A Petition of the thereunder-signed Inhabitants and Visitors of the City of Bath, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners feel themselves called upon to express, in the strongest possible Terms, their just Abhorrence of the late atrocious Attack on His Majesty's Person, by a misguided and wicked Mob, whose Object appears to have been, not only to endanger the Life of their Sovereign, but, by impeding His meeting the Parliament, to controul or over-awe its Deliberations, if not totally to overturn the Legislature; and that the Petitioners have of late observed, with infinite Regret, that frequent disorderly and seditious Meetings have been held, whose Proceedings are calculated to inflame the Minds of the Populace, and to incite them to such dangerous Outrages as above-mentioned; and the Petitioners are the more readily inclined to impute the same to the mischievous Tendency of such unlawful Meetings, from an obvious Coincidence between the late extraordinary Proceedings of a certain Assembly, held in the Vicinity of London, and the Behaviour of the Mob which assaulted the King, in the Approximation of their respective Dates and Circumstances: The Petitioners therefore beg Leave humbly to recommend to the Wisdom of Parliament, to make effectual Provisions, for preventing a Repetition of similar Outrages, and for discountenancing and suppressing all tumultuous and seditious Assemblies, equally subversive of the Peace, and dangerous to the Liberties and Constitution of the State.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Memorandum:

By the Act passed in 1781, intituled, "An Act for establishing an Agreement with the United Company of " Merchants of England trading to the East Indies, &c." the East India Company are required to pay a certain Sum of Money, which is specified in the said Act, in proportion to the Number of Troops sent, or to be sent, to the East Indies, on the Requisition of the said Company.

"This Sum the said Company claim, under the Words of the Act, a Right of paying in the East Indies only; and, as it will be necessary to provide for the Subsistence of the Additionals recruiting for the Regiment of Light Dragoons, and of the Recruiting Companies remaining in Great Britain, there will be -wanting at present for this Purpose, the Sum of 8,345/. 16 s. 2 d.which it will be necessary to vote on Account of the above Estimate.

80 1(3" Novembris. A. 1795.

Ordered, That the said Estimate do lie upon the Table, to be perused by the Members of the House.

Mr. Sargent presented to the House, according to Order, a Bill for the better Relief of the Poor within the several Hundreds and Districts in that part of Great Britain called Englandincorporated by divers

Acts of Parliament, for the Purpose of the better Maintenance and Employment of the Poor, and for enlarging the Powers of the Guardians of the Poor, within the said several Hundreds and Districts, as to the Assessments to be made upon the several Parishes, Hamlets, and Places, within their respective Hundreds and Districts, for the Support and Maintenance of the Poor: And the same was received; and read the First Time.

Resolved, That the Bill be read a Second Time.

Ordered, That the said Bill be printed.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the more expeditious and regular Conveyance of Writs issued for the Election of Members to serve in Parliament: And that Mr. Dent, Mr. Thomas Stanley, and Mr. llobart, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Mr. Hobart, according to Order, reported from th® Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for granting an Aid to His Majesty, by a Land Tax, to be raised in Great Britain, for the Service of the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Ninety-six, was committed, the Amendments which the Committee had made to the Bill, and which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Bill, with the Amendments, in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Amendments were Once read throughout; and then a Second Time, One by One; and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, were agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendments, be ingrossed.

Ordered, That the said Bill be read the Third Time Tomorrow Morning, if the said Bill shall be then ingrossed.

Mr. Hobart, according to Order, reported from the

Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for continuing and granting to His Majesty certain Duties upon Malt, Mum, Cyder, and Perry, for the Service of the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Ninety-six, was committed, the Amendments which the Committee had made to the Bill, and which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Bill, with the Amendments, in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Amendments were Once read throughout; and then

a Second Time, One by One; and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, were agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendments, be ingrossed.

Ordered, That the said Bill be read the Third Time Tomorrow Morning, if the said Bill shall be then ingrossed.

First Report Mr. Ryder reported from the Select Committee, who from Select are appointed to take into Consideration the present on the'hi^h high Price of Corn, and to collect Evidence relative Price of Corn, thereto, and to report the same, from Time to Time, as it should appear to them, to the House, with their Observations thereupon; That the Committee had made some Progress in the Matters to them referred, and had directed him to report the same, together with their Observations thereupon, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

The Select Committee appointed to take into Consideration the present high Price of Com, and to collect Evidence relative thereto, and to report the same, from Time to Time, as it shall appear to them, to the House, with their Observations thereupon;

Proceeded, in the First Instance, to consider such Information as had been already collected concerning the same.

They examined, for this Purpose, the Minutes of the Evidence taken before the Lords of His Majesty's Privy Council, upon this Subject. They received from Sir John Sinclair, One of the Members of the Committee, the Substance of such Accounts of the State of the late Crop of Grain, as the Correspondence of the Board of Agriculture had enabled them, at the present Period, to collect. They had further the Opportunity of receiving from many of their Members a Statement of Facts within their own Knowledge, or communicated by respectable Authorities from their different Counties.

They have received also from His Majesty's Principal Secretary of State for the Home Department, such Returns as had been hitherto made to the circular Letter written by him, by His Majesty's Command, to the Custodes Rotuloru and Sheriffs Depute in England and Scotland, desiring them to obtain Meetings of the Magistrates for the Purpose of procuring an Account of the State of the late Crop: But these Returns are not as yet sufficiently numerous or complete to lead to any precise Conclusion.

On the Whole, however, the general Information derived from the Sources above-mentioned, satisfied your Committee, that, the Crop of other Sorts of Grain than Wheat has been upon the Whole abundant; but that the Produce of Wheat has proved so far deficient, as to require the Adoption of the speediest and most effectual Measures for the Remedy or Alleviation of so great an Evil. They were therefore of Opinion, that they should best perform their Duty by directing v their immediate Attention to the Consideration of such

Vol. 51.

Measures; and have, on that Account, deferred for the present pursuing a detailed Enquiry into the exact Amount of such Deficiency; but they propose to report the same more particularly to the House, when they shall have received such further Information as may enable them to collect more fully the general Opinion, upon a Point which they are sensible it is impossible at any Time to ascertain with any great Degree of Accuracy.

The First and most obvious Mode of supplying this Deficiency is, the Importation of Grain from Foreign Parts — and for the Purpose of forming an Opinion as to what may be the Prospect of Supply from thence, and the most expedient Means to be adopted for procuring it, your Committee proceeded to examine such Persons, from whose Knowledge and Experience in the Trade of Corn they could expect the best Information. It appeared, from their concurrent Testimony, that, though the Crop of Wheat in the United States of America, and in the Countries bordering upon the Mediterranean, was represented as abundant; and in the Northern and Eastern Parts of Europe as not materially deficient; yet, as the old Stock was much exhausted, and the Demand great, the Price, according to the last Advices, was every where uncommonly high. But, though there was upon this Point some Difference of Opinion, it appeared upon the Whole very doubtful whether a Supply, to any considerable Extent, could be depended upon from Foreign Parts, whatever Measures might be adopted. Your' Committee next proceeded to enquire what Measures, in the Judgment of these Persons, afforded the best Probability of obtaining such a Supply. They thought it right to bring distinctly under their Consideration the Alternative of leaving the whole Care of such Purchases to the Executive Government, who would (it was conceived) be in such Case the only Purchasers, and be publicly known to be so; or of leaving the same to the Speculation of individual Merchants encouraged by a liberal Bounty on Importation, and by a public Declaration on the Part of Government (as soon as such Declaration shall be practicable) of the Quantity which they may then have at their Disposal in consequence of former Orders, and of their Intention to give no further Orders for the Purchase of Corn, and to sell what may have been procured in limited Quantities, and at the Market Price. It appeared to your Committee to be the preponderant Opinion amongst those Persons to whom this Alternative was stated, that, upon the Whole, the Restoration of the Trade in Corn to its natural Channel, with the additional Encouragement of a Bounty, was the most eligible Mode of endeavouring to procure from Foreign Parts such Supplies as those Markets might be found able to furnish. Your Committee were further confirmed in this Opinion by the Information they received from some of their Members, that there were Merchants who had stated to them their Readiness, under those Circumstances, to engage in Speculations to a large Extent. After a full Consideration and Discussion of this important Point, your Committee were of Opinion, " That it was expedient for the Executive Government to desist from making any " further Purchases of Com; and that a Bounty should " be granted upon the Importation of certain Sorts of " Grain into this Country, for the Encouragement of " Private Speculation."

Your Committee next proceeded to the Consideration of the Amount and Distribution of such Bounty. They had been informed, that, from the Abundance of the Crop of Wheat in the Countries bordering upon the Mediterranean, there might be a considerable disposable Surplus in those Markets; but that, from the high Price of Freight and Insurance from those Ports, and from the Difficulty of procuring Shipping to go thithar in Ballast, a larger Bounty would be

required to encourage private Speculation in that Quarter than in any other; they were therefore of Opinion, That a Bounty of Twenty Shillings Quarter, and a proportional Bounty per Barrel, should be given on any Number of Quarters of Wheat, weighing not less than 440 lb. Avoirdupois, or on any Number of Barrels of Flour, weighing not less than 1961b. Avoirdupois, which shall be imported into Great Britain from any Port of Europe South of Cape , or from

any Port in the Mediterranean, or in , before the 31st Day of August 1796; until the Quantity of such Wheat and Flour, taken together, shall equal 300,000 Quarters.

They were further satisfied, upon the best Information they could collect, that from the other Parts of

Europe, and from America, a Bounty of Fifteen Shillings

ppr Quarter upon a certain Quantity of Wheat, and of Tqn Shillings per Quarter upon all exceeding it, would be sufficient to give a fair Chance of procuring for the British Markets a large Proportion of whatever Supply those Countries might be expected to furnish beyond their own Consumption: And they were therefore of Opinion, That a Bounty of Fifteen Shillings per Quarter, and a proportional Bounty per Barrel, should be given on any Number of Quarters of Wheat, weighing not less than 440 lb. Avoirdupois, or on any Number of Barrels of Flour, weighing not less than 196 lb. Avoirdupois, which shall be imported from all other Parts of Europe, before the 31st Day of August 1796; pptil the Quantity of such Wheat and Flour, taken together, shall equal 500,000 Quarters. Your Committee were also of Opinion, That a Bounty of Fifteen Shillings per Quarter, and 9. proportional Bounty per parrel, should be given on any Number of Quarters of Wheat, weighing not less than 440 lb. Avoirdupois, or on any dumber of Barrels of Flour, weighing not less than 196 lb. Avoirdupois, which shall be imported from any of His Majesty's Colonies in , or from the United States, before the 31st of August 1796; qqtil the Quantity of such Wheat and Flour, taken together, shall equal 500,000 Quarters. Your Committee were also of Opinion, That a Bounty of Ten Shillings per Quarter, and a proportional Bounty per parrel, should be given on any Number of Quarters of Wheat, weighing not less than 440 lb. Avoirdupois, or on any Number of Barrels of Flour, weighing not less than 1961b. Avoirdupois, which shall be imported into Great Britain before the 31st Day of August 1796, and oh which none of the before-mentioned Bounties shall have been paid.

Your Committee being convinced that if a considerable Quantity of Indiap Corn could be obtained (which from the Abundance of that Crop appeared not improbable) it would afford a material Relief, were also of Opinion, That a Bounty of Five Shillings per Quarter, and a proportional Bounty per Barrel, should be given on any Number of Quarters of Indian Com, or on any Number of Barrels of Indian Meal, which shall be imported into Great Britain before the 31st Day of August 1796; until the Quantity of such Indian Corn and Meal, taken together, shall eqyal 500,000 Quarters. Your Committee were also of Opinion, That a. Bounty of Three Shillings per Quarter, and a proportional Bounty per Barrel, should be given on any Number of Quarters of Indian Cor on any Number. oft Barrels of Indian ‘Meal, which shall be imported into Great Britain before the 31st Day of August 1796; and on which the before-mentioned Bounty shall not have been paid.

Your Committee have some Reason to believe, that there may appear such a Deficiency in the Crop of Pye, as may lead to the Application of similar Measures for the Encouragement of the Importation of tpat Species of Grain, as have beep recompiended respecting Wheat; but they do not yet consider their Information upon that Point as sufficient to authprjze.

them, at the present Moment, to report any Opinion to that Effect.

Your Committee have thought it incumbent upon them, humbly to suggest such Measures as have hitherto appeared, in their Judgment, the most likely to facilitate the procuring without Loss of Time, in the least exceptionable Manner, and on the least unreasonable Terms, the largest Supply of Grain from Foreign Parts, which in the present relative State of the Markets they can be expected to afford. It was particularly with a View to Expedition that they have suggested the proposed Plan of arranging the Bounty. But they feel it at the same Time their indispensable Duty expressly to state, that they are far from entertaining an Opinion that any Supply by Importation can be depended upon to such an Amount as to remove the Necessity of recurring to every other practicable and reasonable Mode by which the present Scarcity may be relieved; and particularly of attending to strict Economy in the Consumption of Wheat and Flour, and of promoting the Substitution, to a certain Extent, of other Articles of Food.

They intend to proceed immediately to the Consideration of these and of other Parts of this extensive and important Subject; and will, with the Permission of the House, report, from Time to Time, such Opinions as they may be enabled to form thereupon.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Chief Petitions Citizens, of the City of Bath, in Common Council assembled, was presented to the House, and read; Yarmmith Setting forth, That the Petitioners, conscious of the respecting' manifold Blessings resulting from the unremitting Care Seditious and Attention of our most Gracious Sovereign to the Meetings. Welfare and Interests of His People, at the same Time contemplating with Abhorrence the insidious Designs and open Violence of Factious Associations to disturb the Tranquillity of His equitable Government, thus humbly pray the House to devise and establish such Measures, as the Wisdom of their Councils may determine, for the effectual Protection of His Majesty's sacred Person, and for the Security of our most excellent Constitution: Impressed with a just Sense of Parliamentary Zeal and Ability to suggest such salutary Means as may avert the impending Danger, the Petitioners beseech the Acceptance of their own Assurances to promote the Effect of such Resolves of the House by the influence of Example, and the Vigour of Exertion.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, Merchants, and Inhabitants of Great Yarmouth, in the County of Norfolk, was also presented to the House, and read;

Setting forth, That the Petitioners have long observed, with Indignation and Horror, the rapid Strides which have been made, by the Disaffected in this Kingdom, to overturn the venerable Fabric of our Constitution, and to involve the Country in Rebellion and Misery;

That Public Meetings have been held, in which Sedition and Discontent, by Inflammatory Harangues, have been propagated amongst our Fellow Subjects:

That the Veil of Reform, under which these Proceedings have been disguised, being at length drawn aside, the Petitioners humbly intreat that the House, in its Wisdom, will adopt such Measures as may be necessary to secure the Person of the Sovereign from Insult, and the People in the peaceable Possession of their Constitution.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Lord Provost, Magistrates, and Council of the City of Edinburgh, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have beheld, with the utmost Horror and Detestation, the late Tumultuous and Seditious Meetings of Persons taking upon them the Name of Societies, and others, whose Principles and Doctrines, hostile to all good Government and Civil Subordination, have a direct Tendency to mislead and inflame the Minds of those who attend such Meetings, as well as others, by many Seditious Publications, circulated and distributed with great Zeal and Industry, against His Majesty's Person and Government: That to these Seditious Meetings and Publications may justly be attributed the most daring and criminal Outrages that were lately committed, Jo the Danger of His Majesty's sacred Person in going to, and returning from, Parliament: That, in order to prevent a Repetition of such Outrage and Insult to His Majesty, as well as to preserve our glorious Constitution, it appears at this Juncture to be necessary for Parliament to adopt such Measures as may effectually prevent such Seditious Meetings and Publications tending to High Treason: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into their most serious Consideration, and to do therein what in their great Wisdom they shall think fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

The other Order of the Day being read, for the Second Reading of the Bill for the more effectually preventing Seditious Meetings and Assemblies;

A Motion was made, and the Question being put, That the said Bill be now read a Second Time;

The House divided.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Chief Petition from Burgesses, of the Borough of Nexvpo in the Isle of e"t'm ^he" Wight, in Common Hall assembled, was presented to saleofCorn, the House, and read; Setting forth, That observing, by the Votes of the House, that a Committee is appointed to take into Consideration the present Corn Laws, the Petitioners beg Leave to observe, that, in their Opinion, an effectual Means of lessening the present high Price of Corn, will be by prohibiting the Sale of Com by Sample, and of course to compel the Farmer to bring his Corn to Market; and that, within the last Ten Years, this Practice of bringing by Sample has become almost universal, and few Loads of Corn are now seen in the Market at Newport, whereas, some few Years back, Two hundred Waggon Loads have been frequently seen there on a Market Day: That the good Effects of bringing the Corn to Market were, that a poor Person might buy a Sack, or small Quantity fitted to his Purse, at the first and cheapest Hand, and, besides, that it contributes to lower the Price, for, the Corn being brought to Market, the Farmer was content to sell it cheaper, rather than carry it back again; and another good and pleasing Effect was produced, that it tended to shew the Stock and Abundance of the Country, when the Farmers from the different Parts exhibited their Stores to Public View: And therefore praying, That the Practice of selling Corn by Sample may be discountenanced by the House, and that such other Measures for reducing the Price of Com may be adopted, as the Wisdom of the House shall suggest

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Bounty of Twenty Shillings per Quarter, and a proportional Bounty per Barrel, should be given on any Number of Quarters of Wheat, weighing not less than Four hundred and Forty Pounds Weight Avoirdupois, or on any Number of Barrels of Flour, weighing not less than One hundred and Ninety-six Pounds Weight Avoirdupois, which shall be imported into Great Britain from any Port of Europe South of Cape Finisterre, or from any Port in the Mediterranean, or in Africa, before the 31st Day of August 1796, until the Quantity of such Wheat and Flour, taken together, shall equal 300,000 Quarters.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Bounty of Fifteen Shillings per Quarter, and a proportional Bounty per Barrel, should be given on any Number of Quarters of Wheat, weighing not less than Four hundred and Forty Pounds Weight Avoirdupois, or on any Number of Barrels of Flour, weighing not less than One hundred and Ninety-six Pounds Weight Avoirdupois, which shall be imported from all other Parts of Europe before the 31st Day of August 1796, until the Quantity of such Wheat and Flour, taken together, shall equal 500,000 Quarters.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Bounty of Fifteen Shillings per Quarter, and a proportional Bounty per Barrel, should be given on any Number of Quarters of Wheat, weighing not less than Four hundred and Forty Pounds Weight Avoirdupois, or on any Number of Barrels of Flour, weighing not less than One hundred and Ninety-six Pounds Weight Avoirdupois, which shall be imported from any of His Majesty's Colonies in America, or from the United States, before the 31st Day of August 1796, until the Quantity of such Wheat and Flour, taken together, shall equal 500,000 Quarters.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Bounty of Ten Shillings per Quarter, and a proportional Bounty per Barrel, should be given on any Number of Quarters of Wheat, weighing not less than Four hundred and Forty Pounds Weight Avoirdupois, or on any Number of Barrels of Flour, weighing not less than One hundred and Ninety-six Pounds Weight Avoirdupois, which shall be imported into Great Britain before the 31st Day of August 1796, and on which none of the before-mentioned Bounties shall have been paid.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Bounty of Five Shillings per Quarter, and a proportional Bounty per Barrel, should be given on any Number of Quarters of Indian Corn, or on any Number of Barrels of Indian Meal, which shall be imported into Great Britain before the 31st Day of August 1796, until the Quantity of such Indian Corn and Meal, taken together, shall equal 500,000 Quarters.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Bounty of Three Shillings per Quarter, and a proportional Bounty per Barrel, should be given on any Number of Quarters of Indian Corn, or on any Number of Barrels of Indian Meal, which shall be imported into Great Britain before the 31st Day of August 1796, and on which the before-mentioned Bounties shall not have been paid.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question, severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That a Bill be brought in upon the said Resolutions: And that Mr. Ryder, Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, Mr. Rose, and Mr. Charles Long, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

And therefore entreating the House to adopt such Measures, for a limited Time, as in their Wisdom shall be deemed most expedient for suppressing all Tumultuous and Seditious Afeetings, and for the better Security of His Majesty's Person and Government.

also by giving vague and discretionary Powers to Magistrates, for the most Part appointed by the Crown and removable at its Pleasure, to prevent any Discussion at their Will, to dissolve such Meetings, and to imprison those who may be present there: That, in both the said Bills, a Latitude of Expression is used in defining the Acts constituting the Crime of Sedition, which may be made to include every Notice of Public Measures, other than approbationary, and is therefore utterly subversive of the Freedom of the Pen, of the Press, and of Speech: That, though the late detestable Outrage against the Royal Person has been used as a Pretence for these Innovations, yet the Petitioners cannot help observing, that the Force of the Laws does not appear to them to have been adequately resorted to, nor the Civil Power to have been duly exerted at the Time, and that it is unfair to conclude from thence, that those Powers, when properly exerted, are insufficient: That the Petitioners are satisfied, from the Experience of Ages, and especially from that of the past Century, during Part of which a great and alarming Disaffection pervaded all Ranks of People, which extended not only to the King's Government, but to his Title and Person, and excited Two formidable Rebellions in the Heart of the Realm, that the present Laws, duly and vigorously administered, are fully adequate to the Punishment of Treason and Sedition, as well as to the keeping of the Peace, and the Protection of His Majesty's Person; and the Petitioners declare their Readiness, in their several Capacities, to enforce them for those Purposes to the utmost of their Power: That the People of this Country being, in general, undoubtedly loyal to His Majesty, and well affected to the Constitution, ought not, collectively, to suffer an Abridgment of their Rights and Liberties for the Act, however atrocious, of a few desperate and obscure Individuals: That the Effect of these Bills will be to destroy all Freedom of Complaint against Oppressions of Laws or Government, however well founded; to annihilate, in Substance, the Fifth Article of the Declaration of Rights; and to create, in Consequence, the most alarming Discontents among His Majesty's Subjects: The Petitioners therefore entreat the House, as they wish to transmit to their Posterity the unimpaired Liberties of their Ancestors, to preserve in the People their Reverence for the Constitution, and to merit their Respect as faithful Guardians of their Rights, to resist all Attempts, under whatever Pretences, to abridge their Liberties, and, specially, not to pass the said Bills.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Inhabitants of the ancient Borough of Gosport, and Parish of Alverstoke, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, observing, with Sorrow, that tumultuous and seditious Meetings are held from Time to Time in various Places, with Horror beholding the atrocious and alarming Effects which they believe have frequently arisen from the Doctrines promulgated at such Assemblies, and filled with a still higher Degree of Abhorrence and Indignation at the late wicked Attack on the sacred Person of our beloved and most excellent Monarch, at a Moment when He was fulfilling one of the most important Duties attached to His exalted Station: Beg Leave humbly to request, That the House would be pleased, in conjunction with the other Branches of the Legislature, to bring forward, and pass into Laws, such Bills as the House, in their Wisdom, may think most expedient for the better Protection of His Majesty's most sacred Person, and for the Prevention of all such tumultuous and seditious Meetings as can be only calculated to inflame the Minds of the Unenlightened, to draw them aside, by Falsehood and Misrepresentation, from their Loyalty and Allegiance, and to introduce into our Country, instead of the present happy Constitution, a System of Violence, Oppression, and Anarchy.

A Petition of the Inhabitants of the Borough of Reading, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have been, in all Ages, distinguished for their Attachment to the Crown, and for their Regard to the Constitution: That on the late atrocious Attack on the Person of His Majesty, the Petitioners were foremost in testifying their Indignation at the horrid Attempt, and their Gratitude to the King of Kings for preserving a Life so deservedly dear to every Loyal Heart: That, during the present Administration, they have been unanimous, to a Degree almost unexampled, in Adherence to their Principles, and in support of their Measures: That they unequivocally disapprove, and will unite their Endeavours to check, the promiscuous and tumultuary Meetings of Persons who are not assembled in a Civil or Political Capacity of Members of a County, Town, or Parish, such as have lately taken place in the Neighbourhood of the Metropolis: That, influenced by the same sentiments of Loyalty and Patriotism, the Petitioners view, with considerable Alarm, Two Bills introduced into the House, the First intituled, A Bill for the Safety and Preservation of His Majesty's Person and Government against treasonable and Seditious Practices and Attempts; the Second, A Bill for the more effectually preventing Seditious Meetings and Assemblies: That in the former they see, with, the most serious Concern, the Revival of those Attempts to increase the Catalogue of Treason which were made in former Ages by weak and arbitrary Administrations, with equal Danger to the Safety of the Monarch and to the Liberty of the Subject; but which a wiser Policy constantly restricted by recurring to the only beneficial Statute on that Subject, a Statute sanctioned by the Experience of more than Four hundred Years, that of the Twenty-fifth of Edward the Third: That the Petitioners consider the Second Bill as subversive of the Fifth Article of the Bill of Rights, of that solemn Compact made at the Resolution between the King and the People for the Establishment of the Religion, Laws, and Liberties of this Country, which acknowledges the Right of Subjects to petition in the Capacity already described, of Members of a County, Town, or Parish, and declares

Petition from Gosport, respecting Seditious Meetings.

Petition against the Bills for the Safety of His Majesty's Person,&c. and for preventing Seditious Meetings.

36 Geo. III. 23° Novem97

declares all Commitments and Prosecutions for such petitioning illegal; that they conceive the free Exercise of this Privilege to be the strongest Argument against Democratic Innovators, whose Theories of universal Suffrage and Annual Parliaments would acquire some Plausibility if the Voice of the People could be suppressed at the arbitrary Command of Two Individuals: That, in the Opinion of the Petitioners, the existing Laws are sufficient to protect the Civil and Political Rights of every Branch of the Constitution; and that if, according to the Opinion of a great Law Character, the Persons who were tried for High Treason had been indicted for Sedition, Public Order would probably have received more effectual Security: That, above all, the Petitioners are apprehensive that the present Uneasiness may be traced to a higher Cause than that which is represented as productive of Public Danger: They therefore humbly implore the House, as Citizens, as Christians, and as Men, to take into their most serious Consideration the Circumstances of a War which, whatever Difference of Opinion may exist in its Principle, must be acknowledged to have been ill-conducted in its Progress, and calamitous in its Consequences: That, conceiving the Restoration of Peace to be better calculated to allay the Public Discontents, by diminishing the Public Burthen?, than the most coercive Regulations, they humbly hope that the House will urge the Necessity of treating with the Executive Power of France, under whatever Form it may be established, on safe and honourable Terms, and particularly, as the more immediate Objects of this Address, they most earnestly entreat that the Bills which they deprecate may not receive the Sanction of the House.

A Petition of the Inhabitants of the City of Bristol, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Bill now brought into the House, intituled, An Act for the more effectually preventing Seditious Meetings and Assemblies, has justly excited, in the Minds of the Petitioners, an anxious Jealousy for the Rights and Liberties which, on the Settlement of the Crown upon the Illustrious House of Hanover, were recognized to be the true, ancient, and indubitable Rights and Liberties of the People of this Kingdom: That the Bill now depending, is intended to preclude the People from the free Discussion of Political Questions, and the unrestrained Right of petitioning against Grievances, the Exercise of which Right is, in the Judgment of the Petitioners, the surest Means of preserving the Constitution inviolate; and the Infringement of which Right, as it blocks up the Avenues through which the Voice of a loyal People has been accustomed to approach the 'Throne, may enable an ambitious Ministry to trample alike on the Prerogative of the Crown and the Liberties of the People: — The Petitioners are not less alarmed by another Bill now depending, intituled, An Act for the Safety and Preservation of His Vql. 51.

Majesty's Person and Government against treasonable and seditious Practices and Attempts: The Petitioners consider that, in a free Country, all Acts, to the Commission of which Pains and Penalties attach, should be defined in Language clear and unequivocal; the contrary being the Tendency of the said Bill, should it pass into a Law, they will be plunged into the calamitous Situation which is well described by a Statute, enacted in the First Year of the Reign of King Henry the Fourth, which says, " Whereas divers " Pains of Treason have been ordained by Statute,

" inasmuch that there is no Man who doth know how " he ought to behave himself, to do, speak, or say, for " Doubt of such Pains — The Petitioners therefore appeal to the House, in the firmest Confidence, That they will reject those violent Measures, which threaten the Destruction of their Liberties, and the Subversion of our glorious Constitution.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, Freeholders, Petition re-and others, Inhabitants of the County of Suffolk, at a specting Se-General Meeting of the County assembled, was also ^tlou*JVIefet* presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That 1Dgs" the Petitioners, with the deepest Regret, lamenting the daring Insult and Outrage lately committed on His Majesty's most sacred Person, to the Interruption of that free Passage to His Parliament which the Spirit of the happy Constitution of these Realms assures, cannot but be convinced that the seditious and treasonable Doctrines, of late held forth, and with so much Industry propagated, have misled the Ignorant, and encouraged the Mischievous, to Acts the most daring against our Liberties and Laws: The Petitioners do therefore most humbly request the House to take into their especial Consideration the Circumstance of all Assemblies professedly called for the Intent of promulgating and disseminating Doctrines subversive of all Religion, Liberty, and Order, and provide such Means as the Temper of the Times for the immediate Purpose requires, and such as shall to their Wisdom seem meet, for the further Security of His Majesty's Person, and of the happy Government of this Kingdom, and for preserving to us the inestimable Blessing of that rational Liberty, which flows from the mild, equal, and free Temperature of our glorious Constitution.

A Petition of the loyal and well-affected Inhabitants Petition in of the Towns and Neighbourhood of Manchester and favour of the Salford, was also presented to the House, and read; forftyis

Setting forth, That, impressed with a due Sense of the Majesty's Value of that Constitution under which they have the Person, &c. Happiness to live, the Petitioners approach the House and for proas the Guardians of their Rights and Liberties, with tiousMeet^' full Confidence that those, to whose Wisdom they are jng8. entrusted, are endued with Integrity to maintain, and Firmness to protect them: That the Petitioners lament, in common with their Fellow Subjects, the Occasion which now calls forth the Exertion of these Qualities to suppress the daring Attempts of unprincipled and Wicked Men, who abuse the venerable Names of Patriotism and Liberty for the Furtherance of Designs which aim at their Destruction: That, when the Petitioners consider the late atrocious Attempt on the Life of their most Gracious Sovereign, they cannot for a Moment hesitate upon the Conclusion they are to draw, nor separate it from a Connection with the Principles which have been so openly avowed, and so industriously circulated, against the Existence of the Constitution itself: That, under these Impressions, the Petitioners beg Leave to express their Approbation of the Principle of the Bills, now before the House, for the more effectual Prevention of Treasons, seditious Practices, and Meetings, the Licentiousness of which the unsuspecting Mildness of our Laws has been hitherto found unequal to suppress:

A Petition of the thereunder-signed Inhabitants of the Town and County of the Town of,

was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners entertain the utmost Abhorrence at the late daring and treasonable Outrage offered to His Majesty's most sacred Person in His Passage to and from Parliament, and sincerely hope that the Perpetrators and Abettors thereof may be brought to condign Punishment: That the Petitioners are impressed with the Sentiments that the Glory and Happiness of their Sovereign, and the Comfort and Prosperity of His People, are so reciprocally united, that the free and perfect Enjoyment of their Freedom is the best and only solid Security of their Affections, and that those Men, who have the Temerity to suggest or advise an Invasion of that Freedom, are Enemies to the King, to the People, and to the Constitution: That the Petitioners, therefore, cannot but entertain the most gloomy Apprehensions from the Perusal of Two Bills now depending in Parliament; the one intituled, An Act for the better Security of His Majesty's Person, &c. and the other, An Act for the Safety and Preservation of His Majesty's Person and Government against treasonable and Seditious Practices and Attempts, it appearing to the Petitioners that the said Laws, by creating new Treasons, by multiplying capital Punishments, and destroying the fundamental Right of the People to assemble peaceably together for the Discussion of Public Grievances, operate to the Subversion of the Constitution, and strike at the Foundation of the Liberties of Englishmen: That the Petitioners are equally Foes to Anarchy and Despotism, but, as free-born , who value

their Liberty more than every other Blessing, they should be wanting in their Duty to their Country, to themselves, and to their Posterity, not to exercise their invaluable Privilege of Remonstrance against the Enaction of Laws, by which the Fences and Outworks, set up by our Ancestors to guard that Liberty, will be beaten down and destroyed: And therefore praying, That the said Bills may not pass.

A Petition of the Inhabitants of the City of Norwich, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, viewing with extreme Surprise, and with great Alarm, the Introduction of Two Bills into Parliament, the one, intituled, An Act for the Safety of His Majesty's Person and Government against Treasonable and Seditious Practices and Attempts, and the other. An Act to prevent Seditious Assemblies, which they conceive to be Infringements upon the Constitution, and Violations of their best Rights and Liberties, have met in Common Hall, to beg of the House, that they will, at this awful Crisis, act as behoves the Representatives of a People jealous of their Liberties, and oppose their Authority to this Innovation, unprecedented since the Resolution of 1688: That the Petitioners have always considered the Law, enacted in the Twenty-fifth Year of King Edward the Third, as since modified by divers Statutes, to be the greatest Safeguard of the Subject, and the best personal Security of the Sovereign: That, whilst the Petitioners lament the late Insult offered to the Person of the King, they cannot but think that the existing Laws are adequate to the Punishment of the Offenders, and, if properly enforced, sufficient to prevent a Repetition, of such Outrages: That the Petitioners, knowing the distressed Situation of the great Majority of the People, are decidedly of Opinion, that to deprive them of the Means of complaining will, in

the Issue, drive them to Measures which the Humanity of the Petitioners most sincerely deprecates: And therefore earnestly praying, That the House will put their decisive Negative upon these Bills, which, if they pass into Laws, will render nugatory the Fifth Clause of the Bill of Rights, and overthrow the most valuable Privileges of Englishmen.

A Petition of the thereunder-written, being Inhabitants of the City of Chester, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners do utterly disapprove of the illegal and violent Proceedings of the Populace on the First Day of the present Session of Parliament, and sincerely rejoice in the Escape of His Majesty from the Danger which threatened His Person: That, from the Information which they have been able to obtain respecting the illegal Occurrences of that Day, the Petitioners believe that they are totally unconnected with the Designs or Actions of any Popular Society — That, wishing for His Majesty all the Security which good Laws can afford, the Petitioners trust that no Act of the Legislature will declare the Safety of the Sovereign to be incompatible with the liberty of the People — Such it appears to the Petitioners is the Import of a Bill, intituled, A Bill for the more effectually preventing Seditious Meetings and Assemblies, now under the Consideration of the House; and the Petitioners do most earnestly deprecate the passing of an Act which, vesting in the Hands of the Magistrate an arbitrary unconstitutional Power, would deprive the People of their unquestioned Right to express their Sense of Measures, the Consequences and Expence of which must be borne by them — That, in the present distressed State of this Country, the Petitioners are convinced that the concluding of a speedy Peace would be the best Means of securing to His Majesty the best Guard of His Person, the Love of His People: And therefore praying, That the House will not suffer the said Bill to pass into a Law.

A Petition of the thereunder-signed Inhabitants of the Town and Neighbourhood of Sheffield, in the County of York, Friends of their Country and its

Constitution, as now established, was likewise presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, in this Moment of Alarm and Anxiety, the Eves of the British Nation are upon the House; the Wishes, the Hopes, and the Fears, of a great and a brave People are centered in their Representatives: The Firmness of the House may save, their Weakness might endanger, the Liberties of their Country: The House are the Guardians of the Constitution, and, while they discharge their Duty, it will remain indissoluble; equally Proof against the Fury of Foreign Foes, and the Conspiracies of Domestic Traitors: That it is with deep Concern the Petitioners observe the Introduction of Two alarming Bills, for the Consideration of the House; the one levelled against Freedom of Speech and the Liberty of the Press, the other framed for abolishing popular Societies: By the Memory of our Forefathers, who purchased with their Lives, and sealed with their Blood, the Liberties of their Country, in the Name of Posterity, whose Blood pleads in our Veins, the Petitioners beseech the House to weigh well the dreadful Principles of these Bills before they venture to pass them into Laws. O ! suffer not the sacred Inheritance of Magna Charta to be mortgaged even by a temporary Surrender of any of its inestimable Privileges; suffer not the Blessings of the Bill of Rights to be forfeited by even a conditional Submission to new Laws, unless it can be proved (which the Petitioners believe it cannot) that the hopeless Necessity of the Times absolutely requires such dreadful Restraints. Let the Petitioners not be compelled to blush when they remember the Virtues of our Ancestors; and let not our Children in their turn blush for the Degeneracy of their Fathers.: To the 'Wisdom and Integrity of the

An Act for granting an Aid to His Majesty by a Land Tax, to be raised in Great Britain, for the Service of the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Ninety-six:

An Act to prohibit the Exportation of'Corn, Meal, Flour, and Potatoes, and to permit the Importation of Corn and other Articles of Provision, for a limited Time, in any Ships whatever, without Payment of Duty:

An Act to continue an Act for permitting the Importation of Organziried Thrown Silk, Flax, and Flax Seed, into this Kingdom, in Ships or Vessels belonging to any Kingdom or State in Amity with His Majesty, for a limited Time.

Then the Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, Inhabitants of the City of Chichester, and its Environs, was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, with that respect which is due to the Representatives of the People, and that Plainness which becomes them, wish to lay before the House their Sentiments on the Convention Bill now pending in Parliament, which they look upon as the most daring and outrageous Attack upon the Constitution of this Nation, and the Rights of the People, that ever was planned and pursued by wicked Men: The Petitioners are convinced that every Briton has an unalienable Right, and that it is the Duty of every Man to watch the Conduct of Administration, that the Constitution be not injured, Vo 1.51.

nor the Rights of the People invaded: The People of England never delegated to their Rulers Authority to alter the Constitution of the Realm, and to change the limited Monarchy thereof into a devouring Despotism; and the Petitioners hope, and do firmly believe, that they still retain so much of their native Courage and Love of Freedom as not to suffer a daring Ministerial Influence to rob them of this Right, the Corner Stone of all the rest: That the Petitioners make this Appeal to the House, who ought to be, and the Petitioners hope, on the present momentous Occasion, will approve themselves the Guardians of our Rights, at the same Time assuring the House, that, much as the Petitioners deprecate the dreadful Alternative, yet they would rather die free than live Slaves.

A Petition of the thereunder-signed Britons, Inha- Petition bitants of London and its Environs, assembled together 1,16 to express their free Sentiments, according to the preventing Tenure of the Bill of Rights, on the Subjects of the Seditious threatened Invasions of their Constitutional Liberties, Meetings, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth,

That the Petitioners approach the House once more to make their Grievances and Apprehensions known, in a legal and Constitutional Manner, to that Branch of the Legislature which, from its legal Stile and Form, was evidently intended to be the Constitutional Guardian of the People's Liberties, and the Champion of its Rights and Privileges — But the Petitioners approach the House, not as heretofore, to claim the Reformation of existing Abuses; if those Claims had been attended to, the Cause of their present Petition could never have existed; The Petitioners come not to repeat their unanswered Arguments on the Necessity of Parliamentary Reform; the very Proposition of the Measures the Petitioners now protest against is a demonstrative Evidence of the Necessity of such Reform; but they approach the- House, with Constitutional Reverence and British Firmness, to conjure them not to drive the People of this distressed and irritated Nation to such Despair, as the Adoption of the coercive System in Agitation before the House, the Petitioners are firmly persuaded, in the End must inevitably produce: The Petitioners conjure the House to remember, that the vital Energies of the British Constitution consist in the Liberties of Speech, and of the Press; that the Safety and Preservation of our Lives and Liberties (next after that immortal Institution of the Trial by Jury) depend upon the strict Observance of the Provisions of that admirable Statute of Treasons extorted by a virtuous House of Commons from Edward the Third: The Petitioners conjure the House also to remember, that the Invasion of these Liberties, and the Violation of this Safety, by arbitrary Institutions and new Theories of constructive Treasons, though sometimes assumed under Pretences of ancient Prerogatives, and sometimes confirmed by corrupt Representatives and arbitrary Acts of Parliament, have never failed of being productive of Consequences the most alarming both to the Government and the People:

That fibe Adoption of those very Maxims and Precedents, upon which the proposed Measures are evidently founded, brought one unhappy Prince of the House of Stuart to the Scaffold, and drove another, with his Posterity, from the Throne; and that therefore to propose and support such Measures is, in Reality, to endanger not only the Tranquillity of the Nation, but the Safety even of His Majesty's Pe.rson and Government, m Support of which these Measures are said to be brought forward: Permit the Petitioners solemnly to conjure the Abuse to recollect the Events that immediately preceded and produced the Resolution of 1688 — the Doctrines advanced in the Justification of that memorable Event, and the Principles which established the House of Brunswick on the Throne:

Let the Petitioners conjure the House also to consider, with due Deliberation, the Limits, and the

Laws which have hitherto been found fully competent to all the just Purposes of free and equitable Government: And, finally, the Petitioners intreat the House to believe, that, when they profess their Abhorrence of all Tumult and Violence, and reject, with the utmost Indignation, the groundless Calumnies that have been spread against their peaceful, orderly, and Constitutional Meetings, they do it from a firm and long settled Conviction, that all Acts of Violence and Outrage are most eminently injurious to that great Cause of National and Constitutional Liberty to which the Petitioners are attached: At the same Time they conjure the House to confide in the Firmness and Temperance of the People of Great Britain, who, the Petitioners trust, have not degenerated from- the Spirit and Bravery of their Ancestors, nor forgotten the important Lessons inculcated by -their Examples.

Measures for those important Purposes, being fully convinced that the Interference of the Legislature is become indispensably necessary to discountenance and defeat those nefarious Principles and Designs, which have a Tendency to introduce the Miseries of Confusion, Tyranny, and Rapine, in the Place of those mild and beneficent Laws which have so long protected the Liberties and Property of the Inhabitants of these Kingdoms.

A Petition of the loyal Inhabitants of the Town and Neighbourhood of Maidstone in, the County of Kent, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are duly sensible of the Happiness they have enjoyed under the mild Laws of this Country, and do contemplate, with peculiar Satisfaction, that most excellent Part of our Constitution which enables the Legislature to provide a Remedy for Evils as they arise: That they cannot see, without the utmost Concern, the factious and republican Spirit which has gone abroad amongst a Part of His Majesty's Subjects, and which has shewn itself in a Variety of disorderly Proceedings, and particularly in the nefarious Attempt lately made upon the Person of our beloved Sovereign, which daring Spirit the Petitioners can attribute to no other Cause than the Influence of certain Political Meetings, in which the greatest Efforts are made, by artful and wicked Men, to sow the Seeds of Discontent and Disaffection, to seduce the People from their Obedience to the Laws, and excite them to Hatred and Contempt of His Majesty's Person and Government: The Petitioners therefore do highly admire and approve the Wisdom and Expediency of the Measures contained in the Bills, which are now under the Consideration of Parliament, and do humbly entreat that the same may he passed into Laws, or that the House will provide such other Remedy, for the present Evils, as shall he deemed expedient.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, and Freeholders, of the County of Buckingham, agreed to at a Meeting held by Public Advertisement, the 21st Day of November 1795, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have observed, with the deepest Concern, the late daring Outrages against the Person of the King in His Passage to and from His Parliament, an Offence which, at the same Time, endangered the personal Safety of a Sovereign justly dear to his Subjects, and violated the most sacred Principles of the British Constitution: That the Petitioners consider these atrocious Acts as the immediate and natural Consequence of those dangerous and seditious Meetings and Publications by which wicked Men have endeavoured to poison the Minds of our Fellow Subjects, and to stir up Sedition, Tumult, and Civil War, within this Country': The Petitioners therefore, duly sensible of the Blessings which we enjoy under our present happy Constitution, and solicitous for the Maintenance of Public Tranquillity and good Order, and for the Protection of the Lives, Properties, and Civil Rights, of the peaceful and loyal Subjects of this Realm, all which are greatly endangered by such Proceedings, do most humbly and earnestly entreat the House to take the same into its most serious Consideration, and to adopt such Measures as the House shall, in its Wisdom, judge most proper for the Safety of His Majesty's Person and Government, and for the more effectual Prevention of all seditious Meetings and Publications.

A Petition of the Inhabitants of the Town and Vicinity of Maidstone, in the County of Kent, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, although the Petitioners sincerely lament the Occasion that has given rise to the Two Bills now before Parliament, the one intituled, An Act for the Safety and Preservation of His Majesty's Person and Government against treasonable and seditious Practices and Attempts, and the other, An Act for preventing seditious Meetings, yet they cannot, so long as the existing Laws are fully competent to the bringing such Offenders to Justice, surrender up One of the most valuable Parts of their Constitution, without

first humbly imploring the House, that they will take into their most serious Consideration the great Innovation they are about to make, and in what Degree it may be likely to affect the Safety of the Constitution, or the Probability of its affording any additional Security to His Majesty's Person and Government: That the Petitioners, so far from believing the re exists any Body of People inimical to the true Principles of the Constitution, do humbly conceive, that whenever Symptoms of Inquietude may have appeared, they solely originated in the real Distress to which the present calamitous War has reduced the Country: The Petitioners do therefore humbly implore the House, That they will use their utmost Endeavours in order to restore to Trade Prosperity, to the Poor Plenty, and to the Nation Happiness, and that the House will reject the above Bills, which the Petitioners conceive tend to infringe on their indubitable Rights and Privileges.

A Petition of the Inhabitants of the Borough of Ilelleston, in the County of was also pre-

sented to the House, and read; Setting forth that the Petitioners have not seen, without the greatest Indignation, the late audacious Attack upon the Person of our most Gracious Sovereign; and the Petitioners have, in common with their Fellow Subjects, offered their sincerest Congratulations to His Majesty on His providential Escape, and are ready to come forward, with their Lives and Fortunes, in Support of the Dignity of the King, and for the Preservation of the Peace of this Kingdom: That though the Petitioners lament, in common with all His Majesty's faithful Subjects, the violent and irregular Proceedings of those Meetings with which this Attack is said to be connected, yet they cannot but view, with the deepest Concern, the Provisions of the Bill, now before the House, for the Prevention of the Evils of which Meetings, so constituted, may in future be productive: That the Petitioners humbly conceive the Principles of the Bill to he, both in Substance and Effect, a direct Infringement upon their just and natural Right of assembling peaceably and lawfully for the Redress of Public Grievances, a Right handed down to them by their Ancestors from the earliest Period, and confirmed to them by the Bill of Rights at the glorious Resolution: That the Petitioners are further of Opinion, that the said Bill is pregnant with serious Evils to the Constitution of this Kingdom, not only as being an Attack upon the sacred Right of Petitioning, but also as being likely to produce, in their fullest Extent, the very Evils which it professes to remedy, inasmuch as the Experience of past Ages has fully proved, that a Nation, debarred of the Rights of expressing its Wants and Grievances free and unrestrained, may be sometimes driven to the desperate Resource of open Resistance: That, notwithstanding, if the House in its Wisdom shall think the Exigency of the Times requires this extraordinary Measure, the Petitioners humbly hope and pray, that it may be temporary only, and limited, at farthest, to the Duration of One Year, lest, through the atrocious Proceedings of a few misguided Individuals, His Majesty's loyal Subjects in general, and their Posterity, be laid under a Stigma of Disaffection, and for ever deprived of One of their oldest and most invaluable Privileges.

His Majesty's Person, being convinced that Licentiousness is inimical to Liberty, and that Anarchy is as much to be dreaded as Despotism: That the most perfect human Institutions are subject to Errors, as well in their original Formation as by Means of successive Introduction, and that Governments, the best administered, are not entirely free from Oppression, on which Accounts it was wisely declared by our Ancestors, in the Bill of Rights, " That it is the " Right of the Subject to petition the King, and that all " Commitments and Prosecutions for such petitioning " are illegal: " That the Petitioners disapprove of the Bill, intituled, An Act for preventing seditious Meetings, because it tends to obstruct the Exercise of this Right, notwithstanding the Experience of more than a Century proves it to have been consonant with the Maintenance of the Public Peace: That the Petitioners disapprove of the Bill, intituled, An Act for the Safety and Preservation of His Majesty's Person and Government against treasonable and seditious Practices and Attempts, because it inflicts heavy Penalties upon every Person who shall speak or write any Thing against the Government and Constitution of this Realm, making no Distinction between the Excellencies of our Constituion and its Defects, and between the Advantages enjoyed under the Government of our Gracious Sovereign, and the Grievances which originate in the Incapacity or Turpitude of His Ministers: The Petitioners conceiving that this will tend to perpetuate Grievances and Errors and to retard that Melioration of human Affairs which Freedom of Writing and of Debate is calculated to promote, they therefore request that the House will not pass these Bills into Laws.

A Petition of the thereunder-signed Inhabitants of the Borough of Saint Alban, in the County of Hertford, was likewise presented to the House, and read j Setting forth. That the Petitioners have beheld, with the deepest Concern, the Introduction in the House of Two Bills, the one intituled A Bill for the Preservation of His Majesty's Persons, and the other, A Bill against seditious Assemblies, which if carried into Effect, will so far restrain the Liberty of the Press, and the Right and Privilege of the Subject of meeting to petition against Grievances, as to render such Right and Privilege of little avail: That being truly sensible of the Value of these Privileges, so long enjoyed by them and their Ancestors, and which they deem their unalienable Right, they cannot refrain from expressing to the House their Alarms at any Attempt to deprive them thereof: And therefore praying, That the House will not pass such Bills into Laws.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Journeymen Taylors resident in Petitions London, Westminster, and Southwark, was also pre- g^sn^rth,® sented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, Safety°ofViia impressed with a deep Sense of the many Advantages Majesty's redounding to us from the mild Auspices of our present Person. &c. Sovereign, the Petitioners sincerely regret, with their an„Jnr Fellow Subjects in general, the violent Outrages which Meet- have been committed on a late Occasion upon the ings.

Sacred Person of His Majesty; but, while the Petitioners thus deprecate so daring an Attempt, they are seriously alarmed at the Introduction of Two Bills into Parliament, which have a direct Tendency to eradicate every Principle of our glorious Constitution, and wrest from Britons those invaluable Privileges transmitted to them by their Forefathers, devised in their Wisdom, and cemented by their best Blood: Believing, therefore, that the best Security of His Majesty's Person and Government consists in the Preservation of those Rights which we have so long enjoyed, and a steady Perseverance in the Execution of the Laws which at present exist, being fully persuaded that they are every Way adequate to the existing Circumstances pointed out in the Bills now pending in Parliament:

The Petitioners further implore, That the House will take into their serious Consideration the unhappy Dilemma in which they will be placed by the Operation of the present Bill; their Societies, though unconnected with political Discussions, and simply associated for the Regulations of their Trade, will then be subject to the Control of a Magistrate, who may, upon any constructive Pretence, disperse their Meetings, or, upon any Remonstrances on their Part, subject them to all the Horrors of Military Execution; it will be evident to the House the Petitioners Numbers, at this Time, are comparatively small, when reviewing them on a former Period, which is greatly to be attributed to the vast Number that have fallen in the present calamitous and destructive War, and now in the Service of His Majesty, struggling to maintain that Constitution which it is the Object of this Petition to preserve inviolate.

A Petition of the thereunder-signed Inhabitants of the Town, Neighbourhood, and Port of Newcastle upon Tyne, was also presented to the House, and read;

Setting forth, That the Petitioners have seen, with great Concern, a late atrocious Attack upon the Person of their beloved Sovereign; and, whilst the Petitioners, in common with every Friend to the Constitution, most sincerely deplore the horrid Attempt, the real Authors of which they earnestly wish may be brought to condign Punishment, they feel themselves inexpressibly alarmed that it should be assumed as a Pretext for the Introduction of Tw'O Bills, one into each House of Parliament, which, if passed into Laws, they humbly conceive, will deprive the People of these Realms of the Rights of free Discussion and Petition, which they trusted had been secured to them at the j£ra of the glorious Resolution: And therefore entreating the House, That those Bills may not be suffered to become a Part of the established Law of these Realms.

A Petition of the Merchants, Bankers, Manufacturers, Traders, and other Inhabitants, of the City of London, was also presented to the House, and read;

Setting forth, That the Petitioners, deeply sensible of the invaluable Rights and Liberties secured to them, in common with their Fellow Subjects, by the existing Laws and Constitution of this Kingdom, and while they regard, with the most grateful Remembrance, the Wisdom of their Ancestors in forming and meliorating, and their firm and manly Defence, from Time to Time, of the glorious Fabrick they had raised — feeling it as they do their bounden and indispensable Duty to endeavour to transmit it unimpaired to their Posterity — considering the Laws now in Force as adequate to
