the Preservation of the Public Peace, and sufficiently coercive and efficacious even as to the momentous Exigencies of the present Times, and conceiving that certain Bills, now pending in the House, intituled, An Act for the Safety and Preservation of His Majesty's Person and Government against treasonable and seditious Practices and Attempts, and A Bill for the more effectually preventing seditious Meetings and Assemblies, are utterly hostile to the true and acknowledged Principles of that Constitution they so sincerely venerate and esteem, and destructive of the undoubted and sacred Rights and Liberties of the People of Great Britain, do most humbly pray, That the House will not pass the said Bills into Laws.

A Petition of the Inhabitants of the Towns of Poi'tsmouth and Portsea, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That tire Petitioners, as Britons, value Liberty as One of the first of Blessings: They account it their Birthright to speak their Minde freely on all Public Matters, and cannot hear, but with Indignation, of being thereby exposed to Fine, Imprisonment, and Transportation: They are confident that it belongs to them to hold Public Meetings, at their Pleasure, without being subjected to the inquisitorial Presence of a Magistrate, or the Danger of Arrest for Freedom of Speech, or feeling the Horrors of Military Execution at refusing to depart at his Command: The general Principles of Freedom which they there imbibe, the Knowledge of their Rights as Men and as Britons, and Information as to their Duties as Members of the social Body, all combine to attach them more strongly to the Constitution, to qualify them to act their Part with greater Propriety as useful Citizens and loyal Subjects: They consider it as their ancient and unquestionable Privilege that the Press should be free, and that Men who, by frank Discussion of the Measures of Government, overawe the Conduct of Ministers, and contribute to the pure Administration of Justice, should not be exposed to the wanton Attacks of an Attorney General, who, by a teazing Prosecution, may deprive them of their Liberty, and rob them of their Fortune: These Rights the Petitioners claim, demand, and insist upon, as essential to the Continuance of the Compact between the King and the People, as it is summed up in the Bill of Rights: Though many of the Petitioners be poor, they are honest and industrious, and by the Labour of their Hands, and the Sweat of their Brow, do not only maintain themselves, but nourish and support, in Affluence, those very Men who would trample upon them, and annihilate their Consequence in Society: The Petitioners beg Leave to remind the House, that, though often, of late, reproached for their Poverty, as Persons who have no Concern with the Transactions of Government, they consider themselves as the great Basis of Society, who, by their Strength and Exertions, support all the superior Ranks, mauy of whom seem to have forgotten whence their Consequence has arisen; and that, were they to withhold their Support, these elated Men must sink to a Level with themselves: The Petitioners would press it upon the Attention of the House, that the great Aim of a good Government is to protect the Poor against the Rich; whereas the Design of these Bills appears to be to arm the Rich against the defenceless Poor: The Poor are the first to feel the Weight of Oppression, consequently the first to complain, by reason of their Weakness: They are filled with inexpressible Horror, that Laws should be framed to stifle the Groans of their Misery, and compel them, in silent Anguish, to pine under the Bitterness of Distress: That those of the Petitioners, who are Persons of Property, consider their poorer Brethren as Men equal in Rights, and as having an equal Stake in Society; because, on the Purity of the Constitution their Happiness, which is their All, depends: While the Petitioners view with the most

u

marked Detestation the Insult offered to the Person of His Majesty (as already signified in their Address from these Towns) they cannot, without the most poignant Grief, behold an arbitrary Accumulation of Treasons, calculated only to harass the Subject without making the smallest Addition to the Security of His Majesty's Person, whose greatest Safety, and whose only impenetrable Shield, consist in the Affection of His Subjects: The Petitioners likewise consider themselves as grievously injured by the studied Ambiguity in describing a Misdemeanor, which, by the Craft and Malice of insidious Spies, might expose the most upright and innocent Man, and most ardent Lover of the Constitution of his Country, to a barbarous Punishment, not heretofore dictated by the mild and benignant Spirit of English Laws — Against the Wrongs here enumerated the Petitioners loudly exclaim, and cannot refrain from saying, that, while Knowledge, Civilization, and Philanthropy, increase, to lessen the Comforts of Society, to arrest the Mildness of Government, and enact Laws full of Harshness and Severity, is equally impolitic and unjust: The Petitioners therefore, as Enemies of Violence and Tumult, and Well-wishers to the Happiness of their Country, cannot conceal from the House the Anxiety and Concern they entertain on a Review of the Consequences which appear inevitably to attend the passing the Treason and Convention Bills, and most earnestly beseech the House to reject those Bills as prejudicial to the Interest and Welfare of the Country, and as a Violation of the Bill of Rights, as destructive *of the inestimable Privileges of the Liberty of Speech, and of the Press, and as an Attack on the Constitution of 1688: And, as a "Duty the Petitioners owe to themselves and Posterity, they call on the House as Legislators not to deprive them of these their ancient and undoubted Privileges, and that the House will continue the Enjoyment of our Constitutional Liberties as the most effectual Means of securing His Majesty's Person, preserving internal Peace, and obtaining a due Reverence to the Laws:

The Petitioners, therefore, most humbly hope and pray, That the House, influenced by a due Regard to that Constitution, which ensures to Englishmen those valuable Privileges as their Birthright, will prevent such pernicious Laws from becoming Part of the Law of the Land.

A Petition of the Publicans of the Cities of London Petitions and Westminster and County of , and Parts

adjacent, was also presented to the House, and read; gafetyof His Setting forth, That the Petitioners conceive, that the Majesty's Bills now pending in Parliament, intituled, An Act Person, Ac. for the more effectually preventing seditious Meet- MdJor Springs and Assemblies, and An Act for the Safety and *

Preservation of His Majesty's Person and Govern- ings. ment against treasonable and seditious Practices and Attempts, will, if passed into Laws, very much affect their Business as Publicans: That certain Clauses in the said Bills, as they now stand, the Petitioners have Reason to fear, will prevent the Meetings of Friendly Clubs and Societies in Public Houses, and which Clubs and Societies will be involved in their Operation, and therefore, if such Bills are passed into Laws, the Petitioners and their Families will, as the Petitioners apprehend, be involved in the Consequences thereof: And therefore praying the House to take their Case into Consideration, and grant them such Relief as to the House shall seem meet, and, if necessary, to be heard by Counsel in Support of their Petition.

A Petition of the Electors and other Inhabitants of the Town and Borough of Southwark, in the County of Surrey, in Town Hall assembled, was also presented to the House and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have heard, with the utmost Detestation, of the late daring Attack made upon the People of England in the Person of His Majesty, in His Passage to

36 LfEO. 111. JXovembns. 107

and from Parliament; and they sincerely hope that the Authors of it will meet with the most speedy and condign Punishment, from whatever Cause or Quarter it has originated, whether from the Wickedness of deliberate Malice, or from any Contrivances with a View to make it the Pretext of depriving the People of England of their true, ancient, and indisputable Rights and Liberties: That it is the Petitioners Opinion, that, as no Reign ever afforded so many Opportunities of trying the Loyalty of the People, so no Prince ever received such repeated and remarkable Demonstrations of Public Love, as His Majesty — That they believe that Lpyalty remains unshaken, notwithstanding the wide and heartfelt Calamities of the Country; and are persuaded that the People do, and will continue to, make a due Distinction between the King, who, by the Spirit of the Constitution, " can " do no Wrong," and the real and responsible Authors of the National Distress and Misery — That the Petitioners would see, with Pleasure, any true Security to His Majesty's Person adopted, if any were necessary to be superadded to the protecting Safeguard of the Laws in being, and the experienced Affections of His People; but that they hear, with Astonishment and Horror, of the Introduction of Two Bills into the House, which, under a Pretence of, but really without, adding to His Majesty's Safety, appear to them, to annihilate the most valid, the most useful, and the most fundamental, of British Rights, thereby libelling the Person of His Majesty, and introducing a Doctrine false as fatal, that the King's Security requires the Extinction of His Subjects most vital Privileges: That the Bills of which the Petitioners complain are, the one intituled, An Act for the Safety and Preservation of His Majesty's Person and Government against treasonable and seditious Practices and Attempts; and the other intituled, A Bill for the more effectually preventing seditious Meetings and Assemblies; That the First of these Bills, besides an arbitrary Accumulation of Treasons in its First Clause, strikes in its Second at every Exercise of the Right of examining Public Affairs, exalting into high Misdemeanors, Words, or Writings, which may be construed to excite Hatred or Contempt of the Government, without further Definition or Exactness; and, ultimately, subjecting Offences, so loose and uncertain, to a Punishment for which there is no Precedent in British Jurisprudence: That the Second of these Bills is still more the Subject of the Petitioners Indignation, inasmuch as it subverts the Right of Petition for Redress of Grievances, which is coeval with our Constitution, as was established at the glorious iEra of the Resolution by a solemn Law, and, from that Period to the present, has never been called in Question: As the Petitioners are persuaded of the Fact, so they beg Leave to state plainly to the House, that the King's Right to sit upon the Throne is not more clear, nor stands upon better Authority, than the Right of the People to petition the Legislature — The King reigns by no hereditary or divine Right in this Country: He reigns in virtue of the Act of Settlement, which transferred the Crown from another Family to the Family of His Majesty; the People petition under the Bill of Rights, which did not create, but which recognized and established (as it was imagined for ever) by the Provisions of a positive Statute, this sacred and unalterable Privilege: Whoever, therefore, attacks the Authority upon which this Right of the People stands, attacks, at the same Time, the Foundation of His Majesty's Title: The Petitioners are aware that it is urged in Defence of these Bills, that they do not take away, but only regulate this Right; but the Petitioners submit to the House, whether to be deprived of the Means of the beneficial Exercise of a Right is not in Reality to subvert the Vot. 51.

Right itself? For, of what Use is the Right to petition, if the Right of the People previously to assemble and freely to deliberate is put in such a Way as virtually to extinguish it? The Petitioners survey, with the utmost Terror the dreadfrd Powers with which the said Bill invests the Magistrate: To employ such Powers without Ruin to the Liberties and Peace of the Community supposes more than mortal Faculties in such Magistrate; he is expected, during the Warmth of a Debate in a Public Assembly, to do what the united Efforts of all the High Judges of the Land, as the Law stands, are unable to accomplish — To say nothing of the possible Ignorance or Corruption of a common Justice of the Peace, the Petitioners humbly entreat the House to consider what Danger there is in confiding to any human Being the Right at his Discretion to arrest any Speaker (however innocent the Speech or wrong the Interference) to disperse any Meeting, and, if disobeyed, to put them under Military Execution, safe and irresponsible himself under the Provisions of this Act: In the other Clauses, the Petitioners see many Mischiefs which, in destroying the Right of Political Discussion, in every other Mode affect our social Enjoyments, and tend to check the Improvement of human Intellect; but these Mischiefs, though great, are absorbed and obscured in the gigantic Evils of the principal Clause — If these Bills should unhappily pass into a Law, which God of His infinite Mercy forbid! it is the Opinion of the Petitioners, that a sullen Calm may for a while succeed, but in the End will prove a Thousand Times more dreadful than all the Seditions which are stated as the Cause of them, even supposing these Seditions to be established by due Inquiry, which the Petitioners conceive is not the Fact: The Irritation and Violence of a Speaker is apt to evaporate with the Oration, while the oppressed Mind, brooding over the Griefs it dares not utter, and stifling the Anguish which consumes it, is likely to burst out in some terrible Explosion, the Effect of which may be too late for Remedy: The Petitioners observe, that the Number of Prosecutions of late Years for seditious Proceedings, the Frequency of Convictions, and the Severity of Punishment, prove that the Laws in being are in full Sufficiency and Vigour, and they take the Liberty of adding, that a Multiplication of the Penal Statutes is a bad Practice and a dangerous Symptom: The alarm and Regret with which the Petitioners are filled by these Bills are not a little aggravated by the Grounds on which (as they are apprized) they were ushered into Parliament; these Grounds, if valid, will not justify the Destruction of the Privileges, which tire the Objects of these Bills, or any other Institution which is the Pride and Birthright of an Englishmen; after such a Restriction, the Petitioners see no Sacredness in the Trial by Jury, the Habeas Corpus, the Freedom of Election, or the Privileges of Parliament, which can secure them from the Effects of Principles which are supposed to sanctify the Abolition of the Liberty of the Press, and the Right of Petition; and though the Petitioners do not desire to agitate Questions respecting the Extent and Limits of the Power of the Legislature, yet they cannot conceive that any Authority can, of Right, adopt such Measures for such Reasons without being, at the same Time, competent to introduce a Resolution in the whole Frame of the Government — They seem to the Petitioners to be little short of asserting that the free Constitution of this Country is no longer compatible with its Quiet, and that our only Security against Anarchy is in the Establishment of Despotism — The Petitioners abhor these States equally, and they see no Refuge from them but in the Constitution of their Forefathers — They entreat the House seriously to call to mind, that in turbulent and difficult Times, prone to Commotion and Change, it was the highest Wisdom

A Petition of the Gentry, Merchants, Freemen, Freeholders, and Inhabitants of the City of Exeter, and its Vicinity, whose Names are thereunder written, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Bill for the more effectually preventing seditious Meetings and Assemblies, which is now depending in the House, appears to the Petitioners an Infringement on the true, ancient, and indubitable Rights and Liberties of the Subjects of this Realm: That the People of Great Britain have hitherto, of Right, assembled for discussing Political Grievances, and, as Circumstances demanded, have instructed their Representatives, petitioned Parliament, or addressed the King: That the Petitioners humbly conceive the Laws already existing provide sufficiently against any riotous or seditious Conduct at Popular Meetings: That the Bill proposed will enable individual Members of the Executive Power to control the Constitutional Liberties of the People; that it will impose unnecessary Restraints on their Assemblies; invest Magistrates with an undefined and discretionary Authority of suppressing fair Discussion; and although no riotous Intentions are manifested, will empower them to imprison their Fellow Subjects, dissolve their Meetings, and endanger their Lives by Military Execution: That the Petitioners have observed, with Concern, another Bill now also depending, intituled, An Act for the Safety and Preservation of llis Majesty's Person and Government against treasonable and seditious Practices and Attempts; a Bill which hazards the Security of the Subject, by extending the most severe Punishments to Offences ambiguously described: That the Petitioners feel the utmost Abhorrence at the Outrages lately offered to the Constitution and to the Person of His Majesty, whose Safety, nevertheless, they humbly conceive, will not be more effectually established by the Bills proposed, than by the Laws already in Existence: The Petitioners therefore humbly and earnestly implore, That the House will prevent the Bills so depending from being passed into Laws, and will preserve inviolate the present Constitution, with the Rights and Privileges of the People.

A Petition of the thereunder-signed Inhabitants of the Borough of Bury Saint Edmunds, in the County of Suffolk, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners approach the House with Sentiments of unfeigned Attachment to the Principles of the Constitution, established by the glorious Resolution of 1688: That the Petitioners have seen with Indignation, the Principles of that Constitution violated by the atrocious Insult lately offered to the Person of llis Majesty; but that the Petitioners view, with the most serious Alarm, the Introduction of Two Bills into Parliament, the one intituled, An Act for the Safety and Preservation of His Majesty's Person and Government against treasonable and seditious Practices and Attempts, the other An Act for the more effectually preventing seditious Meetings and Assemblies, the obvious Tendency of which is to invest the Magistrates with new and arbitrary Powers, to introduce new Penal Laws and constructive Treasons, and to build, upon the Ruins of our dearest Rights, a System incompatible with any free Constitution whatever: That the Petitioners consider the said Bills as unnecessary, impolitic, and unconstitutional — Unnecessary, because the existing Laws are adequate as well to the Detection as to the Punishment of Offenders — Impolitic, because they will lessen that Confidence which should subsist between the People and their Representatives, and that Respect which is due to the Magistrates and the Laws — and Unconstitutional, because they tend to frustrate the Provisions of the Bill of Rights, to deprive the People of the Privileges of Petition and Remonstrance, to prevent the House from a.

being informed of the Wishes of its Constituents, to extend the Influence of the Executive Power, and, by restraining the Constitutional Exercise of Political Discussion, to surrender into its Hands the Bulwarks of Popular Liberty: Therefore the Petitioners most humbly entreat the House not to permit the said Bills to become the Laws of the Realm: That the Petitioners, convinced that the present Apprehensions of Public Danger arise more from the Continuance of a disastrous War, than from any other Cause, are of Opinion that the Restoration of Peace, by lessening the Public Burthens, will better tend to allay Popular Discontent than the most coercive Regulations: They therefore humbly hope that the House will use its best Exertions to obtain a Termination of Hostilities, as the most certain Means of preserving internal Tranquillity.

A Petition of the thereunder-signed Inhabitants of Petition the City, Close, College, and Suburbs, of Winchester, resPcynn8 was likewise presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, impressed with Horror at the late outrageous Insult offered to the Person of our revered and beloved Sovereign, and apprehending the greatest Danger to our happy Constitution, to the Tranquillity of our Country, and to the Security of our Persons and Property, from seditious Assemblies, in which Doctrines are publicly inculcated subversive of all Government, of all Religion, and of all true Civil Liberty, beg Leave to petition the House to concur with the other Branches of the Legislature in passing such Laws as shall more effectually secure His Majesty's Person and Dignity, and prevent such Meetings from being Sources of Sedition and Treason, in whatever Manner to the Wisdom of the House shall seem best.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table.

Nation at the Resolution of it)6S, and recognized by the Union of the Two Kingdoms in the lleign of her Majesty Queen Anne, being essential to the Happiness of the People at large, by securing to them the Freedom of Speech, and Petition in Cases of Grievance, the Petitioners are seriously alarmed at an Attempt, publicly declared to be now in Agitation, to carry through the Legislature Two Bills, the one intituled, An Act for the more effectually preventing seditious Meetings, and Assemblies, and the other An Act for the Safety and Preservation of His Majesty's Person and Government against treasonable and seditious Practices and Attempts; tending and purporting to destroy and do away their essential and invaluable Rights: That the Petitioners, seeing and knowing that a most serious and just Apprehension pervades every of His Majesty's true and faithful Subjects, upon the Grounds of the said purposed Laws, they feel themselves bound, by their Love of their Country and its Constitution, and their Respect for the Person and high Station of His Majesty, to implore the House not to suffer the said Bills, designed to interfere with, and obstruct, the free Discussion of their Rights and Liberties, or their Meetings for such Purposes, and petitioning regarding the same, to pass into Laws: And the Petitioners further add, that, by preventing such Bill or Bills from being carried into Effect as Laws, by whomsoever preferred, proposed, or supported, the House will secure the Love and Attachment of many Hundred Thousand loyal Subjects, who, if such Laws should be passed, will feel no Affection for the Constitution when it shall no longer afford them those invaluable Liberties.

A Petition of the Inhabitants of the Town and Neighbourhood of Birmingham, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, deeply affected at the melancholy Prospect of a further Continuance of the present desolating War, by which our Trade has been mined, Mechanical Labour reduced, and Famine, they fear, will be added to the innumerable Calamities already heaped upon our Heads: Much as the Petitioners are afflicted by the Evils above mentioned, they feel themselves much more so when they contemplate the immense Loss of Blood and Treasure occasioned by the Attempt to accomplish Objects which evidently appear to the Petitioners unattainable: The Petitioners also, considering the pacific Disposition of the present Rulers of France, trust that their Form of Government will not influence the Minds of the House against, or prove an Obstacle to a speedy Restoration of Peace to our once flourishing but now distressed Country: The Petitioners therefore beseech the House to adopt such Measures as in their Wisdom may seem meet to attain so desirable an End: The Petitioners also have heard, with the utmost Abhorrence, of the late daring Outrages committed upon the sacred Person of His Majesty, but venerating, as they do, our excellent and invaluable Constitution,

they beg Leave to state to the House their entire Disapprobation of certain Bills now pending in Parliament, intituled, An Act for the Safety of His Majesty's Person and Government, and, An Act to prevent seditious Assemblies: And, conceiving that the Laws now in Force are adequate to the Preservation of Public Peace, and sufficiently coercive and efficacious as to the momentous Exigencies of the present Times, do most humbly pray that the House will not pass those Bills into Laws.

BUI for pre- ^own , was also presented to the House,

venting Se- and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are not ditious Meet- less deeply affected with the Dangers to which our ing*. Liberty is exposed by the proposed Measure of in-

troducing a Bill into Parliament to prevent Meetings of His Majesty's faithful Subjects than at the late Outrage upon His Majesty's sacred Person, which is held out as the Ground of the proposed Bill: They deprecate the Growth of Disaffection and the Spread of Tumult, and therefore dread the passing of a Bill, of the Nature proposed, into a Law, which would increase the one and promote the other: They would not speak of past Measures which were adopted to circumscribe the Freedom of the Subject; the Petitioners Attention is absorbed in the present Attempt, which, if carried into a Law', will deprive Britons of those Rights which their Ancestors earned with many a Struggle, and purchased at the Price of much Blood: Such a Law', by confining Disaffection, instead of allowing it an Opportunity to spend its Force, will only give it Time to acquire redoubled Energy and renewed Elasticity: It is not the Disease which appears externally, but the secret Poison, which finding no Vent, unseen spreads its Malignity, and undermines the Frame, that is most to be dreaded: The Petitioners know that it is not their Province to dictate, but they conceive it their Duty to pray, that, instead of putting them under further Restraints, the House would apply the Wisdom of Parliament to ameliorate, and the Energy of Government to enforce, Jormer Laws: the Petitioners confess that they are at a Loss to conceive for what Reason the rest of the Kingdom should be deprived or restrained, in their Right of assembling, on Account of the irregular Behaviour of some imprudent or malicious Persons in the Metropolis: The Safety of His Majesty, in the Petitioners humble Opinion, would be more effectually secured by the Affection of a free, than by the Terror of a restricted, People — and who would wish to be defended by the Hedge of Law when he may repose under the Shade of Love: Moderation of Measures, not Severity of Punishment, would regain His Majesty the Love and Affection of the most disaffected. To prevent Disaffection from having Recourse to the dreadful Efforts of Despair, the Petitioners entreat that the House would pause, and, finally, exclude any Bill, which, under Pretence of defending the Person of His Majesty, is calculated to lay unnecessary and unconstitutional Restrictions upon the People: By attending to this Petition, and preserving the Liberty of the Subject inviolate, the House will have an additional Claim upon the Affection of the Country, and the Gratitude of the Petitioners.

Bill, intituled, A Bill for the more effectually preventing seditious Meetings and Assemblies; which Meetings, is at present depending in the House, and which Bill appears to the Petitioners to be an Encroachment on one of the most ancient and Constitutional Rights and Liberties of the Subjects of this Kingdom, namely, that oLpeaceably assembling for the Discussion of their Grievances, and of petitioning Parliament or addressing the King, as Circumstances may require, and which Right of the Subject will, as the Petitioners humbly conceive, be entirely annihilated if clogged with so many Restrictions as are contained in the intended Bill: That the proposed Bill, by enabling an individual Member of the Executive Government to controul, or, by his simple Veto, totally to prevent the Constitutional Right of the People of assembling to discuss the Grievances under which they labour, and of using Constitutional Measures for redressing them, will be a total Alteration of our happy Constitution as established at the Resolution; a Constitution which, the Petitioners doubt not, would (if preserved in its original Purity) continue the Wonder and Admiration of Ages: That the Petitioners have also observed, with the deepest Concern, another Bill, now also depending, intituled, An Act for the Safety and Preservation of His Majesty's Person and Government against treasonable and seditious Practices and Attempts; a Bill which exposes the Subject to the severest Pains and Penalties for the Commission of Offences described with the most vague Ambiguity:

That the Petitioners feel the utmost Abhorrence of the late Outrage committed against the Person of His Majesty, whose Safety, they humbly conceive, is sufficiently secured by the Laws already in Existence, and have therefore to lament that such gross Enormities (from whatever Source originating) have been artfully made a Pretext for enacting Laws which every free born Briton is, in Duty to himself and his Posterity, bound, by every Constitutional Method, to oppose and prevent: When the Petitioners consider the enormous Burthens under which this Country labours, and look forward to a Time when all Hopes of Relief are cut off by the Prevention of dutiful Petitions and Addresses to Parliament and to His Majesty, they cannot anticipate, without Horror, the direful Consequences which are likely to result from the Adoption of Measures so inconsistent with the unalienable Rights of Freemen, and so inimical to His Majesty and His illustrious Family, who were, by the Voice of the People, called to the exalted Throne of these Dominions for the Support of those Rights and Privileges which are thus insidiously attempted to be subverted and destroyed:

A Petition of the Inhabitants of the Borough of Great Yarmouth, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That, whilst the Petitioners have observed, with the most decided Disapprobation, the late Tumultuary Outrage upon the Person of His Majesty, they have observed, with Alarm, the Introduction of Two Bills into Parliament, the one intituled, An Act for the Safety and Preservation of His Majesty's Person and Government against treasonable and seditious Practices and Attempts; and the other, An Act for the more effectually preventing seditious Meetings and Assemblies; which, if passed into Laws, will, in their Apprehension, overthrow the most valuable Privileges of Englishmen, and the latter of which, in particular, they conceive, tends grievously to infringe upon their Right of petitioning the several Branches of the Legislature, as having for its direct Object the total Suppression of all Public Discussion, and of every formal Declaration of Popular Opinion, in any the most peaceable and orderly Assembly, unless conformable to the Will of the local Magistrate for the Time being; every such Magistrate being, according to that Bill, to be armed with a perfectly arbitrary Power of judging concerning Intention, and of summary Arrest: The Petitioners therefore, in Duty equally to themselves and to Posterity, earnestly pray, That the House will put their decisive Negative upon them.

A Petition of the Mayor, Capital Burgesses, Common Councilmen, and principal Inhabitants, of the Borough and Parish of Southm in the County of Devon, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, feeling, in common with the rest of His Majesty's loyal Subjects, the Danger with which the Constitution is threatened by the Obtrusion of certain Doctrines, wholly novel to this Country, and subversive of all the Principles of Order and Government; seeing also the Necessity of counteracting the Growth of this alarming Evil, by stretching out the Laws to meet the peculiar Licentiousness of the Times, take this Method of conveying their Sentiments to the Bar of both Houses of Parliament, humbly imploring them to persist in such Measures, as may appear, to their Wisdom, to be effectual to the putting a Stop to these daring Innovations: The Petitioners particularly look for their Security to the Two Bills now pending in Parliament, for the better Protection of His Majesty's sacred Person, and for the Prevention of traitorous and seditious Meetings, and earnestly pray that the Provisions therein contained may speedily pass into Law: And further pray. That they may be followed up by such other Regulations as may be deemed adequate to the securing the Dignity of Parliament, the Authorities of the Realm, and the Public Peace, from the Inroads of those criminal Movers of Treason and Sedition, who are continually employing every Artifice to seduce the Idle and Illiterate, and to make them the Instruments of their own Ruin, and of the Subversion of the State.

A Petition of the thereunder-signed Inhabitants of the Town of Colchester, in the County of Essex, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners reflect, with the greatest Indignation and Abhorrence, on the insolent and wicked Attack upon the Person of their Sovereign, and trust that the Wisdom of Parliament will be strenuously exerted in endeavouring to discover the real Authors of so daring and atrocious an Outrage; convinced that, whether they be found among open Enemies or (what is altogether as probable) pretended Friends, the Nation will most cordially rejoice at their meeting with their merited

Punishment: That while they sincerely lament that any of their Fellow Subjects could be so unprincipled as to violate, in the Person of their King, that happy Constitution under which they have enjoyed such Advantages, the Petitioners cannot help feeling an extreme Alarm at finding it made the Pretext for bringing Two Bills into Parliament, the one intituled, An Act for the Safety of His Majesty's Person, the other. An Act to prevent seditious Assemblies; the obvious Tendency of which is the Abolition of those Privileges which have always been hitherto considered as their fundamental Rights: That, accustomed to look up to a British House of Commons as the Barrier which is to secure our Lives, Properties, and Freedom, against the Attempts of the Disaffected and the Turbulent, the undue Extension of Prerogative, or the Treachery of abandoned Ministers, the Petitioners cannot sufficiently express their Dissatisfaction and Astonishment at the unexampled Rapidity with which Bills, so important in their Consequences, have hitherto proceeded through all the Stages of their Progress; neither are the Petitioners much less surprized that the Purposes they profess to have in View are the better protecting of His Majesty's Person and Government, and the more effectual Security of the British Constitution: To promote such Purposes as these, the Petitioners trust they shall be found as zealous as any of His Majesty's most loyal Subjects, but they humbly conceive that the Bills, to which they refer, are not only extremely inadequate to effect such Purposes, but, if passed into Laws, will annihilate the Remainder of those Liberties, without which, Existence to a Briton loses Half its Value: That the Petitioners cannot conceive that free Discussion has a Tendency to injure Truth, or the Persons of those who shall wish to support its Authority; that they see not, at present, the slightest Reason to imagine that the late most atrocious Attempt on the Person of our Sovereign has any Connection with the Actions of any Society that has met for the Purpose of discussing Political Subjects, much less do they imagine it can ever sanction an Attempt to prevent us from exercising the most important of our Privileges, the remonstrating with the Legislature or our Sovereign on the Grievances under which we suffer, or censuring the Conduct of His Ministers when encroaching on our dearest Rights: That the Petitioners are fully persuaded that Restraints upon the Liberty of the Press, and the Freedom of Speech, beyond what are already imposed by the existing Laws, not only have the strongest Tendency to produce Discontents, which will always be more dangerous, because they will be always more secret, but will furnish a more reasonable Ground for Dislike of Government than even its most virulent Enemies at present possess: That the Petitioners are thoroughly convinced, that removing the present Grievances and Burthens of the People, in which the War has been so abundantly fruitful, will have a more powerful Effect in recalling the Misled, conciliating the Disaffected, and restraining the Unwary and Imprudent, than any Laws, the most rigid that can be invented, which will always be dangerous in Proportion to their ill-timed Severity: Deeply impressed with the Truth and Importance of these Sentiments, zealous in Defence of our established Constitution (of which Liberty to discuss the Propriety of all Public Measures, and petition against Grievances and Oppression, make so very important a Part) the Petitioners most ardently entreat and supplicate the House, That those Bills, so injurious to our Rights, and oppressive and dangerous in their Consequences, may never be permitted to become a Part of that Code, to which the Petitioners have hitherto looked up with Veneration and Gratitude, and that Peace may be restored, by the Efforts of the House, to a patient and loyal Nation, on which War has accumulated such grievous Burthens and Distress, and whose Prospects,

A 'Petition Of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Assistants, of the 'Borough of Leeds, in Common Iiall assembled, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have long beheld, with deep Concern, the daring Attempts which have been made, by many discontented and ill-designing Persons within these Realms, to overturn the Constitution of this Country, and thereby to bring us into a State of Anarchy and Wretchedness, which the Petitioners most earnestly deprecate: That the Petitioners humbly conceive, that the Laws now existing have not provided an adequate Punishment for the highly seditious Practices which of late have taken place in these Kingdoms, nor have afforded sufficient Means of Prevention against Measures so destructive of Public Peace and good Government, as to threaten the Overthrow of our happy Constitution: The Petitioners therefore do humbly entreat the House, in Concurrence with the other Branches of the Legislature, to enact such Laws as, in their Wisdom, they shall deem most proper for protecting the Person of our gracious Sovereign, the suppressing of seditious Meetings and Practices, and for preventing the Dissemination of such corrupt Principles as endanger the Security of our most excellent Government.

A Petition of the Inhabitants of the City and Suburbs of Winchester, was likewise presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, whilst the Petitioners detest the base Motives and the dastardly Conduct of the Persons who were guilty of so daring an Outrage to His Majesty's most sacred Person in -His Passage to and from Parliament, and sincerely hope that the Perpetrators and Abettors thereof may be brought to condign Punishment; they cannot remain silent on the extraordinary and alarming Tenor of the Bills now pending in Parliament, the one intituled, An Act for the more effectually preventing seditious Meetings and Assemblies; and the other, An Act for the Safety and Preservation of His Majesty's Person and Government against treasonable and seditious Practices and Attempts; as they manifestly appear to proceed on the unjust Grounds of a general Disaffection in the Nation to the King and the other Branches of the Government, and thereby convey an Idea that this brave and generous People are Accomplices of a lawless Mob, and are Friends to Anarchy and Disorder: Knowing it to be the sacred and inviolable Privilege of Britons to take into their serious Consideration every Measure that affects their happy Constitution and their dearest Privileges, the Petitioners beg Leave to state their Apprehensions of the disastrous Effects that may result from their passing into Laws: The Petitioners must therefore, as bound by every Principle of Honour and Virtue, every Thing dear to themselves and their Posterity, humbly remonstrate against the House passing the said Bills into Laws, as they humbly conceive them to counteract the most sacred Principles of our invaluable Constitution, and may lay a Foundation for the Destruction of that glorious Fabric erected by the progressive Wisdom, and cemented by the best Blood of our Ancestors.

A Petition of the Inhabitants, Householders residing in the Parish of Saint Clement Danes, in the City and Liberties of Westminster, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have witnessed, with no less Astonishment than Horror, the atrocious Attempt made on His Majesty's Royal Person, in His Passage to Parliament, on the First Day of the present Session; and are firmly determined to risk their Lives, if called upon, in Defence of our Sovereign, whose Public and Private Virtues have so strong a Claim on the most affectionate Attachment of a dutiful and loyal People: That it is impossible for the Petitioners not to impute the Outrages, which have taken place, to those seditious Assemblies, where Language has been repeatedly held, and Proceedings adopted, calculated to stimulate the Ill-disposed and Disaffected to the Disturbance of the Public Tranquillity, to the most daring Violation of the Laws, to the extreme Hazard of His Majesty's Person, and to the Contempt of His Government: That the Petitioners consider these Outrages as directed, not only against His Majesty's sacred Person, but against the Independence of Parliament, and the established Constitution, and they most anxiously hope, that the House may be enabled, in its Wisdom, to devise some effectual Means to prevent the Repetition of them; at the same Time assuring the House of their most determined Co-operation, and active Exertions, in Defence of the best of Sovereigns, and of those Laws and Liberties, and of that Constitution, the Preservation of which is so intimately connected, not only with the Security of His Majesty's Person, but with the Observance of that Respect due to the First Magistrate.

A Petition of the Inhabitants, Householders of the Petition City and Liberties of Westminster, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners have witnessed, with no less Astonishment than Horror, the atrocious Attempt made on His Majesty's Royal Person, in His Passage to Parliament, on the First Day of the present Session; and are firmly determined to risk their Lives, if called upon, in Defence of our Sovereign, whose Public and Private Virtues have so strong a Claim on the most affectionate Attachment of a dutiful and loyal People: That it is impossible for the Petitioners not to impute the Outrages, which have taken place, to those seditious Assemblies, where Language has been repeatedly held, and Proceedings adopted, calculated to stimulate the Ill-disposed and Disaffected to the Disturbance of the Public Tranquillity, to the most daring Violation of the Laws, to the extreme Hazard of His Majesty's Person, and to the Contempt of His Government: That the Petitioners consider these Outrages as directed, not only against His Majesty's sacred Person, but against the Independence of Parliament, and the established Constitution, and they most anxiously hope that the House may be enabled, in its Wisdom, to devise some effectual Means to prevent the Repetition of them; at the same Time assuring the House of their most determined Cooperation, and active Exertions, iu Defence of the best of Sovereigns, and of those Laws and Liberties, and of that Constitution, the Preservation of which is so intimately connected, not only with the Security of His Majesty's Person, but with the Observance of that Respect due to the First Magistrate.

A Petition of the Persons, whose Names are there- Petition in unto subscribed, Inhabitants of Leicester, was likewise favour of presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That gafet^flSs the Petitioners have seen, with Indignation and Ab- Majesty's horrence, the daring Outrage which lately threatened the Person, 4c.; Safety of His Majesty's Person, and endangered the and forpre-very Existence of the Constitution: That the Petitioners tious Moet^*~ cannot but attribute this nefarious Attempt to the ings. Operation of those Principles which have newly been transplanted in this happy Country, propagated with the most active Industry by its secret Enemies, and founded upon the very Spirit of its open ones; and they humbly submit to the House, that, whilst the Practice of systematically destroying a good Opinion of the Government is suffered to prevail, the Government itself is attacked, and in Danger: That the Petitioners are persuaded that the present Laws do not sufficiently secure the peaceable and the good Subjects against the Machinations of the Disaffected and the Profligate:

They therefore pray the House to pass Two Bills now depending in it, intituled, the one, An Act for the Safety and Preservation of His Majesty's Person and Government against treasonable and seditious Practices and Attempts, and the other, An Act for the more effectually preventing seditious Meetings and Assemblies.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table.

118 26° JVovembris. 1795.

the Candour and Indulgence of the House, in judging thus freely on a Matter that so nearly concerns them, and further beg Leave to remark; that, notwithstanding all those paradoxical Assertions relative to scanty Crops, or those spurious Representations, made by interested Persons, respecting a defective Produce, still the Reverse remains a stubborn Fact; for, from common Observation, and all concurring Circumstances, it appears, that the present Scarcity is an artificial one, brought on by artful and designing Men, long practised in the intricate Windings of Extortion, and through whose avaricious Views we now experience the Effects of Famine: The Petitioners acknowledge, with sincere Gratitude and humble Dependance, our Obligations to the Divine Being, for those munificent Displays of His Providence, in sending us fruitful Seasons, and an ample Supply of all needful Comforts adequate to our Wants and agreeable to our Necessities: We see them with our Eyes as extended by His Bounty; but, alas! before we can partake thereof, we must submit to the exorbitant Exactions of our Fellow Creatures: We feel the Force of Reason in those salutary Laws instituted to secure and preserve the Property of Individuals sacred and inviolate; but seriously lament that it should be in the Power of any Man, or any Set of Men, to cause an artificial Scarcity, or to accumulate Riches and raise Fortunes out of the Calamities of the Poor: We know, and reverence, those equitable Laws instituted to prevent unjust Usury, but know of no Laws applicable or practicable to suppress engrossing by Sample Contracts, or to prevent the baneful Practice of monopolizing many Farms in One, or for prohibiting monopolizing Dealers from engrossing and buying up, at Villages and Farm Houses, all necessary Articles of Subsistence, and thereby, and by Means of their Opulence, Connections, and Combinations, of having in their Power to withhold, keep up, or enhance, the Price of all Articles to what Pitch they please; those pernicious Practices are now become so prevalent as nearly to preclude the Means of purchasing any of the Necessaries of Life but what comes through their Hands, and, thus exposed a Prey to Avarice, the Generality of the Nation are now inevitably reduced to Want and Beggary — Under these unhappy Circumstances the Petitioners beg Leave to appeal to the Justice and Humanity of the House, as the Conservators and Guardians of the Public Welfare; they presume not to dictate or prescribe any specific Mode of Redress, they humbly repose their Remedy in the Wisdom of Parliament, but humbly conceive, and beg Leave to observe, that those Regulations, intended for our Relief, should be easy in their Application, otherwise the Poor will be precluded Benefit by their indigent Circumstances — To this their just and humble Representation, founded on suffering Facts and sad Experience, the Petitioners most earnestly solicit the Care and Attention of the House, and humbly entreat them to take such Measures thereupon as to their Wisdom shall seem most fitting and meet, for the Honour of Parliament, and for the Relief of their humble Dependants.

A Petition of the thereunder-signed Inhabitants of the Borough of Newport, and Parish of Saint Stephens, in the County of Cormcall, was presented to the House,

and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have seen, with great Concern, a late atrocious Attack upon the Person of their beloved Sovereign, and whilst the Petitioners, in common with every Friend to the Constitution, most sincerely deplore the horrid Attempt, the real Authors of which they earnestly wish may be brought to condign Punishment, they feel themselves inexpressibly alarmed that it should be assumed as a Pretext for the Introduction of Two Bills, one into each House of Parliament, which, if passed into a Law, they humbly conceive, will deprive the People of these Realms of the Rights of free Discussion, which they trusted had been secured to them at the Era of the glorious Resolution: And therefore entreating the House, That those Bills may not be suffered to become Part of the established Law of these Realms.

A Petition of the thereunder-signed Inhabitants of the Town and Borough of Launceston, in the County of Cornwall, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have seen, with great Concern, a late atrocious Attack upon the Person of their beloved Sovereign, and whilst the Petitioners, in common with every Friend to the Constitution, most sincerely deplore the horrid Attempt, the real Authors of which they earnestly wish may be brought to condign Punishment, they feel themselves inexpressibly alarmed that it should be assumed as a Pretext for the Introduction of Two Bills, one into each House of Parliament, which, if passed into a Law, they humbly conceive, will deprive the People of these Realms of the Rights of free Discussion and Petition, which they trusted had been secured to them at the Era of the glorious Resolution; And therefore entreating the House, That those Bills may not be suffered to become a Part of the established Law of these Realms.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Burgesses, and Petition from Inhabitants, of the Borough of Wallingford, was pre- Wallingford sented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That gXofCoriu the Petitioners conceive the Practice of selling Corn by Sample is one of the chief Causes of the present high Price of that Article, particularly as it opens an ample Field for Speculation to unprincipled Jobbers, and thus enhances the Price of Grain to the Consumer by the Addition of intervening Profits: That it is the Opinion of the Petitioners, that, if all Kinds of Grain were brought openly and fairly to Market, it would greatly contribute to lower the Prices, as the Farmer having been at the Trouble and Expence of bringing his Corn, would be induced to sell at the Market Price rather than carry it back again; and that the inferior Classes would be thereby enabled to procure so necessary an Article at the First Hand, whereas the prevailing Mode of selling by Sample offers to the Farmer both the Temptation and the Means to withhold his Corn, with a View to procure a Price unbounded as his Avarice: And therefore entreating the

A Petition of the Inhabitants of the Town of Lyme Regis, in the County of Dorset, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners viewing, with great Alarm, the Introduction of Two Bills into Parliament, the one intituled, An Act for the Safety of His Majesty's Person and Government against treasonable and Seditious Practices and Attempts, and the other. An Act to prevent seditious Assemblies; which they conceive to be Infringements upon the Constitution, and Violations of their best Rights and Liberties, have met to request of the House that they will, at this awful Crisis, act as the Representatives of a free People, by opposing their Authority to an Innovation unprecedented since the Resolution: That the Petitioners, though they lament the late Insult offered to the King, cannot avoid expressing their Conviction, that the existing Laws are fully adequate to the Punishment of Offenders, and sufficient to prevent a Repetition of similar Outrages: That the Petitioners knowing the distressed Situation of a vast Number of their Fellow Creatures, and convinced that those Distresses arise from the Continuance of the present most disastrous War,' do most servently implore the House to use every Endeavour to bring about a speedy Peace, as the best Mode of giving Stability to the Throne, Clothing to the Naked, and Bread to the Poor.

A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, Inhabitants of the Town of Leicester, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners view, with the utmost Detestation and Abhorrence, the late daring Insult offered to the sacred Person of the King, and sincerely hope that the Perpetrators thereof may be brought to condign Punishment: That the Petitioners conceive that the Honour and Happiness of the Sovereign are so intimately connected with the Prosperity of the People, that the best Assurance he can have of their Affection must arise from the perfect Enjoyment of their Freedom, and that those who would attempt to diminish that Freedom are Enemies to the King, and to the Constitution: That it appears to the Petitioners, that the Two Bills now depending in Parliament, the one intituled, An Act for the Safety of His Majesty's Person and Government, against treasonable and seditious Practices and Attempts, and the other, An Act to prevent seditious Meetings and Assemblies; are destructive of the Happiness, and of the fundamental Rights of the People, and Vol. 61.

strike at the Foundation of the Constitution, inasmuch as they unnecessarily increase the Number of Capital Punishments, prevent all Public Discussion, and the Declaration of popular Opinion, and, particularly, subvert that invaluable Enjoyment the Liberty of the Press.

With Minds thus impressed, the Petitioners earnestly entreat the House, the legal Guardians of their Rights, to prevent those Bills from passing into Laws, and thereby secure to them and Posterity the Continuance of Privileges which form an essential and iuestimable Part of our excellent Constitution.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the thereunder-written Inhabitants of Petition Southampton and its Neighbourhood, was presented to respecting the House, and read; Setting forth, That, while this Country is bearing its Share of the Calamities under 66 ,ng3'

which all Europe is suffering, they cannot but feel great Concern on seeing its particular Distress increased by internal Discord and Contention, Evils of so alarming a Nature, as to call aloud for the Interposition of the governing Powers, to whose Care the general Welfare is committed: And therefore praying the House to take such vigorous Measures as, in its Wisdom, shall seem most effectual for preserving inviolate our envied Constitution, and guarding it from the insidious Attacks of those who, under the specious Pretext of the Subjects Right, form and encourage Meetings, where the grossest Misrepresentations are held forth, and the most pernicious Doctrines inculcated, tending to excite Discontent in the deluded Multitude, Disrespect to our gracious Sovereign, and Contempt of the Laws, and to destroy all Subordination, that indispensable Bond of social Union, without which no Government can exist, no Nation can enjoy Prosperity or Peace.

Petitions against the Bills for preventing Seditious Meetings; and for the Safety of His Majesty's Person, &c.

134 IMovcmbns.

to the House, and read: Setting forth. That they have beheld, with the utmost Sorrow, a Bill now pending in the House, for the more effectual preventing seditious Meetings and Assemblies; the Operation of which, they humbly conceive, will be to subvert the Liberties and fundamental Laws of this Nation as established at the glorious Resolution: To complain under Oppression has hitherto been considered the Right of Englishmen; but, by the present Bill, the Petitioners humbly conceive that they will be utterly deprived of that Freedom of Discussion in Public Assemblies, by which alone the true Extent and Pressure of Grievance can be ascertained — because this Bill requires the Intervention of a Magistrate at every Meeting convened for the Purpose of lamenting Grievances, where the General Voice may be overawed by his Authority — Discontent may be misinterpreted into Disloyalty — and Perseverance in Complaint may be menaced with the Horrors of Martial Law: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Burgesses, Tradesmen, and other Inhabitants, of the Borough of Newcastle under Lyme, in the County of ,was also pre-

sented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are informed there are Two Bills now depending in the House, intituled, An Act for the more effectual preventing seditious Meetings and Assemblies, and, An Act for the Safety and Preservation of His Majesty's Person and Government against treasonable Practices and Attempts: That considering the Constitution of this Kingdom, as by Law established, is wisely calculated, and sufficiently powerful, to secure the Person of the Sovereign, enforce due Obedience and Submission to the Government and Laws, as well as to provide for the Peace and Happiness of the Nation, and the Liberty and Prosperity of the People, and humbly conceiving that the said Two Bills tend to prevent the free Discussion of Public Measures, the undoubted and one of the most important Rights of British Subjects, and also viewing them as Innovations of that Constitution, which the Petitioners wish always to support, maintain, and deliver to Posterity inviolate, they therefore pray, That the said Bills may not pass into a Law.

A Petition of the Gun-makers residing in the Cities of London and Westminster, and Parts adjacent, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners observe, with great Concern, Two Bills now before the House, severally intituled, An Act for the Safety and Preservation of His Majesty's Person and Government against treasonable and seditious Practices and Attempts, and, An Act for the more effectually preventing seditious Meetings and Assemblies; which the Petitioners insist are totally subversive of the true Principles of the Constitution, as established at the glorious Resolution in 1688: That the Petitioners further represent to the House, that Public Meetings, of every Description of the People, are the only Security they possess against the Abuses of Power: That the Petitioners, deeply sensible of the Dangers which impend over this Country, and smarting under the Calamities and Distress occasioned by the War in which they are unfortunately involved, do most humbly entreat the House not to aggravate their Sufferings by passing the present Bills into Laws, and thereby destroy the best Rights and Liberties of Englishmen.

A Petition of John Cartwright, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioner, in the strongest Manner, condemns and reprobates all such Outrages on Peace and Order, and all such flagitious Insults, as appear to have been offered to His Majesty on the first Day of the present Session of Parliament; and thinks the Offenders ought, if possible, to be discovered, and, if discovered and

convicted, to be punished in the most exemplary Manner; and he presumes the Laws now in being fully adequate to that salutary End, as well as to the still more important one of preventing, as far as Law can prevent, the high Crime of Treason, provided those Laws be duly resorted to, and faithfully administered: Holding these Sentiments, the Petitioner has viewed, with the deepest Horror, the Attempts now making in both Houses of Parliament, by certain Persons in Power, to introduce into the Criminal Law of England such a Change as, in the Opinion of the Petitioner, must, if successful, remove from his Mind every Idea of his living under a free Government: The Petitioner humbly conceives the proposed Bill for the Safety and Preservation of His Majesty's Person and Government against treasonable and seditious Practices and Attempts; and another Bill for the more effectually preventing seditious Meetings and Assemblies, to be wholly unnecessary to the Laws of this Country, injurious to the Interests, subversive of the Liberties, and dishonouring the Character, of the Nation, and pernicious also in the highest Degree, inasmuch as those Bills, if made Law, would have, to the Apprehension of the Petitioner, a manifest Tendency to foster and to aggravate the Discontents of one Part of the People; and, as soon as the Prejudices of others shall by Experience be done away, to beget in the Community at large a settled and rooted Dislike of the Government, under which they should be doomed to live. The Petitioner certainly does believe, and indeed he knows, that great Discontent at certain Abuses and Corruptions of the Constitution does exist amongst many of the People, whose anxious Attachment to the Constitution has taught them to study its Principles, and to consider by what Line of Conduct, both on the Part of the People, and of their Rulers, that Constitution is to be preserved: That Sort of Discontent, the Petitioner is not ashamed to own, he himself has long and deeply felt, and largely shared; nor does he wish to conceal from the House, that the Views he has taken of the Abuses and Corruptions he speaks of, have filled his Mind with the most melancholy Presages of the approaching Loss of British Liberty; nor can he now entertain a better Hope, unless certain Measures, congenial with the true Principles and obvious Maxims of our Constitution, be speedily adopted by the House; he need not say they must be Measures of a Complexion as different from the dreadful Bills now pending, as Light from Darkness: Here the Petitioner most humbly entreats the House to look into its own Journals for a Petition presented to it on the 6th Day of May 1793, and to review the said Petition with that serious Attention, that full Deliberation, and that impartial Regard to the most important Right of Englishmen, which the subject Matter of that Petition so well deserves to have bestowed upon it: That Petition, as the present Petitioner is credibly informed and believes, states, amongst a great Variety of Particulars of high Importance, the following Facts and Inferences, and in the following Words; namely — " That, at " the present Day, the House of Commons does not " fully and fairly represent the People of England, " which, consistently with what your Petitioners conceive to be the Principles of the Constitution, they " consider as a Grievance; and, therefore, with all " becoming Respect, lay their Complaints before your " Honourable House" — Again, Your Petitioners,

" in affirming that your Honourable House is not an " adequate Representation of the People of England, " do but state a Fact, which, if the word, ‘ Representation' be accepted in its fair and obvious Sense, " they are ready to prove; and which they think detrimental to their Interest, and contrary to the Spirit " of the Constitution" — Again, " Your Petitioners " must now beg Leave to call the Attention of your

" Honourable

" Honourable House to the greatest Evil produced by these Defects in the Representation" [Referring to a long Enumeration of Defects besides those here " quoted] " of which they complain; namely, the Extent of Private Parliamentary Patronage; an Abuse, which obviously tends to exclude the great Mass " of the People from any substantial Influence in the " Election of the House of Commons, and which, in " its Progress, threatens to usurp the Sovereignty of " the Country, to the equal Danger of the King, of " the Lords, and of the Commons" — Again, " The " Operation of the first Species of Patronage is direct, and subject to positive Proof: Eighty-four " Individuals do, by their own immediate Authority, " send One hundred and Fifty-seven of your Honourable Members to Parliament; and this your Petitioners are ready, if the Fact be disputed, to prove, " and to name the Members and the Patrons — The " second Species of Patronage cannot be shewn with " equal Accuracy, though it is felt with equal Force ‘ — Your Petitioners are convinced, that, in Addition u to the One hundred and Fifty-seven Honourable M Members above-mentioned, One hundred and Fifty more, making in the whole Three Hundred and Seven, are returned to your Honourable House, not " by the collected Voice of those whom they appear " to represent, but by the Recommendation of Seventy " powerful Individuals, added to the Eighty-four " above-mentioned, and making the Total Number " of Patrons altogether only One hundred and Fiftyfour, who return a decided Majority of your Honourable House. — If your Honourable House will accept " as Evidence the common Report and general fieUef of the Counties, Cities, and Boroughs, which " return the Members alluded to, your Petitioners are " ready to name them, and to prove the Fact; or, if " the Members in Question can be made Parties to " the Inquiry, your Petitioners will name them, and " be governed by the Testimony which they themselves Hshall publicly give:" If, then, the Allegations here recited be true — and the Petitioner has been credibly informed, they were not so much as questioned by any Member of the House, when placed on its Journals — he hopes he may, without giving Offence to the House (all Intention of which he sincerely disclaims, as on this solemn Occasion he should think such Conduct highly indecent and represensible) he hopes, he says, he may ask. Where are to be found the Three distinct, independent, and balancing Powers of the English Constitution ? — Monarchy, and Aristocracy, indeed, hold their respective Places, undiminished in Splendour, and apparently possessing their Constitutional Shares in the Government; but, when the Petitioner looks for Democracy, when he seeks the awfully-majestic Representative Body of this great Nation emphatically stiled, " The Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled," presumed to emanate from, and to be identified with, the great Mass of the People, — touched by their every Grievance and sympathizing in all their natural and honourable Feelings, does he find such a Representative Body to exist? Do not the Journals of the House, on the contrary, inform him, that a decided Majority of the House are returned, " not by the collected Voice of those whom " they appear to represent," but under the private Patronage, or by the immediate Authority, of One hundred and Fifty-four Individuals? If these alarming Allegations be true — if One hundred and Fifty-four Persons can, and actually do, at their own independent Will and Pleasure, to the grievous Wrong of the People, seat in the House a Majority of its Members, must not those Persons, of course, have its Determinations at Command ? and will not such a State of Things amount to the Demonstration of a Fact, which, keenly as it may be felt by the Petitioner, rather than express, he will leave to be inferred by the House: If these Vol.31.

afflicting Allegations be true, has there not crept into the Government, through an insensible Decay which needs to be repaired, an alarming, a portentous Power, a mighty irresistible Something, distinct from, and paramount to, all the Constitutional Estates of the Realm ? — a Power of a Character utterly unknown to our Constitution, and abhorrent to the Principles of our Government; — a Power for which Political Writers have, indeed, an appropriate Appellation; but one so odious, that the Petitioner, out of Respect to the House, and from his Feelings of Reverence for the genuine Constitution of his Country, will forbear to express: And, if such a dreadful Power have, in the Nature of a Disease, grown out of the gradually increasing Decay of popular Representation; and have at its Disposal the Public Purse and consequently dependent on its Will the Supplies to the Executive Magistrate, can even His Majesty be supposed to be beyond the Reach of its overbearing Sway ? — must not the Peerage be eclipsed by the One hundred and Fifty-four ? — and all the just Ends of Representation to the People be defeated, while their every Interest shall be submitted to the Power of Men, in whose Election or Appointment they, have neither Share, Controul, nor Influence?. And if it be likewise true, as farther stated in the aforesaid Petition of the 6th of May 1793, and of which the then Petitioners tendered " legal Evidence, that Forty Peers, in Defiance of your Resolutions, have possessed themselves of so many " Burgage Tenures, and obtained such an absolute " and uncontrouled Command in very many small " Boroughs in the Kingdom, as to be enabled, by their " own positive Authority, to return Eighty-one of " your Honourable Members;" and that the said then Petitioners also had the most reasonable Grounds to " suspect" (which Grounds of Suspicion they declared themselves ready to shew at the Bar of the House) " that no less than One hundred and Fifty of your " Honourable Members owe their Elections entirely " to the Interference of Peers" — if these Things be true, then the Petitioner humbly conceives, while Alarms are so industriously propagated of Attempts and Conspirings against the Constitution, that Attempts such as these, Conspirings so daring and so criminal, Strokes so sweeping, to remove the Pillars of the Fabric, ought not to pass without a full and rigid Investigation; and the more so, as the Truth or the Falsehood of the Allegations can so easily be ascertained by the House: Lord Chancellor Somers, as every Member of the House must know, in a Treatise on Government, has truly said, that " Treason is a betraying of " the State; and the greatest and highest Treason is " that which is committed against the Constitution." If, then, the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled, be a Part, a vital, a sacred Part of the Constitution; — if it be only on the Principle of Representation that the House can be entitled to that Appellation; — if sitting in the House constitutionally implies Popular Election; — and if a Loss to the People, either by Encroachment or otherwise, of a Majority of the Seats in the House, have actually taken place, as so strongly set forth without Denial or Question in the Petition on the Journals to which the present Petitioner now refers; then he humbly presumes it will follow as a necessary Conclusion, that the Constitution has indeed received a deep and deadly Wound. There may not have been Treason.in the Intention; but no Man can deny, that he, who more or less destroys the Essence of the House of Commons, betrays the State. Should any Men beneath the Degree of Baron, even Meml>ers of the House, usurp, but for a Day, Seats among the Peers, arrogating to themselves the Functions of Lords of Parliament, would not Astonishment and Indignation strike every Breast ? and would not the Constitution itself shake to its Centre, if Possession could be held of such Seats, to pass as Private
