Property from Hand to Hand ? — or if any Privy Councillor should dare to step with the King into his Throne on the Meeting of Parliament, and hidden Fetters should also be discovered under the Royal Robe, would not a Cry of " Treason " burst from every Tongue? — Are there, then, the Petitioner humbly asks the House, only Two Estates of the Realm which are to be hedged in and secured by a sacred Inviolability; while the Third, like a neglected Common, is to have its Fences trampled under Foot, and to become the Spoil of every lawless Trespasser? — No; the House will doubtless awaken to the Necessity of expelling Invaders, and guarding against future Encroachment. And it is for the House seriously to consider, whether reflecting Men can believe, that either of the Two Bills now pending would ever have seen the Light, had not their Movers been encouraged to such Attacks on the Liberties of the People, from the Traces of Popular Representation in the House being so nearly worn out and obliterated. As these Bills have been ushered in, like other inauspicious Acts of their Authors, with dark Insinuations of Criminality against Men known to profess themselves the Advocates for a Reform in the House, and such insinuated Criminality of these Men is made the indecent, the monstrous Pretext for uprooting the Freedom of all Men, it may not be unworthy of the House to bestow a few Moments of their Attention on some Circumstances respecting those who come within the general Description of Friends to Parliamentary Reform; Men who, although differing in Opinion on subordinate Points, are agreed in that One Object from which the Appellation has been given them. The Reformers are charged with Discontent: So far from denying this Charge, they have, for the last Fifteen Years, from Time to Time, come to the House to make known this Discontent, to shew its Cause, and to pray for the Removal of both Cause and Effect: If they are not yet disburdened of their Grief, it is because the House hath not yet thought proper even to enquire into the Justness of their Complaint. The Reformers are accused of conspiring to overthrow the Constitution: False and extravagant as is this Accusation, they may not be surprized at it; and for the following Reasons: l st, Because, by their Exertions to bring to Light the Conspirings of other Men against the Constitution, the Truth was Daily becoming manifest to the Nation: — 2dly, Because Men, interested in upholding the Corruptions of the State, which caused the Discontent complained of, had in their Hands the Annual Application and Expenditure of Seventeen Millions of Public Money; and, as appears to the Petitioner, without being under any sufficient Controul: — 3dly, Because the said Men had also in their Hands every other Means which the Government and Patronage of a great Empire can be supposed to afford for influencing the Public Opinion; and, if capable of so atrocious a Crime, of spreading through the Land false Alarms and Delusions, which not even Truth could resist or oppose without the Aid of Time: — And, lastly, Because the very Nature of the Case required that, in order to divert the Public Attention from those Corruptions and Decays in the very Frame of the Government, and those Conspirings against the Constitution which the Reformers were so successfully exposing, they themselves should be charged with the Crime, and their Cause, if possible* brought into Disrepute — Fraud, Panic, and Delusion, have had their Day; but the Petitioner trusts in Time, as well as in the Wisdom of the House, and the Discernment of an English People, for a true Judgment being passed between the Reformers and their Opponents: The House cannot be ignorant that, with particular Reference to the pretended Plots of the Reformers, and to the State of these Men's Minds — certainly not in a State of unfeeling Apathy, but suffering under a quick Sense of unredressed Wrongs — and as

a special Reason for not administering that Political Medicine, a Parliamentary Reform, it has by their Opponents been urged that the Times are too Feverish, and yet they now behold Bills proposed by their Opponents which, if the People of England are not become, Politically speaking, a Nation of Dead Carcases, must spread a Flame through the Land. If, in an Inflammatory State of the natural Body, it were to be assigned as a Reason for withholding a Powerful Febrifuge, that the Fever ran too high, and at the same Time the Essence of whatever was most inflammatory and irritating were thrown in, to work up the Fever into a Phrenzy, would not the House think that a Physician, so acting, were either a Madman or a Murderer? The House will recollect at what Period it was, that the Proceedings of the Reformers first gave Ministers serious Disturbance of Mind, and, as all the subsequent Matters must be fresh in its Memory, the Petitioner will not do more than just touch on the most prominent Objects of Attention; namely, the Activity of the Reformers, and the Hopes of Success with which they were animated; the Censures they hereupon incurred, the Imputations thrown out against them, the Spies placed around them, the Seizure of Papers containing all their Plans of Operation, the Imprisonment of conspicuous Persons, their Indictment for High Treason; and, after a considerable Period of most anxious Suspence to the Nation, the Trials that ensued. — And what at last appeared? Why, it appeared, that mixed with the Proceedings of some of these Men, in their great and virtuous Cause, there were on the Part of Individuals Marks of Indiscretion, Rashness, and Folly; for they were Men; and some of them without the Advantages of Education; — It also appeared, that the Fervours of some had even, in the Judgment of Juries, hurried them into Expressions deemed seditious. But Sedition, the Petitioner begs Leave to observe to the House, is an undefined, and perhaps undefinable Crime; an Error of that peculiar Nature, that, in bad Times, the base and the servile are perhaps less likely to fall into it, than those who feel a generous Indignation at their Country's Wrongs. A Sidney and a Russell were accounted seditious, when a Jefferies was the Pattern of Loyalty — The only Person whom the Petitioner recollects to have been convicted of Treason (except a Man whom he believes was afterwards pardoned) was an acknowledged Spy, and under Circumstances that may account for his Conduct in the Line of his Vocation; a Man, if his own Account of himself may be credited, tinctured with Fanaticism, if not with Insanity — But the Petitioner, with much Deference, asks again, What, after all the agitating Alarms, after all the successful Diligence of Government in securing Persons and Papers, and after Trials, such as never before oppressed the Bench and the Bar with the Labours of Investigation, what has been brought to Light respecting the Reformers, that it imports the Nation to know ? — The Petitioner will tell the House what has been brought to Light. This has been brought to Light: — That the Constitution has already been grievously injured and undermined; and that nothing but the Measures which the Reformers point out, and have been pursuing — Measures which they have again and again pressed upon the Attention of the Public, and of the House, can avert its speedy Destruction — And the Petitioner, with great Humility, will also beg Leave to inform the House what has not been brought to Light concerning the Reformers: In all this sifting of their Actions, and even of their very Thoughts, there was not discovered the smallest Ground for charging them with criminally conspiring to seize on One hundred and Fifty Seats in the House, and sell them to Peers; or with any Attempt at transferring a decided Majority of those Seats to One hundred and Fifty-four Men, to be held and inherited as Private Property; giving the Possessors of those Seats such irresponsible

A Petition of the thereunder-signed Inhabitants of Petition the City of Bath, was also presented to the House, *

and read; Setting forth, That a Bill is now before the preventing

House, intituled, An Act for the more effectually Seditious preventing seditious Meetings and Assemblies, which appears to be entirely subversive of the well known Saiet^of* ancient Liberty of the Subject, as declared and recog- His Majesty's nized in the Filth Article of the Bill of Rights: That, Person,&c. when both Houses of Parliament made a solemn Tender of the Crown to their Highnesses the Prince and Princess of Orange, and their Successors, they did claim, demand, and insist upon, the Right of the

People to petition, and therefore to meet and assem-

ble, without Restraint, for that Purpose, as their undoubted Right and Liberty; and the Petitioners cannot see, without extreme Anxiety, a Bill before the House, which threatens to deprive them of this acknowledged and invaluable Right: That the Petitioners, under the united Impressions of Horror and Indignation, feel and lament the daring Outrage against His Majesty's Royal Person in Flis Passage to Parliament, on the Opening of the Session; but they have a Consolation in reflecting, that the Laws now in being have made ample Provision for the due and condign Punishment of all such audacious Offences:

That the Petitioners, with these Sentiments, humbly beg Leave to represent to the House, that they consider a Bill, now likewise depending, intituled, An Act for the Safety of His Majesty's Person and Government against treasonable and seditious Practices and Attempts, as not only unnecessary, from the Existence of the present Laws for the Punishment of such Attempts and Practices, but, without affording any additional Security to His Majesty's Person or Government, as oppressing the Subject with Punishments hitherto unknown in the System of English Jurisprudence, for ambiguous and undefined Crimes and Misdemeanors, which they conceive to be also inconsistent with the Tenth Article of the Bill of Rights: That the Petitioners, from these Considerations, do most humbly and most earnestly implore the House to reject the said Bills, and to continue to them those Rights and Liberties which were claimed, demanded, and insisted upon, and which, they trust, will be transmitted, without Infringement or Restriction, to their latest Posterity.

Resolved, That the Bill be committed to Mr. Thomas coairuUlt Stanley, Mr. Blackburne, &c.: And they are to meet this Afternoon, at Five of the Clock, in the Speaker's Chamber.

The House, according to Order, resolved itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the Bill for the more effectually preventing seditious Meetings and Assemblies.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Mr. Sargent took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Mr. Sargent reported from the Committee, That they had gone through the Bill, and made several Amendments thereunto; which they had directed him to report, when the House will please to receive the same.

Ordered, That the Report be now received.

Mr. Sargent accordingly reported from the said Committee, the Amendments which the Committee had made to the Bill, and which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Bill, with the Amendments, in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Report was read.

Ordered, That the said Report be taken into further Consideration upon Tuesday Morning next.

Ordered, That such a Number of Copies of the said Bill, as amended by the Committee, be printed, as shall be sufficient for the Use of the Members of the House.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, made in the Thirty-fourth Year of His present Majesty's Reign, for making a Navigable Canal from the River Rennet, at or near the Town of Newbury, in the County of Berks, to the River Avon, at or near the City of Bath, and also certain Navigable Cuts therein described, was read: Then,

Mr. John Rennie, an Engineer, being examined, said.

That some Progress has been made in the said Works, and that it appears, by Surveys lately made, that if the Line of the Canal was varied in certain Parts in the County of Wilts, namely, from a certain Place between Upper and Lower Foxhanger, in the Parish of Rowd, by Seend and Semington, to Lady Dozen Farm, near Trow-

bridge, and from Wolf hall Lane, leading to Wolf hall Farm, to Brintslade House, and from a Close in the Parish

of Saint John the Baptist, in Devizes, to a Road leading from Potshot to Rowd, and from a Piece of Land near Widbrook, in the Parish of Bradford, to a Road adjoining Clay Farm House, in the same Parish, and from the South Side of the River Avon, a little above Avon Cliff Mills, in the Parishes of Westwood and Bradford, to the North Side of the said River, a little below the said Mills, and from the East Side of the said River near Stoke Bridge, in the said Parish of Bradford, to the West Side of the said River, in the Parish of Moncklon Coombe, in the County of Somerset, the Line of the said Canal will be much shortened, and be more convenient to the Public, a better Junction with the Wiltshire and Berkshire Canal will be formed, a Tunnel of great Length avoided, a very material Saving of Water in the Lockage at Devizes will be made, a considerable Quantity of deep Cutting near Widbrook saved, better Situations for crossing the River Avon will be obtained, and an Aqueduct and expensive Embankment across the Mitford Valley avoided; which Variations will pass over a smaller Quantity of Land, and be executed at less Expence, and be more convenient to the Public than the present Line of the Canal. — That the making a Branch from such varied Line between Foxhanger and Lady Down Farm to Trowbridge, with a Bason at the End thereof, would be of great Advantage to the said Town and Neighbourhood, and of Public Utility: — And that it would tend to the better carrying the Purposes of the said Act into Execution, if some of the Powers and Provisions thereof were altered and amended.

A Petition of the Court of Directors of the East India Company was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have beheld, with Horror, the late daring Attempt on the sacred Person of His Majesty, at the Moment when he was proceeding to exercise a Prerogative of the Crown most dear to Britons, that of assembling the Representatives of the People: Whatever may have been the Circumstances that immediately led to this wicked Attempt upon His Majesty and the Constitution of this Country, the Petitioners cannot but acknowledge, with deep Concern, that it appears to them to derive its Origin from dangerous Doctrines, calculated to corrupt the Public Mind, and to disturb the Peace of the Country: Doctrines which have been disseminated with most criminal Industry by seditious Persons, disaffected to His Majesty and the happy Constitution under which we live: That the Petitioners beg Leave to express their Detestation of all Meetings for such destructive Purposes, and their confident Reliance, that the House will, in the Bill now before them, adopt such Measures for the Prevention of Assemblies of that Nature, and for the Preservation of the Public Peace of the Country, as in their Wisdom they shall see fit.

A Petition of the Noblemen, Gentlemen, Clergy, Freeholders, and Inhabitants, of the County of Northumberland, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have learnt, with inexpressible Alarm, that a Bill hath been brought into the House, intituled, An Act for the more effectually preventing seditious Meetings and Assemblies; the Provisions of which Bill are, in the humble Apprehension of the Petitioners, destructive of the Constitution, and subversive of their ancient, true, and undoubted Rights and Liberties: That the Laws of England are the Birthright of the People thereof; that the Right of Public Discussion, and petitioning for the Redress of Grievances, is their unalienable Privilege, confirmed to them by divers Statutes of this Realm; and that any Attempt to restrain the People, in the Constitutional Exercise of this their undoubted Franchise, has a Tendency to overthrow the Fundamental Laws of the Kingdom, and to alienate the Affections of the People from the established Government: That the Petitioners, on the Part of the People of England, solemnly disowning the Charge of Disloyalty which the said Bill imputes to them, do humbly represent, that, in their Judgment, the Laws in being are sufficient, if duly executed, for the Preservation of the Public Peace, and that, if they were not, it is inconsistent with the Justice of the House, that, for the Transgressions of a Few, the Whole should be disfranchised: And therefore praying the House, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law. The Petitioners beg Leave further to Represent to the House, that the Bill now depending in the House, intituled, An Act for the Safety and Preservation of His Majesty's Person and Government against treasonable and seditious Practices and Attempts, hath created great Disquietude and Alarm in the Minds of the Petitioners: That the Petitioners conceive the said Bill to be unnecessary, the old Laws of this Realm having, for Centuries past, been found fully adequate to all the Exigencies of the State, and any occasional

A. 1795.

Deviation from the same, by the Introduction of newfangled Treasons, having proved no less dangerous to the Safety of the Sovereign than fatal to the Liberties of the Subject: That the vague and ambiguous Terms in which the Offences created by the said Bill are described, render the Lives and Liberties of the People of England precarious and insecure, so that no Man will know how he ought to behave himself, to do, speak, or say, for Doubt of such Pains of Treason: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law, and that it may be accorded, that, in no Time to come, any Treason be judged otherwise than was ordained by the Statute of King Edward the Third.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, Merchants, Tradesmen, and other Inhabitants of Liverpool, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That with a due Sense of the Value of that excellent Constitution under which the said Town, and the Kingdom at large, have so long flourished, the Petitioners humbly represent to the House, as the Guardians of their inestimable Rights and Liberties, the full Assurance they have that those, to whose Wisdom these Rights and Liberties are entrusted, will, in Conjunction with the good and loyal People of this Land, use their best Endeavours to protect, maintain, and support our gracious King and that glorious Constitution: That the Petitioners cannot but seriously la-

ment the daring Outrage which some misguided People, who must have been deluded by the Arts of'factious, desperate, and designing Men, have been led to commit against the Life of our most gracious Sovereign, and feel with Anxiety the consequent impending Danger to which our happy Form of Government in Church and State is, by such treasonable and seditious Practices, exposed — Under these Impressions, the Petitioners cannot but approve of the Principle of the Two Bills now before the House, for the Safety and Preservation of His Majesty's Person and Government; and for the more effectually preventing seditious Meetings and Assemblies; and beg to express their Hope and firm Reliance, that the Wisdom of Parliament will be able to provide such Remedies as may be adequate to prevent these growing Evils: And therefore praying, That these Bills may pass into a Law, subject to such Regulations and Amendments as shall seem expedient to the Parliament of Great Britain.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Bailiffs, and Common Councilmen, of the Town of Liverpool, in the County of Lancaster, in special Council assembled, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, deeply affected with the glaring and wicked Outrage lately offered to our most gracious King, by misguided and deluded Persons, lament, with still increasing Concern, that there should appear such a regular and systematic Connection between the seditious Societies, now in Existence, and the Perpetrators of this horrid Crime, so as to leave very little Room for Doubt that the Blow, aimed at our beloved Sovereign, was, in His Person, intended as a virtual Attack upon our glorious Constitution: And, thoroughly persuaded of the superior Excellence of the British Constitution above that of any other Nation, the Petitioners fully approve, of the Principles of the Two Bills, now depending in Parliament, for the Safety and Preservation of His Majesty's Person and Government; and for the more effectually preventing seditious Meetings and Assemblies; as the best and most efficacious Means for checking the Progress of the nefarious Tenets and Doctrines now spread abroad amongst us, so totally subversive of good Order, and for putting a Stop to those atrocious Acts, so immediately calculated to sap the Foundation of our happy Constitution and Government, in Church and State: And therefore prayng. A Petition of the thereunder-signed Gentlemen, Merchants, Bankers, Tradesmen, and other Inhabitants, of the Town of Liverpool, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners feel themselves peculiarly called upon, at this important Crisis, humbly to express to the House their Anxiety respecting certain Bills now depending in Parliament; one of which is intituled, An Act for the more effectual preventing seditious Meetings and Assemblies, and the other, An Act for the Safety and Preservation of His Majesty's Person and Government against treasonable and seditious Practices: That, by the Purport of the first-mentioned Bill, it appears to the Petitioners that the Constitutional Right of the Subjects of this Realm to meet and consult together on their Common Grievances, and to petition the Legislature for Redress, is restrained and impeded by Difficulties, which are evidently inconsistent with its free and proper Exercise — That new and arbitrary Powers, affecting the Lives and Safety of the Subject, are proposed to be vested in Individuals, who are expressly discharged from all Responsibility — That an Englishmen is to be subjected to Capital Punishment without the Judgment of his Peers; and that the whole Bill bears rather the Character of Military Law than of a Civil Regulation: That, by the last mentioned Bill, new Treasons are created that subvert the established Law on that Subject, which has subsisted, the equal Bulwark of the Sovereign and of the People, for upwards of Four hundred Years — That, contrary to the Spirit of the Constitution, the Criminal Intention, which may be falsely imputed, is punishable instead of the Overt Act, which may be proved — That the Crime of Sedition, which, by the existing Laws, already subjects the Offender to Fine and Imprisonment, is converted into Treason; and those Popular Strictures on Public Men and Public Measures, which are the Criterion and Essence of a free Government, are liable to be misconstrued into Sedition, and are subjected, in the Second Instance, to a Species of Punishment at which Humanity recoils: That, under the Influence of those serious Impressions, occasioned by the sudden Adoption of Measures so dangerous in their Consequences, the Petitioners cannot conceal from the House the Apprehensions by which they are actuated; Apprehensions which are greatly increased by an avowed Intention, on the Part of His Majesty's Ministers, to support in the Country a Military Force, contrary to the Practice of our Ancestors and the Spirit of the Constitution, and still more by Insinuations, from Men high in Office, respecting the Destination of that Force, tending to create Dissensions amongst His Majesty's Subjects, and unnecessarily adverting to Circumstances which cannot be too much deprecated — Impelled by these serious Considerations, and conceiving that the existing Laws of the Country, if properly carried into Effect, are sufficient for the Purposes professed to be intended tty the said Bill, the Petitioners humbly entreat the House, That the said Bills, or such of them as may be yet depending in the House, may not pass into Laws.

A Petition of the Mayor, Bailiffs, and Burgesses, of Petitions in the Borough of Newcastle-under-Lyme, in the County fa. Hr of tL® of Stafford, in Common Council assembled, was also BlU - pre‘

presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That it is with the deepest Concern the Petitioners are persuaded, as well from Daily Observation as from the Reports of the Two Houses of Parliament, during the last Session, that there has been, and still exists, an internal and traitorous Conspiracy, threatening the vital Interests of these Realms: A Conspiracy the more formidable, as its Advances have been systematical and regular; branching out into various Classes and Societies, united by secret League and Correspondence, and acting in Concert for the more effectual Propagation of the same seditious Principles: By these Schools and Seminaries of Disloyalty, more dangerous from the Union than the Number of their Members, who exert, in the Prosecution of their Designs, a Zeal and Activity which might be creditable in a better Cause, those inflammatory Writings have been lately issued, and those intemperate Harangues at Public Meetings been encouraged, which, if not restrained by the Wisdom of Parliament, the Petitioners apprehend may go well nigh the Ruin of our Constitution, both in Church and State: That the Petitioners are the more convinced of the imminent Danger of such Societies, from attending to the intimate and visible Connection between the Tendency of their Principles and the late atrocious and desperate Attack upon the Person of their most gracious Sovereign: Feeling, moreover, that the Prevention of Crimes is much more to be wished for than the Punishment of Offenders, the Petitioners observe, with Satisfaction, that the Vigilance of Parliament is wisely occupied in providing against these extensive and complicated Dangers, by the salutary Precautions of the Bill now pending for preventing seditious Meetings and Assemblies: In the Adoption of such timely and wise Precautions, the Petitioners are convinced that there is no essential Departure from the Spirit of the Constitution, or the Usage of our Ancestors; they recognize in it that Saving Wisdom which, by an Alteration of Parts, maintains Consistency in the Whole, and deviates from Forms to preserve Essentials; they reject, with Indignation, that narrow-minded Policy, which, in Times pregnant with Alarm, would refuse to the Executive Power additional temporary Sanctions and Securities, proportionate to the Exigency of the Danger; they trust that the Bill, now proposed to the Consideration of the House, a Bill which secures to the good Citizen the Exercise of his legal Rights, whilst it is a Curb upon the disloyal and seditious Subject, will be found adequate, as they are persuaded it is necessary, for the Remedy of the Evil: They pray therefore, That it may pass into a Law.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Common Council, Gentlemen, Clergy, Tradesmen, and other loyal Inhabitants, of the ancient City of Chester, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That convinced of the inestimable Value of that Constitution under which we have so long enjoyed the greatest Blessings, the Petitioners approach the House, confident of its Wisdom, Justice, and Firmness, to protect their Rights and Liberties: The Petitioners lament, in common with all well-disposed Subjects, the Necessity of applying the most effectual Means to prevent the insidious Designs, and suppress the violent

Further, the Petitioners are sensibly affected with the general Distress which arises from the Scarcity and high Price of Corn and other Provisions, whereby the Middle Ranks of Society are deprived of the rational Comforts of Life, and the Body of the People suffers the real Misery of actual Want: In the present unfortunate War alone can be found the Origin of such a dreadful Calamity, which the Continuance of the War must not only prolong, but aggravate in a Degree which, the Petitioners apprehend, cannot much longer be supported; they therefore further petition the House to put a Period to this Calamity, in bringing about a speedy Peace by those Means which the Constitution has lodged in its Hands, in order to be employed upon an Emergency like the present.

A Petition of the thereunder-signed Inhabitants of Petition the County of Hants, was also presented to the House, against the and read; Setting forth, That a Bill has been brought into the House, subversive of the Liberties which ^ltloU3 the People of this Kingdom, at the Period when ings; and for they transferred the Crown of England to the illustri- the Safety of ous family at present upon the Throne, did claim, pe^n^lT* demand, and insist upon, as their true, ancient, and indubitable Rights; and the said Bill is intituled, An Act for the more effectually preventing seditious Meetings and Assemblies: That the only Mode by which the Petitioners and the People of Great Britain can express their Sentiments, to make their Grievances known, is by meeting together either to instruct their Representatives, to petition Parliament, or to address the King; this is their Privilege, and subject to the existing Laws, which have already provided against the Abuse of it, the Petitioners do, in the Language of their Forefathers, claim, demand, and insist upon, the Exercise of it, as their true, ancient, and established Right: The Allowance and Encouragement of free, honest, and open Discussion of all Matters Political and Judicial, while it has afforded the surest Controul upon the Encroachments of the Executive Government, has tended most effectually to secure the upright Administration of Justice: The House is humbly reminded, that the Right of the People to such Meetings is the best Security they possess against the Abuse of Power: If they, who are delegated to defend their Liberties, basely or corruptly betray them; if they, who are sent to watch over Ministers, become their Accomplices, what may the People do, if they may not remonstrate? By the Bill now depending no Meeting can be called except with the Knowledge of a Magistrate, whose Presence is made necessary, not merely for the Preservation of the Peace, but for the Purpose of controuling the Sentiments to be uttered; he is constituted sole Judge of the Manner in which a Grievance may be stated, ora Right asserted; to differ with him in Political Opinion is made a Breach of the Peace; to maintain that Opinion is made a Riot, and to persist in it is to incur the Horrors of Military Execution: The Petitioners further beg Leave to call the Attention of the House to a Bill now depending, intituled, An Act for the Safety and Preservation of His Majesty's Person and Government against treasonable and seditious Practices and Attempts; they humbly represent, that this Bill contains an arbitrary Accumulation of Treasons, calculated to harrass and oppress the Subject, without adding any Security to the Person of His Majesty; that it also describes the Misdemeanor, at which another of its Clauses is pointed, with such studied

A Petition of the Lord Provost, Magistrates, and Common Council of the City of Glasgow, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, for several Years past, the Petitioners have seen, with the deepest Concern, a certain Description of Men endeavouring to diffuse Opinions, and inculcate Doctrines, totally repugnant to the Principles of our happy Constitution; and it is to those Opinions and Doctrines that the Petitioners must ascribe that Spirit of Sedition and Tumult which has manifested itself upon many Occasions, and has recently proceeded to the extreme and unwarrantable Length of disturbing the Deliberations of Parliament, and endangering the Life of our most Gracious Sovereign: The Petitioners, therefore humbly request, That the House may be pleased speedily to adopt such Measures as they, in their Wisdom, shall think proper for the more effectual Security of His Majesty's Person and Government, and for preventing in future all seditions Meetings and Assemblies, which, the Petitioners conceive, cannot be better accomplished than by passing into Laws the Two Bills lately brought into Parliament for these Purposes.

A Petition of the Dean of Guild, and the Merchants House of Glasgow, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners have observed, with the deepest Concern, the great Pains which have been taken to disseminate Doctrines through the Country, tending to infuse Discontent, and stir up Sedition in the Minds of the People, which have, at length, operated so strongly, as to have inflamed a lawless and unprincipled Mob to the Commission of the most daring Acts of Violence: The Petitioners are humbly of Opinion, that the Two Bills, now under the Consideration of Parliament, for the better securing His Majesty's Person and Government; and for more effectually preventing all seditious Meetings and Assemblies; are well calculated to answer the Ends proposed, and appear, under the present Circumstances, to be indispensably necessary for the Peace and Happiness of these Kingdoms: And therefore praying, That the House will steadily follow out such Measures as are not only calculated to secure the Life of our most gracious Sovereign from the Attacks of the wicked and misguided, but to protect the Constitution from the insidious Attacks of seditious and discontented Persons, and thereby enable us to transmit the invaluable Blessings, we at present enjoy, to our Posterity.

A Petition of the Inhabitants of the City of York, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the superior Rank and Importance of Great Britain, in the Scale of the Nations of the World, have depended upon the superior Excellence of her Political Constitution, the Spirit of which recognizes a due and equable Balance between the legal Prerogatives of the King and the Rights and Liberties of the Subject, which Balance can only be maintained by the Continuance of free, open, frequent, and unrestrained Communications between the People and the Legislative Body; and such Communications were considered, at. the iEra of the glorious Resolution in 1(588, as a Part of that wise and happy System Vol. 51.

which placed the illustrious House of Bi'unswick upon the Throne of these Realms, as appears by a distinct Substantive Clause in the Bill of Rights: That Two Bills, now depending in Parliament, the one intituled,

An Act for the Safety and Preservation of His Majesty's Person and Government against treasonable and seditious Practices and Attempts, and the other,

An Act for the more effectually preventing seditious Meetings and Assemblies, are, in their Spirit and Tendency, repugnant to that System, and subversive of the true Principles of that Resolution, by creating new and accumulated Treasons, and by subjecting free Deliberation upon Laws or Grievances to Checks and Control, as unprecedented as they are incompatible with fair Discussion and the Rights of private Judgment, and thereby alienating the Affection of the People from the Constitution, and lessening their Respect for the Laws: That the Laws now in Forpe are fully adequate to the Security of His Majesty's Person, and sufficient to restrain or punish the improper Use or licentious Abuse of the Constitutional Right of the People to prefer their Petitions, or present their Remonstrances, to all or any of the Branches of the Legislature: And therefore praying, That the said Bills may not pass into Laws.

Then the Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, Inhabitants of the Ward of Castle Baynard, was brought up, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners, highly sensible of the Happiness they enjoy under the Government of our most Gracious Sovereign, and possessing the utmost Abhorrence of the late daring Outrage committed against His Majesty's sacred Person, and being of Opinion that such Outrages are countenanced and encouraged by sundry treasonable and seditious Methods now in Practice to entlame the Minds of the People, and particularly by seditious Meetings and Assemblies held for that Purpose, do think it their Duty to express their Confidence in the Wisdom of Parliament, That such Laws will be speedily enacted as will tend effectually to suppress such Meetings and Assemblies, and to preserve to the Nation a Continuance of the Blessings enjoyed under our present glorious Constitution.

A Petition of the thereunder-signed Merchants, Traders, and Inhabitants, of the Town and County of Poole, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners hold in the utmost Abhorrence the late atrocious Attempt on the Person of His Majesty: That, feeling an anxious Care for our Liberties, they are, notwithstanding, alarmed at seeing Two Bills, intituled, An Act for the better Preservation of His Majesty's Person, &c.; and, An Act for preventing seditious Meetings and Assemblies, brought into the House, as they appear to the Petitioners inconsistent with the Principles of our Constitution, and, if passed into Laws, will destroy one of our best Rights, " A free Communication of Thoughts and Opinions:" That this Right has been always a Securky to us against the Encroachments of Power,

A Petition of the Weavers and other Inhabitants of Spitalfields, Bethnal Green, and its Environs, was likewise presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, from the melancholy Effects of a most unfortunate and deplorable War, and from the fearful Apprehensions operating in every serious Mind for the Consequences of still greater Distresses likely to ensue if the present Bills, intituled, A Bill for foe Safety of His Majesty's Person and Government against treasonable and seditious Practices and Attempts; and, A Bill for the more effectually preventing seditious Meetings and Assemblies, should pass into Laws; which Bills, being fabricated to constitute new Offences, and to award the Punishments of Death and Transportation on Conviction of such newly-created Offences, the Petitioners are filled with foe deepest Concern and Anxiety, and can only look up for Consolation and Relief to the Public Spirit and Philanthropy of foe House: The Petitioners beg Leave to declare that, though their Station in Life is confined to the Sphere of Manual Labour, and their Means of Daily Support depend entire^ upon foe Sweat of foeir Brow, yet they feel an

equal Degree of Sympathy for the afflicted, and equal Zeal for the Honour ana Felicity of their Superiors, and as sincerely and ardently long for the Prosperity and Peace of Great Britain as the richest of her Peers: The Appellation of Englishmen surely warrants their Supplication to the House, where every Man's Right should have a steady Watchman and Protector in every Member of it — In this earnest Manner, under the present Circumstances, while they experience every Inconvenience arising from an unexampled high Price of every Necessary of Life, and under as unparalleled a Scarcity of Employ, neither of which Calamities they are sensible of being accessary in occasioning, and both which Evils, as well as the Execrations of Millions against the new Operations which lurk in the Bills above-mentioned, they firmly believe will cease, if foe House will condescend to the Prayer of their !

united Petition, which is, That the said Bills be not,

passed into Laws, and that Peace be restored on fair and honourable Terms. !

Low Wines or Spirits; accordingly, the Petitioners began Business, and entered into Contracts for the Delivery of large Quantities of Spirits at specified Periods, which, as the Law presently stands, they reckoned themselves well warranted to do; nor had they any Reason to suspect, that an Act, which was productive to the Revenue, and, in the distilling of Spirits from Melasses, attended with no Injury to any Description of People, would soon be repealed; and that the Petitioner, Mr. , only began to

distil about a Week ago, nevertheless he was under the Necessity of paying the Duties since the 10th of October last, in Terms of the Statute: That no Part of the said Act, in as far as it relates to the distilling of Spirits from Melasses, has been repealed hitherto, but the Petitioners understand, that there is a Bill now depending before the House, which, if passed into a Law, will not only put an End to their Trade, but must have the Effect of involving them and their Families in Poverty and Ruin, unless Provision is made in it for fair Indemnification, similar to that introduced in the Distillery Prohibition Bill passed in June last; that, if the Object of the Bill is to preserve Melasses for Food, the Petitioners arc ready to prove, that the People of Scotland do not use Melasses in that Way; the Bill therefore, while it will certainly be very prejudicial to the Revenue, is not likely to be productive of any real Advantage to the Country: If, however, the Petitioners are prohibited from carrying on their Business, they surely have a Claim to Reimbursement of the Duties they have paid, and an adequate Compensation for the Expence they have been led into under the existing Laws of the Land; besides, as their Stock will become an Article of no general Use in Scotland, they will be under the Necessity of exporting it, at a very great Loss, to the only Market for its Consumption — Under these Circumstances, and as the Petitioners are the only People in Scotland who distil Spirits from Melasses, and that only to the Extent of about Eleven Puncheons of Melasses in a Week, they trust, that, before the proposed Bill is allowed to take Eft'ect, reasonable Time will be given to enable them to work oft' their Stock on Hand, and that ample Provision will be made for their Indemnification in other Respects: And therefore praying, That, in Case it shall appear a proper Measure to the House, to prohibit Distillation from Melasses, a reasonable Time may be allowed them, not less than Three Months, to work off their present Stock, or, at any Rate, that Provision may be made, in the Bill, for allowing the Petitioners a fair Indemnification for the Loss to which they must be exposed, as Individuals, from a Measure of general Benefit to the Country, or that the House will grant the Petitioners such other Relief in the Premises as to them shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the said Committee.

A Petition of the Merchants, Manufacturers, Traders, and other Inhabitants of the City of Glasgow, and its Neighbourhood, was presented to the House, and react; Setting forth. That the Petitioners esteem it a Duty which they owe to themselves, and to the Public, to petition the House, that the Bill, now depending in Parliament, intituled, A Bill for the more effectually preventing seditious Meetings and Assemblies, may not pass into a Law: The Petitioners beg Leave humbly to represent, that the Right of petitioning the King, or Parliament, for the Redress of Grievances, is a fundamental Principle in the British Constitution, and particularly secured by an express Article in the Bill of Rights, that Charter of our Liberties established at the Resolution: It is, therefore, with the utmost Concern and Astonishment, that the Petitioners see an Attempt made to overturn and destroy this Privilege, by subjecting all Meetings of the People, for the Purpose of deliberating on Public Affairs, to the discretionary and uncontrouled Power of Magistrates, appointed by the Executive Government. In a mixed Form of Government, like that of Great Britain, any Innovation, subversive of the popular Part of our Constitution, ought to be regarded as equally destructive of our Liberties and Rights with a direct Invasion of the Prerogatives of the Crown: Sensible of the Necessity of repressing Sedition and Disorder, the Petitioners are, at the same Time, convinced that the Laws already existing, and by which Peace and good Order have been so long maintained, are fully sufficient for that Purpose; and they fear that additional Restrictions, accompanied by unusual and rigorous Penalties, might excite such Discontents as would endanger the Peace of the Country: It must impress every good Subject with Sorrow and Regret, to observe that the late atrocious Attempt against the Person of His Majesty, which could only proceed from the most abandoned and worthless Part of the Community, has been made the Pretence for attempting Innovations destructive of our Rights and Liberties.

A Petition of the Merchants, Bankers, Manufacturers, Traders, and other Inhabitants, in the City of Glasgow, and Neighbourhood, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, desirous to live quietly in the lawful Prosecution of their own immediate Concerns, and to be free from the Agitation which Political Dissensions create, with much Reluctance obtrude their Opinions upon either Branch of the Legislature; but observing, with Regret, that Two Bills, now depending in the House, the one, for the Safety and Preservation of His Majesty's Person and Government against treasonable and seditious Practices and Attempts; the other, for the more effectually preventing seditious Meetings and Assemblies; are laid hold of by restless and discontented Men, as Pretences for keeping the Public Mind in a State of Alarm, they feel it their Duty, in the present Situation

A Petition of the Booksellers, Stationers, Printers, Paper-Makers, and others immediately connected with the Liberty of the Press, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Liberty of the Press has materially contributed to the flourishing Condition which this Country, previous to the Commencement of the present War, had happily attained: That the Petitioners are enabled to state to the House, that the happy Privilege of the Freedom of the Press, hitherto so beneficially enjoyed in this Country, has afforded, and does at this Time afford, a comfortable Subsistence to many Thousands industrious and reputable Families, the greater Part of whom, by the Invasion of this Privilege, must inevitably be reduced to Misery and Ruin: That the Petitioners, speaking professionally, to which, on this Occasion, they wish to confine themselves, beg Leave to represent to the House, that the Bill lately introduced into the House of Lords, and now lying under the Consideration of this House, intituled, An Act for the Safety and Preservation of His Majesty's Person and Government against treasonable and seditious Practices and Attempts; will operate, if passed into a Law, to the Annihilation of the Liberty of the Press hitherto enjoyed, will thereby inevitably cause the Bankruptcy and Ruin of many hitherto flourishing and respectable Traders, while, at the same Time, it will, deprive of all Means of honest Livelihood an alarming Number of Persons in the lower Orders of Society connected with the various Branches of Trade and Manufacture dependant upon the free Exercise of the inestimable Art of Printing: The Petitioners therefore pray the House to take these Matters into their most serious Consideration, and to relieve them from the Anxiety, Apprehensions, and Ruin, with which they are threatened by the vague and indefinite, and therefore vexatious and oppressive, Clauses of the said Bill, and to guard, with jealous Intrepidity, that great Palladium at once of the Liberties and Prosperity of Britain — the Freedom of the Press.

A Petition of the Aldermen, Freemen, Clergy, and other Inhabitants, of the Borough of Saint Alban, in the County of Hertford, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, having heard that a Petition to the House has been drawn up and hastily signed by several Inhabitants of the said Borough, conveying Sentiments on certain Bills, now pending in Parliament, diametrically adverse from their Opinion of such Bills, conceive it highly expedient that the House should be informed of their Thoughts on this Subject, that they may not be implicated in the same Opposition: They beg Leave, therefore, humbly to address the House, and to represent that in the present Temper of the Times, they have Reason to think some Measure is absolutely necessary to be adopted to restrain, within due Bounds, such Meetings as have lately been the Means of propagating Principles of Sedition, totally subversive of our present happy Constitution, and the Domestic Peace of these Kingdoms, and which, if permitted to continue, must, by seducing the Minds of the People from their Duty and Allegiance, ultimately produce Anarchy and Confusion in Vol. $1.

A Petition of certain Electors of the ancient Town and Borough of Southwark, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners have observed, with deep Concern, the various Efforts of wicked and designing Persons to mislead the Understandings of some of the People, to seduce them from their Allegiance to our lawful Sovereign, and to fill their Minds with Disaffection to our excellent Constitution — the glory of every honest , and the Envy of all Foreign Nations: That the Petitioners have strong Reasons to suspect that the Contrivers of the late seditious Meetings, and of their consequent Outrages, are leagued with the natural Enemies of these Kingdoms, and would betray the People into their Hands; the Petitioners therefore rely on the Wisdom of the House to avert such Evils from this Land, that such Laws may be enacted as may effectually secure the Life of our beloved Sovereign, His Crown and Dignity, and as may be adequate to the Preservation of the future Peace and Safety of the Subjects of these Realms, and the Permanence of our happy Constitution, without infringing the sacred Rights of the People, to deliberate, with due Decorum, on any Public Grievance, or to petition or remonstrate, as often as they may think necessary, to the King's Executive Government, or to any of the Branches of the Legislature.

A Petition of the Friendly Association of Merchant

Shipwrights of the River Thames, was likewise presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners view, with extreme Surprize and Alarm, the Introduction of Two Bills into Parliament, the one intituled, An Act for the Safety and Preservation of His Majesty's Person and Government against treasonable and seditious Practices and Attempts; and the other, An Act to prevent seditious Assemblies; which they conceive to be Infringements upon the Constitution, and Violation of their best Rights and Liberties, have met to beg of the House, that they will, at this awful Crisis, act as behoves the Representatives of a Free People jealous of their Liberties, and oppose, with all their Authority, this Innovation, unprecedented since the glorious Resolution: The Petitioners therefore earnestly pray, That the House will put their decisive Negative upon those Two Bills, which lay the Axe to the Root of British Liberty, and, if passed into Laws, will render nugatory the Filth Clause of the Bill of Rights, and overthrow the most valuable Privileges of Englishmen.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table.

Mr. Sheridan reported from the Committee, appointed to enquire who was the Author of the Pamphlet, intituled, " Thoughts on the English Government — " addressed to the Quiet Good Sense of the People " of England; in a Series of Letters — Letter the First, " on the National Character of Englishmen — The Nature of the English Government — The Corruptions u caused in both by the Introduction of French

"ciples — The Effects produced by the Reformation " and the Resolution upon Political Principles — The Conduct of the Whig Party — The Character of the " modem Democrats — London, Printed for J.

" N* 168, Piccadilly — 1795. — " and who were empowered to report their Proceedings, from Time to Time, to the House; That the Committee had enquired into the Matter to them referred; and had directed him to make a Report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Mr. John Owen being examined, said, That he is a Bookseller, and lives in Piccadilly.

And being asked, If he knew a Publication, intituled, " Thoughts on the English Government?" he replied, Yes; his Name was signed to it

After this Declaration, Mr. Owen declined giving any further Information to your Committee, on the Plea that it might tend to criminate himself.

And being finally asked, Whether he persisted in refusing to answer any Questions the Committee might put to nim? he replied, Yes.

Mr. John Lake being examined, said, That he knows Mr. Wright, the Printer, in Peterborough Court, as also Mr. Street and Mr. Stump.

And being asked, Whether be ever heard these Persons speak of a Pamphlet, intituled, " Thoughts on the " English Government ?" he said. He had.

And being asked, Whether he ever heard them speak of the Author of the Pamphlet? be said, Yes; and that he heard Mr. Me Dowall*s Brother acknowledge that he composed the Press for the Pamphlet, particularly those Parts which have been deemed libellous by the House of Commons; and also that Mr. Reeves had been backwards and forwards at the Office, and the Pamphlet was commonly known throughout the Office by the Name of Mr. Reeves's Pamphlet. — That Mr. Wright, the Printer, was commissioned by Mr. Reeves to get a Person to publish the said Pamphlet; and in consequence Mr. Wright applied to several Booksellers, who refused to publish it, Mr. Wright refusing to give up the Author; and Mr. Owen, in Piccadilly, undertook to publish it, and Mr. Wright's Porter delivered it, by the Name of Mr. Reeves's Pamphlet, to Mr. Owen; and the Witness thinks Mr. M'Dowalts Brother said, that Mr. Reeves made some Interlineations at his Frame while composing, and that Mr. Reeves generally corrected the Press.

Mr. Charles MeDowall being examined, said, That he is Compositor to Mr. Wright. That he recollects the Pamphlet, intituled, " Thoughts on the English " Government," being printed at his Office.

And being asked, Whether the Press was corrected

during the printing of the Pamphlet from the Manuscript Sheets ? he said, It was.

And being asked, What Persons he saw superintending the Press, and correcting the Proofs ? he replied, No one, but Mr. Reeves.

And being asked. If he knew Mr. Reeves by Sight ? he said, Yes; he lives in Cecil Street.

And being asked, Whether he saw Mr. Reeves frequently during the printing of the Pamphlet, superintending the Work ? he said, Yes.

And being asked, If he ever saw Mr. Reeves write on or correct any of the Proofs ? he said, He was not certain.

And being asked, Whether he ever spoke to Mr. Reeves at Mr. Wright's ? he said. Yes; frequently.

And being asked, Whether Mr. Reeves's Conduct at Mr. Wright's was such as to lead the Witness to believe him to be the Author of the Pamphlet? he replied. Yes.

And being asked, Whether he knew the Hand-writing of Mr. Reevesfhe said, Yes; the Hand-writing that

goes for his.

And being asked, Was the Hand-writing of this Pamphlet, in his Opinion, the same as the Hand-writing that goes for Mr. Reeves's ? he said, Yes.

William Augustus Miles, Esquire, being examined, was asked, Whether he has any, and what Reason, to know who is the Author of the Pamphlet, intituled, " Thoughts on the English Government?" he said. Yes. In the first Instance, from Mr. Owen's having presented it to him as Mr. Reeves's Pamphlet; and in the Course of a few Hours afterwards, meeting Mr. Reeves turning out of the Treasury, he (the Witness) informed him, that he had received a Pamphlet written by him. — Mr. Reeves asked him the Title. He told him. — Mr. Reeves then enquired, if John Owen had informed him, that he (Mr. Reeves) was the Author. From Delicacy to the Bookseller, he said, No; but the Secret was revealed by a Printer's Man, who, by Mr. Owen's Declaration, he understood to be Mr. Wright's Man. — Mr. Reeves then earnestly recommended him to read the Pamphlet; and to the best of his Recollection, Mr. Reeves desired him to let him know what he thought of it. — That the Witness, on his Return, read it, and found the following Passage:

" In fine, the Government of England is a Monarchy; the Monarchy is the ancient Stock from " which have sprung those goodly Branches of the " Legislature, the Lords and Commons, that at the " same Time give Ornament to the Tree, and afford " Shelter to those who seek Protection under it But " these are still only Branches, and derive their Origin " and their Nutriment from their common Parent; " they may be lopped off, and the Tree is a Tree " still; shorn indeed of its Honours, but not like " them cast into the Fire. The Kingly Government " may go on, in all its Functions, without Lords or " Commons," so repugnant to the Principles of the Resolution of 1688, that the Witness immediately sent a Transcript of it to the Chancellor of the Exchequer, accompanied by a Letter; and on the Morning following the Witness wrote a Letter to Mr. Reeves; a Copy of which Letter was delivered in to the Committee, and read, the Witness requesting it might stand a Part of his Examination; and is as follows:

" Pall Mall, 1795.

" I have read your Pamphlet, Sir, with equal Attention and Concern; with Attention, because you recommended it strongly to my Perusal, and with Concem, because I was hurt that any Man, acquainted " with the Principles of the English Constitution, should " have the Indiscretion or Effrontery to misrepresent " them in a manner so very gross and unpardonable. —

" Such Writings tend to bring Monarchy much more

" into

36 Geo. III. 1° Decembris. 155

" into Disrepute than the Harangues of Mr. Thelwall " and Go.; and Monarchy in this Country does not require to be sustained by Trick and Contrivance; it " has the Support of Reason, Policy, and Experience. " The Nonsense and Falshoods of Writers, who only " prove their Ignorance or Servility, will endanger it; " and if my Advice should be asked, 1 would seriously " recommend you to defend the Excellencies of our " Constitution by its Excellencies — for they plead far " more eloquently in its Favour, than either your " Writings, or those of Mr. Burke. The Misfortune " is, that you confound the Abuses of Government " with the Government itself; and having by far a " much greater and more decided Interest in the Preservation of the one than of the other, your Anxiety " for the latter is merely a Contingency on the former, " and becomes a mere secondary Consideration. I will " tell you very candidly, that I thought you were " going greater Lengths than either Facts or Policy " warranted, in November 1792; and I am inclined to " believe, that your present Labours are more likely " to do Mischief than Good. What you have said in " Pages 12 and 13, would, in the Reign of George " the First, have sent you to the Pillory; and if Ministers discharge their Duty, they must discourage " the Publication in Question — for it is no less incumbent on them to discountenance Attacks on the " Constitution from one Description of Men than " from another. Whether it is assailed by the intemperate Zeal of Royalists or Republicans, it ought " to be defended; for it has equal Danger to apprehend from the extravagant Pretensions of the one, " and the rancorous Animosity of the other, and as an " Individual interested in its Preservation, I will ofpose, coute quit coute, any Innovation on the Part " of the Crown, as vehemently as I would on the Part " of Democracy; and if you held the Blessings of a " free Constitution in as much Reverence, and the " Smiles of Lord Hawkesbury as cheap as I do, your

*l Name would not be so generally detested, and the " Part that you would have taken in those Political " Questions which unhappily divide us, would have " been much more to your Credit, though not so lucrative. — I should not have said thus much, if you " had not pressed me to read a Pamphlet that is very ill calculated to allay the Ferment in Men's Minds, " and which I consider as a Libel on the Constitution " — injurious to the Interests and to the Dignity of the " Crown, and an Insult to that Good Sense to which " you have appealed — I have only to add, that I " shall most cordially rejoice when these Disputes " are at an End, and when Questions of this Nature " cease to animate our Conversations, and to sour " Men's Dispositions towards each other — such Questurns cannot benefit the Cause you wish to serve, " but they may ruin it; and it well behoves you, Sir, " to pause and think!

" I am, &c."

" To John Reeces, Esquire,

" Cecil Street, Strand."

And the Witness being asked, Whether he received any Answer from Mr. Reevesdisavowing his being the Author of the Pamphlet ? he said, He did not.

And being asked, If he has any Reason to know that Mr. Reeves received the Letter? he replied. Yes; from Mr. Reeves having exposed it to Mr. in Consequence of a Paragraph in the Morning tuck of the 9th Instant, in which the offensive Extract was included; in consequence of which Mr. Wright came to Mr. Owen, and found Fault with him for having accused Mr. Reeves of being the Author, informing Owen that he (the Witness) must have sent that Extract to the Morning Chronicle; in consequence of which the Witness wrote to Mr. , a Letter, of

which the following is a Copy; which was read; viz. Yot. 51.

" Sir, " Pall Mall, Nov. 11, 1795.

" Your Printer has insinuated, that the libellous " Extract from your Pamphlet, which appeared in the " Morning Chronicle on the 9th Instant, was sent by " me, and he draws that Conclusion from having seen the private Letter that I addressed to you on that " Subject, the 6th Instant. It is merely to refute a " Falshood, which may be the Foundation of much " Calumny and Misrepresentation, that I assure you I " was perfectly ignorant of the Extract, or any Comment on it, having been sent to any of the Public " Prints. — It is however incumbent on me to add, " that I perfectly approve of the Exposure, from the " full Conviction I have, that such Doctrines have a " direct Tendency to Mischief, and to alienate the

Affections of the People from His Majesty and His " Government. As you have judged it expedient to " expose my Correspondence in Part, I call on your " Candour to produce the Whole of it, or I shall be under the Necessity of sending Copies of my Letter " to the different Papers in Defence of myself.

" I am, Sir,

" Your humble Servant,

" Miles."

" To John Reeces, Esquire,

Cecil Street."

Mr. Benjamin Hinton being examined, said, That he is Porter to Mr. Wright the Printer, and delivers out the Publications. — That he remembers delivering out a Pamphlet, intituled, " Thoughts on the English Government." — That he delivered it to Mr. Owen the Bookseller in Piccadilly — That he had been printing an Address from Mr. Reeves to the King — That when he delivered the Pamphlet to Mr. Owen, he (the Witness) said it was Mr. Reeves's Pamphlet — That he has seen Mr. Reeves come into Mr. Wright's Printing Office — That he knows Mr. Reeves's Person — As near as the Witness can guess, the Pamphlet came into his Hands about a Fortnight ago; and before that he has seen Mr. Reeves at the Office several Times.

Mr. Thomas Wright, a Printer, being examined, was asked, Whether he knew the Author of the Pamphlet, intituled, " Thoughts on the English Government?" he replied, He declined giving up the Name of the Author.

And being asked, Upon what Principle he refused to answer the Question ? he said, One of the First Lessons inculcated on a Printer upon his Initiation into his Profession is, that the Name of the Author of a Manuscript committed to his Care or Keeping is a most sacred Deposit, from which he is never to part without the Assent or Permission of the Author, unless compelled by Public Justice.

And being asked, Whether he should think himself justified in printing any Manuscript on any Political Subject brought to his Office? he said, No, by no Means; he would exercise that Judgment and Discretion which he possesses, in determining whether it contained Matter of a libellous Nature, whether pub? lie or private, or any Thing that was against what is called contra bonos Mores — That he has endeavoured to exercise that Judgment in all the Publications which he has been concerned in.

And being asked, Whether he bad read the Pamphlet in Question ? he replied, Yes; and if he bad seen

any

any Tiling he thought objectionable he would not have printed it.

And the Witness being asked, Would not the Authority of the Person bringing him a Work weigh with him as well as his private Judgment? he replied. The Authority of the Person bringing him a Work to print would weigh with him (as he believes it would with every other Printer) as well as his private Judgment.

And being asked. Whether he had ever conversed with Mr. Reeves on the Subject of the Pamphlet in Question? he said, Yes.

And being asked, Whether he meant to say, that he had not conversed with Mr. Reeves for this Month past, on the Subject of the Pamphlet ? he said, Not as the Author of it, to his Knowledge, but as the Person who superintended the Correction of the Press.

And being asked, In what respect did Mr. Reeves superintend the Correction of the Press? he said, In correcting the Proofs, which he might do for a Friend.

And being asked. When the Publication was printed, to what Publisher did he send it? he replied, To the Person whose Name is at the Bottom of the Pamphlet.

And being asked, Whether he did not know that Person was Mr. Owen ? he said, Certainly.

And being asked, By whose Advice or Direction did he send the Pamphlet to Mr. Owen ? he said, By the Advice and Direction of no Person — it was his own doing entirely — he employed Mr.

And being asked, Whether he had ever any Conversation with Mr. Reeves respecting Mr. Owen being the Publisher? he said, Not previous to it; but as Mr. Reeves had corrected the Pamphlet, lie mentioned it to him as the Gentleman who had corrected the Pamphlet.

And being asked, Had this Pamphlet not answered in Point of Sale, from whom should he expect to be paid ? he said, From no one; the Loss would have been his own, and he understands the Profit would also be his.

And being asked, From what Authority he understood the Profit of this Pamphlet would have been his, if it sold well ? he replied, From the Gentleman from whom he received the Manuscript.

And being asked, Who was that Gentleman ? he replied, The Gentleman who corrected the Pamphlet.

And being asked, Was not that Gentleman Mr. Reeces ? he answered, He had said that above.

And the Evidence being read to the Witness, he was asked, Whether he had any Explanation to add to the Answers he had already given ? he said, He had not.

Mr. John Gillet being examined, and shewn the Pamphlet, intituled, " Thoughts on the English Government," he was asked, Whether he had not heard Mr. Owen declare that Mr. Reeves was the Author of that Pamphlet? he replied, Yes, in his own Shop frequently.

Mr. Thomas Gillet being examined, was asked, Whether he was not in Mr. Owens, Shop on or about Saturday, the 21 st November he said, Yes.

And being asked to relate any Conversation he heard respecting the Circulation of the Pamphlet, intituled, " Thoughts on the English Governmenthe informed your Committee, That Mr. Reeves came into the Shop, and he said to Mr. Ozven, " Where is " this Pamphlet, that is ascribed to me?" — Mr. Owen pointed to the Pamphlet. — Mr. Reeves took One up and doubled it, and put it in his Pocket, and asked whether it had sold well — he then desired him to send Half a Dozen to some Person's Office in Westminster, but he (the Witness) did not distinctly hear to whose Office.

Mr. Stephen Jones being examined, said, He is employed in Mr. Wright's Office as Overseer in his Business, and is Superintender of all the Publications in his Office.

Being shewn the Pamphlet, intituled, " Thoughts " on the English Government," he was asked, Whether he superintended the Progress, through the Press, of that Pamphlet? he said, He did.

And being asked, Whether he corrected the Proofs ? he said, He did.

And being asked, Whether he and he alone corrected the Proofs? he said, No — he corrected them in Conjunction with Mr. Wright. — Mr. Wright invariably corrected them the First or the Second Time — No Sheet went to the Press without his reading it.

And being asked, Did no other Person superintend the correcting the Press besides himself and Mr. Wright? he said, Yes, there did.

And being asked, Who was that Person ? he said, Mr. Reeves.

And being asked, If he received Directions from any Person superintending or correcting the Press of a Manuscript printed at his House, should he think himself bound to attend to those Directions, unless he considered the Person giving them either as the Author, or acting for the Author ? he said, He should certainly not; he should not suffer any One Correction to be made under such Circumstances.

And being asked, Whether he attended to any Direction or Correction given to him in the Case of printing the Pamphlet in Question, from Mr. Reeves ? he replied, Yes.

Then, in Point of Fact, he was asked, Did he consider Mr. Reeves as the Author, or acting for the Author ? he replied, Most certainly.

And being asked, Whether he has any Part of the original Copy ? he said, He believes there may be some about the House.

And being asked, If there are any Proof Sheets about the House, corrected by Mr. Reeves ? he said.

He is inclined to think there are.

Mr. Wright being again examined, was asked, How long Mr. Jones had superintended his Business? he said, Four or Five Years.

And being asked, Whether he had ever had Reason to doubt of Mr. Jones's Veracity or Accuracy ? he replied, That he never had the least Doubt of his Veracity or Accuracy. Then,

Mr. Jones (having been directed by the Committee' to endeavour to find the Proof Sheets alluded to in his Evidence) returned, and was again examined; and being asked, If he had found any of the Proof Sheets ? he replied, He had brought the first he could lay his Hands on. — They are not complete.

Then the Witness produced the said Sheets, and said. That a few of the Alterations in the Margin may be his own, which would be confined to Typographical Errata: That he cannot speak positively to all the others, but some are Mr. Rs, to the best of his Recollection.

And being asked, Whether he had not himself seen Mr. Reeves write ‘ upon some One of the Papers now delivered in by him to the Committee ? he said, He had seen Mr. Reeves make Alterations on certain of the Sheets, but he could not from Memory state which they are.

And being asked, Whether he knew Mr. Reeves's Hand-writing ? he said. He thinks he does.

He was then desired to look over the Proof Sheets delivered in by him, and point out what Notes or Observations are, to the best of his Knowledge, Mr. Reeves's Hand-writing.

And the Witness having looked over the said Sheets, he said, He finds all the Passages now marked by him with a Cross are, to the best of his Belief, Mr. Reeves's Hand-writing.

And being again asked, Whether he had not himself actually seen Mr. Reeves in the act of marking the Proof Sheets, or some of them, now delivered in by him? he said, He had.

And

36 Geo. III. 1 ° Decembris. 157

And being asked, In whose Hand-writing is the separate Paper included in the Sheets delivered in by him, which separate Paper appears to be Part of the Title of the said Pamphlet ? he said, He believed it to be Mr.

Reeves's.

And being asked, Whether he has had Knowledge of Mr. Reeves printing other Publications at Mr. Wright's Office? he replied, Yes, very many. He has been in the Habit, and had the Opportunity of knowing Mr. Reeves's Hand-writing.

And being asked, With those Means and Opportunity of knowing his Hand-writing has the Witness any Doubt that this separate Paper, and the Observations and Notes in the Sheets, are in Mr. Reeves's Handwriting r he said, He had not.

And being asked, What Mr. Reeves is the Person referred to by him, as the Corrector of the Proof Sheets, and Superintender of the Publication of this Pamphlet? he answered, Mr. John Reeves, the Chairman of the Association for protecting Liberty and Property against Republicans and Levellers.

The Evidence having been read over to the Witness, he was asked, Whether he had any Explanation or further Observation to make upon it? he replied, He had not. — Then,

Mr. Wright was further examined, and asked, Whether he conceives Mr. Jones has a Right to send out Proof Sheets or Pamphlets without any direct Communication with him ? he said, Yes; he is in the Habit of doing so, as well as all other Overseers in Printing Offices.

And being asked, From his Knowledge of Mr. Jones, does he suppose he would deliver any Proof Sheets, as from his Office, that were not printed there ? he said, He should suppose not.

And being asked, If he ever knew an Instance of his doing so ? he replied, No.

And being asked, Whether Mr. Jones has not an Authority, from his Situation with him, to deliver any Proof Sheets of Works printed at his (the Witness's) Office, if required, without an immediate Application to him; the Witness? he replied, He certainly has; no Printing could go on, without a Person in Mr. Jones's Situation having that Power.

Mr. Wright being again examined, was asked, Whether he recollected a Conversation with Mr. Reeves on the Subject of a Letter received by Mr. Reeces from Mr. Miles?he replied, Yes; and that Mr. Reeves had

shewn it him.

Being shewn the Proof Sheets delivered in by Mr. Jones, he was asked, If he knew whether the separate Paper, included therein, was Mr. Reeves's Hand-writing? he said, He believes it is; and that he is familiar with Mr. Reeves's Hand-writing.

And being asked, Whether he had seen Mr. Reeves since his last Examination by the Committee ? he replied, Yes, and conversed with him on the Subject of this Publication.

And the Witness desired to add to his former Evidence, as the Committee had called on him to add any Explanation he thought proper — That Three or Four Proof Sheets had been sent to other Gentlemen, and some Corrections received from them on the Proof Sheets; particularly he can point out one in Page 7, and another in Page 12. — But on being shewn the Correction in Page 7, he admitted the Hand-writing to be Mr. Reeves's, but from the Blackness of it he supposes the Words to be traced over Writing in Pencil — The Word " active," in Page 12, he thought not to be Mr. Reeves's Hand-writing.

And the Witness being asked, Whether he meant that he had sent these Proofs to those other Gentlemen; and received the; Corrections back from them himself? he answered, No — That he only knew of them through Mr. Reeves, whom he supposed to have sent the Proofs, and that it was to Mr. Reeves Vou51.

they were returned, and he adopted the Corrections where he chose it.

And being asked, Who the Person was that brought the Pamphlet to him; he answered, The Person who corrected the Press — Mr. Reeves.

And the Witness desired to add, That as he had been asked on a former Examination, whether the Authority of the Person bringing him the Pamphlet would not weigh with him, as well as his own Judgment, on the Publication; he meant to declare that the Authority of Mr. Reeves bringing him the Pamphlet in Question had operated with him as an Inducement to publish it.

And being asked, Whether he had not read the Manuscript ? he answered, Only Parts of it.

And being asked, Wrhether the Manuscript was not in the same Hand-writing as the separate Paper now shewn to him, and which contains the Title of the said Pamphlet? he said, That to the best of his Judgment and Recollection, such Parts as he had seen were of the same Hand-writing.

Mr. Owen being further examined, and being shewn a Passage in Mr. Miles's Evidence, he was asked, Whether he recollected receiving from Mr. Reeves the Directions therein stated, to send Six Copies of the Pamphlet in Question to Lord Hawkesbury's Office $ and whether he had executed those Directions-? he answered, He had; that he had sent them, directed to Mr". Chalmer, at Lord Hawkesbury's Office.

And being asked, To whose Account he had charged them, he said, To Mr. Reeves's.

And Mr. Owen being now apprized of the Consequences of the Answer he had made in his previous Examination refusing to answer any Questions that might be put to him; — the Witness begged Leave to retract that Answer, and apologize to the Committee; yet he still hoped the Committee would not press him to give up the Author, as, notwithstanding the Confession he had made of being the Publisher, he thought it might tend to criminate himself.

And your Committee having, as they conceive, abundant Proof from the Body of Evidence already before them, did not examine the Witness further.

And your Committee, conceiving any further Evidence respecting the Person responsible as Author or Publisher of the Pamphlet in Question wholly unnecessary, did not proceed in the Examination of many Persons, whose Testimony they have Reason to believe would still further establish the Facts stated by the preceding Witnesses. They have only to add, in Discharge of the Duty committed to them by the House; viz. To esquire who was the Author of the Pamphlet, intituled, ‘ Thoughts on the English Government, &c.' declared by the House to be " a malicious, scandalous, " and seditious Libel, containing Matter tending to " create Jealousies and Divisions among His Majesty's " loyal Subjects; to alienate their Affections from our " present happy Form of Government, as established " in King, Lords, and Commons, and to subvert the " true Principles of our free Constitution; and that the " said Pamphlet is a high Breach of the Privileges of " this House;"

That it appears to the Committee, That John Reeves, Esquire, of Cecil Street, in the Strand, is the Author, or has acted as the Author, of the said Publication.

Ordered, That the said Report be taken into further Consideration upon Friday Morning next.

Ordered, That such a Number of Copies of the said Report be printed, as shall be sufficient for the Use of the Members of the House.

The House being informed, that Charles , Esquire, was very much indisposed;

Ordered, That the said Charles Yorke, Esquire, have Leave to go into the Country, for a Month, for the Recovery of his Health.
