The other Order of the Day being read, for taking into further Consideration the Report from the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for the more effectually preventing seditious Meetings and Assemblies, was committed;

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, That the Amendments made by the Committee to the said Bill be now read a Second Time.

An Amendment was proposed to be made to the Question, by leaving out the Word " now," in order to add, at the End of the Question, the Words " Tomorrow Morning."

And the Question being put, That the Word " now " stand Part of the Question;

It was resolved in the Affirmative.

Then the main Question being put;

Ordered, That the Amendments, made by the Committee to the said Bill, be now read a Second Time.

The said Amendments were accordingly severally read a Second Time, and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, were, with Amendments to several of them, agreed to by the House.

A Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, directing that the Notice sent by the Persons signing it to the Clerk of the Peace, and by him to the Justices, shall be as effectual as if published in the Newspaper.

And the said Clause was Twice read, and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House to be made Part of the Bill.

Then several Amendments were made, by the House, to the Bill.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendments, be ingrossed.

Ordered, That the said Bill be read the Third Time upon Thursday Morning next, if the said Bill shall be then ingrossed.

Ordered, That Mr. Kempe have Leave to make a Motion, it being after Nine of the Clock.

And he moved the House accordingly; and presented to the House,

A Petition of the Inhabitants of the ancient Borough of Lewes, and of the Cliffe, and in the County of Sussex.

And the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners entertain the most gloomy Apprehensions from the Perusal of Two Bills now pending in Parliament, One for the Safety and Preservation of His Majesty's Person and Government against treasonable and seditious Practices and Attempts; and the other, for the more effectually preventing seditious Meetings and Assemblies; it appearing to the Petitioners that the said Bills, by creating new Treasons, by multiplying Capital Punishments, and by destroying the fundamental Right of the People to assemble peaceably together for the Discussion of Public Grievances, operate to the subversion of the Constitution, and strike at the Foundation of the Liberties of Englishmen: That the Petitioners detest Anarchy, and abhor Despotism, but, as free born Britons, who value their Liberty as their choicest Blessing, they would be deficient in their Duty to their Country, to themselves, and to their Posterity, not to exercise their invaluable Privilege of petitioning against the Enaction of Laws by which the Fences and Outworks set up by our Ancestors, to guard that Liberty, will be beaten down and destroyed: They therefore pray the House, That the said Bills may not pass.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Bill for prohibiting the making of Spirits from Wheat, &c. reported.

Mr. Hobart, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill to continue, for a further Time to be limited, an Act, made in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act to prohibit, for a limited Time, the making of " Low Wines or Spirits from Wheat, Barley, Malt, " or any other Sort of Grain, or from any Meal, Flour, " or Bran; and for permitting Home-made Spirits, " deposited in the Warehouses for Exportation, to be " taken out for Home Consumption, on Payment of " Duty," and to prohibit the Distillation of Spirits " from Potatoes, was re-committed, the Amendments which the Committee had made to the Bill, and which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Bill, with the Amendments, in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Amendments were Once read throughout; and then a Second Time One by One: and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, were agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendments, be ingrossed.

Ordered, That the said Bill be read the Third Time Tomorrow Morning, if the said Bill shall be then ingrossed.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Common Petitions Council, and Livery, of the Town and County of the npainstths Tow n of Nottingham, was presented to the House, and g^["r0lfh^ read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners approach Majesty's the House, to request of them, as the Guardians of our Personae. Rights, and of that liberal Constitution, which after many Struggles, was at the Resolution committed to us to enjoy, and to the House to protect and defend, that they will appease the National Alarm which the Bill now pending in the House, intituled, An Act for the Safety and Preservation of His Majesty's Person and Government against treasonable and seditious Practices, has so justly excited — It is a Bill which, if carried into a Law, can alone endanger His Majesty's Person and Government, by rudely tearing asunder the Bond of Affection between the Subject and the governing Power; each have their Rights, and a Harmony of Rights can alone secure the Public Good.

To subject the most innocent Acts and the most dignified Characters, to an undefined Law of Treason, to a discretionary Construction of Treason, and to subject those Acts and those Characters to Sentences of the most awful Terror, is to establish an absolute Tyranny of Law; it is to revive the Law of Libel of Imperial Rome in all its Horror: "With Wisdom and Temperance our glorious Ancestors have fully provided for the Dignity and Security of Government; to their Wisdom the Petitioners chearfully submit, and their Wisdom, the Petitioners trust, will be the Rule of the House: It is therefore their earnest Prayer, That the House will not suffer this novel, this alarming Bill, to pass into a Law.

A Petition of the Inhabitants of Nottingham, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth,

That the Petitioners, the Gentlemen, Merchants, Tradesmen, and other Inhabitants, of the Town and County of the Town of Nottingham, respectfully approach the House, as the Guardians of that Constitution, whose genuine Principles the Petitioners revere, as the best Security for the Dignity of the Crown, and the Rights of the People, to request the serious Consideration of the House of a certain Bill, now pending in the House, intituled, An Act for the Safety and Preservation of His Majesty's Government against treasonable and seditious Practices and Attempts: That the Petitioners sincerely deplore the late atrocious Attack upon His Majesty's Person, in His Way to the Houses of Parliament, at the Opening of the present Sessions, and would chearfully assist, by every Means in their Power, in bringing to immediate Punishment the Authors and Abettors of that daring Outrage; for this Purpose the Petitioners are persuaded the excellent

Laws, which distinguish the venerable Fabrick of our Constitution, aided by the Testimony of competent Witnesses, are fully adequate: The extensive and generous Fffusions of Loyalty which His Majesty will experience on this Occasion, will sufficiently convince the House, that the misguided Conduct of a few Individuals was far from proceeding from National Disaffection: The Petitioners rely Upon the Wisdom of the House, to perceive the Injustice of indicting a Nationul Punishment for Individual Offences; they assure themselves of the Discernment of the House, that popular Esteem and Affection is the best Security to His Majesty's Person and Government, and that these may be conciliated by Acts of Kindness, but cannot be commanded or enforced by Acts of Power: The Petitioners are convinced that our present Constitution (containing within itself the Power of perpetual Improvement) has obtained, and still enjoys, the Affection and Esteem of the great Body of our Countrymen, because, until the present Period, it has assured to the People of these Realnis the Right of Public and Private Discussion — tile Liberty of the Press — and the Right of petitioning all the Branches of the Legislature, without the Interference of Ministers, the Controul of Magistrates, or the Dread of Military Execution: The Petitioners are persuaded that the Bills, which have been presented for the Sanction of the House, directly violate, or insidiously attempt to regulate, the Exercise of these Rights, upon the Existence of which, in the Frame of our Constitution, and upon the Respect paid to them by the Ministers of the Crown, depends the Happiness of the People, and their Attachment to the Constitution: Therefore, as the House affectionately regard the Dignity of the Crown, which must ever find its best Security in a Nation's Love — as the House respect themselves — as they admire the general and zealous Attachment to the Constitution, which, at present, glows in the Hearts of Britons — in fine, as the House wish the great Body of the Nation from henceforth to believe in the Existence of the Constitution, or to consider the House as their genuine Representatives, the Petitioners earnestly implore the House not to permit the said Bill to pass into Law.

A Petition of the Noblemen, Gentlemen, Clergy, Freeholders, and other Inhabitants, of the County of Southampton, was also presented to the House, and read: Setting forth, That the Petitioners, assembled upon the interesting and awful Occasion of the late alarming Danger to the sacred Person of His Majesty, and to express their Sentiments of Indignation and Resentment against the Authors of that Parricidal Attempt, are naturally led to search for the Cause of an Outrage, which, not less from the Virtues than frbtn the Station of the Sovereign now seated on the Throne, seemed to be beyond any the worst Idea of Human Ingratitude and Wickedness: In pursuing this Investigation, the Petitioners can discover no morb probable Source of such atrocious Mischief than the seditious Instigation of certain Societies and Meetings* in Which, to the Abuse of the Indulgence of the Law, Principles and Doctrines are avowed and circulated of most dangerous Consequence to the Preservation of true Liberty, as well as to the Safety of the State: That the Petitioners have contemplated with anxious Sdrprize, and are now induced to mention with earnest Uneasiness, the Risk to which the well-disposed Part of the Community have been suffered to be exposed by the progressive Audacity, and unchecked Diffusion* of false and poisonous Suggestions, to create Discontent, and to incite Revolt, against some of the best Maxims of our Government, and surest Defences of our Rights and Franchises: The Application of a preventive Remedy to a Mischief of a Nature so intimately affecting the dearest Foundation of our social Tranquillity and Happiness, - Vol. .51.

must be an Object wolthy of the earliest and most serious Consideration of the Legislature: In Justice to themselves and to Posterity, and in grateful Concern for the general Welfare of the Country, the Petitioners cannot dispense, with Obedience to their Duty upon such momentous Occasion, to recommend to the Wisdom of Parliament the Adoption of some effectual Measures to secure the Continuance and Enjoyment of our true Constitutional Privileges, by a moderate but adequate Restraint on the Excess to which the Enemies of the Constitution would licentiously carry the Perversion of its real and excellent Arrangements for the Maintenance of Individual Freedom and National Prosperity: The Petitioners humbly conceive (although they do not venture to dictate the particular Provisions of any Bill for this essential Object) that it may be framed with successful Insurance of the Blessings which, by our Constitution, they have a Right to claim and to protect, and with decisive Controul of those licentious Proceedings, which the desperate Wickedness of a Few would make the Crime and consequent Destruction of the Whole.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, Freeholders, Petition in and other Inhabitants of the County of Rutland, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, SafetvofHii That the Petitioners have viewed with the utmost In- Majesty'* dignation and Horror, the daring Attack made upon Person, &e. the Person of His Majesty on His Passage to Parliament; and they are persuaded this Attack has been made by Russians w'hose Minds have been seduced from their Duty and Allegiance to their Sovereign by the Arts of seditious, designing, and evil-minded Men, to subvert our happy Constitution, and to riot in its Subversion: That the Petitioners observe, with the greatest Satisfaction, the Steps which the Wisdom of the House has taken to prepare, and bring in, a Bill for the greater Safety of His Majesty's Person, the clearer Definement of the Laws of Treason, and to give more speedy and effectual Checks to that Spirit of Sedition and Disaffection which has for some Time spread its Poison under the specious and popular Terms of Liberty and Reform: That the Petitioners should be entirely forgetful of their Duty to themselves, to the best of Sovereigns, and to their Country, if they did not present the House with this unequivocal Testimony of their Attachment to their Sovereign, their Desire to preserve the Constitution, which makes us happy, their cordial Regard for their Fellow Subjects, and their fixed Determination to support the House against all the Attempts of a Faction, now reduced, by the Dread of salutary Laws, to Violence and Desperation: That the Petitioners have requested the Representatives of their County to present this Petition to the House, humbly praying, That the Commons of Great Britain will ever continue to be the watchful Guardians of the Constitution as by Law. established.

A Petition of the Merchants, Traders, and other Petition in Inhabitants, of the United Towns of Port Glasgow and fofth* Nexvark, was also presented to the House, and read; Safety of Hi* Setting forih, That the Petitioners have beheld, with Majesty's Concern, Dissentions sown and nourished in these Person, &c.; Kingdoms, for some Time past, by certain discontented and seditious Persons, in Opposition to the established t;ous Government and Constitution, atld lately a most atro- ings. cious Act of Outrage committed against the Person of His Majesty: That the Two Bills, now depending in Parliament, for the better securing His Majesty's Person and Government; artd for the more effectually preventing all seditious Meetings and Assemblies; appear to the Petitioners to be the best Remedies for preventing the Dangers to be apprehended from the daring Attempts of the Factious: And therefore praying, That the House may pass the said Two Bills into LatvS for such limited Time as to their Wisdom shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Magistrates and Town Council of the United Boroughs and Towns Corporate of Glasgow and Newark, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the continued seditious Attempts of certain discontented Persons to create Anarchy, and a Spirit of Revolt against the present happy Constitution of these United Kingdoms, and the recent daring Outrage against the Person of His sacred Majesty, urgently call for strong and speedy Measures for preventing any future Repetition of such Crimes: That the Bills now depending in Parliament, for the better securing His Majesty's Person and Government; and, for the more effectually preventing all seditious Meetings and Assemblies; appear to the Petitioners to be best calculated for the Purpose of such Prevention: And therefore praying, That the House may pass the said Two Bills into Laws, for such limited Time as to their Wisdom shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Nobility, Gentry, Clergy, and Freeholders, of the County of was likewise

presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Laws, provided by the Wisdom of our Ancestors against High Treason, Political Libels, and Tumultuous Assemblies, have been found, by the Experience of many Ages, to be a sufficient Safeguard to the Person of the King, and perfectly adequate to the Suppression and Punishment of all Offences against the Quiet and Security of the State: That it is, therefore, with the utmost Surprize and Grief, that the Petitioners have heard of the Introduction of Two Bills into Parliament, severally intituled, An Act for the Safety and Preservation of His Majesty's Person and Government against treasonable and seditious Practices and Attempts; and, An Act for the more effectually preventing seditions Meetings and Assemblies; One of which removes the ancient Boundaries of Treason, describes libellous Speeches and Writings with such Latitude as to comprehend all Political Speeches and Writings which are not Panegyricks on the Government, and subjects to a Penalty, which the Humanity of the Laws of England has hitherto confined to the most foul and infamous Offences; and the other subjects the Deliberations of Public Meetings, in which alone the Right of Petition can be exercised with Effect, to the Caprice or Corruption of Magistrates, thereby defeating all substantial and beneficial Exertion of that sacred Right itself, claimed and demanded by our Ancestors in the Bill of Rights, as the Inheritance of Englishmen, secured to them by the fundamental Laws — That the Petitioners cannot but deprecate the Adoption of Measures, which, by depriving the People of that Controul over Public Affairs which they derive from free and open Discussion, tends to enfeeble and extinguish their Love for the Constitution, to bring into Hatred and Contempt the existing Government of the Country, and thus equally to endanger the Peace and Liberty of the Nation: The Petitioners, therefore, most earnestly implore the House, That the said Bills may not pass into Laws.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Steward, Bailiff, and Inhabitants, Petition of the Borough of Cirencester, in the County of Glou- respecting cester, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners see, with Concern and In- gs‘ dignation, that the Endeavours of factious and seditious Men to overturn the Constitution of this Country, and to reduce us to a State of Anarchy and Wretchedness, are still continued with indefatigable Assiduity, and that the Effect of the pernicious Principles, which they have disseminated, has been strongly proved by the late daring Attempt against the Life of our beloved Sovereign; and the Petitioners think themselves called upon, at the present Moment, to declare their determined Resolution to support, by every Exertion in their Power, whatever Laws Parliament, in its Wisdom, shall think proper to enact: The Petitioners therefore entreat the House, in Concurrence with the other Branches of the Legislature, to adopt such Measures, as it shall deem most effectual, to suppress these daring Attempts.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Members of the Benefit Societies, Petition for a and other Inhabitants, of Nottingham, and its Vicinity, ReP^ of was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth,

That, at the present alarming Crisis, when we have Bounty on already suffered one distressing Scarcity, and are told the Exporta-that we are on the Eve of another, the Petitioners of Corn think it their indispensable Duty to claim the Attention c‘ of the House to the Evils under which we labour —

The Petitioners have entertained more than Doubts of the Policy which dictated the Regulations with respect to the Exportation and Importation of Corn, and cannot be reconciled to either the Prudence or Humanity of, in Effect, bribing Foreign Nations to take the Bread out of the Mouths of our Labourers and Manufacturers, neither can they see the Justice or

Necessity

Petition respecting Seditious Meet ings.

Necessity of taxing at any Time that Supply which we might draw from another Country; the Petitioners therefore pray the House to endeavour to procure a total Repeal of such Statutes as allow a Bounty upon the Exportation of Corn, and also of those which impose such heavy Restrictions upon its Importation, as the Petitioners hope it will be found, upon Experience, that such Repeal would be beneficial to the Nation. — Another Evil, of which the Petitioners complain, is the Monopoly of Farms, which has swallowed up the Cottages and small Farms, whose Occupiers, from their Circumstances, were obliged to come regularly to Market; an Evil which has increased, is increasing, and ought to be diminished: Further, they beg the Interference of the House with respect to the Practices of Regrating, Forestalling, Engrossing, and selling Corn by Sample; Practices which tend to advance the Market, and extremely distress those whose scanty Incomes enable them to live only from Hand to Mouth — Lastly, convinced, by melancholy Experience, that the present War, whether just or unjust in its Principle, has been the leading and productive Source of all the Calamities which the Petitioners deplore, they conjure the House, by all the Respect they bear to the Welfare of our common Country, to use their utmost Efforts to put an End to the ruinous Hostilities which daily impose such vast and heavy Burthens upon us, and which have swept the Husbandman, and the Fruits of his Industry, into one common Grave; and the Petitioners trust, that the House will feel a due Sense of the Importance of these Subjects, and will decide, in relation to them, with that Discretion and Humanity, which they seem to require.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Select Committee, who are appointed to take into Consideration the present high Price of Com.

A Petition of the Mayor, Magistrates, Gentlemen, Clergy, Bankers, principal Traders, Manufacturers, and others. Inhabitants of the City of , was

presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners approach the House, convinced of its Wisdom and Firmness in protecting and securing their Rights and Privileges: They deeply lament (in common with every good Subject) the daring Attack made upon the Person of His Majesty, while He was proceeding to exercise one of the most important Functions of His High Office; and they cannot but impute this alarming Outrage to the Propagation of Doctrines promulgated at seditious Meetings and Assemblies, frequently called together by artful and designing Men, for the pretended Purpose of deliberating upon Grievances, but the real Object of which is the Subversion of all regular Government: Impressed with this Belief, the Petitioners are firmly persuaded of the Necessity of preventing seditious Meetings and Assemblies: And they humbly pray the House to adopt such Regulations, as to their Wisdom may seem meet, for the Purpose of effecting an Object which appears to the Petitioners essentially necessary for the Preservation of the Right of Petitioning itself, and for the Security of every Privilege they enjoy under our free and happy Constitution.

A Petition of the Inhabitants of the Borough of Bridport, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, firmly attached to the Principles of the Resolution, the Glory of their Ancestors, consider as the chief Excellence of the British Constitution the establishing a due Balance between the Prerogative of the Crown and the Liberty of the Subject, by which the Dangers of Despotism on the one Hand, and the Evils of Anarchy on the other, are equally avoided: That, to preserve these Principles pure and inviolate, the Petitioners conceive it the

Vol. 51.

Duty of every Lover of his Country to watch with a jealous Eye, and legally to oppose, every Measure that has a Tendency to infringe the Right of Petitioning, which has hitherto been held most sacred, and which has been expressly stipulated by the Bill of Rights; they cannot therefore, without Alarm, observe the Introduction of Two Bills into Parliament, the one intituled, An Act for the Safety and Preservation of His Majesty's Person and Government against treasonable and seditious Practices and Attempts; and the other, An Act for the more effectually preventing seditious Meetings and Assemblies; which Bills they consider to be unnecessary and impolitic; unnecessary, because they believe the existing Laws to be sufficient for the Punishment of Offenders; and impolitic, as tending to alienate the Affections of His Majesty's Subjects, as well as inimical to free Discussion, and frequent Communication of the Public Sentiment on important Questions involving the Liberty and Happiness of the British Nation: Possessing these Sentiments, and apprehending that those Alterations, which the Committee has thought proper to adopt, do not materially correct the dangerous Principle of the said Bills, nor render them less obnoxious to their numerous and respectable Opposers, the Petitioners therefore pray the House not to pass them into Laws.

A Petition of the Burgesses and thereunder-signed Inhabitants of the ancient Borough of Arundel, in the County of Sussex, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, impressed with the deepest Concern at the late daring and outrageous Insult offered to the Person of our beloved Sovereign, think it a Duty incumbent on them, for the Preservation of those inestimable Blessings which they have so long, and still continue to enjoy, to express their Abhorrence of so detestable a Proceeding, and to pray that the House will adopt such Measures as in its Wisdom shall appear most likely to discover the Abettors and Perpetrators thereof, and bring them to meet the Punishment' due to their daring and atrocious Offences: That the Petitioners, apprehending the greatest Danger to our happy Constitution, to the Tranquillity of this Country, and to the Security of their Persons and Property, from the daring Attempts of those seditious Assemblies, whose Doctrines are a Libel upon all Government, tending to subvert the Principles of true Civil Liberty, and evidently intending to introduce Discord and Anarchy, and firmly believing that the existing Laws are not adequate to repel effectually the Malignity of the Evil, humbly pray, That the House will speedily pass such Laws as shall more effectually secure the Person and Dignity of our most gracious Sovereign, suppress all seditious Meetings and Practices, and, finally, prevent the Dissemination of such corrupt Principles as may endanger the Security and Existence of our most excellent Government.

A Petition of the Inhabitants of the Borough of Arundel, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners believe, that the late atrocious Outrage offered to His Majesty's sacred Person is more attributable to the Distresses of the Kingdom, greatly heightened by the present calamitous War, than to any other Cause: That the Petitioners see, With serious' Concern, Two Bills brought into the House, One intituled, A Bill for the Safety and Preservation Of His Majesty's Person and Government against treasonable and seditious Practices and Attempts; and the othet, A Bill for the more effectually preventing seditious Meetings and Assemblies; the first of which Bills alters the long established Laws of the Ladd respecting Treason, and unnecessarily adds a long Catalogue thereto, as the Petitioners conceive the Efficacy of the present Laws to be fully adequate for the Punishment and Prevention of that horrid Crime, and the latter the Petitioners consider as an Infringement of the happy Constitution of this Country, attd a direct Violation against the Bill of Rights; as established at the glorious Resolution: That believing the Blessings of Peace will tend more to allay the Discontents of the People, and be more conducive to the Happiness Of all, than the most Coercive Measures, the Petitioners earnestly pray, That the House will use their utmost Efforts for the Attainment of an honourable Peace, and that the Two Bills above-mentioned may be rejected by the House.

Value of rational and genuine Liberty, and feel that the Essence and true Spirit of it are only to be preserved by wholesome Restraints on the Seditious and the Profligate; they deprecate the Evils of Licentiousness, and the Horrors of Anarchy; they rely, with Confidence, on the Wisdom of Parliament, to frame such Laws as the Exigencies of the Times require, and that no greater Restraints will be imposed on natural Liberty than are necessary for the general Good: The Petitioners therefore humbly pray, That the House will, with regard to each of the Bills above specified, do that which, in their Wisdom, shall appear to be most conducive to the Safety and Welfare of our King and Country.

A Petition of the thereunder-signed Inhabitants of Plymouth and its Vicinity, convened by Public Notice from the Worshipful the Mayor of the said Town, and assembled at the Guildhall of the same on the 30th Day of November 1795, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, confiding in the Wisdom of Parliament for taking such Measures as might best tend to the Security of His Majesty's Person, and the Constitution of this Kingdom, were willing to have silently awaited the Result of its Deliberations on those interesting Subjects; but, having seen certain printed Resolutions of a Meeting held in the Long Room at Stonehouse on the 23d Day of November, purporting to be the Resolutions of the Inhabitants of PlymouthPlymouth Dock, and Stonehouse, in which Resolutions Two Bills, now pending in Parliament, the one for the Preservation of His Majesty's Person and Government, and the other for preventing seditious Meetings, are severely reprobated, not only as completely subversive of the Principles of the Constitution, but as absolutely needless, think it incumbent upon them to disavow those Sentiments, being themselves of Opinion, that the Provisions of those Bills, both in their Design and probable Operation (being hostile only to the licentious Abuse of our Constitutional Privileges) are therefore friendly to a just, rational, and honest Liberty: That, though the Necessity of new Restrictions is, no Doubt,. to be lamented, yet Laws must conform to Exigencies; that therefore the extraordinary Licentiousness which has of late prevailed, in disseminating the Principles and Doctrines of Sedition and Disaffection, has itself created the Necessity of extraordinary Restraints: That the late atrocious Insult on the King's Majesty in His Way to the House of Parliament, which the Petitioners cannot forbear connecting, in their own Minds, with those Principles and Doctrines, has sounded a dreadful Alarm to every true Friend of the Constitution,

and exacts of the Legislature, its faithful Guardian, correspondent Measures of Vigilance and Vigour for its Protection, and for the Safety and Preservation of His Majesty's Person and Government: And therefore, under the Impression of these Sentiments, the Petitioners pray the House to adopt such Provisions as to their Wisdom shall appear best calculated for the Attainment of those great Ends.

of Staff ord, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was preventing also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. Seditious That it is with the deepest Concern, die Petitioners are Meetings, persuaded, as well from daily Observation as from the Reports of the Two Houses of Parliament during the last Session, that there has been, and still exists, an internal and traitorous Conspiracy, threatening the vital Interests of these Realms; a Conspiracy the more formidable, as its Approaches have been systematical and regular, branching out into various Classes and Societies united by secret League and Correspondence, and acting in Concert for the more effectual Propagation of the same seditious Principles: By these Schools and Seminaries of Disloyalty, more dangerous from the Union than the Number of their Members, who exert, in the Prosecution of their Designs, a Zeal and Activity, which might be creditable in a better Cause, those inflammatory Writings have been lately issued, and those intemperate Harangues at Public Meetings been encouraged, which, if not restrained by the Wisdom of Parliament, the Petitioners apprehend may go well nigh the Ruin of our Constitution both in Church and State: That the Petitioners are the more convinced of the imminent Dangers of such Societies, from attending to the intimate and visible Connection between the Tendency of their Principles, and the late atrocious and desperate Attack upon the Person of their most gracious Sovereign: Feeling, moreover, that the Prevention of Crimes is more to be wished for than the Punishment of Offenders, the Petitioners observe, with Satisfaction, that the Vigilance of Parliament is wisely occupied in providing against those extensive and complicated Dangers, by the salutary Precautions of the Bill, now pending, for preventing seditious Meetings and Assemblies: In the Adoption of such timely and wise Precautions, the Petitioners are convinced that there is no essential Departure from the Spirit of the Constitution, or the Usage of our Ancestors; they recognize in it that saving Wisdom, which, by an Alteration of Parts maintains Consistency in the Whole, and deviates from Forms to preserve Essentials; they reject, with Indignation, that narrow-minded Policy which, in Times pregnant with Alarm, would refuse to the Executive Power additional temporary Sanctions and Securities proportionate to the Exigency of the Danger; and they trust that the Bill, now proposed to the Consideration of the House, a Bill which secures to the good Citizen the Exercise of his legal Rights, whilst it is a Curb upon the disloyal and seditious Subject, will be found adequate, as they are persuaded it is necessary, for the Remedy of the Evil: They pray therefore, That it may pass into a Law.

A Petition of the Inhabitants of the Ward of gate, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners feel the deepest Indignation and Abhorrence at the late most abominable Outrage on His Majesty's Person, and most earnestly hope the Perpetrators thereof will soon meet the Punishment justly due to so desperately criminal an Offence: That the Petitioners have observed also, with great Concern, the Attempts that have been made to disturb the Public Tranquillity, by various seditious Meetings and Publications, which have lately multiplied in the Metropolis and its Environs, obviously tending to poison the Minds of the People, and excite them to Acts of Outrage and Disorder; and the Petitioners cannot help expressing their Concern and Surprize at an Attempt to pass a Censure on the Conduct of John William Anderson, Esquire, Alderman of their Ward, in a Petition presented to the House, purporting to be from their said Ward; whereat the Petitioners beg to assure the House, that the Duties of a Magistrate have never been on every Occasion, more ably or honourably performed than by their present said Magistrate: The Petitioners therefore humbly entreat the House to adopt such Measures, for a limited Time, as, in their Wisdom, shall be deemed most expedient for the better Security of His Majesty's Person and Government, and for preventing all tumultuous and seditious Meetings.

A Petition of the Inhabitants of the Borough and Foreign of Kidderminster, in the Parish of Kidderminster, and County of Worcester, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Inhabitants of the said Borough and Parish have been, in all Ages, distinguished for their Attachment to the Crown, and for their Regard to the Constitution: That on the late atrocious Attack on the Person of His Majesty, the Petitioners were ready in testifying their Indignation at the daring Attempt, and their Gratitude to the King of Kings for preserving a Life so dear to every loyal Heart: That, influenced by these Principles of Constitutional Loyalty and Patriotism, the Petitioners view with great Alarm Two Bills introduced into the House, the first intituled, A Bill for the Safety and Preservation of His Majesty's Person and Government against treasonable and seditious Practices and Attempts; the second, A Bill for the more effectually preventing seditious Meetings and Assemblies: That, in the former, they see, with the most serious Concern, a Revival of those Attempts to increase the Catalogue of Treasons which were made in former Ages by weak and arbitrary Administrations, with equal Danger to the Safety of the Monarch, and the Liberty of the Subject; but which a wiser Policy constantly restricted by recurring to the only beneficial Statute on that Subject, a Statute sanctioned by the Experience of more than Four hundred Years — that

Vol. 51.

of the Twenty-fifth of Edward the Third: That the Petitioners consider the second Bill as subversive of the Fifth Article of the Bill of Rights, of that solemn Compact made at the Resolution, between the King and the People, for the Establishment of the Religion, Laws, and Liberties of this Country, which acknowledges the Right of Subjects to petition, and declares all Commitments and Prosecutions for such petitioning illegal: That, above all, the Petitioners are apprehensive that the present Uneasiness may be traced to a higher Cause than that which is represented as productive of Public Danger; they therefore implore the House, as Citizens, as Christians, and as Men, to take into their most serious Consideration the Circumstances of a War, which, whatever Difference of Opinion may exist on its Principles, must be acknowledged to have been ill conducted in its Progress, and calamitous and ruinous in its Consequences — That, conceiving the Restoration of Peace to be better calculated to allay the Public Discontents, by diminishing the Public Burthens, than the most coercive Regulations, they humbly hope that the House will urge the Necessity of treating with the Executive Power of France, under whatever Form it may be established, on safe and honourable Terms: And, particularly, as the more immediate Object of this Address, they most earnestly entreat. That the Bills, which they deprecate, may not receive the Sanction of the House.

A Petition of the thereunder-signed Merchants, Tradesmen, and other Inhabitants, of the Town of Kilsyth, in the County of Stirling, was likewise presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are of Opinion, that it is the sacred and inviolable Right of every Briton to meet and deliberate freely on any Public Measure, particularly on what concerns their Rights and Liberties, as settled at the Resolution in 1688 .-.Under the Influence of these Principles, the Petitioners feel their Hearts beat, with the most painful Emotions, when they reflect that the Bill now pending in Parliament, intituled, A Bill for the more effectually preventing seditious Meetings and Assemblies; is in its Nature evidently calculated to deprive us of the very Essence of these our invaluable Privileges: Along with the genuine Friends of Liberty and Order, the Petitioners abhor and detest all Irregularities and Excess, and mark, with Detestation, the late Insult offered to His Majesty, and are impressed with the deepest Sorrow, when they recollect that the Act of a few Individuals should be made a Pretext, by designing Ministers, to criminate the whole Nation, and bring it under the Bondage of the most oppressive Tyranny: The Petitioners therefore entreat that this, their humble Petition, may be taken into the most serious Consideration of the House, and, for the Sake of their Lives and Liberties, they pray, That the said destructive Bill may not pass into a Law.

And the Question being put. That the said Clause be brought up;

It passed in the Negative.

Another ingrossed Clause was offered to be added to the Bill by Way of Ryder, declaring, that no Payment to a Schoolmaster shall be deemed a Payment of Money for Admission to Lectures within the Meaning of this Act

And the said Clause was Thrice read; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the Bill, by Way of Ryder.

Then the Amendments following were severally proposed to be made to the Bill; viz.

Pr. 16. 1. 20. After " Discourses" to insert shall " be delivered, or public Debate " shall be had."

1. 25. To leave out from " Kingdoms" to " for," in 1. 27.

Pr. 18. 1. 4. After " aforesaid " to insert " knowing such House, Room, Field,

" or Place to be opened or used " for such Purpose."

And the said Amendments were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House; and the Bill was amended at the Table accordingly.

The Amendments following were also proposed to be made to the Bill; viz.

Pr. 24. 1. 7. To leave out " for Three Years"

and insert " until the 25th Day " of March 1797" instead thereof.

And the Question being put, That the Words " for Three Years" stand Part of the Bill;

It was resolved in the Affirmative.

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, That the Bill do pass;

A Petition of the Weavers and others, Inhabitants of the City of Coventry, who were prevented from signing the Petition presented to the House against the Two Bills now pending in Parliament, on Account of the Shortness of the Time allowed for that Purpose, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners beg leave to represent to the House the great Concern they feel for the Prosperity of the Nation and the Liberty of British Subjects: and, being alarmed at the Bills now pending in Parliament, the one intituled, An Act for the Safety of His Majesty's Person and Government against seditious and treasonable Attempts; the other, An Act for die more effectually preventing seditious Meetings and Assemblies; which Bills, in the Petitioners Apprehension, Btrike at the Root of British Freedom, by depriving the Subject of his dearest Rights, the liberty of free Discussion: They humbly pray, That the House will not permit the said Bills to pass into a Law, the existing Laws being, in the Petitioner's Opinion, fully adequate for the Security of His Majesty's Person, the Preservation of good Government, and the Happiness of the People.

Resolved, That the Bill do pass: And that the Title be, An Act for the more effectually preventing seditious Meetings and Assemblies.

Ordered, That Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer do carry the Bill to the Lords, and desire their Concurrence.

The Order of the Day being read, for the Third Reading of the Bill (now ingrossed) to continue, for a further Time to be limited, an Act, made in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act to prohibit, " for a limited Time, the making of Low Wines or " Spirits from Wheat, Barley, Malt, or any other Sort " of Gram, or from any Meal, Flour, or Bran; and for permitting Home-made Spirits, deposited in the " Warehouses for Exportation, to be taken out for " Home Consumption, on Payment of Duty and to prohibit the Distillation of Spirits from Potatoes;

And the House having continued to sit till near Three of the Clock on Friday Morning;

Ordered, That the said Bill be read the Third Time this Day.

The other Orders of the Day being read;

Ordered, That the Report from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty, be received this Day.

Ordered, That the Report from the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill to prevent Obstructions to the free Passage of Grain, and of other Provisions, within the Kingdom, was committed, be received this Day.

And then the House adjourned till this Morning, Eleven of the Clock.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, Freeholders, and Inhabitants of the Town of Sunderland near the Sea, in the County of Durham, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have observed, with inexpressible Anxiety, the frequency of seditious Meetings and Assemblies within these Kingdoms, and conceive that to the Fermentation Excited in the Public Mind by such Assemblies may be justly imputed the late atrocious, but happily unsuccessful, Attempt on the Life of our beloved Sovereign; and that the Petitioners have learnt, with infinite Satisfaction, that a Bill has been brought into the House for the Purpose of preventing such Seditious Conventions, which, should they be permitted, would indisputably operate to the Introduction of Anarchy and Confusion, and to the Destruction of all Order and good Government within these Realms: That the Petitioners are under no Apprehension lest the Bill, now before the House, should at all interfere with the just Rights and Liberties of His Majesty's Subjects; and they rely, with full Confidence, on the Wisdom and Integrity of the Legislative Body: And humbly pray, That the most effectual Measures may be taken, by a Law' enacted for that Purpose, that the late tumultuous Proceedings, wdiich have disgraced this Country, may be suppressed, and that the treasonable Designs of Faction may be disappointed.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for regulating the Conveyance of printed Votes, Proceedings in Parliament, and printed Newspapers, by the Post, in Great Britain: And that Mr. Bernard, Sir William Young, and Mr. Garthshore, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Ordered, That the Order of the Day, for the Second Reading of the Bill to amend so much of an Act, made in the Ninth Year of the Reign of King George the First, intituled, "An Act for amending the Laws " relating to the Settlement, Employment, and Relief of the Poor," as prevents the distributing occasional Relief to Poor Persons in their own Houses, under certain Circumstances and in certain Cases, be now read.

And the said Order being read accordingly;

The said Bill was read a Second Time.

Resolved, That the Bill be committed.

Resolved, That the Bill be committed to a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Monday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the said Bill.

A Petition of the Mayor, Jurats, and Freemen, and other Inhabitants, of the ancient Town of Rye, and its Neighbourhood, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners beg Permission humbly to intrude on the most serious Deliberations of the House, and to express their Hopes and Prayer, That the Two Bills now pending in Parliament, the one intituled, A Bill for the Security of His Majesty's Person and Government, the other, A Bill for the more effectually preventing seditious Meetings and Assemblies; so necessary, in their Opinion, to the Safety of His Majesty's Person, Crowm, and Dignity,

and to the Protection of the existing Government of this Country, may pass into a Law: That the Peti- , tioners, having full and entire Confidence in the Wis- dom and Loyalty of the House, should not have presumed to have offered their Opinions or Petition, had not a Petition from several of the Inhabitants of the said Town been obtained, by Misrepresentation, against the said Bills, and without any Public Notice having been given of the said Petition.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Petition in A Petition of the Inhabitants of the Borough of favour of the Penryn, in the County of Cornwall, was presented to Sat'etf° of the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Peti-I^ Majesty's loners, impressed with the highest Veneration for that Person, Ac.; Constitution under which this Nation has so long ami for pre- happily flourished, beg Leave to approach the House tiousMeet-1* firmest Reliance on its Wisdom, Integrity,

iilfcr3 and Firmness, in the Preservation and Protection of

their dearest Rights and Liberties: That the Petitioners, were struck with the greatest Horror at the late atrocious Attempt on the Life of the best of Sovereigns, an Attempt evidently connected with, and springing from those abominable Principles so openly and daringly avowed by wicked and desperate Persons, who, associating together, under the specious Pretence of reforming the Government, and who, abusing the sacred Names of Liberty and Patriotism, aim only at the Destruction of our glorious and happy Constitution, and the Introduction of Anarchy and Confusion: That, under these Impressions, the Petitioners beg Leave to express their Approbation of the Principle of the Bills, now before Parliament, for the Prevention of Treasons and Seditious Meetings, convinced that the Restrictions proposed by them are calculated for the Protection of the Life of the Sovereign, and the inestimable Rights and Liberties of Englishmen, and will be felt as a Grievance only by those whose Principles and Attempts are treasonable and hostile to the Welfare of their Country: And therefore praying, That the said Bills may pass into Laws.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the thereunder-signed Freeholders of Petition Yorkshire, was presented to the House, and read; Set- ting forth, That, by the Fifth Article of the Bill of safety of Rights, the People of this Land are entitled to the His Majesty's Privileges of free Discussion, and free Petition to the Person, &c.; Legislature — those Rights, like every other Political Right, are liable to be abused; but, if they have been tious Meet-abused by any rash and misguided Individuals, the togs. Petitioners conceive, that, for the Fault of a few desperate Persons, the whole People of England ought not, and justly cannot, forfeit those invaluable Privileges, and such Forfeiture would be more especially grievous, when their general Loyalty, their Love of Order and Tranquillity, and their Attachment to the Constitution, are certain and unquestionable: The Petitioners have seen, therefore, with Grief and Astonishment, that Two Bills, one of which is intituled, An Act for the Safety and Preservation of His Majesty's Person and Government against treasonable and seditious Practices and Attempts; the other, A Bill for the more effectually preventing seditious Meetings and Assemblies; have been offered to Parliament by His Majesty's Ministers in the present Session, by which the Petitioners humbly conceive such Restraints are proposed to be laid on the Exercise of our Rights of free Discussion, and free Petition to the Legislature, as would u amount,

having informed the Chancellor of the Exchequer of his Readiness to treat for the Loan, he was invited to the Treasury on the said 25th Day of November last, which Day was fixed for the Communication of the Nature and Extent of the Loan, in order that the intended Bidders might be fully prepared against the Time fixed for the Bidding, which was the Friday following: That the said James Morgan was then, for the first Time, requested to declare whether he would agree to bid for the Loan, on Condition that the Offer, made by him (should it turn out to be the most advantageous for the Public) should be at the Option of Messrs. Boyd and others, the Contractors for the last Loan, to supersede by offering to advance the Money at a Rate more advantageous to the Public, by Half per Cent, or Ten Shillings on every One Hundred Pounds to be borrowed: That the Petitioners represent that, in their Minds, there cannot exist any good or sufficient Reason why such Preference ought to be given to the Contractors for the last Loan, more especially as they are informed that many of the Persons who furnished the last Loan to Government, as standing on the List of Messrs. Boyd and others, the then Contractors, are not the same Persons as are upon their List for the present Loan; and that, in Case it should appear that any Terms were made on the Contract for the last Loan, those Terms could only apply to the same Persons with whom such Terms were made, or who were liable to be affected thereby: They further represent to the House, that, relying in full Confidence on a fair Competition being allowed in offering to make the Loan to the Public, they have been induced to prepare large Sums of Money, ready to be applied to the Use of the Public, should the Offer, made on their Part, have been found the most advantageous: That the Plan of a Competition being destroyed by the Conditions stipulated in favour of the Contractors for the last Loan, they have been deprived of an Opportunity of making any Bidding for the Loan, which Opportunity, they humbly insist, they were entitled to, as well from the declared Terms of a Competition being allowed, as of the great Benefit to arise to the Country therefrom, whereby the Petitioners have sustained great Injury, not having any Provision made for the Ke-investment of their Money, by them necessarily called in to be prepared to make the usual Deposit, and such Payments as might be fixed for an early Period: That, in regard the Petitioners are advised that the Contracts made by the Chancellor of the Exchequer for all Public Loans are upon Condition of the Sanction of Parliament for the Terms thereof: The Petitioners therefore, for the Reasons before stated, most humbly pray the House will not sanction the Contract made with Messrs. Boyd and others for the Loan for the ensuing Year, and that the Petitioners may be heard, by Counsel, in Support of this their Petition.

A Petition of the thereunder-signed Inhabitants of the Town and Neighbourhood oi Huddersfield, in the GEORGE R.

County of York, was also presented to the House, and His Majesty thinks proper to acquaint the House read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners approach the of Commons, that a considerable Sum is likely to arise

House with Sentiments of unfeigned Attachment to the Principles of the Constitution established by the glorious Resolution of 1688: That the Petitioners have seen, with Indignation, the Principles of that Constitution violated by the atrocious Insults lately offered to the Person of His Majesty; but that the Petitioners view, with the most serious Alarm, the Introduction of Two Bills into Parliament, the one intituled, An Act for the Safety and Preservation of His Majesty's Person and Government against treasonable and seditious Practices and Attempts; the other. An Act for the more effectually preventing seditious Meetings and Assemblies; the obvious Tendency of which is to invest the Magistrates with new and arbitrary Powers; to introduce new Penal Laws and constructive Treasons; and to build, on the Ruins of our dearest Rights, a System incompatible with any free Constitution whatever: That the Petitioners consider the said Bills as unnecessary, impolitic, and unconstitutional; unnecessary, because the existing Laws are adequate as well to the Detection as to the Punishment of Offenders; impolitic, because they will lessen that Confidence which should subsist between the People and their Representatives, and that Respect which is due to the Magistrates and the Laws; and unconstitutional, because they tend to frustrate the Provisions of the Bill of Rights, to deprive the People of the Privileges of Petition and Remonstrance, to . prevent the House from being informed of the Wishes of its Constituents, to extend the Influence of the Executive Power, and, by restraining the Constitutional Exercise of Political Discussion, to surrender into its Hands the Bulwarks of Popular Liberty: And therefore die Petitioners most humbly entreat the House not to permit the said Bills to become the Laws of the Realm.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table.

Mr. Ryder reported from the Select Committee, w'ho Second Re-were appointed to take into Consideration the present Port froni high Price of Corn, and to collect Evidence relative thereto, and to report the same, from Time to Time, as pointed)® it should appear to them, to the House, with their consider the Observations thereupon; That the Committee had made high Price a further Progress in the Matters to them referred, and had directed him to report the same, together with their Observations thereupon, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

The Select Committee appointed to take into Consideration the present high Price of Comr and to collect Evidence relative thereto, and to report the same, from Time to Time, as it shall appear to them, to the House, with their Observations thereupon;

Have received, since their last Report, further Information respecting the Deficiency in the Crop of Rye, and the great Want of that Article in those Parts of the Country where it forms the principal Subsistence of the People; and they are thereby induced to think, that similar Measures ought to be adopted for the Encouragement of the Importation of that Species of Grain, as have been recommended respecting Wheat. They beg Leave therefore to submit their Opinion to the House, that a Bounty of Ten Shillings per Quarter should be given for every Quarter of Rye, weighing not less than 50per Bushel, which shall be imported into Great Britain before the 30th Day of September 1796, until the Quantity of such Rye ' shall equal 100,000 Quarters; and also that a Bounty of Six Shillings per Quarter should be given for every Quarter of Rye which shall be imported into Great Britain before the 30th Day of September 1796, exceeding the Quantity to which the before-mentioned Bounty is limited.

Your Committee are also inclined to reepmmend an Extension of the Period for which the several Bounties on Grain and Flour are proposed to be granted.

They observe, from the Weekly Returns of the Price of Wheat in the whole Kingdom, and of the Price and Quantity in the London Market, since January last, that the highest Price and the greatest Scarcity took place during the Months of July and August, and particularly in the latter. These, therefore, are the Months for which it is most important to provide; and they are led to fear, that if the Bounty is confined to such Corn as may arrive before the 31st of August,

Merchants may be discouraged from sending Supplies j

to this Country during that Month, by the Apprehension

3 E that

198 8° Decembris. A. 1795.

that they may not arrive in Time to be entitled to the Bounty. They beg Leave therefore to suggest an Extension of the Time to the 30th of September; and they submit, whether it might not also be expedient to place, in proper Hands, a discretionary Power of allowing the Bounties to such Ships as may arrive before the 15th of October, upon Proof of their having actually set Sail for Great Britain, from their respective Ports, at such Time that they might, in the ordinary Course of their Voyage, have arrived before the 30th of September.

Your Committee have also received a Suggestion, from Merchants trading to the Southern Parts of Europe and to Africa, that it would be advisable to enlarge the Quantity to which the highest Bounty upon Corn brought from those Quarters, was proposed to be limited: They do not state an Expectation that the Whole of that Quantity can be procured; but they are apprehensive that the original Limitation may tend to check Speculation, by the Fear of exceeding the Quantity specified — and they propose, therefore, that the highest Bounty should be extended to 400,000 Quarters.

Your Committee have also examined several Merchants, respecting the Proportion which the Bounty upon Flour ought to bear to that upon Wheat: They have been satisfied by this Examination that, in Consideration of the various Size and Weight of the Barrels used in different Countries, it would be more advisable to grant a Bounty upon the Hundred Weight of Flour than upon the Barrel, as had been at first suggested: That it is expedient to adopt, upon the Importation of Wheat and Wheat Flour, the same Proportion of Bounties which has been already established by the Legislature upon the Exportation of the same, (i.e.) One Shilling and Six Pence per Hundred Weight of Wheat Flour as equivalent to Five Shillings per Quarter of Wheat; and that the same Rule ought to be applied to Indian Corn and Meal.

In suggesting in their former Report that the Bounty given on Wheat ought to be limited to such as weighed not less than at the Rate of 55 per Bushel, your Committee proceeded upon Information then received, that Wheat of a lower Weight was usually of so inferior a Quality, as to be unfit for the Use of Man; and under a full Persuasion of the Necessity of fixing some Limit, in order to prevent tire Object, for which the Bounty is given, from being defeated by the Importation of Corn inapplicable to the Subsistence of the People. They have since received further Information, which has satisfied them, that Wheat, naturally of somewhat a lower Weight, may produce wholesome Food; and that Cargoes, not unfrequently, arrive out of Condition, in consequence of which the Weight is for the Time diminished, though it soon recovers; and that it might prove an inconvenient Restraint upon Speculation, if the Merchant were exposed to lose the Whole of the Bounty, by a slight Inattention of his Agents abroad, or by a temporary and accidental Deterioration of the Article imported: They are therefore of Opinion, that a Bounty, equal to Four Fifths of the proposed Bounty, should be given on all Wheat weighing not less than at the Rate of 531, per Bushel.

Your Committee having stated such further Observations as they have thought necessary, respecting the Amount of the Bounties, and the Limitations as to Weight and Quantity, and Time, beg Leave to recommend, for the Prevention of Fraud, that all Corn and Flour imported for Bounty, should be subject, in Addition to the Inspection of the proper Officers of the Customs, to the Examination of Persons qualified to judge thereof; that without the Certificate of such Persons, stating that the Article is merchantable and fit for making Bread, no Bounty should be paid; find that the Importation of Corn add Flour for

Bounty, should be confined to such Ports in which it is probable that Persons so qualified may be found.

Your Committee have also received Information, that there are Ships now in the Port of this Country laden with Corn, which are intended to be reported for Exportation; and that other Ships may arrive, the Consignees of which may send their Cargoes to Foreign Ports, unless tempted by the Bounty to unload them here; and they beg Leave, therefore, to submit the Expediency of extending the Bounty to the Cargoes of all Ships which may now be in the Ports of this Country, or may arrive here previous to the passing of the Act by which it is to be granted.

Ordered, That the said Report be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of the present hitjh Price of Corn.

Ordered, That such a Number of Copies of the said Report be printed, as shall be sufficient for the Use of the Members of the House.

Ordered, That the Order of the Day, for the Call of the House, be now read.

A Motion was made, and the Question being put. That the said Order be discharged;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, the several Rates and Duties on Vellum, Parchment, or Paper, upon which any Receipt, or the Discharge for any Legacy left by any Will or other Testamentary Instrument, or for any Share or Part of a Personal Estate divided by force of the Statute of Distributions, or the Custom of any Province or Place, shall be ingrossed, written, or printed (and which said Duties were granted by several Acts of Parliament made in the Twentieth, Twenty-third, and Twenty-ninth Years of the Reign of His present Majesty) shall cease and determine.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, a Duty be charged upon every Legacy, and upon every Share or Residue of the Personal Estate of any Person dying and leaving such Estate of the clear Value of One hundred Pounds or upwards, which shall pass either by Devise, or by force of the Statute of Distributions, or the Custom of any Province or Place, to any of the Kindred of the Deceased in tire several Degrees herein after mentioned, according to the Rates following, that is to say: Where any Legacy, or any Share or Residue of any such Personal Estate, shall pass to a Brother or Sister of the Deceased, or to any the Issue of a Brother or Sister of the Deceased, there shall be charged a Duty of Two Pounds for every hundred Pounds of the Value thereof, and after that Rate for any greater or less Sum or Quantity: Where any Legacy, or any Share or Residue of any such Personal Estate, shall pass to a Brother or Sister of a Parent of the Deceased, or to any the Issue of a Brother or Sister of a Parent of the Deceased, there shall be charged a Duty of Three Pounds for every hundred Pounds of the Value thereof, and after that Rate for any greater or less Sum or Quantity: And where any Legacy, or any Share or Residue of any such Personal Estate, shall pass to any the Issue of a Brother or Sister of a Grandfather of Grandmother of the Deceased, there shall be charged a Duty of Four Pounds for every hundred Pounds of the Value thereof, and after that Rate for any greater or less Sum or Quantity.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, a Duty of Six Pounds be charged for every hundred Pounds of the Value of any Legacy, or any Share or Residue of the Personal Estate of any Person dying and leaving such Estate of the clear Value of One hundred Pounds, or upwards, which shall pass either by Devise, or by force of the Statute of Distributions, or the Custom of any Province or Place, to any Person in any more distant Degree of Collateral Consanguinity to the Deceased, than is before charged, or to any Stranger in Blood to the Deceased, and after that Rate for any greater or less Sum or Quantity.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, a Duty be charged upon the clear Value of any Real Estate that, upon the Death of any Person, shall descend, or pass by Devise, or by force of any Gift, Grant, or Conveyance, or by Act or Operation of Law, to, or to the Use of, or in Trust for, any Person or Persons of the Kindred of the Deceased in the several Degrees herein after mentioned (except Purchasers for valuable Consideration actually paid) in Fee Simple, Fee Tail, or for Term of Life or Lives, according to the Rates following, that is to say: Where any such Estate shall pass to a Brother or Sister of the Deceased, or to any the Issue of a Brother or Sister of the Deceased, there shall be charged a Duty of Two Pounds for every hundred Pounds of the Value thereof, and after that Rate for any greater or less Sum or Quantity: Where any such Estate shall pass to a Brother or Sister of a Parent of the Deceased, or to any the Issue of a Brother or Sister of a Parent of the deceased, there shall be charged a Duty of Three Pounds for every hundred Pounds of the Value thereof, and after that Rate for any greater or less Sum or Quantity: And where any such Estate shall pass to any the Issue of a Brother or Sister of a Grandfather or Grandmother of the Deceased, there shall be charged a Duty of Four Pounds for every hundred Pounds of the Value thereof, and after that Rate for any greater or less Sum or Quantity.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, a Duty of Six Pounds be charged for every hundred Pounds of the clear Value of any Real Estate that, upon the Death of any Person, shall descend, or pass

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to llis Majesty, every Person who shall keep, and use, any Horse, Mare, or Gelding, for the Purpose of riding, or for the Purpose of drawing any Coach, Berlin, Landau, Chariot, Calash, Chaise, or any other Carriage, by whatsoever Name such Carriage is now, or hereafter may be, called or known (for or in respect, whereof any Rate or Duty heretofore under the Management of the Commissioners of Excise, and now transferred to and under the Management of the Commissioners for the Affairs of Taxes is payable) shall be charged with a further additional Annual Duty of Ten Shillings for each such Horse, Mare, or Gelding.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, every Person who shall keep Two Horses, Mares-, or Geldings, and no more, for the Purpose of riding, or for the Purpose of drawing any Coach, Berlin, Landau, Chariot, Calash, Chaise, or any other Carriage, by whatsoever Name such Carriages now are, or hereafter may be, called or known, shall be charged with a further additional Annual Duty of Live Shillings for One of such Horses, Mares, or Geldings.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, every Person who shall keep Three, Four, or Five Horses, Mares, or Geldings, and no more, for the Purpose of riding, or for the Purpose of drawing any Coach, Berlin, Landau, Chariot, Calash, Chaise, or any other Carriage, by whatsoever Name such Carriages now are, or hereafter maybe, called or known, shall be charged with a further additional Annual Duty of Seven Shillings and Six Pence for each Horse, Mare, or Gelding, exceeding the Number of One.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, every Person who shall keep Six or more Horses, Mares, or Geldings, for the Purpose of riding, or for the Purpose of drawing any Coach, Berlin, Landau, Chariot, Calash, Chaise, or any other Carriage, by whatsoever Name such Carriages now are, or hereafter may be, called or known, shall be charged with a further additional Annual Duty of Ten Shillings for each Horse, Mare, or Gelding, exceeding the Number of One.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, every Person who shall keep any Horse, Mare, or Gelding, not charged with any former Rate or Duty, or any Colt or Filley, or any Mule, shall yield and pay Annually a Duty of Two Shillings for each such Horse, Mare, Gelding, Colt, Filley, or Mule.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, the several Duties on Persons exercising the Trade and Business of an Horse Dealer, and who shall take out a Licence to use and Exercise the Trade and Business of an Horse Dealer, imposed by an Act of the Twenty-fourth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, shall cease and determine.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, every Person exercising the Trade or Business of an Horse Dealer within the City of London, or the City or Liberties of Westminster, the Weekly Bills of Mortality, the Parishes of S Mary le Bone or Saint Pancras, in the County of Middlesex, or the Borough of Southxcark, in the County of Surrey, and who shall

take out a Licence to use and exercise the said Trade and Business of an Horse Dealer, shall yield and pay Annually the Sum of Twenty Pounds.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, every Person exercising the Trade and Business of an Horse Dealer without the City of London, and City and Liberties of 1 Pest mins terthe Weekly Bills of Mortality, the Parishes of Mary le Bone and

Saint Pancras, in the Cquuty of Middlesex, and the Borough of Southwark, in the County of Surrey, and who shall take out a Licence to use and exercise the said Trade anil Business of an Horse Dealer, shall yield and pay Annually the Sum of Ten Pounds.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, an additional Excise Duty of One Penny Farthing be charged for every Yard Square of Paper which shall be printed, painted, or stained, in Great Britain, to serve for Hangings, or other Uses (over and above the Duties payable for such Paper before the printing, painting, or staining thereof) and so in Proportion for any greater or lesser Quantity.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, an additional Excise Duty of Five Pence be charged for every Yard in Length, reckoning Yard Wide, of Foreign Callicoe and of Foreign Muslin, which shall be printed, stained, painted, or dyed, in Great Britain (except such as shall be dyed throughout of One Colour only) and so in Proportion for any greater or lesser Quantity.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, an additional Excise Duty of Two Pence Halfpenny be charged for every Yard in Length, reckoning Yard Wide, of all Linens, and of all Stuffs made either of Cotton or Linen, mixed with other Materials, Fustians, Velvets, Velverets, Dimities, and other figured Stud's, made of Cotton and other Materials, mixed, or wholly made of Cotton Wool wove in Great Britain, which shall be printed, stained, painted, or dyed, in Great Britain (except such as shall be dyed throughout of One Colour only, and Stuffs made of Woollen, or whereof the greatest Part in Value shall be Woollen) and so in Proportion for any greater or lesser Quantity.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, an additional Excise Duty of Tw'o Pence Halfpenny be charged for every Yard in Length, reckoning Yard Wide, of Stuffs wholly made of Cotton Wool, wove in Great Britain, commonly called British Manufactory, and of British Muslins, which shall be printed, stained, painted, or dyed, in Great Britain (except such as shall be dyed throughout of One Colour only) and so in Proportion for any greater or lesser Quantity.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Allowance for Waste on White and Rock Salt, carried Coastwise, be discontinued.

The First Resolution of the Committee being read a Second Time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

The Second Resolution of the Committee being read a Second Time, several Amendments were proposed to be made thereunto, by leaving out the Words " Six Shillings and Six Pence," in that Part of the Resolution where it is said, that the Contributor is to be entitled to an Annuity to that Amount, and inserting the Words " Four Shillings and Six Pence" instead thereof.

And the Question being put, That the Words " Six " Shillings and Six Pence" stand Part of the said Resolution;

It was resolved in the Affirmative.

Then the said Resolution was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

The subsequent Resolutions of the Committee being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

The other Orders of the Day being read;

A Petition of the Inhabitants of the Town and Neighbourhood of Taunion, convened by Public Advertise-

ment the 30th Day of November 1795, to prevent the selling of Wheat by Sample, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, sensible of the Imposition to which the Community at large is exposed, and impressed with Concern for the Hardships and Sufferings experienced by the lower Orders of Society from the present exorbitant Price of Wheat, beg Leave to approach the House, and submit to their Consideration the few following Particulars: The Petitioners conceive it to be an incontrovertible Maxim, that the Value or Rise and Fall of any Commodity should be in proportion to its Scarcity or Abundance; in the present Instance it is fortunate that the Degree of Scarcity of Wheat can be pretty accurately ascertained — It appears, from the best Authorities, the Returns of the Magistrates to the Lord Lieutenants of the different Counties, that the Failure of the Crop this last Season may be set down at One-third of the usual Produce: Supposing the n, the Average Price of Wheat, in Years of common Fertility, to be Six Shillings per Bushel, in Compensation to the Farmer, for the Failure of this last Crop, Three Shillings ought to be added, and the present Price of Wheat will be Nine Shillings per Bushel, i. e. taken unconnected with any other Circumstance; but it appears also, by the authentic
