Mr. Giles again called in, and examined.

4G6. Had you any Conversations with Mr. Morgan, in October and November last, on the Subject of the expected Loan?

As to the Time, I can't exactly speak, but I think it was in November, Mr. Morgan called upon me at the Rank, and told me he had an Intention of making a List, and if I would be upon it, and my Friends, he would be very glad to have my Name; he then stated that in the Formation of his List he should subject every Subscriber to the signing a Letter that they should not be in any other List but his — I told him that if that was the Case I could not be in his List, for I had already engaged with the other Two Parties to be upon their List — he said, he would exempt me and my Friends from signing such a Letter — and then, or soon after, I gave him the List which I now deliver in.

Air. Morgan afterwards came and told me, if the Loan should be for Seventeen Alillions, I might take as far as 15,000l. more, and if Eighteen Alillions, 35,000l. more; which I assented to, but not for myself.

467. Did you, in any of these Conversations, give him any Information respecting the Manner in which (as you understood) the Chancellor of the Exchequer meant to settle the Loan, that is, whether by open Competition or otherwise ?

I could not do it when this Alatter was first talked of, because I did not know it; but I did afterwards, I believe on the 22d or 23d of November, tell him that it was to be by Competition, and we were to go up on Wednesday.

468. Did you at any Time express to Mr. JMorgan your Opinion that the Loan would not be settled by

open Competition, but that it would be given to Alessrs. Boyds ?

Certainly not in such Words as those — I confess that I did in private confidential Conversation, which I apprehend with Deference no Gentleman could deem himself justified in divulging, tell him that I had my Suspicions that Air. Boyd's Party would, or might, have a Preference.

469. At what Time ?

I believe I did repeatedly, but I don't recollect the Dates; but it was all previons to Monday the 23d Day

of November.

470. Upon what Grounds wrere your Suspicions formed ?

Aly Reasons were, that I conceived Air. Boyd's Party, in point of good Faith, had a Claim to some Preference from the Conditions stipulated at the making of the preceding Loan having been deviated from, and I thought them too sagacious to omit availing themselves of that Circumstance.

471. Did you state that Reason to Air. Morgan

No — I-don't know that I ever mentioned it to any

body — I did not to him.

472. Did you state to him any other Reason for your Suspicion ?

No; I don't recollect that I did; I had no other Reason.

473. Did you state to him that there had been a Aloney Transaction in the Course of the Summer to the Amount of 900,000l., in which Alessrs. Boyds had accommodated Government?

Certainly not; whether Air. Morgan first spoke to me of Treasury Bills, or I to him, I really don't know, but we had a Conversation about them, and I believe it was Air. Morgan who first mentioned them to me; I told him I knew nothing of the Transaction officially, but I had a great many of the Bills put into my Hands, and had discounted Two or Three of them in my private Capacity — Air. Morgan knew as much or more of the Transaction than I did, as it seemed to me by his Conversation.

474. Of what Nature were those Treasury Bills ?

If I recollect right, they were drawn by a Boyd, junior, dated at Hamburgh, to the Order of Boyd, Benfield, and Company, on the Commissioners of the Treasury, of different Dates, and accepted by Air. Long.

475. Was your own private Opinion, that a Preference w ould be given to Air. Boyd, in any Degree founded upon this Transaction ?

Had there been no other Reasons in my Alind, I should certainly have not suspected that any Preference would be given to Air. Boyd on that Account, but it was natural for me to think that it could not impede that Preference; I mean simply this, that it could not put him in a worse Situation.

476. Do you not think it put him in a better Situation ?

I really did not turn this in my Alind so as to have those distinct Ideas about it; I never went further in Conversation with Air. Morgan, than to say, in Effect, that I had my Suspicions, which I did repeatedly.

477. Did you ever in Conversation with Air. Morgan, upon the Subject of his Intention to become a Bidder for the Loan, say, that you thought that he would be tricked, or use Words to that Effect?

Never in my Life, to my Know ledge — but I can't be sure that I did not use such a Word, but if I did, it certainly was in a joking Way — but I don't recollect it.

36 Geo. III. 9° Febru 341

478. Did the Chancellor of the Exchequer, at any Time in the Course of the last Year, apply to the Bank for Money to be advanced in Anticipation of the last Loan ?

Neither last Year nor ever — I never knew such a Thing.

479. Do you recollect perfectly that Mr. Morgan said, he should subject every Subscriber to the signing a Letter that they should not be in any other List but his?

So I understood it, and he put a printed Form of a Letter in my Hand, and left it with me.

480. Did you not understand Mr. Morgan to allow the same Latitude or Indulgence to the Friends in your List, as to yourself, to be in the Lists of the other Parties offering for the Loan ?

Most certainly.

481. Were the Friends on your List all Directors of the Bank ?

No — about One Half were not.

482. Did you ever tell Mr. Morgan that you did not consider any Thing which passed at the settling of the Loan in November 1794, for the Service of the Year 1795, as a Pledge, or entitled to Weight in Favour of the Pretensions of Messrs. Boyd and Co. to have a Preference to the Negotiation for the Loan of 1796 ?

I don't recollect that I did — it is possible that I might say to Mr. Morgan, that Mr. Boyd's Party had some Right to claim a Preference, owing to this Loan being made before the other was extinct.

483. Did you ever say to Mr. Morgan that you thought they had not such a Right ?

No — never, certainly.

484. In any of those Conversations with Mr. Morgan to which you have alluded, did he express to you his Opinion, that the Transaction of the Hamburgh Bills would be productive of any Degree of Preference to Messrs. Boyds in the Negotiation for the Loan ?

No, never — and I believe that Mr. Morgan never suspected that Messrs. Boyd would have a Preference at all, I believe he always thought it would be by Competition.

485. In the several Public Loans which you have known, has it or has it not been understood by the Parties, that no Second Loan should take place till after the last Payment of the former, or that if political Events should render such Second Loan necessary, the former Contractors had a Right to a Refusal of that Second Loan, or to some other adequate Compensation ?

I don't recollect any Loan made for the Receipts to come out before the others were totally extinct — Mr. Newland looked back a great Way, but since the Establishment of the Bank, no new Loan has been made when two Payments of the preceding One were not fulfilled, as in the present Case.

486. On what Days were those Two last Payments to be made on the Loan for 1795 ?

On the 27th of November and the 15th of January — and there were 3,356,265/. floating Receipts, of the English and Imperial Loan, in the Market on the 24th of November.

I had no particular Communication with them on that Subject, I was in the Room with the rest of the Gentlemen — I thought in my own Mind they would not accept of it — I should not in their Place have accepted of the Proposal.

499. Do the principal Contractors for Loans ever deliver the Scrip Receipts to the Persons on their Lists till they have made the Deposit on the first Payment ?

They have no Receipts to deliver — they give the Names of those Gentlemen upon their Lists to Mr. Nezvland, and those Gentlemen pay in the Deposit without Receipts, and have a Right to fetch the Receipts away when delivered.

500. Is not all Risk to the Contractors from the Sub-subscribers at an End when that Deposit has been made ?

Certainly not, for if the Loan was to fall under 10 per Cent, which is generally the Amount of the First Payment, the Contractors would undoubtedly be responsible to the Public — I have known it fall G per Cent.

302. Do you consider the Contractors, as to the Claim which you have mentioned, possess that Claim independently of the Subscribers?

I really should think so.

503. What Injury would the Contractors sustain from the Negotiation of a new Loan, previous to the last Payments on the preceding one ?

That would depend on the Quantity of Stock which they had left.

304. Would not that apply equally to the Subscribers ?

Yes, if they had their Stock remaining.

505. Do you then think that the Contractors have a Right, on Account of the superior Risk which they incur, and of the Duties which they perform, to sanction or oppose a new Loan, previous to the Expiration of the Term of their Contract, without any Consideration of the Subscribers ?

I will not go so far as to say they have a Right, but I, as a Contractor, should think myself very unfairly dealt by, if Conditions were proposed and made at making of the Loan, which should afterwards be broken through.

306. If Mr. Boyd had stated to you that, in the Preference which he claimed for himself, he did not consider the Subscribers as entitled to any Share, or to any Compensation for any Injury they might sustain from the Introduction of a new Loan, should you have thought his Claim to such a Preference well founded ?

I should, as the Contractor for the last Loan.

507. Whether as a mere Subscriber, not a Contractor, if any of the Conditions made at the Time of making the Loan were broken through, should you not consider yourself in that Case entitled to complain?

If I had sold my Stock I should not trouble my Head about it — if I had not I should.

50S. Supposing the Contractors to have sold all their Stock, should you think that they had any Reason to complain ?

Certainly not — unless they felt for the rest of the People that had it — they could not be injured.

509. You have stated that Mr. having

searched in the Cooks of the Bank, had been able to find no Instance in which a new Loan had been negotiated whilst Two Payments on the former Loan remained to be made; did he find any Instance where only One Payment remained to be made?

lie could find none, where anew Loan was made, and the Receipts came out before all the Payments on the former.

510. When did you first converse with the Chancellor of the Exchequer, on the Subject of a Loan, for the Service of the Year 1796?

I believe it was on Monday the 23d of November.

511. Had the Chancellor of the Exchequer, in the Months of October or November, made any Reference to you on the Subject of Mr. Boyd's, Claim ?

Never till the 23th of November — I never heard of it before, nor ever suspected it — that is Mr. Boyd's Claim; but I had the Suspicion in my Mind, as before stated, that he had a Right to claim some Preference.

512. On the 23d of November did the Chancellor of the Exchequer declare to you, for the Information of the Parties who might intend to bid for the Loan, that it should be disposed of by public Competition ?

I asked him pointedly the Question, Whether it was to be by Competition, and he told me, certainly it would, and that I might tell the Gentlemen — and then my Suspicions were done away.

313. Did the Chancellor of the Exchequer at that Time know who were to be the Competitors?

I told the Chancellor of the Exchequer there would be but Three that I knew of; viz. Mr. Boyd's Party — Mr Mcllish — and Mr. JSIorgmi; and I added to him, that Mr. Jllorgan was very respectable in Point of Solidity and Character, but that he had not pour People to subscribe to the Obligation w'hen he made the Loan, and that in Lieu thereof he would pay into Mr. Nc:eland's Hands 330,000/4 or 400,000l., as a Deposit, which the Chancellor of the Exchequer was perfectly satisfied with.

514. Did the Chancellor of the Exchequer then state to you, that he was under an Engagement to admit Mr. Boyd and his Party to a Conference with him on the Subject of their Ciaim, previous to his receiving any other Competitors ?

No — he never said a Word about it.

I can't recollect the Date, but as soon as of any body else — I think it was in the Beginning of November that I received a Note from Mr. , inti-

Certainly I did, by Letter, but I was more on Mr. ]\Iorgans List than upon any of the other Two.

I conclude from Circumstances that it was — I have not a Doubt about it.

525. Do you mean that you conclude it from Circumstances that they were considerably more ?

No — I had no Guide to enable me to judge how much.

526. May it not frequently happen, the Parties may be so situated as to make it an Object to them to obtain the Loan on Terms more advantageous to the Public than the Chancellor of the Exchequer might propose ?

Certainly.

527. When did you first understand that the Chancellor of the Exchequer meant finally to settle the Loan on the 25th instead of the 27th of November ?

I understood it first on the 25th of November.

anti Mr. Morgan before they left Street on

No otherwise than by giving him the Price of the Stock of the Day — the Chancellor of the Exchequer then referred to some Papers, which I did not see; and then asked the Deputy Governor and me whether 65 I. was not a fair Price to put the 3 per Cents, at — I think I might say it was a fair Price — the Quantum of Long Annuities he settled himself — I think then the Chancellor of the Exchequer mentioned it would be raising the Money at about 4/. 13$. or Cent. No, not greatly — I think it ought always to be in their Favour.

The Chancellor of the Exchequer had the Reserve, and mentioned it.

Certainly something less.

No — Nobody but the Deputy Governor and myself, unless the Two Secretaries of the Treasury were there.

I don't recollect any particular Reply, but he seemed to me that he comprehended by that, he had in some Measure committed himself; nothing further passed on that Subject.

542. Was it not pretty generally understood, previous to the 23d of November, that the Loan would be for Sixteen Millions and upwards?

I never heard of more than Sixteen Millions — I heard it would be for that Sum.

543. Was not the Amount of the Navy Debt floating in the Market, generally understood about that Time to be about Five Millions ?

I never made a Calculation in my own Mind — if I had guessed it, I should have thought it more. — I never thought about it.

544. What Effect do you think the Power reserved of funding Five Millions of Navy Bills during the current Year, instead of paying them in Money, ought to have on the Terms of the Loan ?

I don't think it would have had much — perhaps One WdXiper Cent. — but I don't know what exact Sum to say.

545. Do you think that funding Five Millions of the Navy Bills payable in the Course of this Year out of the Money voted for the Services of the Year, instead of their being paid in ready Money, would have an Effect on the Terms of the Loan; and to what Extent?

Certainly that would; but to what Extent I am not competent to say.

546. Do you mean to say more than One Half per Cent. ?

Yes — I think so — much more.

547. Do you consider it to be the Knowledge that a Loan, to any given Extent, is coming into the Market, which affects the Price of the existing Funds, or merely the making the first Payment on such Loan after it is settled.

The Knowledge certainly.

548. Would the Bargain for a new Loan being concluded before the making of the last Payment on the preceding Loan, although the first Payment on that new Loan was not to take place till some Time after all the Payments on the former Loan should be completed, operate as strongly in affecting the Value of the Funds, as if the first Payment on such new Loan were to take place before those on the previous Loan should be completed ?

Certainly not.

549. Would not that depend chiefly on the Sum which remained to be paid up on the old Loan ?

In a Degree, certainly.

550. Are you, as a Director of the Bank, acquainted with any Thing which passed there respecting the Bills drawn from Hamburgh on the Treasury, before alluded to ?

I never knew any Thing of them officially — I am not a Director, and do not perform the Functions of one.

551. Has the Sum of Loan, allotted to be divided between the Governor and Deputy Governor of the Bank of England, been always the same as the present?

For the 3 or last Loans they have been the same — about 3 or Years ago, a Sum of 50,000l. each was given to them by the Contractors, independent of their Share of what is given to the Bank, and that has been continued ever since.

556. It has been stated, that the Chancellor of the Exchequer gave as a Reason why he applied to Mr. Boyd for an Anticipation of the Payments of the last Loan, that perhaps the Bank of England might not find it convenient to make it — <lo you understand what is meant by that Expression ?

As the Chancellor of the Exchequer never made an Application, I do not.

557. Do you think, from your Knowledge of the Circumstances attending the Advance made by Mr. Boyd, that the Treasury must have considered themselves as much indebted to him for the Accommodation ?

I don't know how to answer that Question — I fancy Mr. Boyd was most benefited by the Transaction; as I naturally apprehend, though I know nothing of the Matter, that Mr. Boyd might have some Commission, or other Profit.

558. Do you know whether any of the Hamburgh Bills were received as Cash in making the Deposit of the present Loan?

Certainly not — they could not have been; the Act of Parliament requires Money.

559. To the best of your Knowledge, were not the Transactions with respect to the Hamburgh Bills new and unprecedented ?

I never saw or knew of any such before.

560. Would or would not the Credit of any private

House be thought to suffer from Bills pretended to be drawn at Hamburgh, if such Bills were actually drawn in London ?

I should think so; and the Bills themselves I should think are invalid, by not being stamped.

561. Do you know whether any of those Bills were presented to the Bank to be discounted ?

I really can't tell.

562. Have you had Occasions to advert to the Circumstances relating to Public Loans for some Time past.

Yes — at different Times.

563. Do you recollect what has been the usual Interval between the fixing the Bargain and opening the Budget ?

I believe in general 2 or 3 Days — sometimes a Day more; and sometimes a Day less.

564. Before the Two last Loans, do you ever recol lect so long an Interval as 12 Days ?

Certainly not.

565. Does it occur to you, that any Advantage is likely to accrue to the Public from an Interval so unusually long?

I do not conceive there can.

566. Are you acquainted with the particular Cir cumstances which occasioned those Bills which were in Fact drawn or written in London, to be dated as from Hamburgh ?

I know no more of that, than what has been read to me as Part of Mr. Boyd's Evidence.

567. Do you mean to say that Bills bearing Date as at Hamburgh, though actually written in London, under all the Circumstances belonging to those particular Bills in Question, would be injurious to the Credit of a private Mercantile House?

I have not heard all the Circumstances.

568. Have you heard any Circumstances relative to the Transaction of these Hamburgh Bills, that would make you think differently with respect to them, from what you have expressed yourself to think of other Transactions of the like Description ?

No.

569. Would the Bank discount for any Commercial House whatever. Bills which were known to be drawn under the Circumstances which have been stated to belong to the Hamburgh Bills ?

I believe not.

570. Do you think that it is one of the Advantages attending Loans by Competition, that the Public generally obtain the Sum to be borrowed upon better Terms?

I should think so.

Christopher Terry, Esquire, called in, and examined.

672. Were you included in the List of Persons who intended to subscribe for the Loan under Mr. James Morgan ?

I was.

673. In consequence of Mr. Morgans Disappointment, were you deputed by any of the Subscribers to his List to wait on the Chancellor of the Exchequer?

At a General Meeting, a Committee was appointed, which Committee deputed me and Mr. Brawn to wait on the Chancellor of the Exchequer.

674. Can you state what passed at that Meeting?

I went with Mr. Brawn, on or about the 2d of December, to the Chancellor of the Exchequer — We stated to him the Reason of our Attendance, which was, that the Gentlemen of the Committee wished to represent their Grievances, owing to his not having allowed a Competition for the Loan — The Chancellor of the Exchequer, in Reply, related what had passed at the Meeting when Mr. Morgan attended for settling' the Preliminaries; and said, he wished to satisfy Mr. Brawn and me, that what he did was for the Benefit of the Public at large — he also read the Letter that he had received from Mr. Boyd, the Night previous to the intended Meeting: He said, after reading and considering it, he thought " that Mr. Boyd's " Claim deserved some Degree of Attention" — I think those were his very Words; but he acknowledged that in his Opinion, Mr. Boyd had no legal Preference. — -The Chancellor of the Exchequer said, he had wished to ascertain, whether any Agreement had been made, at the Time of making the former Loan, respecting Mr. Boyd's Claim; on which he consulted with the Governor of the Bank, with respect to any Conversation which had passed at the former Loan. — That the Governor of the Bank informed him that it had not been usual to make a new Loan till the last Payment of the former one was made. — The Chancellor of the Exchequer was asked, Whether it was his Intention to have settled the Loan on that Day ? — he said, that it was not — that his Reason for settling it on that Day was that Mr. Morgan and Mr. Mellish, having refused to become Competitors, he was left with the other Parties only — that he first consulted with the Governor and Deputy Governor of the Bank on the Terms, and then closed' with Mr. Boyd.

675. Have you any Reason to apprehend that a better Bargain would have been made for the Public, if Mr. Morgan had been admitted to a Competition for the Loan ?

I have Reason to think so.

676. Did you give to any Gentleman Authority to state in Parliament, that Mr. Morgan would have made an Offer by at least Two per Cent, more Advantageous for the Public, had he then been permitted to bid?

I did.

677. Was not that Authority derived in Part from Conversations with Mr. Morgan f

It was.

Appendix, N* 1.

Kensington Gore, N<nr. 16, 1795.

SIR,

I have the Honour to acquaint you, that, considering it to be your fixed Principle in all possible Cases to dispose of Loans by Competition; I have formed a List to enable me to offer for the ensuing Loan, to the Amount of 15 Millions, and to be extended if necessary — The Subscribers are about 400 real Stockholders, and monied Men, and are prepared to make the Payment. — I have at my Bankers upwards of 300,000l., and can have 200,000l. more at a Moment's Notice, to deposit as a Security. — It has been my Aim to have no Subscribers for large Sums, but to diffuse the Subscription; and I can with Confidence assure you, Sir, That the List is complete and proper for the Purpose, and will tend to advance the Price of the Contract. — And considering, that in conducting so important a Concern, it is proper for me to be prepared to meet all possible Events; and reflecting, that Circumstances may make it necessary, and Parliament may agree to guarantee a further Loan to be raised in England for his Majesty the Emperor; in that case, I am ready, on Behalf of my List of Subscribers, to conform to your own Conditions, by a positive or eventual Agreement: having entire Confidence that you always act with the best Intentions, and conformable to Justice, — I have the Honour to be,

SIR,

Your most

The R' HonWe Wm Pitt.

Appendix, N* 3.

Sir, Sackville Street, 24 November 1795.

We beg Leave to represent to you, on Behalf of ourselves and the other Contractors for the Loan of last Year, that the Contract was entered into under the Condition that no other Public Loan for this Country should be made, until the Period fixed for the last Payment of the Loan then contracted for should have elapsed.

4 X We

354

9° Februa

A. 1796.

Inquiry re- We conceive, that on this Account we have an un-specting the doubted Right to object to the Negotiation of the Loan Loan* now proposed to be contracted for, until the Period

assigned us for the Sale of our Scrip shall expire, viz. the 15th January next. This is not one of those Rights of which litigious People sometimes avail themselves, for the mere Purpose of giving Trouble — It is a Right which is founded in Justice, and the Nature of Things, recognized by constant Practice and public Opinion, and which we cannot relinquish without evident Loss. That this may appear to you perfecdy clear, we beg Leave to state, that there is at this Moment still floating in the Market the Value of Five Millions of Money in Scrip, which remains to be converted into Stock. Several of the Contractors for the last Loan are Holders of this Scrip, and they must inevitably sutler by the Introduction of Eighteen Millions more into the Market, while so large a Portion of last Year's Scrip is still on Hand.

While we thus assert our Right to prevent the Negotiation of the Loan now in Contemplation, we are loth to exercise this Right to, your Inconvenience, or to the Detriment of the Public, and are therefore willing to wave it, upon Condition that the Injury which must result from the Introduction of so large a Sum of Scrip into the Market, before (if we may so express ourselves) our exclusive Lease of the Market expires, be compensated to us by the Chance of Advantage to arise from the new Loan, on which Ground we presume to claim the Preference of contracting for it.

By the monied Powers of our Party we are enabled to give the highest Price that ought to be given, and we can assure you, with great Sincerity, that in the Event of your consenting to a private Negotiation, our Offer shall be fully as liberal as if we had no Preference whatever, and that it shall equal your Expectations.

We are aware that your Acquiescence in this Proposal must meet with Difficulty in your own Mind, on Account of your Predilection in Favour of public Competition; but to reconcile as much as possible the Principle of Competition with what we conceive to be our undoubted Right, we are willing to admit of it on the present Occasion to a certain Degree.

We are willing to allow the proposed Loan to be exposed to Competition, upon Condition that the Option shall be expressly reserved to our Party of taking the Loan at such a Price as shall be equal in Value to one Half per Cent, upon the whole Sum borrowed above the highest Offer of the Competitors.

If any solid Objections can be made to both these Proposals, we shall be happy to adopt any other Measure more agreeable to you, by which you may on the one Hand be secured against undue Advantage on our Part, and on the other we may preserve our Right, or obtain in lieu of it such a Preference as we conceive to be justly due to our particular Situation.

We have the Honour to be, with great Respect,

Sir,

Your most obedient humble Servants,

Walter Boyd. Abram. Robarts.

Rt. hon. William Pitt, &c. &c.

Appendix, N* 5.

(Copy.) Sackville Street, 23 November 1795. Sir,

Having heard that this Day had been appointed for an Interview' between you and the Persons intending to offer for the ensuing Loan, Mr. Robarts and I were upon our Way from the City to desire an Audience of you previous to your receiving the Candidates, when we learned at the Bank that the Meeting was put off till Wednesday.

I beg Leave to solicit, on the Part of Mr. Robarts and myself, as representing the whole Contractors for last Year's Loan, the Honour of an Interview with you as early Tomorrow' as may be consistent with your Convenience, that we may have an Opportunity of stating certain Circumstances peculiar to our Situation, which it is of great Importance should be well understood before any public Interview respecting another Loan takes place. I had, upon the Assurance that you gave me that you would send for our Party previous to any such Interview, acquainted them that they would not be deprived of a proper Opportunity of stating what they had to say, before any other Steps W'ould be taken about another Loan; and I was therefore mortified to find that a Meeting was on the Point of taking place, without any such previous Opportunity having been afforded them.

I have the Honour to be, &c.

(Signed)

Walter Boyd. The Right honble Will"1 Pitt.

Appendix, N* 6.

Kensington Gore, December 2 2d, 1795.

Sir,

Reflecting on the Question, if I would ask the Gentleman that I expected an Answer from on the 29th October, for Leave to give in his Name; it now appears to me, as the Circumstance was mentioned merely to account for my stopping on that Day to receive Subscriptions, that it is improper for me to make any Application, or in any Manner endeavour to involve Persons in Questions arising from a Transaction in which they have not been concerned, and have not the least Knowledge of There were a great many Offers and Applications as well as that attended to, which were refused or rejected on various Grounds, and which I consider as private and confidential; and therefore I humbly hope the Honourable Committee will not press such Questions to me.

I have the Honour to be, Sir,

Your most obedient humble Servant,

James Morgan.

William Smith, Esq. Chairman of the Committee of the Honourable House of Commons.

Appendix, N° 7.

(Copy.) Sackville Street, 26 August 1795. Sir,

When I had the Honour to suggest to you the Plan by which I proposed to give the Treasury the Anticipation of that Part of the Loan which becomes due in November, December, and January, I fully explained that it was by Means of Acceptances of the Treasury for these Periods that I could accomplish this Anticipation — I stated to you the Necessity there would be (however full of Money my House might happen to be occasionally) for me to have in Hand negotiable Effects, by which I might at any Time be able to replace the Money which we might have advanced, declaring however my Readiness to make the first Advance without any such Effects, because I imagined they could not be prepared before the first Advance might be wanted.

Agreeably to this Explanation, and the Arrangement that seemed to be understood between us, I expected to have made the first Payment last Week, and to have been authorized to order Drafts to be made upon the Treasury, in the Proportions and at the Periods that might have best suited the Purposes of the Arrangement for the first and future Payments, by which Means, while I should have had the Satisfaction of promoting the public Service, I should also have been sure that no possible Inconvenience could result to myself from it. — Such having been my Ideas of the Arrangement, you will not be surprised, that the Uncertainty as to the Periods of making the Advances, which you appeared to be in Yesterday, should lead me to fear that you may not have precisely the same Ideas of it; and that thus unpleasant Disappointments might arise to both Parties. It is to prevent the Possibility of any such Disappointments that I trouble you with this Letter.

My only Object in the Business, is to accomplish in a satisfactory Manner the Wish of Government, and taking beforehand the necessary Steps for insuring Success; if upon Examination you find you can dispense with the Whole as you have already found Means to dispense with the Half of the original Sum, I shall be extremely happy at it, because the Business is by no Means so much an Object of Desire as of Care and Anxiety; 'tis not an Advantage that I long to reap, but a Service of some Difficulty and Delicacy which I am solicitous to perform with Success; 'tis not a Thing that can be done at any Time on the shortest Notice, but an Operation that, with the necessary previous Concert of Measures, may be carried through with Success. — It is not necessary that Government should sustain the Loss of a single Day's Interest more than their Occasions require, although the Acceptances of the Treasury may be granted before they receive the Value of them in Money.

What I wish particularly to be at a Certainty about, is, whether or not the Anticipation will be wanted; when the different Instalments will be required; and if I may positively reckon upon receiving the Acceptances of the Treasury as I may call for them, in Return for Money or Effects falling due at the particular Periods when the Money happens to be wanted — If the Business is to go on, official Letters on these Points will be necessary, because, in an Affair of so vast a Magnitude for One House, there must not exist a Possibility of Mistake or Delay.

I have the Honour, &c.

Boyd.

To the Right honbl* Will" Pitt.

(Copy.) Loan.

Sir,

I am commanded by the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty's Treasury to inform you, that the public Service requiring the Anticipation of the Receipt of those Parts of the Instalments of the last Loan, and of the Payments to the Lottery, which are not yet due, it is their Lordships Desire that you should make these Anticipations, by paying into the Office of the Paymaster General of His Majesty's Forces the following Sums:

500,000l. on or before the 20th Instant.

500,000l. on or before the 20th October.

And in order to reimburse the Advances so to be made, it is their Lordships Order that you should draw or cause to be drawn, at such Times and in such Sums as you may find most convenient to you, Bills of Exchange upon their Lordships, payable at the following Periods; viz.

To the Amount of £. 500,000 payable 30th 1795.

500,000 - - 24th 1796.

£. 1,000,000

Together with Interest at 5 per Cent, upon the Advances you may have made, from the Dates of these Advances until the Dates at which the Bills upon their Lordships become payable.

Should Circumstances happen to render any Change necessary in this proposed Arrangement, there will be Time to give you Notice of it before you order the Drafts for the Payment in October.

I am, Sir,

Your very obedient Servant,

Charles Long.

Treasury Chambers,

September 12th, 1795.

Walter Boyd, Esq.

It is perfectly understood, that you are to be allowed Interest at the Rate of 5 per Cent, upon such Sums as your House shall have been, or in future may be in Advance for the Service of Government.

Appendix, N* 9.

(Copy.) Sackville Street, 14 September 1795.

Sir,

In consequence of the Letter with which you honoured me on the 12th Instant, I beg Leave to inclose Bills of Exchange on the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty's Treasury, for 505,668/. 10$. 0 dated Hamburgh, 31st August, at Three Months Date, which I request you will have the Goodness to accept, and return me Tomorrow. The Value shall be paid on Saturday into the Office of the Paymaster General of His Majesty's Forces, agreeably to your Directions.

My Cousin, Mr. Boyd, Junior, having been at Ham^ burgh the 30th August, I thought proper to get him to draw the Bills, in order to keep the Operation as much as possible within the Knowledge of my own House, and to save the Expence of a Commission, which we must have paid had we employed any House to draw on their Lordships.

I am, &c.

(Signed)

Charles Long, Esq. Walter Boyd.

Secretary to the Treasury.

Appendix, N® 11.

Kensington Gore, January 16th, 1796.

Sir,

I have the Honour to acquaint you, that, at a Meeting of the Subscribers in the List formed to enable me to bid for the Loan, it was their Opinion that the public Interest is not connected with the making of the said List, and that it will be improper for me, as a confidential Agent, to produce the same in any Manner. And I beg Leave to observe, that it is the Principle of free and open Competition, not to give Room for Suspicion, or Occasion for Scrutiny. The Responsibility of the Contractors to secure the Deposit is the only Object on the Part of the Public; and, I believe, it was particularly so declared by the Right honourable the Chancellor of the Exchequer, on the Opening to Parliament the Terms of the Contract for the Loan for 1794, which was the last disposed of by fair Competition. I have the Honour to be,

Sir,

Your most obedient humble Servant,

James Morgan.

William Smith, Esq.

Chairman of the Committee of the Honourable House of Commons, appointed to enquire into the Circumstances of the Negotiation of the late Loan.

Appendix, N* 12.

Kensington Gore, January 16th, 1796.

Sir,

I have the Honour to acquaint you, that the Gentlemen who offered to be the Securities with me for making the Deposit, in case the Proposal I made the 7th December last to contract for the Loan had been approved and accepted, have severally cancelled their Names, and consider the Purpose to be entirely at an End, as the Proposal was rejected. And they now think it will be improper for me to produce their Names in any Manner, as it may tend to involve them

in Questions, concerning which they are totally uninformed. I have the Honour to be,

Sir,

Your most obedient and humble Servant,

James Morgan.

William Smith, Esq.

Chairman of the Committee of the Honourable House of Commons, appointed to enquire into the Circumstances of the Negotiation of the late Loan.

Appendix, N* 13.

Kensington Gore, January 20th, 1796.

Sir,

The Committee having asked me, what I thought would have been the Difference between the Offers likely to have been made by the Parties at the Bidding, in case it had taken place; I have the Honour to acquaint you for their Information, that the Loan for

1,100,000 I. Sterling was disposed of by fair Competition the 7 th March last, and that the greatest Difference in the Offers was 12 7 per Cent. Annuity

for 15 Years, which, valued at 10 Years Purchase is 61. 5 s. 10 d.per Cent, and the least Difference was

7 s. 1 d.per Cent. Annuity, amounting to 3/. 10*. 10

per Cent.

And I beg Leave, Sir, to take this Opportunity to recommend to the Attention of the Committee, the Proposal from the Government of Ireland for making of the Loan, because I know it is essential to the public Interest, and can with the greatest Confidence declare, that the Proposal was the best possible that could be offered under the then Circumstances, although the great Merit of it has not been noticed by the Public. When the printed Proposal was sent over, I read it with Astonishment, because the Principle was the direct Reverse to the ruinous System followed here, in making Loans in Capitals at a great Discount, and thereby unnecessarily accumulating immense Sums to the Debt to be redeemed. I have the Honour to be,

Sir,

Your most obedient and most humble Servant,

James Morgan,

William Smith, Esq.

Chairman of the Committee of the Honourable House of Commons, appointed to enquire into the Circumstances of the Negotiation of the late Loan.

Appendix, N* 17-

Sir, Kensington Gore, 25th 1796.

In the Minutes of ray Examination before the Committee, it appears from my Answer to a Question as if I meant to state, " that the Governor of the Bank had " mentioned the Money Transaction for 900,000l. as " the Ground for Mr. Boyd's having the Loan," without the necessary Explanation that I conceived it to allude to his Doubts of the Competition, and to the Confidence he observed in Mr. Boyd's Party that they should have the Loan. I beg Leave to acquaint you. Sir, that I am very desirous to explain and correct that Answer before the Committee, and I am.

Sir,

Your most obedient humble Servant,

James Morgan.

William Smith, Esq.

Chairman of the Committee of the Honourable House of Commons for enquiring into the Circumstances of the late Loan.

Sir,

I am, Sir,

Your obedient humble Servant,

IV. Smith.

Appendix, N* 21.

(Copy)

Memorandum, 8th January 1795.

It is still intended to propose to Parliament to enable His Majesty to guarantee a Loan to Austria, to the amount of 6,000,000l., on the Terms which have been specified; provided the Emperor agrees in Return to enter into Engagements to the Extent desired. But Circumstances have occurred which make it a possible Case, that an Agreement may be concluded for proposing to guarantee a Loan to a smaller Amount; but at the lowest not less than 4,000,000 /., in Return for less extensive Engagements on the Part of Austria. In order to save Time, and to be prepared for either Alternative, it becomes necessary to ascertain what Variation should take place in the Amount of the Long Annuity, on every 100l. in the Loan for this Country, in consequence of any Abatement of the Amount of the Austrian Loan. The estimated Difference being 4 s. between the Case of the Austrian Loan taking place to the full Extent of 6,000,000l., and of its not taking place at all, the Allowance to be made in any intermediate Case should be in the same Proportion — viz. An Augmentation to the Annuity at the Rate of 8 a. for every Million abated from the Amo'unt of the Austrian Loan.

theft* frame to that Gentleman, theft* Wish that in the inquiry re-Event of the Imperial Loan being reduced to Four e

Millions, the Annuity, which by Calculation woiuld be gs. 10d. may be made 10#. to avoid Fractions, and they hope this Favour will not be refused to them in Return for their liberal Conduct in contracting for the Loan on Conditions so favourable to the Public.

Mr. Boyd accordingly did make this Request to Mr.

Pitt on Sunday the 1 ith of January, and he was pleased to consent to it.

(Signed) W. Boyd.

We agree, in case the Imperial Loan shall not be settled at the Time of proposing the Loan of 18,000,000l. for the Service of the present Year, to>-make the Deposit on the said Sum of 18,000,000 /., for which Receipts are to be given at the Bank in the usual Manner.

If Provision shall not afterwards be made for guaranteeing any Loan to Austria, an Addition to be made of 4 s.to the Long Annuity, as specified in the Agreement signed by us on the 12th of December last; if Provision should in this Session be made for a Loan to Austria, but to a less Amount than 6,000,000 /. an Addition then to be made to the Long Annuity in the Proportions mentioned in the Memoranda of the 8th and 10th of January last.

The first Payment on the 27th of this Month.

The Discount on the Advance for completing the Payments on or before the 13th March next, to be computed from the 23d January, and any other Discounts to be computed from the Times on which the Payments shall be so completed.

It is further agreed, that on the Deposits being made on the English Loan of 18,000,000l., there shall be reserved lor the Public Companies Three Fourths of the Sums specified in the Agreement of the 12th of December.

We agree to the above Proposal on the Part of the Chancellor of the Exchequer, it being understood that the Payment of the Deposit upon both or either of the Loans shall not take place until the Agreement between England and Austria for the Amount of the Imperial Loan shall be finally settled, so as that the precise Quantity of the several Articles of the General Omnium may be properly known, and the Receipts prepared accordingly.

was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, by an Act, made in the First Year of the Reign of Queen Anne, for re-building and repairing the Piers of the Town and Port of in the County of York, several Duties were granted upon all Ships and Vessels entering within the Piers of the said Port, and upon certain Goods and Merchandizes therein particularly mentioned, landed within the Haven or Piers of the said Port of Whitby, and shipped off from Whitby aforesaid, and also a Duty of One Farthing per Chalder on all Coals loaded at certain Places therein mentioned, for the Term of Nine Years, to commence from the 1st Day of May 1702, with such Provisions for the due collecting, accounting for, and applying of the said Duties, and other Powers, Matters, and Things relating thereto, and for keeping clear the said Harbour, as in the same Act is particularly mentioned; and that, by another Act, made in the Seventh Year of her said late Majesty's Reign, the said recited. Act was continued until the 1st Day of May 1723; and, by another Act, made in the Seventh Year of King George the First, the Duties and Sums of Money granted and imposed by the said recited Acts (save and except the Duty of One Farthing per Chalder) were made perpetual, and enacted to be paid to the Trustees therein named, and their Successors for ever, to the End that the Piers and Harbour of Whitby aforesaid might be preserved, kept, and continued in good Repair; and that, by another Act, made in the Eighth Year of his late Majesty King George the Second, for lengthening the West Pier of the said Harbour of Whitby, and for improving the Harbour, the said Duty of One Farthing/>er Chalder, granted by the said Act of the First Year of Queen Anne, and continued by the said Act of the Seventh Year of her Reign (but which had ceased from the 1st Day of May 1723) was revived, continued, and directed to be paid, for the further Term of Thirty-one Years, to

be computed from the 1st Day of June 1735; and, by another Act, made in the Sixth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, the said Duty of a Farthing per Chalder upon Coals was continued for tire further Term of Thirty-one Years, to be computed from the 1st Day of June 1766, which Term is near expiring; and that, in pursuance of the said Acts, a considerable Sum of Money hath been borrowed upon the Credit of the said Duties, which still remains due, and the said Piers have been for some Time past, repairing, and considerable further Repairs and Improvements are necessary to render the said Harbour more extensively useful, and the Entrance thereto more safe and easy, but which Repairs and Improvements cannot be effected without a further Continuance of the said Duty of One Farthing per Chalder on Coals; and that some of the Powers and Provisions contained in the said Acts require Alteration and Amendment: And therefore praying, that Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the Continuance of the said Duty of One Farthing a Chalder upon Coals, for such further Term, and for altering and amending the said Acts, in such Manner, and under such Regulations, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Common Council Men, Free Burgesses, and Inhabitants of the Town and Borough of Great Grimsby, in the County of Lincoln, also of the several Proprietors of Estates there, and in the Vicinity thereof, and of the Farmers and Occupiers thereof, and also of the several Merchants, Traders, and others, whose Names are thereunto respectively subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Port of Grimsby

is a very ancient Port, and the Haven there, which extends from the Two Bridges, or Sluices, in the Parish of Great Grimsby aforesaid, to the River Humber, was formerly deep, and capacious enough to admit Ships of nearly 400 Tons Burthen, which used to float by the said Bridges, or the One of them; and that the said Haven is now so silted and warped up as to- be navigable only for Sloops of about 40 Tons Burthen, which are frequently neaped for Ten or Twelve Days together, the same being seldom able, when loaded, either to get up or out of the said Haven but at Spring Tides, and, consequently, it is now become almost impracticable for any Ship to navigate so far up the Haven as to reach the legal Quays, Wharfs, or Landing Places of the said Port, by Means whereof the Trade of the Town of Great Grimsby is gone to almost entire Decay, to the great Loss, Prejudice, and Inconvenience, as well of the Inhabitants thereof, and of the adjacent Country, as of the Public at Jarge; and that, if the said Haven was widened, deepened, and rendered more straight, and the Course thereof in Part varied, and also, if the Water of a certain Beck called Freshney, which runs in or between the Two adjoining Parishes of Great Coates and Little Coates, and in or between Great Coates and Great Grimsby aforesaid, was brought into the said Haven, the same would be rendered navigable more constantly, and for Vessels of larger Burthen, whereby the Trade and Commerce of the said Town would be restored, and considerably increased, and the Public in general greatly benefited: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for widening, deepening, enlarging, straightening, and improving the said Haven, or otherwise to alter and vary, in Part, the Course and Direction thereof, also for taking, and conveying into the same Haven the Water of the said Beck, called Freshney, and for that Purpose to make new Cuts or Drains from the said Beck through the intervening Lands, lying in the said Parishes of Little Coates and Great Grimsby, or otherwise to widen, deepen, enlarge, and straighten the Old Drains, Cuts, or Ditches, extending from the said Beck through certain other Lands, lying in the said Two last mentioned Parishes, to the said Haven, and also for other beneficial Purposes, subject to such Orders, Rules, and Regulations, Provisoes and Restrictions, as the House shall judge to be expedient and proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report, the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Dudley North, Mr. Harrison, 8cc.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker's'Chamber; and have Power to send for Persons, Papers, and Records.

present Majesty's Reign, intituled, "An Act for dividing and inclosing the Open and Common Fields, " Common Pastures, and all other the Commonable " Lands, in the Parish of Hanley Castle, in the County " of Worcester" it was enacted, that the said Open and Common Fields, Meadows, and Grounds, and a Tract of Land therein mentioned, called Hanley Common, and all other the Commonable Lands and Waste Grounds within the said Parish of Hanley Castle, should, as soon as conveniently might be, be divided, set out, and allotted, by certain Commissioners therein named, and their Successors, to be appointed in Manner therein mentioned; and, it was further enacted, that all Persons, having or claiming any Lands or Rights of Common in or upon the said Common Fields and other Commonable and Waste Lands, thereby directed to be divided and inclosed, should, and were thereby required, by themselves or their Agents, to lay their respective Claims in Writing under their Hands, or under the Hands of their Agents, before the said Commissioners, or any Three of them, at their First or Second Meeting to be holden for the Purposes of the said Act, and that no such Claims should be received by the said Commissioners after their Second Meeting, except for some special Cause to be by them allowed, and that, if any Dispute or Difference should arise between the Parties interested in the said Division touching or concerning any such Claim, or any other Matter or Thing relating to the Division and Allotment of the said Lands and Grounds, it should be lawful for the said Commissioners, and they were thereby empowered and required, by Examination of Witnesses upon Oath, and upon such other Evidence, Enquiry, and Proof, as they should think proper, to hear and determine the same, and every such Determination should be binding and conclusive to all Persons whomsoever; but, the said Act recites, that the Owners of several Estates lying in the Parish of in the said

County of Worcester, and the Owners of several Estates in the Parish of Cohcall, in the County of Hereford, claimed to be entitled to Common of Pasture in and upon the said Tract of Land, called Hanley Common, as appurtenant to their several Estates, and might be desirous of trying such Claims at Law, it was there- fore enacted, that the said Commissioners, or any Three of them, should, and they were thereby authorized and required, by Examination of Witnesses upon Oath, and by such other Ways and Means as they should think proper, to hear and determine the said Claims of the Owners of Estates in the Parishes of Mathon and Cohcall, and each of them, and forthwith to reduce such Determination into Writing, and the same should, at all seasonable Times, be open to the Inspection of all Persons claiming to be interested, or their Agents, without Fee or Reward, and that, in case any Person should object to such Determination of the said Commissioners, or any Three of them, and should give Notice thereof to the said Commissioners, or any One of them, under his Hand, or the Hands of his Agent, within Fourteen Days after such Determination, it should and might be lawful for any One or more of the Persons seised of any of the Estates within the said Parishes of Mathon and Colwall, or either of them, to commence and prosecute, in any of His Majesty's Courts of Record at Westminster, One or more Action or Actions against any of the Persons having Lands within the said Parish of Hanley Castle, and claiming Right of Common in and upon the said Tract of Land, called Hanley Common, for ascertaining the Right of the Person or Persons claiming such Right of Common as aforesaid, and to declare therein upon a feigned Wager, as usual in Declarations for trying Issues directed by Courts of Equity, and that such Declaration or Declarations, in case the Parties should not agree in settling the same, should be settled by the proper Officers of the Court wherein the Action

or Actions should be brought, and, after delivering such Declaration or Declarations, the Defendant or Defendants should forthwith appear, accept the same, and plead to Issue, and the Plaintiff or Plaintiffs therein should proceed to the Trial of such Action or Actions, at the Summer Assizes, in and for the County of Gloucester, next after the passing of the said Act, and the Verdict or Verdicts to be given should be final and conclusive, unless the Court, wherein the Action should be brought, should set aside the same, and order a new Trial or new Trials to be had, which it should be lawful for the Court to do, as is usual in other Cases, and that, after any Verdict or Verdicts should have been obtained, and not set aside by the Court, the Party or Parties for whom such Verdict or Verdicts should be obtained, should and might procure his and their Costs of Suit to be taxed by the proper Officers of the Court where such Action or Actions should have been brought, and the same should, in case the Right were found for such Owner of Lands in the said Parishes of Mathon and Colwall, or either of them, be paid by the said Commissioners, or any Three of them, out of the Money to be raised for defraying the Expences of obtaining and passing the said Act, and carrying the same into Execution, as therein mentioned; and the said Agent having made such Request, the said Thomas Hornyhold, and the Solicitor for passing the said Act, consented thereto, but it was apprehended, that the Introduction of any new Words or Matter in the said Act would prove fatal to it, and therefore the Agent of the Petitioner, upon the Assurance of the said Thomas Hornyhold and the said Solicitor, that no Difficulty should be thrown in the Way of the Petitioner in trying his Right, or Claim, at Law, in the Event of the Mathon and Colwall Proprietors establishing their Claim, consented to withdraw the proposed Amendment, and to permit the Act to pass into a Law; A Petition of Henry Earl of Exeter, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer (by His Majesty's Command) acquainted the House, that His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was Drought up, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioner, by virtue of several Grants from the Crown, is seised in Fee of the Woods, Underwoods, Woodlands, and other Hereditaments, within the Haye or Walk of , within the Bailiwick of Clive, otherwise Cliffe, in the Forest of Rockingham, in the County of Northampton, except Herbage for the King's Deer and Wild Beasts, and all Royal Mines upon the Premisses, and is also seised in Fee of the Office of Forester or Keeper of the said Haye or Walk, and of all the Deer and Wild Beasts therein, and divers Persons have used and enjoyed Rights of Common upon the said Woods, Underwoods, Woodlands, and Premisses; and that the said Woods, Underwoods, Woodlands and Premisses, are capable of Improvement, and for that Purpose it will be expedient to set out and allot Lands belonging to the Petitioner in lieu of such Rights of Common, but, as

Vol. 51.

such Improvement cannot effectually be carried into Execution so long as the Deer of die Forest are at Liberty to go into the said Woods, Underwoods, Coppices, Woodlands and Premisses, the Petitioner has made his humble Suit to His Majesty, that He will be graciously pleased to give Leave that a Bill may be brought into Parliament to enable His Majesty to grant to the Petitioner, his Heirs and Assigns, in Fee Simple, all the Estate, Right, Title, and Interest, now remaining in His Majesty, in, over, and upon the said Haye or Walk, upon a full and adequate Consideration to be paid for the same, to which His Majesty has been pleased to give His Consent: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the Purpose aforesaid, under such Restrictions and Regulations as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Mr. Powys and Mr. Dickins do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A Petition of the Governor and Company of Merchants of England trading into the Levant Seas, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer (by His Majesty's Command) acquainted the House, that His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That the Trade between this Kingdom and Turkey has, for a long Series of Years, been carried on by a Society of Merchants, incorporated by Charters, and regulated by Acts of Parliament; and that, in order to carry on the said Trade with Safety, and to protect His Majesty's Subjects in the Turkish Dominions, it has been found necessary that an Ambassador should be sent from England to reside at Constantinople, and that Consuls, and Vice Consuls, and other Officers and Servants, should be established in the different Parts of Turkey where British Subjects reside, and where the English Merchants carry on Trade; and the Charge of the said Establishment is borne by the Turkey Company, which, together with other Expences incident to carrying on the Trade, have, of late Years, amounted to about 8,oooo/. per Annum; and that the Petitioners acknowledge, with Gratitude, the several Grants they have, from Time to Time, received from the Bounty of Parliament, and, although they did not apply for Assistance in the Course of the last Session, as they found themselves in a Situation to support their Expences,.yet they are sensible they should not discharge the Duty incumbent on them by their Charter, nor the Justice they owe to the Public (for whom they consider themselves as Trustees) if they did not declare their present Inability to support their necessary and unavoidable Expences unless relieved by Parliament: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and grant them such Relief as may be thought necessary and proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of those, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Persons residing within the Town and County of the Town of Nottingham, and in the Neighbourhood thereof, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Road from Nottingham Trent Bridge, to the Town of Nottingham, is at present in a very ruinous State, having been greatly damaged by the Flood in the Spring of the Year 179,5; and that the Passage over the said Bridge, called The Trent Bridge, being extremely narrow and inconvenient, it is essential to the Accommodation of the Public that the said Trent Bridge should be re-built upon such a Plan as to render the same more commodious and easy of Passage, and that the Road should be raised, and other additional Bridges and Arches, sufficient for the Passage of the Flood Water, should be erected on the said Road, in order to render the same safe and commodious, and protected at all Seasons from the Flood to which it is peculiarly exposed; and that it appears to the Petitioners, that the leading Entrances into the said Town of Nottingham, by Chapel Bar and Hollow Stone, are, at present, in njany Places extremely narrow, inconvenient, and unsafe for Travellers and Carriages, and the Road through the Town is in a ruinous Condition; and that the said Entrances cannot be widened or improved, or the said Road effectually widened and repaired, by the ordinary Course of Law: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for establishing a Toll at the Trent Bridge, for rebuilding or improving the Trent Bridge, for repairing the Road leading from the same to the Town of Nottingham, the Chain and Flood Bridge, and also the Leen Bridge on the said Road, and for constructing such other Flood Bridges on the said Road as may be thought necessary, and for making, repairing, and widening, a Road from the Leen Bridge, near to the said Town of Nottingham, to join the Mansfield Turnpike Road, and for widening the Entrance and Road into the said Town, by Way of Chapel Bar, for paving and improving the said Road, and for contributing to the Improvement of the Road from Chapel Bar to the Top of the Sand Hills.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Pierrepont, Mr. Robert Smith, &c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker's Chamber; and have Power to send for Persons, Papers, and Records.

Another Petition of those, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Persons residing in the Town and County of the Town of Nottingham, and in the Neighbourhood thereof, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Road from Nottingham Trent Bridge, to the Town of Nottingham, is at

present in a very ruinous State, having been greatly damaged by the Flood in the Spring of the Year 1795, and it is essential to the Accommodation of the Public, and particularly of the Town of Nottingham and its Neighbourhood, that the Road should be raised, and that other additional Bridges and Arches, sufficient for the Passage of the Flood Water, should be provided in order to render the said Road safe and commodious, protected at all Seasons from the Flood, to which, from its Situation, it is peculiarly exposed: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for establishing a Toll at the Trent Bridge, for repairing the Roads from the Trent Bridge to the Town of Nottingham, the Chain and Flood Bridges, and also the Leen Bridge, and for constructing such other Flood Bridges as may be thought necessary on the said Roads.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the preceding Petition is referred: And that they do examine the Matter of this Petition; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

Commonable Places, and Pieces of Waste Ground, are capable of very great Improvement, and, if the same were divided and allotted among the several Persons entitled thereto and interested therein, and the several Allotments inclosed, it would be of great Advantage to all Parties concerned: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for dividing, allotting, and inclosing the said Moor, Common, Wastes, Commonable Places, and Pieces of Waste Ground, in such Manner, and with such Powers and Provisions, as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the several Proprietors, and Inhabitants, within the Towns of Pontefract and in the West Riding of the County of York, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That, by an Act lately passed, for dividing the Park of Pontefract, in the County of York, and for other Purposes therein mentioned, a certain Portion or Allotment of the said Park was set apart, and severed from the Residue thereof, for the Use of the Inhabitants of Pontefract and Tanshelf, in the Manner and subject to the Regulations and Restrictions, mentioned in the said Act, but several Amendments are found wanting, to render the same more useful to the Inhabitants of the said Towns: That there are Means of supplying the Inhabitants of the said Towns more plentifully and conveniently with Water, and the said Towns would be greatly improved, if proper Powers were obtained, not only for procuring such Supply, but also for paving, lighting, and cleansing, the same, and for removing Annoyances therein, the Execution of which said Powers might be greatly facilitated by obtaining the proposed Amendments in the above-mentioned Act of Parliament; and that the greatest Part of the late Fields and Open Grounds, within the said Townships vf Pontefract and Tanshelf, and the Manor of Tanshelf, have been inclosed, but some small Parts thereof yet remain open, which is, in a great Measure, owing to Property held in Mortmain, and by Persons under various Incapacities to alienate, lying intermixed therewith; and that the unalienable Property in the said Towns of Pontefract and Tanshelf and the said Manor of Tanshelf, is otherwise productive of great Inconvenience, and it would be of great Utility if proper Powers of exchanging, and of flatting, or lying together, were obtained; and that Regulations, respecting the Poor and divers Hospitals in the said Towns, and respecting a Charity School in the said Town of Pontefract, and the Property belonging to those Institutions respectively, would be of great Benefit to the said Inhabitants and Proprietors: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill, or Bills, for effecting the Purposes above-mentioned.

Stepney Po- A Petition of Jonathan Eade, of Stoke Newington, in

lice Petition, the County of Middlesex, Esquire, Lord of the Manor of Stepney, in the said County, and of the several other Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Inhabitants within the said Manor, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the said Manor is very extensive and populous, and such of the Streets, Lanes, Public Ways, and other Public Passages and Places, within the said Manor, as are not included under any particular Act of Parliament for paving and regulating, are not paved, or very ill paved, and repaired, and are greatly obstructed, and rendered incommodious, by various Nuisances and Annoyances, and divers Offences are frequently committed therein; and that the Petitioners apprehend the said Inconveniences are, in a great Measure, owing to the Want of sufficient Powers being lodged in the Court Leet of and belonging to the said Manor, and in the Steward of the said Court, to compel proper Persons to take on them the Office of Jurymen in the Court Leet, to present such defective or ruinous Pavement, and also such Nuisances, Obstructions, and Annoyances, and such Offences as aforesaid, within the said Manor, and also to the Want of an easy and effectual Method of levying and recovering the Amerciaments set and imposed by such Jury; and that great Frauds and Abuses are committed within the said Manor by the Use of false Weights and Measures, which the present Powers of the said Court Leet are not competent to detect, prevent, or remedy, and it would greatly tend to the Safety, Advantage, and Accommodation, of all Persons residing within the said Manor, or such Parts thereof as aforesaid, and be of Public Utility, if sufficient Powers were given to the Lord of the said Manor to enforce the Attendance of proper Persons on the Leet Jury within the said Manor, and if sufficient Powers were also given to the said Court Leet to levy and recover the Fines or Amerciaments that might be set and imposed on all Persons neglecting to pave or repair the Pavement they are by Law required to make or repair, and on all Persons, within the said Manor or Parts thereof as aforesaid, committing, or causing, Nuisances, Annoyances, or Obstructions, or committing Offences within the same, and also, if the said Court Leet were enabled to enforce the Use of due and legal Weights and Measures, and to punish Persons using false Weights and Measures, svithin the said Manor: And therefore praying, That

A Petition of the Coalheavers working on the River Coalheavers Thames, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was Petition, presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That an Act was passed in the Tenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act to repeal an " Act, passed in the Thirty-first Year of the Reign of " his late Majesty King George the Second, intituled,

" An Act for Relief of the Coalheavers working upon " the River Thames, and for enabling them to make " Provision for such of themselves as shall be sick,

" lame, or past their Labour, and for their Widows " and Orphans; and to regulate the Price of their " Labour; to prevent Frauds and Impositions on such " Labourers; and for their further Relief;" and that the said Act of the Tenth Year of His present Majesty's Reign was made for relieving Labourers employed in unloading Ships laden with Coals, usually called Coalheavers, from the Impositions and Frauds practised upon them by Persons called Coal Undertakers, employed to procure Coalheavers to unload such Ships in the River ITiames; but, it being declared, in and by the last mentioned Act, that the same was to continue in force for Three Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament only, the said Act has long since expired, and the Petitioners are deprived of the Benefit arising from the Regulations therein contained; and that the Petitioners have for several Years past laboured under the greatest Hardships, through the Impositions of some of the Coal Undertakers, who oblige the Petitioners to give them Part of what they earn, in order to obtain Employment from them, by which Means the Coalheavers and their Families are frequently reduced to great Distress, and Disturbances and Inconveniences are occasioned; and that the Coal Trade would be much better carried on, if the Coal Undertakers were under proper Controul, and the Wages or Earnings of the Petitioners secured to them by the Authority of Parliament: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for regulating the aforesaid Coal Undertakers, for ascertaining and settling the Price of Labour to be paid to the Petitioners, and others, working as Coalheavers on the River Thames, and for protecting them from Frauds and Abuses in the Payment of their Wages, in such Manner as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Alderman Anderson, the Lord Mayor of London, &c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker's Chamber; and have Power to send for Persons, Papers, and Records.

son of the Practice among Persons retailing Malt and other Liquors within the Cities of London and Westminster, and Places adjacent, of carrying the same out in Pewter Pots, and leaving such Pots with their Customers, and of the Ease and Temptation thereby given to dishonest and indigent Persons to dispose of the Pots so let to Receivers of Stolen Goods, the Petitioners sustain Yearly such very heavy Losses that it is become an alarming and increasing Grievance, which Losses the Petitioners conceive can in no Way be effectually prevented but by the Interposition of Legislative Regulations, restraining all Persons, selling Malt Liquors by Retail, within prescribed Limits, from leaving Pewter Pots at any private House or Place to which such Liquor shall be ordered to be brought; and such Regulations would also tend to remove the Temptation which the dishonest, iudigent, and immoral, now have to commit those Crimes, the Prosesution and Punishment of which is so frequent, troublesome, and expensive, to the Petitioners: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and that Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the Purposes aforesaid, under such Regulations and Restrictions as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the thereunder-signed Inhabitants of Petition from the Hundred of Home, in the County of Suffolk, was Ho.we for presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That Jh^wndows the Petitioners are Occupiers of Farms in the said of Dairy Hundred, in which the Manufacture of Cheese and Rooms from Butter is carried on to a great Extent, and certain DutX-Rooms with large Windows, not made with Glass, but with Splines, are absolutely necessary in the Manufacture aforesaid; and that the Petitioners, in general, living in Houses only tenanted by them, and that only for a certain Period, have it not either in their Power or Ability to make those Buildings (agreeable to the Determination of the Judges) detached from such Dwelling Houses, which are, in many Instances, old and inconvenient Buildings; and that the Petitioners, having hired those Houses with their Farms, in many Cases at high Rents, possessed of an Exemption from the Window Duties for Rooms so employed, and being at this Time greatly oppressed by the alarming Increase of the Poor Rates, and other Parish Charges, find themselves greatly distressed by this additional and unlooked for Burthen: And therefore entreating the House, That those Rooms, used only for the Purposes of the Manufacture of Cheese and Butter aforesaid, may be exempted from the Duties on Windows, as has ever been the Case in the said Hundred, until the late Decision of the Judges of His Majesty's Court of Exchequer.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Sum of Two Millions be raised by Loans or Exchequer Bills, to be charged on the first Aids to be granted in the next Session of Parliament; and such Exchequer Bills, if not discharged, with Interest thereupon, on or before the 5th Day of April 1797, to be exchanged and received in Payment in such Manner as Exchequer Bills have usually been exchanged and received in Payment.

A Petition of the Magistrates of the County of Petition Chester, assembled at the General Quarter Sessions of J/j1,1"81 t,ie the Peace, held for the said County at the Castle of Chester, on the 12th Day of January 1796, was pre- Wages of sented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Labourers in Bill to explain and amend so much of an Act, made Hust)andry-in the Fifth Year of the Reign of Queen Elizabeth, intituled, "An Act containing divers Orders for Artificers, Labourers, Servants of Husbandry, and " Apprentices," as empowers Justices of the Peace, at or within Six Weeks after, every General Quarter Sessions held at Easier, to regulate the Wages of Labourers in Husbandry; and Setting forth, That it appears to the Petitioners that the Principle of the said Bill, and several of the Clauses therein contained, will tend to the Oppression of Labourers in Husbandry, and prevent their being employed by the Day in the Manner in the said Bill mentioned, and that several of the Provisions in the said Bill will be found extremely difficult, if not wholly impossible, to be carried into Effect by the Magistrates of the respective Counties, Cities, and Towns, within this Kingdom, by Reason of the Difficulty of obtaining correct Information as to the particular Circumstances of each Labourer within their respective Jurisdictions, and the Amount of the Earnings of such Labourers, and more especially in determining as to the Extent of the Abilities of old and infirm Persons to work as Labourers in Husbandry; and that the said Bill, if passed into a Law, would, in many Instances, be the Means of wholly depriving such last mentioned Labourers of Employment, and bring additional Burthens upon the Parishes, Townships, and Places, to which they belong:

The Petitioners therefore submit to the Consideration. of the House, that Labourers in Husbandry would be placed in a worse Situation by the Operation of the said Bill, if passed into a Law, than they are in at present under the existing Laws, and the general Usage of Farmers and other Persons employing such Labourers, for which Reasons the Petitioners desire the said Bill may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second Time.
