To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act for making and maintaining a Navigable Canal out of and from the Warwick and Birmingham Canal, now cutting, or intended to be cut, in the Parish of Bud-brooke, in the County of Warwick, into the Oxford Canal, in the Parish of Braunston, in the County of Northampton, was read: And,

Mr. Charles Handley being examined, said, That the Company have proceeded in the Execution of the said Act, mid made a considerable Part of their Canal, but now find, that if the same was to be completed in the Line prescribed by the said Act, between a Place or Road called The Fosse Road, in the Parish of Off church,

in the County of Warwick, and the Parish of Braunston aforesaid, it would be attended with much Inconvenience and Prejudice to the said Company, and would be incommodious for Navigation, as a Tunnel of more than 800 Yards in length must be made thereon. That the Company have lately caused Surveys to be made, whereby it appears that if the above-mentioned Part of the Line of their Canal was abandoned, and instead thereof it was carried from the said Place or Road, called The Fosse Road, in the Parish of Offchurch aforesaid, through the several Parishes, Hamlets, Townships, or Places of Offchurch, Bascote, Long -ington, Stockton, Burdingbury, Lemington, Hastings, Broadwell, Grandborough, Caldecot, and Napton, in the County of Warwick, into the said Oxford Canal, in the Parish of Napton, in the County of Warwick, and certain Collateral Cuts or Branches made therefrom, it would be much more beneficial to the said Company, more commodious for Navigation, and be of greater Advantage to the Public.

And the Witness added, That some other Amendments and Alterations are requisite in the said Act.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for authorizing the Company of Proprietors of the Warwick and Braunston Canal Navigation to vary the Course of a certain Part of the said Canal, and for amending and altering the Act, made in the Thirty-fourth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for making the said Canal: And that Sir George Augustas.

William Shuckburgh Evelyn and Sir John Mordaunt do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Sir John Mordaunt presented to the House, according to Order, a Bill for enabling the Company of Proprietors of the Warwick and Birmingham Canal Navigation to finish and complete the same, and for amending the Act of Parliament, passed in the Thirty-third Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for making the said Canal: And the same was received; and read the First Time.

Resolved, That the Bill be read a Second Time.

Sir John Mordaunt reported from the Committee,

to whom the Petition of the Manufacturers of Buttons, and of the Merchants and Factors dealing in that Article, in the Town and Neighbourhood of Birmingham, in the County of Warwick, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. William Smith, a Button Maker of Birmingham, being examined, said, That the manufacturing and vending of Metal Buttons, particularly of plated and gilt Buttons, has for many Years been one of the principal and most increasing Branches of Trade in the said Town, in which many Thousands of Men, Women, and Children ace employed, and great Quantities of such Goods are sent to Foreign Markets: Then,

Mr. Humphrey Vale, another Button Maker of Birmingham, being also examined, said, That great Frauds and Deceits have lately been discovered to be practised in the marking of Metal Buttons, which were neither gilt nor plated, with the Words " gilt" or " plated," or other Words or Marks, intimating, contrary to Truth, that the same were gilt or plated, to the great Injury of the Purchasers; whereby the Honour and Credit of the Merchant, Factor, and Manufacturer hath been lessened in the Opinion of Foreigners, and the Use and Wear of gilt and plated Buttons greatly diminished both at Home and Abroad.

And the Witness further said, if such fraudulent Practices are suffered to continue, the said valuable Manufacture may ultimately be lost to this Country, the existing Laws being insufficient to check the same.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to regulate the making and vending of Metal Buttons, and to prevent the Purchasers thereof from being deceived in the real Quality of such Buttons: And that Sir John Mordaunt, Sir George Augustus William

Voi.51.

Shuckburgh Evelyn, Mr. Hawkins Browne, and Mr.

Whitmore, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Sir George Augustus William Shuelcburgh Evelyn Coventry, reported from the Committee, to whom the Bill for ^jr^rk'n,g enlarging the Term and Powers of Two Acts, passed Gutter Hoad in the Twenty-seventh Year of the Reign of his late Bill, reported. Majesty King George the First, and in the Sixteenth

Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for repairing the Road from the City of Coventry to Warwick, and from Coventry to Martyns Gutter, and also several other Roads therein mentioned, so far as the said Acts relate to the said Road from Coventry to Warwick, and from Coventry to Martyns Gutter, was committed;

That the Committee had examined the Allegations of the Bill, and found the same to be true; and that the Committee had gone through the Bill, and made several Amendments thereunto, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Bill, with the Amendments, in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Amendments were Once read throughout; and then a Second Time, One by One; and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, were agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendments, be ingrossed.

Sir George Augustus William Shuckburgh Evelyn pre- Bill for

sented to the House, according to Order, a Bill for au- amending the thorizing the Company of Proprietors of the Warwick and Braunston Canal Navigation to vary the Course of £anai Act a certain Part of the said Canal, and for amending and presented. And the same was received; and read the First Time.

Resolved, That the Bill be read a Second Time-

An ingrossed Bill for dividing, allotting, and in- Dunton closing, the Open and Common Fields, Meadows, and Another Commonable Grounds and Places, of and within 1 '

the Parish, Lordship, and Liberties, of Dunton Bassett, in the County of Leicester, was read the Third Time.

An ingrossed Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, by Way of Ryder, for making an Allotment to the Vicar, as a Compensation for the Tythes of old inclosed Lands.

And the said Clause was Thrice read; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the Bill, by Way of Ryder.

Resolved, That the Bill do pass: And that the Title be, An Act for dividing, allotting, and inclosing, the Open and Common Fields, Meadows, and other Commonable Grounds and Places, of and within the Parish, Lordship, and Liberties of Dunton Bassett, in the County of Leicester.

Ordered, That Mr. Pochin do carry the Bill to the Lords, and desire their Concurrence.

Mr. Hobart according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of W ays and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Sum of Two Millions Five hundred thousand Pounds be raised, by Loans or Exchequer Bills, to be charged on die first Aids to be granted in the next Session of Parliament.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That such Parts of the several Rates and Duties on Vellum, Parchment, or Paper, upon which any Receipt, or the Discharge for any Legacy left by any Will, or other Testamentary Instrument, or for any Share or Part of a Personal Estate, divided by Force of the Statute of Distributions, or the Custom of any Province or Place, shall be ingrossed, written, or printed (and which said Duties were granted by several Acts of Parliament, made in the Twentieth, Twenty-third, and Twenty-ninth Years of the Reign of His present Majesty) in respect whereof any Duty shall be imposed by any Act of the present Session of Parliament, do cease ana determine.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Charge of the Pay and Cloathing of the Militia, in that Part of Great Britain called England, for One Year, beginning the 25th Day of March 1796, be defrayed out of the Monies arising by the Land Tax granted for the Service of the Year 1790.

A PETITION of the Mayor, Bailiffs, and Commonalty, of the City of Exeter, in Chamber assembled, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Hill for making a Navigable Canal from the River Fxc, near the Town of Topsham, in the County of Devon, to the River Tone, near the Town of Taunton, in the County of Somerset, and for cleansing and making Navigable a certain Part of the said River Tone, and for making certain Cuts from the said Canal; and Setting forth, That, hv the said Bill, it is proposed that Powers should be given to the Proprietors of the said Undertaking to erect or construct Reservoirs in the Valley of the River Culm, in the said County of Devon, and to make Channels to convey Water from the said Reservoirs, and from the said River Culm, to join or communicate with the said intended Canal at the Places mentioned in the said Bill, and that the said Proprietors should he authorized to supply the said intended Canal, Cuts, and Reservoirs, with Water from the said River Culm, and from all such Springs' as shall be found in making the same, and from all Rivers, Springs, Brooks, Streams, and Watercourses, which shall be found within a certain Distance, to be ascertained, from any Part of the said Canal and Cuts, and from the Reservoirs belonging thereto, and for that Purpose to.deepen, enlarge, or straiten, any such Rivers, Brooks, Streams, or Watercourses, or any others, which may come or be brought into the same, respectively, and to make such Feeders and Aqueducts, and erect such Weirs, Engines, and Machines, for supplying the said Canal,

Cuts, and Reservoirs, with Water, and for. conveying Water from the said Reservoirs to the said Canal ana Cuts, as the said Proprietors shall, from Time to Time, think proper and expedient: That the River Culm falls into the River Eat Stoke Canon, in the County of Devon, about Four Miles above the City of Exeter, and forms a very considerable Part of the River Exe, in its Passage at the City of Exeter, and, in dry Seasons, the Supply of Water in the River Exe principally depends on the Quantity produced by the River Culm; and that the Petitioners are possessed of a

Navigable Canal from Exeter to Topsham, originally formed by virtue of Powers given to the Mayor, Bailiffs, and Commonalty of the said City, by an Act, passed in the Reign of King llenry the Eighth, for amending the River and Port of Exeter, which Canal is supplied with the Water of the River Exe at or near the said City of Exeter, and hath, since that Period, from Time to Time, been greatly improved by the Petitioners and their Predecessors at a very great Expence, whereby a large Debt has been incurred, and still remains due from the Petitioners; and that, for upwards of One hundred Years past, the said Canal has been made capable of conveying from Topsham to Exeter not only Lighters and Boats, but Ships of heavy Burthen, which hath been found to be of great Convenience and Advantage, and tended greatly to the Increase of the Trade and Commerce of the City, and hath also produced a considerable Income to the Petitioners for defraying the Expence of maintaining the Navigation, so necessary and highly beneficial to the Trade of the said City, and also for the Payment of the Interest of the Debt due thereon; and that the said City is principally supplied with Water from the River Exe, by Means of an Engine erected by the Petitioners Predecessors, and leased out by them for the Purpose of conveying Water in Pipes throughout the greatest Part of the City — That in the Summer Season there is but a scanty Supply, and at particular Times a total Want of Water in the River for working the said Engine, and for the Use of the Inhabitants of the said City — That there are likewise many Fulling Mills on the River Exe, necessary for carrying on the Woollen Manufacture, established in the said City, and Corn Mills belonging to the Petitioners and their Lessees, and, within a few Years past, a large Mill has been established near the City, adjoining to a certain Weir, called Trews Weir, for spinning Cotton, under a Lease from the Petitioners, which Mill was erected at a great Expence; and that any Diminution in the Water of the River Exe would be highly injurious and prejudicial to the said Navigation from Topsham to Exeter, as well as to the said Water Engine, Fulling Mills, and Corn Mills, and Spinning Engine, established on the said River, and all the Water taken from the River Culm must, in the same Proportion, lessen the Quantity of Water in the River Exe, at Exeter, whereby the several Interests before-mentioned will be most materially injured: That the Petitioners, under many ancient Charters and Grants from the Crown, hold the City of Exeter at Fee Farm, for which they pay a large Rent to the Crown, by virtue thereof, as well as by Prescription and immemorial Usage, the Petitioners are entitled to receive various Petty Customs, or Town Dues, on all Goods imported into the Port of Exeter, and are also possessed of a Quay at Exeter, and an ancient Crane or Quay at Topsham, which they also hold under the Crown, paying a large Rent for the same, and the Petitioners, in Right of the said Quay at Topsham, as Fanners under the Crown, are

entitled to certain Rates on all Goods, Wares, and Merchandize, laid on Land, laden, or unladen, upon the said Quay, or in ary other Place, being dry Land, within the Precincts of the Manor of ;and

that the Petitioners conceive that, if a Navigable Canal should be made from Taunton to Topsham, according to the Line, and in the Manner proposed by the

A Bill for dividing, inclosing, and allotting, the Open and Common Fields, Common Meadows, Common Pastures, Lammas Grounds, Waste Lands, and other Commonable Lands and Grounds, in the Parish of Little Brickhill, in the County of Bucks, was read a

Mr. Manning reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Merchants and others residing in or near the Cities of London and Westminster, the Borough of Southwark, and Parts adjacent, in the Counties of Middlesex and Surrey, was referred; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, relative to Navigation Bills, had been complied with; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Robert Milligan, Esquire, being examined, said, That he is a West India Merchant. — And being asked, Whether, from the great Increase of the Trade and Commerce of London, Westminster, and Southwark, and the Parts adjacent, the present Legal Wharfs and Quays on the River Thames, and those used as Legal Wharfs and Quays by Sufferance, have not been found inadequate to the Accommodation of the Shipping coming thereto, and to the Purpose of landing and shipping Goods, Wares, and Merchandizes thereat? he said, Completely so; totally inadequate to the Business, which is at present confined to the Legal Quays. — Being asked. Whether he does not think that the Sufferance Wharfs, in Addition to the Legal Quays Vol. 51.

and Wharfs, are sufficient for the Accommodation of the Commerce ? he said. He does not think that either the Legal Quays, or the Sufferance Wharfs, are properly calculated for the Business now carried on there, particularly the West India Trade. — Being asked, What he meant by properly ? he said, In the first Instance, the West India Ships, homeward bound, draw so much Water, that many of them are obliged to discharge their Cargoes into Lighters at Deptford, and very few of them go higher up the River than Bell Wharf. — Being asked, Whether he did not think that the present Legal Wharfs and Quays, with the Sufferance Wharfs and Quays, are capable of being so improved as to answer all the Purposes of Trade ? he said, He does not think they are capable of such Improvement. — Being asked, If he thought the Situation pointed out for the Wet Docks is the most commodious for Docks for the Accommodation of Shipping, and the Trade in general ? he said, He perfectly approves the Principle of Wet Docks, and thinks that it will be the only effectual Way of preventing the excessive Plunderage daily committed upon the present System, which is now carried on to an Extent almost incredible. — Being asked, Whether he thought Wet Docks, constructed at the Isle of Dogs, would be more sufficient? he said, He thought so, and he is still inclined to think so, but he has not considered the other Situation so fully as now to be prepared to decide upon it — Being asked, Whether he did not think that in Time of Peace the Legal Quays and Sufferance Wharfs are sufficient for the Accommodation of the Trade of the Port of London ? he said, He does not think that even in Times of Peace they are at all calculated for the India Trade. — Being asked, Why they are not calculated for that Trade? he said, Because the Ships, by unloading their Cargoes into Lighters at so great a Distance from the Free Quays, must continue to be liable to very considerable Plunderage on the River, and the long Detention frequently happening in the Discharge of those Lighters, even after they are brought to the Free Quays, makes them also liable to Plunderage. — Being asked, What is the Reason of that long Detention at the Free Quays, and if it is not owing to the Free Quays being blocked up ? he said, It certainly is occasioned by the Wharfingers frequently undertaking to do more Business than they can properly execute, more than the Quays are competent to execute, particularly in War Time. — Being asked, Whether the Wharfingers have not frequently applied to the Merchants to clear away their Goods, and without Success ? he said, Not to his Knowledge. — Being asked, Whether the Merchants always make their Entries as soon as the Ship reports ? he said, Generally as soon after the Ship reports as they are able to work out their Cargo — the prime Entry is then made — the post Entry cannot be made until the Goods pass the King's Beam. — Being asked, If there is any Loss suffered on the Quays ? he said, He presumes there must be considerable Damage and Loss upon the Quays, and he has seen them exposed to the Weather there without any Covering. — Being asked, Whether that is not in general for Want of the post Entries ? he said, He believes not; for in general, as soon as the Landwaiter delivers in the Note of the Weights at the King's Beam, the post Entry is made. — Being asked, If it is not common for the Landwaiters to make repeated Applications to the Merchants for the post Entries ? he said, He does not know it in the Course of his own Business. — Being asked, Whether it is not usual for the Merchants to send the Cooper to the Warehouse where the Sugars are, for a Sample? he said, Certainly. — Being asked, What Quantity the Cooper is directed to bring away for the Sample ? he said, He believes Two Pounds is deemed sufficient for a Sample. — Being asked. If he does not know, that from Three Pounds and an Half to Four Pounds have often been brought ? he said, He

5 K has

4U2 ltr Pebruam . 17 yb.

has heard so, and a great deal more. — Being asked, Whether he knew of any Instance in Time of Peace of the Goods remaining in Lighters Five or Six Weeks? he said, No. — Being asked, Whether it can ever happen in Time of Peace ? he said, He thinks it is likely. — Being asked, Whether his principal Reason does not arise from there not being Depth of Water sufficient at the Quays and Sufferance Wharfs for the Ships to discharge their Cargoes there ? he said, It is certainly a very material Reason, but it is not by any Means the most material, because he thinks the Difficulty of the Navigation for such Ships as have hitherto been obliged to discharge their Cargoes at Deptford, ‘ for the Want of a sufficient Depth of Water, and other Impediments, from the crowded State of the River, would not thereby be removed. — Being asked, Whether he knew of any Instance, within the last Two Years, of any Lighter of Sugar lying so long at the Quays as Five or Six Weeks, or even Two or Three Weeks? he said, Two or Three Weeks in many Instances. — Being asked, Whether that did not happen in 1793 ? he said, He knew several Instances in 1793 of Lighters being detained Five or Six Weeks at the Wharf. — Being asked, Whether he has ever seen the Quays so crowded, by Casks being piled on the Quays Five or Six Hogsheads high, for Want of Room, so as to impede the Business of the Quays? he said, Yes, he has seen them several Hogsheads high. Being asked, Whether that Difficulty does not arise from the under ones having paid the Duty, and the upper ones not ? he said, He could not tell. — Being asked, Whether he knew the Extent of the Sufferance Wharfs? he said, He did not. — Being asked, If he had ever been upon the Sufferance Wharfs, and made such Observations as to enable him to state whether they contain proper Accommodation for the landing and Delivery of Goods, or not ? he said, He has been upon many of them, and had Occasion to employ them in 1793, and thinks them even worse calculated for the Accommodation of the West India Trade than the Free Quays. — Bein» asked, On which Side of the Water were those Sufferance Wharfs ? he said, On the Surrey Side. — Then,

Mr. John Dailey being examined, said, That he is Assistant to the Register General of Shipping. — And being asked, Whether the Shipping using the Port of London has not increased very considerably within the last Fifty Years? he said, It has. — Being asked, Whether he could tell in what Degree ? he said, It appears by the Books in the Custom House that it has more than doubled. — And being asked, What was the State of the Shipping in 1793, in the Foreign Trade, inwards? he said, There were 3,541 Ships, amounting to 655,124 Tons, entered inwards in 1793.

Mr. Jaynes Duncan being then examined, said, That he is a Ship Broker, and has commanded Vessels in the King's and Merchants Service many Years. — Being asked, Whether he is not acquainted generally with the Situation of the Trade in the Port of London ? he said, He is. — And being asked, Whether many Inconveniences, Delays, Accidents, and Damages have not been occasioned to the Trade and Commerce of the Port of London from the crowded State of the River? he said, There has, many more than he can remember. — And being asked, Whether, from the very great Increase of the Navigation of the River, many very heavy Damages and Delays have not been frequently sustained by the Owners of, and Persons interested in, Ships and Vessels resorting to the Port of London ? he said, There has, a great many. — And being asked, If good and sufficient Wet Docks or Basons, Canals or Cuts, with proper Outlets, and other necessary Works, were made in convenient Situations near the River, for receiving and discharging Vessels, whether the several Grievances complained of might not thereby be removed, Protection and Dispatch given to Shipping, Accommodation to Commerce, and Security to the Revenue ? he said, Most undoubtedly.

Mr. Daniel Alexander, Junior, being then examined, was asked, Whether it will not be necessary, for carrying into Effect the Purposes proposed by the Petitioners, to purchase several Lands, Buildings, and other Premisses ? he said, It will: that the Buildings in general consist of old Houses.

Mr. John Rennie being examined, was asked, Whether he has surveyed the Situation of the proposed Docks, and other Works, and also the Line of the intended Canal? he said, He has, and that it is very practicable to make them.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for making Wet Docks, Basons, Cuts, and other Works, for the greater Accommodation and Security of Shipping, Commerce, and Revenue, within the Port of London, and for making a Navigable Canal from Blackmail to the said Docks in And that

Mr. Manning, Sir William Young, Mr. Samuel Long, Mr. Dcvaynes, Mr. Hobart, Mr. and Mr. Whit-

Mr. Dudley North reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Common Council Men, Free Burgesses, and Inhabitants, of the Town and Borough of Great Grimsby, in the County of Lincoln, also of the several Proprietors of Estates there, and in the Vicinity thereof, and of the Farmers and Occupiers thereof, and also of the several Merchants, Traders, and others, whose Names are thereunto respectively subscribed, was referred; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, relative to Navigation Bills, had been complied with; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. George Babb being examined, said, That the Port of Great Grimsby is a very ancient Port; and the Haven there, which extends from the Two Bridges or Sluices in the said Parish to the River Humber, was formerly deep and capacious enough to admit Ships of nearly 400 Tons Burthen, but that it is now so silted and warped up as to be navigable only for Sloops of about 40 Tons Burthen, which are frequently neaped for Ten or Twelve Days together, and seldom able, when

loaded,

Cranford Bridge, Slough, &c. Roads Bill, reported.

Great Grimsby Haven Petition, reported.

loaded, either to get up or out of the Haven but at Spring Tides; and consequently, it is now become almost impracticable for any Ship to navigate so far up the Haven as to reach the legal Quays, Wharfs, or Landing Places of the said Port, by Means whereof the Trade of the Town is gone almost to entire Decay, to the great Loss, Prejudice, and Inconvenience, as well of the Inhabitants thereof, and of the adjacent Country, as of the Public at large. And being further examined, he said, That if the said Haven was widened, deepened, and rendered;more straight, and the Course thereof in Part varied, and if the Water of a certain Beck, called Freshney, was brought into the said Haven, the same would be rendered navigable more constantly for Vessels of large Burthen, whereby the Trade ana Commerce of the Town would be restored, and considerably increased, and the Public in general greatly benefited.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for widening, deepening, enlarging, altering, and improving, the Haven of the Town and Port of Great Grimsby, in the County of Lincoln: And that Mr. Dudley North and Mr. Harrison do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A Petition of George Stainfo Esquire, Messenger attending the Great Seed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioner observes, by the Votes, that a Bill for the more expeditious and regular Conveyance of Writs, issued for the Election of Members to serve in Parliament, is now depending in the House, which, if passed into a Law, the Petitioner is apprehensive will much affect the Fees belonging to him upon the Carriage and Conveyance of Writs for the Election of Members to serve in Parliament: And therefore praying, That if the said Bill shall pass into a Law, the House will be pleased to make some Compensation to the Petitioner for the Loss he may sustain, by the Diminution of his Fees, in Consequence of the Provisions intended in the said Bill.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

Mr. Alderman Anderson reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Proprietors of the Bank or Fund, called The Million Bank, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, certain Indentures, bearing Date the 19th of July and the 19th of February 1695, were produced and read, by which it appeared, that divers Persons agreed to erect the said Bank or Fund for certain Purposes, to be founded upon certain Annuities, and Parliamentary or other good Securities; and that several Sums of Money had been subscribed as a Capital Stock or Fund for carrying on such Undertaking, which was to continue for 199 Years, unless sooner determined by the Order and Consent of the Proprietors having Two Third Parts of the said Capital Stock, or by some inevitable Accident; and that at the Expiration or other sooner Determination of the said Term of 199 Years, the said Capital Stock, and such Part of the Profits as should not have been before divided, shall be then divided amongst the Proprietors, in Proportion to each Person's Interest in the said Capital Stock and Profits.

It also appeared to your Committee, that the Capital Stock of the said Bank or Fund is 500,000l.; and that the said Society purchased the Reversions of divers Exchequer Annuities for the Remainder of a Term of 96 Years, by the falling in of which the Society have been enabled, for several Years past, to make a Dividend of 5 /. per Centum per , and for the last Half Year an extraordinary additional Dividend of Ten Shillings per Centum upon the said Capital Stock; and by investing the Surplus in Government and other Public Securities, there is a large Accumulation on the said Capital Stock. That the said Term of 96 Years expired on the 5th of February 1792, from which Time the Business of the said Bank has wholly consisted in the Receipt of the Dividends becoming payable on the Stocks and Securities composing the said Capital Stock, and the Accumulations thereof, and in the Payment of the Dividends upon the said Stock or Fund, and in the Investment of the Surplus thereof in Government or other Securities. That the Expence of conducting the Affairs of the said Society is between Six and Seven hundred Pounds per Annum.

Mr. Henry Johnson being examined, said, That no Profit now results to the Society from the Continuance of the said Bank or Fund, but on the contrary (besides the above Annual Expence of Management) the Petitioners Property therein is subject to Loss upon every

Sale thereof, the same producing considerably less in Proportion than their Shares in the Securities in which the said Capital Stock is invested would produce, was the said Capital Stock or Fund divided amongst them.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for dissolving a certain Partnership Society or Undertaking, called The Million Bank, and for dividing the Joint Stock and Funds, belonging thereto, amongst the Members thereof: And that Mr. Alderman Anderson and Mr. Alderman Lushinglon do prepare, and bring, in, the same.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.,

William Cross, Surveyor to the said Company, being examined, said. That by virtue of Two Acts of the Sixth and Tenth Years of His present Majesty's Reign, a Navigable Canal from the Trent to the Mersey hath been made and completed; and by another Act of the Sixteenth Year of His said Majesty, another Navigable Canal hath also been made and completed, from the said first-mentioned Canal on the South Side of Harecastle, in the County of Stafford, to Froghal and a Railway from thence to or near Caldon, in the said County.

And the Witness further said, That by Surveys lately taken, it appears, that a Navigable Cut or Canal may be made from the last mentioned Canal, near the Village of Endon, to the Town of Leek, in the said County of Stafford, which will be of great Advantage to the Trade and Commerce of the said Town, and of Public Utility; and that for supplying the said Canal with Water, a Reservoir may be conveniently made in a certain Vale called Rudyard Vale, near to the said Town of Leek; which Canal and Reservoir the said Company, at their own Expence, are w illing and desirous to make and maintain.

Mr. Powys reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of Henry Earl of , was referred;

That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, several Letters Patent, dated the 4th of April, the 30th of May, and the 23d of July, in the Fourth Year of the Reign of King Charles the First, were produced and read; whereby it appeared that the said Earl of Exeter is seised in Fee of the Woods, Underwoods, Woodlands, and other Hereditaments within the Hay or Walk of Westhay, within the Bailiwick of Clive, in the Forest of Rockingham, in the County of Northampton, except Herbage for the King's Deer and Wild Beasts, and all Royal Mines upon the Premisses; and is also seised in Fee of the Office of Forester or Keeper of the said Hay or Walk, and of all the Deer and Wild Beasts therein: And,

John Bramston, Esquire, being examined, said, That

divers Persons have used and enjoyed Rights of Common upon the said Woods and Premisses, which are capable of Improvement, and for that Purpose it is proposed to set out and allot Lands belonging to the said Earl in lieu of such Rights of Common; but as such Improvement cannot be effectually carried into Execution so long as the Deer of the Forest are at Liberty to go into the said Premisses, His Majesty, upon Application being made to him, has been graciously pleased to give his Consent, that a Bill should be brought into Parliament to grant to the said Earl of Exeter, his Heirs and Assigns, in Fee Simple, all the Estate, Right, Title, and Interest now remaining in His Majesty in, over, and upon the said Hay or Walk, ipon a full and adequate Consideration to be paid for the same.

Ordered, That the said Report be referred to the Consideration of a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House will, Tomorrow Morning, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the said Report.

Mr. Powys reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of George Finch Hatton, Esquire, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Letters Patent, dated the 5th of July, in the Twenty-fifth Year of the Reign of Queen Elizabeth, were produced and read; whereby it appeared that the Petitioner is seised of the Custody of the Launde of Benefield, within the Forest of Rockingham, in the County of Northampton, with the Office of Valet and Groom-keeper of the same Launde, and the Wild Beasts therein, and also of the Office of Keeper of divers Woods within the said Forest of Rockingham, and within the Bailiwick of Rockingham, in the said Forest, and the Custody of the Wild Beasts within the Launde, Offices, Woods, and Bailiwick aforesaid, and is also seised of the Messuage called The Launde Lodge, within the Launde aforesaid, and of the Herbage and Paunage of the said Laundq: And,

' John Bramston, Esquire, being examined, said, That the Petitioner and others are entitled to divers Woods,

Lands, and Grounds in the said Bailiwick, over which the said Office extends, and in or over which the Deer of the said Forest have Right to feed and depasture. —

And the Witness added, that divers Persons have used and enjoyed Rights of Common upon the Woodlands and Premisses; and that the said Launde, Woods,

Lands, and Premisses are capable of Improvement, and for that Purpose it will be expedient to set out and allot Lands in lieu of such Right of Common; but as such Improvement cannot be effectually carried into Execution so long as the Deer of the Forest are at Liberty to go into the said Launde, Woods, Lands, and Premisses, the Petitioner has obtained His Majesty's Consent that a Bill may be brought into Parliament, to enable His Majesty to grant to the Petitioner, his Heirs and Assigns, in Fee Simple, all the Estate, Right, Title, and Interest now remaining in His Majesty in, over, and upon the said Launde, Woods, Lands, and Premisses, upon a full and adequate Consideration to be paid for the same.

Ordered, That the said Report be referred to the Consideration of a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House will, Tomorrow Morning, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the said Report.

Mr. Poztys reported from the Committee, to whom Petition for the Petition of John Earl of Westmorland, was referred; a Grant of That the Committee had examined the Matter of the ^elt said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, moriandin as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Rockingham Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at Forestre-the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as P°rte<l* followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, several Grants from the Crown were produced, by which it appeared, that the Petitioner is seised in Fee of all the Woods, Underwoods, Woodlands, and other Hereditaments within the Hay or Walk of Sulehay and Short-wood, and within the Hay or Walk of Morehay, within the Bailiwick of Clive, otherwise Cliffe, in the Forest of Rockingham, in the County of Northampton, except as therein is excepted; and that the Petitioner is also entitled to the Office of Master Forester or Keeper of the said Bailiwick, called Cliffe Bailiwick, and all the Herbage and Deer Browse within the said Hay or Walk of Sulehay Farms and Shortzcood, and the said Hay or Walk of Morehay, with Power to the Petitioner to take all the Deer to his own Use, and to inclose the said Woods and other Premisses, and convert the same into Tillage, and such other Uses as the Petitioner should think fit: And,

John Bramston, Esquire, being examined, said, That the Petitioner has not yet destroyed the Deer, in regard the Woods being commonable to several neighbouring Parishes, the Cattle could not be excluded beyond the usual Time, and the Removal of the Deer would have no other Effect than leaving a greater Portion of Herbage for the Commoners without any Advantage to the Petitioner. — That the said Premisses might be improved if the Commonable Cattle were excluded therefrom, for which Purpose the Petitioner is desirous to make a full Compensation to the Commoners for their Common Rights; but such Improvement cannot be carried into Execution so long as the Deer of the Forest are permitted to go into the Woods and Premisses; and His Majesty has been pleased to consent that a Bill may be brought into Parliament to enable His Majesty to grant to the Petitioner, his Heirs and Assigns in Fee Simple, all the Estate now remaining in His Majesty in and upon the said Hays or Walks, upon a full and adequate Consideration to be paid for the same.

Ordered, That the said Report be referred to the Consideration of a Committee of the whole House.

Ordered, That Mr. Charles Long do make the Report from the Committee, who were appointed to inquire what Laws are expired, or near expiring; and to report their Opinion, from Time to Time, to the House, which of them are fit to be revived or continued.

Mr. Charles Long accordingly reported from the said Committee; That the Committee had inquired accordingly, and had come to several Resolutions, which they had directed to be reported to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered. it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Resolutions of the Committee were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That so much of an Act, made in the Eighth Year of the Reign of His Majesty King George the First, intituled, "An Act for giving further Encouragement " for the Importation of Naval Stores, and for other " Purposes therein mentioned," as relates to the Importation of Wood and Timber, and of the Goods commonly called Lumber, therein particularly enumerated, from any of His Majesty's British Plantations or Colonies in America, free from all Customs and Impositions whatsoever, which was to be in Force for Twenty-one Years from the 24th Day of June 1722, and which, by several subsequent Acts, made in the Sixteenth, Twenty-fourth, and Thirty-first Years of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the

Second, and the Fourth, Twelfth, Nineteenth, Twenty-sixth, and Thirty-third Years of His present Majesty's Reign, was further continued until the 29th Day of September 1795, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament, is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That so much of an Act, made in the Eighth Year of the Reign of his Majesty King George the First, for the Encouragement of the Silk Manufactures of this Kingdom, and for taking off several Duties on Merchandizes exported, and for reducing the Duties upon Beaver Skins, Pepper, Mace, Cloves, and Nutmegs, imported, and for Importation of all Furs, of the Product of the British Plantations, into this Kingdom only, and that the Two Corporations of Assurance, on any Suits brought on their Policies, shall be liable only to single Damages and Costs of Suit, as relates to the Encouragement of the Silk Manufactures of this Kingdom, and to the taking off several Duties on Merchandize exported, which was to continue in Force for Three Years, from the 25th Day of March 1722, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament, and which, by several subsequent Acts, made in the Eleventh Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, and in the Second, Eighth, Fifteenth, Twentieth, Twenty-sixth, and Thirty-second Years of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, and in the Sixth, Fourteenth, Twenty-second, and Twenty-ninth Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, bath been continued until the 24th Day of June 1795, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament, is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the Eighth Year of the Reign of his Majesty King George the First, intituled, "An Act to prevent the clandestine running of Goods, " and the Danger of Infection thereby, and to prevent Ships breaking their Quarantine, and to subject Copper Ore, of the Production of the British " Plantations, to such Regulations as other enumerated Commodities of the like Production are subject," which was to be in Force for Two Years, from the 25th Day of March 1722, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament, and which, by several subsequent Acts (except the Clauses obliging all Ships and Vessels to perform Quarantine) was to have further Continuance to the 1st Day of June 1747, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament, and which, by an Act, made in the Twentieth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, was intended to be further continued to the 1 st Day of June 1754, but, by Mistake, the Year 1747 was inserted therein, instead of the said Year 1754, and which, by several subsequent Acts, made in the Twenty-first, Twenty-seventh, and Thirty-third Years of the Reign of his said late Majesty, and in the Seventh, Fourteenth, Twenty-first, and Twenty-eighth Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, was further continued from the Expiration thereof until the 29th Day of September 1795, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament, is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the Fifth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, for the Encouraging the Growth of Coffee in His Majesty's Plantations in America, which was to continue in Force from the 25th Day of March 1735, until the 25th. Day of March 1739, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament, and which, by several subsequent Acts, made in the Eleventh, Nineteenth, Twenty-fifth, and Thirty-second Years of his said late Majesty's Reign, and in the Sixth, Fourteenth, Twenty-

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the Fourth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for importing Salt from Europe into the Province of " Quebec, in America, for a limited Time," which was to continue in Force from the 24th Day of June 1764, for the Term of One Year, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament, and which, by several subsequent Acts, made in the Sixth, Thirteenth, Twentieth, Twenty-sixth, and Thirty-first Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, was further continued until the 24th Day of June 1795, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament, is near expiring, and fit to be . continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for encouraging the Manufacture of Leather, by lowering " the Duty payable upon the Importation of Oak Bark, when the Price of such Bark shall exceed a " certain Rate, for a limited Time," which was to continue in Force for the Term of Five Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament, and which was, by another Act, made in t:he Seventeenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, continued for the further Term of Five 'Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament, and which Act, by another Act,

North Level Lord William Russell reported from the Committee, Drainage to whom the Petition of Francis Duke of Bedford, Petition, Lord of the Manor of and the humble Peti-

reporte . jjon of the Governor, Bailiffs, and Commonalty of the Company of Conservators of the Great Level of the Fens, and of the several other Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, Proprietors of Lands lying in the North Level, Part of the Great Level of the Fens, called Bedford Level, and in other-

wise Great Porsand, in the County of Lincoln, was referred; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, relative to Drainage Bills, had been complied with; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, passed in the Eleventh Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, to enable the Corporation of the Governor, Bailiffs, and Commonalty of the Company of Conservators of the Great Level of the Fens, called Bedford Level, to complete and maintain the principal Banks and Works necessary to the well draining and preserving the North Level, Part of the said Great Level, and for laying Taxes on the Lands within the said North Level, and on divers Lands adjoining thereto, in the Manor of was read;

whereby it appears, that the Lands and Grounds within the said North Level, are Yearly rated and assessed as follows; (that is to say) all the said Lands and Grounds within the said North Level (except as therein excepted) with aTax of Six Pence for every Acre; and the said Lands called Portsand, otherwise Great Porsand, with a Tax of Three Pence ere: And, Mr. Thomas Steed Watson being examined, said, That

the said Taxes have been duly collected and applied, pursuant to the Direction, and for the Purposes of the said Act: Then,

Mr. John Gotobed being examined, said, That he is Deputy Register of the Bedford Level Corporation: That the Corporation have borrowed upon Bonds the Sum of 25,000l. being the whole Sum they are empowered to borrow on Account of the said North Level, which Money still remains due; that the Yearly Produce of the said Taxes and Revenues, after deducting the Interest of the said Debt, Officers Salaries, and other incidental Expences, amounts to the Sum of 944 /., which Sum is insufficient for the repairing, maintaining, and supporting the Works and Banks of the said Level: That for the maintaining of the Works absolutely necessary for the preserving and well draining of the said Lands, it is requisite that a further Tax should be laid upon those Lands, and that Power should be given to the said Corporation

to raise Money on the Credit of such additional Tax, for the more expeditious and complete Execution of the Works requisite: And,

Mr. Thomas Pear, the Superintendant of the said Banks and Works, being examined, said, That the Great Outring Banks of the said North Level, comprize a Distance of Twenty-five Miles and Six Furlongs, or thereabouts; and that the Annual Taxes and Revenues at present chargeable on the said Lands, are insufficient for the due maintaining, supporting, and executing the said Banks and Works, and of roding and cleansing the several Rivers and Drains belonging thereto, and very inadequate in Times of Flood of finding and providing Boats, Materials, and other Things necessary: — And being further examined, he said, That the Maintenance and Support of the said Banks and Works are essential to the Preservation of the said Lands, and that in order to maintain, support, and keep the same in Repair, it will be necessary to lay an additional Tax on the said North Level, and in otherwise Great Porsand; and for the better and more expeditious executing and completing the said Works, and preserving the said Banks, it will be requisite that the said Corporation of Bedford Level should have Powers given to them to borrow Money upon the Credit of the said additional Tax.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for laying an additional Tax upon the Lands within the North Level, Part of the Great Level of the Fens, called Bedford Level, and on Portsatid, otherwise Great Porsand, in the County of Lincoln, for the further Support and Preservation of the principal Banks and Works of the said North Level: And that Lord William Russell and Lord John Russell do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Mr. Alderman Harley reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Company of Proprietors of the Leominster Canal Navigation, under their Common Seal, was referred; That the Committee had examined,. and found that the said Petition is not within the Standing Orders of the House, relative to Navigation Bills, it not being intended to give Power for raising any further or additional Rates, Tolls, or Duties, or for varying the Line of the Canal; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, passed in the Thirty-first Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for making a Navigable Canal from Kington, in the County of Hereford, by or through Leominster, to join the River Severn, near Stourport Bridge, in the County of Worcester, was read: And,

Vol. 51.

Mr. Jacob Wyles being examined, said, That the Company have proceeded in making the said Canal, but have met with many unforeseen Difficulties in carrying on the Work, which have occasioned a very great additional Expence from what was expected at the Time the said Act was passed, particularly in making a Tunnel at Putnal Field: That the said Company have expended nearly the Sum of 80,000l. in carrying on the Work, and find, that unless they have Power to raise an additional Sum of Money beyond the Sum they are authorized to do by the said Act, they cannot be able to complete the said Tunnel and Canal: And the Witness added, That some other Amendments are necessary to be made in the said Act.

Mr. John Rennie being then examined, said, That he has surveyed the Works already done in Execution of the said Act, and finds that it will require a very considerable Sum of Money in order to complete the said Canal, in Addition to what the Company are authorized to raise by the said Act.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring iq a Bill to enable the Company of Proprietors of the Leominster Canal Navigation to finish and complete the same: And that Mr. Alderman Harley and Mr. Hunter do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A Petition of the Rulers, Auditors, Comptrollers, and Assistants, of the Society or Company of Watermen, Wherrymen, and Lightermen, upon the River Thames between Gravesend and Windsor, under their Common Seal, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for making Wet Docks, Basons, Cuts, and other Works, for the greater Accommodation and Security of Shipping, Commerce, and Revenue, within the Port of London, and for making a Navigable Canal from Black to the said Docks in Waj/ping; and setting forth, that the said Company of Watermen, Wherrymen, and Lightermen, consist of Ten thousand Persons, and upwards, many of them having numerous Families, and the Whole of their Subsistence is drawn from the Navigation of Boats and Vessels upon the said River, and if the said Bill should be permitted to pass into a Law, the Boats and Vessels of the Petitioners employed upon the said River will be rendered, in a great Measure, useless, and a great Majority of the Petitioners, and their numerous Families, deprived of the Means of Subsistence; and that, by an Act, passed in the First Year of the Reign of King James the First, the Petitioners are empowered to appoint a certain Number of Watermen to ply upon the said River between

Vau.rhall, above London Bridge, and Limehouse, upon the Lord's Day, and the Overplus of the Earnings of such Watermen are directed by the said Act to be applied to the Use of the poor, aged, decayed, and maimed Watermen and Lightermen, of the said Society and Company, and their Widows, and that, by the Overplus of the Earnings of such Watermen so plying on the Lord's Day, upwards of Five hundred aged and necessitous Persons are now, and have been for some Time past, Annually relieved; and that the greater Part of the Earnings of such Watermen, so plying on the Lord's Day, arise from the carrying of Seamen and other Persons on Board the Vessels lying in the said River, but if the said Bill should pass into a Law, such Earnings will be wholly lost to the Petitioners, and the numerous Objects of Distress which are supported by the said Charity will be thereby deprived of its Relief and Assistance: That, for several Years last past, the Average Number of Apprentices bound into the Service of the Petitioners amounts to Three hundred and upwards Annually, and the Petitioners have Reason to believe that the Annual Number of such Apprentices would be reduced to less than Fifty if the said Bill should pass into a Law; and that, in the Course of the present War, near Four thousand Men have been furnished from the Body of the Petitioners, who are now serving, either as impressed Men or Volunteers, in His Majesty's Navy, and, if the Petitioners should be compelled to desert their Employments, by the passing of the said Bill

Ex- Mr. Hobart reported from the Committee, who were Vw--»gLws. appointed to enquire what Laws are expired, or near expiring, and to report their Opinion, from Time to Time, to the House, which of them are fit to be revived or continued; That the Committee had made a further Enquiry, and had come to several other Resolutions, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Resolutions of the Committee were read; and are as followed; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That so much of an Act, made in the Thirty-third Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for the Regulation of Distilleries in Scotland, and the Exportation of British made Spirits Vol.5I.

" from England to Scotland, and from Scotland to " England, for a limited Time," as imposes Duties on Spirits made or manufactured in that Part of Great Britain called Scotland, and imported from thence into that Part of Great Britain called England, which was to continue in Force until the 1st Day of December 1795, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament, is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the Nineteenth Year of the Reign of His late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, "An Act more effectually to prevent the " Frauds and Abuses committed in the Admeasurement of Coals within the City and Liberty of Westminster, and that Part of the Duchy of Lancaster " adjoining thereto, and the several Parishes of Saint " Giles in the Fields, Saint Mary le Bon, and such Part

" of the Parish of Saint Andrew, Holborn, as lies in the County of Middlesex," which was to continue in Force from the 24th Day of September 1746 for the Term of Three Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament, and which was continued by several Acts, passed in the Twenty-third, Twenty-fourth, Thirty-first, and Thirty-second Years of the Reign of his said late Majesty, and the Sixth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, and was amended and further continued by an Act, passed in the Twenty-first Year of His said present Majesty's Reign, until the 24th Day of June 1795, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament, is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Air. Dent reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of George Stainforth, Esquire, Messenger attending the Great Seal, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Alatter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read j and is as followeth; vis.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Stainfoi'lh produced to your Committee an Account of the Profit of his Office, which he has held for Three Years, from August 1792 to August 1795, by which it appeared, that the Annual Average Profit has been 586/. 7$. arising from Thirty-eight YVrits in each Year, which Account is hereunto annexed. And Mr. Stainforth stated to your Committee, that in the said Sum is included Alileage upon the Carriage of Writs, and also 78/. 45. for the Carriage of Four Proclamations to Edinburgh, amounting to 38.5/. 7s. and the 51. 5 s. given upon the Delivery of each Writ, as Fees amounting to 201 /.

Besides the above Sum of 586/. 7 he receives from the Hanaper Office the Sum of 276/., for summoning a new Parliament in England and Scotland; which, on the Supposition that a Parliament exists Six Years, amounts to 46 I.per Annum, which being

5 Quadded

Mr. Stain-forth's Petition, reported; |

426 22° FebruariL A. 1796.

added to the Sum of 586/. 7 makes the Sum of 632/. 7 8.his Average Annual Income, exclusive of

Fees he may receive on a General Election, and which if estimated according to the Rate hitherto received, and supposing a new Parliament is chosen every Six Years, will produce an Increase to his Income of above 480/. each Year; but this Part of his expected Income he has not yet had an Opportunity to ascertain, no General Election having intervened since he has held the Office. Exclusive of the Fees above-mentioned, his Deputy has always received 2/. 2 on every Writ, for his own Use.

Mr. Stainforth also acquainted your Committee, That wdien he came into his Office, he found the Fees arbitrary and extravagant to such a Degree as to occasion great Complaint, which he has reduced to a fixed, and

what he trusts has been considered as a moderate Rate; and assured your Committee of his perfect Acquiescence to any Regulations which the Legislature, for the beneficial Regulation of the Office, should think fit to make, expressing at the same Time a Hope, that if it should be thought proper to leave the Office of Messenger of the Great Seal, as far as respects the Delivery of Parliamentary Writs, subject to a real and bond side. Responsibility, the Legislature would take into their Consideration the Propriety of an increased Allowance under the Head of Mileage; and if, with the same View of Public Benefit, it should be thought right to regulate the Office upon any other Plan, they would consider what Compensation the Office may properly receive on Account of the Circumstances before-mentioned.

A Petition of the Governor and Company of the Petition from Water Works and Water Houses in was pre- Waxworks

sented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Company Petitioners are the Proprietors of certain Water Works against Lon-and Water Houses established in the Parish of Saint ‘Jon P?.^3' Paul. Shadwell, in the County of Middlesex, which c" 1 Works have been carried on under the Authority of an Act, made in the Third and Fourth Year of the Reign of King William and Queen Mary, to the present Time, and the said Parish, and several other Neighbouring Parishes, have been supplied with Water from the said Works by Means of Engines, Pipes, and Cisterns, erected and laid for the Passage and Conveyance of it, to the great Accommodation of the Inhabitants of the said Parishes, and at the great Expence and Risk of the Petitioners and their Predecessors; and that the said Works have been found to be of great Public Utility, upon the Success whereof depends the Health and Comfort of many Thousands of the Inhabitants of the Neighbourhood; and that the Petitioners are informed, by the Votes of the House, that a Bill is depending for making Wet Docks,

Basons, Cuts, &c. and for other Purposes, in the said Parish of Shadwell, and other Parishes adjoining thereto,

and, if the said Bill should pass into a Law, the Petitioners will be very much injured in their Property. their Works destroyed, and the Inhabitants in the Neighbourhood deprived of their Comforts, and be put to the greatest Inconvenience: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill, and that the same may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for making Wet Docks, Basons,

Cuts, and other Works for the greater Accommodation and Security of Shipping, Commerce, and Revenue, within the Port of London, and for making a Navigable Canal from Blackmail to the said Docks in Wapping, be read a Second Time; and that the Petitioners be then heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunder written, on Behalf of themselves and others, Owners and Lessees of Fulling and other Mills on the River Exe, and Dyers and other Persons concerned in the Woollen Manufacture in and near the City of Exeter, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for making a Navigable Canal from the River Exe, near the Town of in

the County of Devon, to the River Tone, near the Town of Taunton, in the County of Somerset, and for cleansing and making navigable a certain Part of the said River Tone, and for making cerain Cuts from the said Canal; and Setting forth, That the said Mills are held by the Petitioners, some of them by Leases for Years determinable on the Deaths of Lives, others for long Terms of Years absolute, and some at Yearly Rack Rents, and notwithstanding the River Culm now flows into the Exe, the Supply of Water is very frequently insufficient for the Petitioners said Mills, particularly in the Summer Months; and that, if the Company of Proprietors of the said intended Canal should bo permitted to take Water from the said River Culm, it will be highly prejudicial and injurious to the Petitioners Property, and tend to the Ruin and Decay of the Woollen Trade carried on in and near the City of Exeter: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by their Counsel and Agents, against the said Bill, and that the same may not pass into a Law, or that they may have such Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second Time; and that the Petitioners be then heard, by their Counsel, or Agents, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

Marshland Mr. Coke of Norfolk reported from the Committee, Drainage and to whom the Petition of the several Persons, whose ^Petition ^ames are thereunto subscribed being Owners and reported. ' Proprietors of Messuages or Houses, or Tofts, having Rights of Common upon and over certain Tracts of Common and Waste Lands called Marshland Smeeth and Marshland Fen, lying within the Country of Marshland, in the County of Norfolk, was referred; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, relative to Bills of Drainage and Inclosure, had been complied with; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it iappeared to them, to the House; and he read the

Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

Mr. Thomas Bean being examined, said, That there are within the Country of Marshland, in the County of Norfolk, certain large Tracts of Common and Waste Lands, called Marshland Smeeth and Marshland Fen, containing together, by Estimation, 8,oooo Acres, or thereabouts, bounded and described as in the Petition is mentioned: And that the Owners and Proprietors of certain ancient Commonable Messuages or Houses, or of Tofts (being the Scites of ancient Commonable Messuages or Houses) are respectively entitled to Rights of Common in, over, and upon the same. —

And being further examined, he said, That the said Tracts of Common and Waste Lands, for Want of a proper and effectual Drainage, are of little Benefit to the several Persons having Rights of Common in, over, and upon the same; and that it would be of great Advantage to the Parties interested, if the said Tracts of Common and Waste Lands were drained, '

inclosed, divided, and allotted among the several Parties, according to their Rights and Interests therein:

And the Witness added, That it would be of Advantage to the Parties interested, if the Stocking, Feeding, and Depasturing of the said Smeeth and Fen were regulated and stinted until the Inclosure, Division, and Allotment thereof.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for draining and improving, and for inclosing, dividing, and allotting, certain Tracts of Common and Waste Lands, called Marshland Smeeth and Marshland Fen, lying within the Country of Marshland, in the County of Norfolk; and for stinting and regulating the Stocking, Feeding, and Depasturing, of the said Smeeth and Fen, until the Inclosure, Division, and Allotment thereof: And that Mr. Coke of Norfolk, Mr.

Hobart, and Mr. Charles Yorke, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons, of the City of London, in Common Council assembled.

And then they withdrew.

And the said Petition was read; Taking Notice of the Bill for making Wet Docks, Basons, Cuts, and other Works, for the greater Accommodation and Security of Shipping, Commerce, and Revenue, within the Port of London, and for making a Navigable Canal from Blackwall to the said Docks in Wapping and Setting forth, That the Mayor and Commonalty and Citizens of the City of London, by virtue of, and under divers Charters, recognized and confirmed by divers Acts of Parliament, have had and exercised, and ought and have accustomed themselves to have and exercise, the Office of Bailiff and Conservator of the Water of Thames, to be exercised and occupied by the Mayor of the same City for the Time being, during the Time of his Mayoralty, or by his sufficient Deputies in, upon, and about, the Water of Thames (that is to say), from the Bridge of the Town of Staines, in the County of Middlesex, and towards the East unto London Bridge, and from thence to a certain Place called Kendall, otherwise Yenland, otherwise Yenleet, towards the Sea and East, and in Medway, and in the Port of the City of London aforesaid, and upon whatsoever Bank, and upon every Shore, and upon every Wharf, of the same Water of Thames, within the Limits and Bounds aforesaid, and in, upon, and about, all and every of them, and also, for all the Time aforesaid, have had and taken, and ought and have accustomed themselves to have and take, to their own proper Use, by the Mayor of the same City for the Time being, during the Time of his Mayoralty, or his sufficient Deputies, all Wages, Rewards, Fees, and Profits, belonging to the same Office of Bailiff; and that, if the said Bill should be passed into a Law, the Rights and Privileges of the Petitioners would be invaded, and the Trade and Commerce of the said Port of London, where it has flourished for a great Length of Time, to the great Benefit and Advantage of the City of London, and the Kingdom in general, would, in a very material Degree, be removed to a new Scite, out of the Controul and Superinten-dance, as well as out of the Care and Protection of the Petitioners; and that such Removal would not only be a Violation of the ancient Privileges of the Petitioners, but also be productive of the most ruinous and distressing Consequences to divers incorporated Societies and Companies, as well as to great Numbers of Individuals, the Value of whose Property, or the Profits of whose Labour and Industry, in a great Measure depend on the Trade and Commerce of the City and Port of London being continued to be carried on within the Limits Vo i.. 51.

and Jurisdiction of the said City That the Petitioners and their Predecessors, ever careful of the Rights and Welfare of their Fellow Citizens, and anxious to accommodate, promote, and increase, the Trade and Commerce of the City of London, have, from Time to Time, devised, and offered to execute, Plans conducive to those Ends, and actuated by these Motives, as well as in Consequence of divers Applications made to them in that Respect, have formed a Plan for increasing the Accommodation of the Port of London, which by the Aid and Authority of Parliament, they have Reason to believe may be carried into Execution, without the Necessity of creating a new Corporation, or other expensive Establishment, without Injury or Inconvenience to Individuals, and without infringing on the ancient Rights and Privileges of the City of London, or bur-thening the Trade of the said Port to the Extent proposed by the said Bill, and the Petitioners pledge themselves to the House to bring forward, and if duly enabled, to carry those Plans into Execution; and that as, by carrying of the Petitioners Plan into Execution, the Public at large would derive every Benefit and Accommodation which the Commerce of London can require at a moderate Expence, and perfectly consistent with the Safety of its Shipping, and the Security of the Revenue, and, as the Petitioners do not thereby take, or mean to take, any Emolument or Advantage to themselves, they rely on the Justice of the House that no new Corporation shall be established, as proposed by the said Bill: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by their Counsel, Agents, and Witnesses, against the said Bill, and that the same may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second Time; and that the Petitioners be then heard, by their Counsel, or Agents, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

Petition from A Petition of the Wardens and Assistants of the shf of'car* Fellowship of Carmen, London, on Behalf of them-men against selye3 and the rest of the Free Carmen of London, was London presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That Docks, &c. the Petitioners are, and have been, from Time imme-1 ' morial, a Body of Freemen and Citizens of London,

originally incorporated, and, as they humbly conceive, essentially necessary for the Accommodation and carrying on of the Trade and Business of the City and Port of London, and are placed by the Authority of Parliament under the Legislation, Controul, and Regulation, of the Magistrates of the said City, at their Court of Session, with respect to the Price, Manner, and other Circumstances of performing their Labour, whereby the possibility of Imposition upon the Merchants and Traders is entirely prevented; and the Petitioners pay an Annual Sum of near 400l. to Christ's Hospital, for the Quit Rent of certain Licences, by which they exercise the exclusive Privilege of working their Carts for Hire within the said City; and that the Petitioners have seen a Bill, depending in the House, for making Wet Docks, Basons, Cuts, and other Works, for the greater Accommodation and Security of Shipping, Commerce, and Revenue, within the Port of London, and for making a Navigable Canal from Black-wall to the said Docks in and if the Scheme

proposed by the said Bill should be carried into Effect, the Trade and Business of the City and Port of London would, in a great Degree, be removed to a new Situation out of the Limits and Jurisdiction of the City, where any Man, or Set of Men, might exercise and carry on the Trade and Business of the Petitioners, whereby the Petitioners would be deprived of that exclusive Privilege they apprehended to be secured to them when they entered into and embarked their Capitals in their Business, the Consequence of which must be very material Injury and Distress, if not total Ruin, to the Fellowship Carmen of London and their Families: And therefore praying, That they may be heard by their Counsel, Agents, and Witnesses, against the said Bill, and that the same may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second Time; and that the Petitioners be then heard, by their Counsel, or Agents, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

Mr. Hobart accordingly reported from the said Committee, the Resolution which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Bounty of One hundred Pounds be allowed to each Master, and Fifty Pounds to each Surgeon, of every Ship employed in conveying Slaves from the Coast of Africa, upon Proof being made, that not more than Two Slaves, in each Hundred that shall have been taken on Board such Ships, have died; and of Fifty Pounds to each Master, and Twenty-five Pounds to each Surgeon, where not more than Three Slaves, in each Hundred, have died within a certain Period.

The said Resolution being read a Second Time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.
