Mr. Fox reported from the Committee, to whom the Victuallers-Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are Potion re-thereunto subscribed, being licensed Victuallers or Re- *{^n|pew, tailers of Malt and other Liquors, was referred; That ter Pots, rathe Committee had examined the Matter of the said ported. Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

William Broivn being examined, said, That there are, within the Cities of London and the Borough of Southwark', and the several Towns, Villages, and Places in the Neighbourhood of the same, more than Seven thousand licensed Publicans, many of whom sustain very heavy Losses by having their Pewter Pots secreted and stolen. — That the Witness was present at a very numerous Meeting of the Publicans lately held, at which the Losses of several of them were stated to be so high as 6o/. or 70/. Annually, but that upon a moderate Computation the Average could not be less than from 15/. to 20/. which (reckoning the whole Number of licensed Houses within the Limits aforesaid) amounts to the Sum of 100,000l. or upwards.

That the Custom of leaving Pewter Pots at the Houses and Habitations of the Customers supplied with Malt or other Liquor, is the principal Cause of such Losses; a Custom which (aided by the experienced Confidence reposed by Thieves in the Receivers of Stolen Goods) affords to the indigent and dishonest frequent and easy Temptations to secrete, steal, melt, and destroy the Pots so left: And (notwithstanding the many Prosecutions, Convictions, and Punishments for Offences of that Nature, at a very heavy Expence and Loss of Time to the Prosecutors) the Witness believes that nothing but Legislative Regulations, restraining all licensed Victuallers, within stated Limits, from leaving their Pots at the Houses or Habitations of their Customers, can effectually stop the Mischief complained of, or destroy the Source of such immoral and dishonest Crimes in the indigent and lower Class of People, so injurious to Individuals.

Mr. Alexander Weir being also examined, confirmed the above Evidence.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to prevent the secreting, purloining, or destroying Pewter Pots, and other Vessels, belonging to Persons retailing Malt or other Liquors, within the Limits to be therein mentioned: And that Mr. Fox and the Lord Hood do prepare, and bring in, the same.

The House, according to Order, resumed the adjourned Debate on the Motion, made upon Monday last, That it appears to this House, That the Principle of making Loans for the Public Service by free and open Competition, uniformly professed by the Chancellor of the Exchequer, has been very generally recognized, as affording the fairest Prospect of Public Advantage.

And the Question being again proposed, That it appears to this House, That the Principle of making Loans for the Public Service by free and open Competition, uniformly professed by the Chancellor of the Exchequer, has been very generally recognized, as affording the fairest Prospect of Public Advantage;

An Amendment was proposed to be made to the Question, by leaving out the Words, " free and open " Competition, uniformly professed by the Chancellor " of the Exchequer, has been very generally recognized, as affording the fairest Prospect of Public " Advantage," and inserting the Words, " Competition, which was introduced, and has in general been " acted upon, by the present Chancellor of the Exchequer, has been productive, in many Instances, of " great Public Advantage; but, that this Principle " could not be applied in its full Extent to the Bargain " for the late Loan, consistently with the peculiar " Circumstances of the Case, and with that Attention " to the equitable Claims of Individuals, which ought " always to be shewn in Transactions with them on the " Behalf of the Public," instead thereof.

And the Question being put, That the Words proposed to be left out stand Part of the Question;

The House divided.

Resolved, That it appears to this House, That the Principle of making Loans for the Public Service by Competition, which was introduced, and has in general been acted upon, by the present Chancellor of the Exchequer, has been productive, in many Instances, of great Public Advantage; but, that this Principle could not be applied in its full Extent to the Bargain for the late Loan, consistently with the peculiar Circumstances of the Case, and with that Attention to the equitable Claims of Individuals, which ought always to be shewn in Transactions with them on the Behalf of the Public.

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, That it appears to this House, That, in all the Communications relative to the Formation of the late Loan, which passed between the Chancellor of the Exchequer and the Governor of the Bank of England, or any of the Parties concerned, previous to the 24th of November last, the Chancellor of the Exchequer did invariably profess a Resolution to adhere strictly to the Principle of free and open Competition;

And the previous Question being put, That that Question be now put;

It passed in the Negative.

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, That it appears to this House, That on the 25th of November 1795, the Day appointed by the Chancellor of the Exchequer for a Meeting of the several Competitors for the Loan, to settle the Preliminaries thereof, and when they were all assembled, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, after a separate Conference with Messrs. Boyd and his Party, did propose to the other Competitors, viz. Mellish and , to bid for the Loan, " on Condition that an Option should be " reserved to Boyd and his Party, of taking the Loan " at such a Price as should be equal in Value to One Half per Cent, on the whole Sum borrowed, above " the highest Offer of the Competitors

And the previous Question being put, That that Question be now put;

It passed in the Negative.

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, That it appears to this House, That the said Mellish and Morgan, having refused to become Competitors on a Condition, to which they deemed it almost impossible to submit, the Chancellor of the Exchequer did, immediately after, without proposing any other Terms, agree for the Loan with Boyd and his Party, although it was understood, by all the Parties, that they were not to come to a final Settlement on that Day

And the previous Question being put, That that Question be now put;

It passed in the Negative.

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, That it appears to this House, That, by giving this Preference to Boyd and his Party, the Chancellor of the Exchequer did totally depart from the Principle of free and open Competition, after having, by a Communication through the Governor of the Bank, only Two Days preceding, expressly invited Persons to bid on that Principle, and who had also previously made Preparations for that Purpose;

And the previous Question being put. That that Question be now put;

It passed in the Negative.

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, That it appears to this House, That the Preference, so given to Boyd and his Party, was claimed by them on the Foundation of a supposed Fact in the Settlement of the preceding Loan for the Service of the Year 1795, between the Chancellor of the Exchequer and the said Boyd and his Party; namely, that " the Contract was entered into under the Condition,

" Right, which was founded in Justice and the Nature " of Things, recognized by constant Practice and " Public Opinion;"

And the previous Question being put, That that Question be now put;

It passed in the Negative.

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, That it does not appear to this House, That the Chancellor of the Exchequer has any where admitted the Reality of such Engagement or Condition having been made by him with tire said Boyd and his Party, but, on the contrary, that he did state to the Parties assembled at his House on the 25th of November, " that the Circumstances had come but recently " to his Knowledge," and that he did not admit any Obligation to exist, although the said Boyd contends that his Right was not only founded in Justice and the Nature of Things, but recognized by constant Practice and Public Opinion;

And the previous Question being put, That that Question be now put;

It passed in the Negative.

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, That it appears to this House, That no such Condition is, in fact, either expressed or implied, in any of the Papers laid before this House, in which the Particulars of the Contract for the said Loan appear to have been fully adjusted and settled between the contracting Parties;

And the previous Question being put, That that Question be now put;

It passed in the Negative.

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, That it appears to this House, That such a Restriction is introduced into the Memorandum of the Contract for the Loan for the Service of the present Year; and that no Precedent is any where alleged for the Introduction of a Stipulation so new, and of which the Consequences may be extremely important;

And the previous Question being put, That that Question be now put;

It passed in the Negative.

And the previous Question being put, That that Question be now put;

It passed in the Negative.

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, That it appears to this House, That the said Boyd, in his Addresses to the Chancellor of the Ex-

chequer, on the Subject of his supposed Right to a Preference over the other Competitors, supported that Right by Arguments drawn from his Situation as an Holder of Scrip of the preceding Loan, and from the Injury which he and the other Contractors for that Loan must inevitably suffer, as Holders of that Scrip, by the Introduction of Eighteen Millions more into the Market, while a large Portion of the last Years Scrip was still on Hand; and that it does not appear that the said Boyd did ever allege, or pretend, to the Chancellor of the Exchequer, that he had an unalienable inherent Right to a Preference for the Loan then depending, which belonged to him exclusively, as a Contractor for the preceding Loan, though he should have disposed of the Whole of his Share therein;

And the previous Question being put, That that Question be now put;

It passed in the Negative.

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, That it appears to this House, That it is, generally, to the Negotiation of a new Loan before a certain Period, to which the said Walter Boyd objects in all his Communications with the Chancellor of the Exchequer; and that the Principle of his Objection to such Negotiation applies equally, whether the Deposit on such Loan be appointed to take place shortly before or after the last Payment on the preceding Loan;

And the previous Question being put, That that Question be now put;

It passed in the Negative.

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, That it appears to this House, That the Value of the existing Funds is affected in a far greater Degree by the Negotiation for a new Loan, and the Settlement of the Terms thereof, than by the making the Deposit on such Loan after it is settled;

And the previous Question being put, That that Question be now put;

It passed in the Negative.

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, That it appears to this House, That, before all the Payments were made on the Loan for the Service of the Year 1794, the Chancellor of the Exchequer did negotiate a new Loan with the said Boyd and his Party for the Year 1795; and that, although considerable Sums of the Loan for 1794 were then outstanding as floating Scrip, though the Funds were considerably affected by the Transaction, and though the Deposit was expected to be speedily called for, yet neither James Morgan, Esquire, nor any other of the Contributors to the former Loan, either objected to the Negotiation, or made any Complaint on Account of it;

And the previous Question being put, That that Question be now put;

It passed in the Negative.

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, That it appears to this House, That, waving all Consideration of the Interests of the contracting Parties, Cases may arise in which it might be highly prejudicial to the Public Service if the Chancellor of the Exchequer should be precluded from entering into a Negotiation for a new Loan, or from fixing the Deposit to be made on such Loan on some day previous to the last Payment on the preceding one;

And the previous Question being put, That that Question be now put;

It passed in the Negative.

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, That it appears to this House, That the said Walter Boyd, Esquire, has declared that no Part of his Right to a Preference, as a Contractor for the new Loan, was grounded on the Transaction of the Bills dated at Hamburgh, and circulated by him for the Service of Government; that he never had any Expectation of that Sort; and that he took no Merit at all to himself in having consented to that Operation;

And the previous Question being put, That that Question be now put;

It passed in the Negative.

A Motion was made, and the Question being put,

That it appears to this House, That no such Declarations on the Part of a Contractor, palpably preferred, and immoderately benefited, by the Gift of a Loan of Eighteen Millions Sterling, on such Terms, and accompanied with such Arrangements, as to create a Profit of 12 per Cent, or 2,160,000l., before the First Payment became due, can acquit the Chancellor of the Exchequer of having departed from the Principle of free and open Competition in Favour of Waller Boyd, Esquire, in a Manner incompatible with the Interest of the Public;

It passed in the Negative.

A Motion was made, and the Question being put,

That it appears to this House, That, in every Part of the Transaction of the late Loan, the Public Interest has been sacrificed by the Chancellor of the Exchequer; and that the Profits to the Contributors, at the Expence of the Nation, have been so exorbitantly swelled, as to have risen, even before the Deposit was made thereon, to an Amount greatly exceeding the Deposit itself, viz. on a Loan of Eighteen Millions to the enormous and incredible Sum of Two Millions One hundred and Sixty thousand Pounds Sterling; .

It passed in the Negative.

Resolved, That it appears to this House, That the Terms of the Loan were fixed with a due Regard to the Magnitude of the Sums borrowed, and provided for, as well as to the Market Price of the Funds, and the Situation of Public Affairs, at the Time the Bargain was concluded.

Resolved, That it appears to this House, That, in every Part of the Transaction of the late Loan, the Conduct of the Chancellor of the Exchequer was actuated by a View to the Public Interest; and that there is no Ground to suppose that any Interference took place on the Part of any Persons connected with Government in the Distribution of any Part of the said Loan.

Petition A Petition of the Inhabitants of the Parish of Saint

iTvt f Olaoe, Southwark ,was presented to the House, and

St. 01ave,° re®d; Taking Notice of the Bill for making Wet Docks, Southwark, Basons, Cuts, and other Works, for the greater Accom-againstLon- modation and Security of Shipping, Commerce, and &c BmkS' Revenue, within the Port of , and for making

a Navigable Canal from Blackwall to the said Docks in Wrapping; and Setting forth, That the Petitioners are greatly alarmed at the Tendencies of the said Bill, inasmuch as it would occasion the Removal of a great Part of the Trade of the Port of London away from its ancient and accustomed Channels, to the great Injury of the Inhabitants of the said Parish, in which (from the natural Advantage of its Situation) many of the principal Sufferance Wharfs have been, from Time immemorial, established: That many Lightermen and Watermen, Officers of the Customs, and others, engaged in Employments on the said Wharfs, are Householders in the said Parish, and the Removal of so much of the Trade to a remote District would either deprive them of their Business, or compel them to remove to new Situations, under great Uncertainty of their being able to procure Establishments therein — That the said Wharfs, and the Warehouses belonging, are rated in the Parish Books at a Rental of more than u,oooo I. per Annum, and contribute Annually upwards of 8oo I. to the Maintenance of the Poor, and to other Public Rates in a still larger Proportion — That the said Parish is greatly burthened with Poor, and that a Measure, which so directly tends to diminish the Trade, and, consequently, to lessen the Rental of the Wharfs and Warehouses, would prove an irreparable Injury to the Petitioners: And therefore praying, That they may be allowed to be heard themselves, and by their Counsel, against the said Bill, and against the several Clauses therein, and in Support of these Allegations by proper Witnesses, and, finally, that the said Bill may not pass into a Law.

Petition from A Petition of the there-undersigned Owners, Lessees, certain Own- and Occupiers, of Sufferance Wharfs at the Port of Sufferance London, within the Limits approved of by the Ho-Wharfs nourable the Commissioners of His Majesty's Customs, against D° was also presented to the House, and read; Likewise Bill. taking Notice of the said Bill; and Setting forth, That

many of the Allegations contained in the Preamble thereof, and upon which the pretended Necessity and Propriety of the said Bill particularly rest, are either wholly unfounded in Fact, or are calculated, in the Frame of them, to mislead the Judgment of the House, and that such of the Inconveniences, suggested in the said Bill, as really exist, are in a great Degree exaggerated, for the Petitioners do with Confidence assure the House, that every Inconvenience which can reasonably be complained of in respect to the legal Quays and Sufferance Wharfs within the said Port, or in respect to the Mooring and Navigating of Vessels in the River Thames, arises entirely from the Want of due Regulations and Arrangements relative to those Subjects, and from no other Cause whatsoever, and that the same are capable of being remedied in such a Manner as will neither infringe the Rights, or injure the Properties, of any Individual, or Class of Individuals whatsoever: That the Petitioners have embarked very considerable Fortunes, and employed the Labour and Industry of their lives, in raising and maintaining Wharfs and Warehouses, which have been established and sanctioned by the Approbation of the Commissioners of His Majesty's Customs, and at which the Business of Landing, Shipping, and Housing Goods, has been far many Years past conducted equally to the Satisfaction of that Board, the Accommodation of Vol. 51.

Merchants, and the Advantage of the Public, the Wharfs and Warehouses belonging to the Petitioners having been erected in such Number, Succession, and Extent, as the Increase of the Commerce of the said Port has from Time to Time required, such Wharfs and Warehouses being now of more than Three Times the Extent of the legal Quays described in the said Bill, and being also, from their local Situation, peculiarly calculated to secure and protect the Public Revenue, and in every Respect adequate to the due Landing,

Shipping, and Housing, of all such Goods and Merchandize, as the legal Quays of the Port of London cannot with due Convenience receive; and the Petitioners apprehend and doubt not but they shall also be able to prove, to the Satisfaction of the House, that there is in the River Thames a Quantity of convenient Room, amply sufficient for the proper Mooring and Navigating of all Ships and Vessels resorting thereto; and that the Petitioners humbly conceive, and are prepared by Evidence to prove, that the Project of establishing a Dock Corporation, of the Nature and Extent sought for by the said Bill, is not only useless and unnecessary, but mischievous, as far as respects the Public Convenience, highly dangerous to the Revenue, burthensome to Traders in general, and peculiarly unjust and oppressive in respect to several very numerous and useful Classes of His Majesty's Subjects, and most especially to the Petitioners: And therefore praying to be heard, by themselves, Agents, or Counsel, against the said Bill, at the Bar of the House, and to offer such Proofs and Arguments in Opposition to the same as they shall be advised, and that the said Bill may not pass into a Law.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table until the said Bill be read a Second Time; and the Petitioners are to be then heard, by themselves, their Agents, or I

Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petitions, if they think fit.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petitions.

A Petition of the Trustees for the River Lee, and others, Traders and Navigators on, and Persons interested in, the Navigation of the said River, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Navigation of the River Lee from the Towns of Hertford and Ware to the River Thames is an ancient Navigation, and has been long used for conveying from the Counties of Hertford, Essex, and Cambridge,

Seat Quantities of Malt and Flour to the Cities of ondon and Westminster, and Timber to His Majesty's Vol. 51.

and other Dock Yards on the River Thames, to great Advantage in the Supply of those Articles in such Quantities as could not be otherwise so well conveyed; and that, about Thirty Years ago, the said Navigation was much improved, at a great Expence, under the Aid and Authority of an Act of Parliament, for which Purpose large Sums of Money were borrowed upon Annuities, and at Interest, most Part whereof still remains due to the Creditors, who relied on the Security given by the said Act, and which, from such Improvement of the said Navigation, and the consequent Increase of Trade thereon, has continued sufficient and satisfactory; and that the Petitioners, perceiving, from the Votes of the House, that a Bill has been lately brought in for making Wet Docks, Basons, Cuts, and other Works, for the greater Accommodation and Security of Shipping, Commerce, and Revenue, within the Port of London, and for making a Navigable Canal from to the said

Docks in Wapping, and understanding that such Canal, so to be made, is intended to intersect and cross the Canal of the Navigation of the River Lee from Bromley to Limehouse, are much alarmed on Account of that

Part of the said Navigation, which, as appears to the Petitioners, must unavoidably be interrupted and prejudiced, and subject to a great Diminution of the Tolls hitherto received on their said Canal, as well as to the Risque of being driven again down the old circuitous and dangerous Navigation into the Thames below Blackwall; and the Petitioners fear, that the prejudice to that Part of the Navigation may so extend itself, that not only the said Canal from Bromley to Limehouse may be rendered of little or no Service, but that, from the Loss of the Use thereof, the Whole of the said Navigation may become less valuable to the County for the Purposes intended by the said Act of Parliament for its Improvement, and, consequently, the Security of the said Creditors may be much lessened, and their Faith on Parliament diminished: And therefore praying to be heard, by themselves, or their Counsel, against the said Bill, as to the making the said Canal from Blackwall to the said Docks, in order to their obtaining such Protection and Relief in the Premises for the said Navigation and its Creditors, as to the House may seem meet.

Ordered, That the -said Petition do lie upon the Table until the said Bill be read a Second Time; and that the Petitioners be then heard, by themselves, or Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

A Petition of Malthcxo Physician, and

EverardHome, Esquire, Surgeon, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have received, in Trust, a Collection of Preparations illustrating the various Parts of the Animal (Economy, the Property of the late John Hunter, Esquire, Surgeon General to the Army, deceased, to be disposed of in the Manner specified in the following Clause of his Will, dated the nth of 1793 — " I also

" give to the said Matthew Baillie and Everard Home,

" all my Collection of Natural History, and the Cases, " and other Things belonging thereto, or used therewith, upon Trust, that they offer the same to Sale,

" in One entire Lot, to the Government of Great Britain, at such Price that may be considered as " reasonable between both Parties, and, in case of " Refusal, then that it may be offered to Sale to any " Foreign Government or State upon the like Terms, " and, in Failure of such Sale, then to dispose of the " same in an entire Lot, in such Manner as they shall " think proper;" and that the Petitioners, in pursuance of the Obligation imposed upon them by the Testator's Will, humbly renew their Application to the House, and are prepared to submit to the House the Testimony of Persons eminently qualified to explain and prove the Nature and Utility of the Collection, it's Importance to the Advancement of Medical Science, that it forms a Systematical Series so arranged that it cannot be replaced if suffered to be dispersed, and that it is prepared in a Manner to insure it's Durability for Centuries: That the Petitioners were prevented from presenting a Petition for Leave to bring in a Bill for effecting the Purchase above-mentioned, before the Expiration of the Period limited by the House for receiving private Petitions, by Reason that His Majesty's Approbation of their Application was not at that Time obtained; And therefore praying, That they may be permitted to present a Petition for Leave to bring in a Bill for the above-mentioned Purpose, although the Time fixed for presenting Petitions is elapsed.

A Petition of Benjamin Pugh, M. D. was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That a Bill is depending in the House for making and cutting a Canal through different Meadows in the Parish of South Stoke, in the County of Somerset, which Bill, if suffered to pass into a Law, will very materially injure the Petitioner, he being informed, and according to a Plan he has seen, that it is the Intention and Design of the Proprietors of the said Canal to cut through a very valuable Orchard, Garden, and Meadow, called Great Meadow (in his Writings) belonging to him: And therefore praying the House to take his Case into their Consideration, and admit him to be heard, by himself or Counsel, against the said Bill, and afford him such Relief as to the House shall seem right.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Bill to vary and alter the Line of a Canal authorized to be made by an Act, passed in the Thirty-fourth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act " for making and maintaining a Navigable Canal, with " certain Railways and Stone Roads, from the several " Collieries in the County of Somerset, to communicate " with the intended Kennet and Avon Canal, in the " Parish of Bradford, in the County of Wilts," and to alter and amend the said Act, is committed; and that the Petitioner be heard, by himself, or Counsel, before the said Committee, upon his Petition, if he thinks fit.

Petition from A Petition of the Register and Rulers of the Society of of Ticket Porters of the City of in Behalf of

themselves and their Brethren Ticket Porters, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are a large Body of Men, consisting of about 2,000 Persons in the Whole (and many of them with large Families) who have been deputed and authorized by the Corporation of the City of London, from Time immemorial, to unlade and house all Manner of Goods and Merchandizes coming to the Port of London from the British Plantations, America, the East Country, and other Places, and likewise to ship off and re-lade the same when exported, and the Petitioners, upon their Admission as Ticket Porters, enter into- a Bond, with Two Sureties, in the Penalty of tool. each Person, for the due Performance of their Duty, whereby the Merchant is secured in case of any Loss or Damage happening to the Goods or Merchandizes entrusted to their Care; and that the Petitioners have seen a Bill, depending in the House, for making Wet Docks, Basons, Cuts, &c. for the greater Accommodation and Security of Shipping, Commerce, and Revenue, within the Port of London, and also for the making a Navigable Canal from Blackwall to the said Docks in Wapping; and, if the same should pass into a Law, the Trade and Business of the City and Port of London will, in a great Degree, be removed to a new Situation, out of the Limits and Jurisdiction of the City, where any Man, or Set of Men, may exercise and carry on the Business and Employment of the Petitioners, whereby they will be deprived of the exclusive Privileges granted to them by the Corporation of the City of London, and will be attended with great Injury ana Distress, if not the total Ruin of themselves and Families: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table, until the Bill for making Wet Docks, Basons, Cuts, and other Works, for the greater Accommodation and Security of Shipping, Commerce, and Revenue, within the Port of London, and for making a Navigable Canal from Blackwall to the said Docks in Wapping, be read a Second Time; and the first-mentioned Petitioners are to be then heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

Mr. John White, a considerable Consumer of Hay and Straw, being examined, confirmed the foregoing Evidence.

thereof entitled to Right of Common in and upon all the Commons and Waste Grounds there, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the fiill for improving, dividing, and inclosing, the Commons, Waste Grounds, and Mosses, in the Parish of Cartmel, in the County Palatine of Lancasterand Setting forth, That the said Commons and Waste Grounds are, for the most Part, exceedingly mountainous, greatly covered with Rocks, incapable of Improvement, and fit only for the Purpose of depasturing young Cattle and Sheep, and not more than One Eighth Part thereof can by any Means he converted into Tillage, and that, of the small Quantity of Land capable of being so converted into Tillage, the greatest Part thereof is frequently overflowed by the Sea, and the Remainder not only frequently overflowed by a Rivulet, called Pool, but by great'

Quantities of Water running and flowing from the Mountains; and that considerable Stocks of Sheep are kept upon the said Commons and Waste Grounds, to the Advantage not only of the Petitioners and others holding landed Property within the said Parish, but to the Woollen Manufactory of this Country, and if the same should be divided and inclosed, few, if any. Sheep could be kept thereupon, as. breeding Stocks of Sheep will not do well if confined in small Inclosures; and that many Parts of the said Commons and Waste Grounds are so barren, that the Expence of fencing in and inclosing the same would greatly exceed the real Value thereof, and, if the said Bill should pass into a Law, and more particularly in its full Extent, it will greatly injure the Petitioners and others entitled to Right of Common in and upon the said Commons, Waste Grounds, and Mosses: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and that the Petitioners may be heard, by their Counsel, or Agents, against the said Bill, or such Parts thereof as may affect them.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second Time; and that the Petitioners be then heard, by their Counsel, or Agents, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

Ordered, That the said Bill be read a Second Time upon Friday Morning next.

Petition from A Petition of the Gentlemen, Farmers, Graziers, shirtTfora Breeders of Sheep, and others, whose Names are thereto TjucobDogs, subscribed, residing in the County of Leicester, and in the adjacent Counties, in Behalf of themselves and the rest of His Majesty's Subjects in that Part of the Kingdom, was presented to the House and read; Setting forth, That many fatal, afflicting, and calamitous Events have of late very frequently happened, both to the human and brute Species, in the Neighbourhood of the Petitioners, from Canine Madness, and great Mischiefs and Injuries have, for some Time past, been almost incessantly done, in and about the said Neighbourhood, by various Kinds of Dogs, particularly by their Destruction of vast Numbers of Sheep and Lambs of the best Breed, the Value whereof in that Part of the Kingdom is inestimable; and that the Petitioners are fully persuaded that, at a Time like the present, when the Scarcity of Meat of all Kinds, and various other Necessaries, is felt in a most unexampled and alarming Degree throughout the Kingdom, it is become a Public Grievance that so large and increasing a Number U¥' Vox.. 51.

of useless carnivorous Animals should be permitted to be kept, the supporting of which must be highly injurious to the Means of Subsistence of labouring and necessitous Persons, it being well known that many Hundreds of Families in that useful Class of Society might be amply provided for, and maintained, with what is daily consumed by the Multitude of unnecessary Dogs: And the Petitioners, therefore, relying on the Wisdom of the House, and its Attention to alleviate the Hardships of the Times, and redress the Public Grievances, humbly pray, That, as a principal Means conducive thereto, an Impost, Taxation, or Duty, may be laid upon Dogs, and that a Bill may be brought into the House, this Session, for that Purpose, and passed into a Law, with such Regulations and Restrictions as to the House shall seem meet and expedient.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Masters of the Tackle Houses of the Twelve superior Companies of the City of

a.

London, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was agaiut Lon-presented to the House and read; Setting forth, d°n Dpcb, That the Petitioners legally hold their Appointments from the Lord Mayor and Commonalty, and Citizens of the City of J^ondon, and the Special Nomination of the Masters, Wardens, and Courts of Assistants, of their several Companies, whereby they are deputed to execute the Office of Tackle Portage within the Port of the said City and Liberties thereof, for the Term of their respective Lives; and that a very considerable Part of the Goods and Merchandize, imported and exported at and from the present legal Wharfs and Quays, are, and must, according to Law, be landed and shipped, under the Care and Custody of the Petitioners, who respectively advance their Money, and are always responsible for Accidents, Damages, and Losses, by Theft or otherwise, while the same are in their Charge, and that, as Occasion may have required, the said Masters of the Tackle Houses have never failed to indemnify the Owners of all such Goods and Merchandize, by which Means the Trade snd Business of the said Port of London have been greatly secured and benefited, and the Emoluments attached to the Immunities of the Office, or Business, of the Petitioners, is the only Source of Subsistence for themselves and Families; and that the Petitioners have seen a Bill depending in the House for making M et Docks, Basons, Cuts, and other Works, for the greater Accommodation and Security of Shipping, Commerce, and Revenue, within the Port of London, and for making a Navigable Canal from Blackzcall to the said Docks in Wapping, and, if the Scheme proposed by the said Bill should be carried into Effect, the Trade and Business of the City and Port of London would, in a great Degree, be removed to a new Situation, out of the Limits and Jurisdiction of the City, w here any Man, or set of Men, might exercise and carry on the Trade and Business of the Petitioners, whereby the Petitioners would be deprived of that exclusive Privilege they apprehended to be secured to them when they obtained their respective Appointments, and embarked their Capitals in their Business, the Consequence of which must be very material Injury and Distress, if not total Ruin, to themselves, and Families; and that if certain practicable Improvements were made at and near the present Legal Quays and Wharfs, and proper Jiegulations adopted for facilitating the landing, loading, carrying, housing, and for shipping, of Goods and Merchandize thereon, and therefrom, every necessary Accommodation and Dispatch might be had and given, notwithstanding the increased Trade of the Port of London: And therefore praying. That they may be heard, by their Counsel, Agents, and Witnesses, against the said Bill, and that the same may not pass into a Law.

A Petition of the Governors and Directors of the petition from Poor, and other Inhabitants, paying to the Relief of the Cover-the Poor, of the Parish of Saint John, Southwark, in nors of the the County of Surrey, was also presented to the House, habitants of*

and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have st. John, been informed, that a Bill for making Wet Docks, Southwark, Basons and Cuts, in JPopping and and also against D*

for making a Navigable Cut from Blackwall to the 1 ' said Docks is now depending in the House, and they are greatly alarmed at the Introduction of the said Bill, and the Clauses thereof, as the Petitioners conceive it to be a mischievous Project, tending to create exclusive Privileges, and to restrict the Liberty of Trading as heretofore, with an arbitrary Exaction and Levy of Tonnage that will necessarily raise the Prices of every Article of Merchandize to the Consumers: That the Situation of the Parish of Saint John, Southwark (which comprises a Line of Wharfing upon the Bank of the River Thames nearly 3,000 Feet in Length, opposite to the Custom House and

Tower

36 Geo. III. 3° Martii.

Tower of London, in the very Heart and Seat of Commerce, with Depth of Water convenient for 'Ships of great Tonnage to lay and unload at the Quay) pointed out in former Times so many natural Advantages for Trade, that, in the Course of the last Sixty Years, many Individuals have been induced to lay out and risque very considerable Capitals in erecting and establishing Wharfs and Warehouses for the immediate Accommodation and Convenience of landing, shipping, and storing, all Sorts of Merchandize, and the Commissioners of His Majesty's Customs have successively annexed thereto the Privileges of Sufferance Wharfs, and the said Commissioners have also, upon mature Deliberation, as appears by their Resolutions of the Year 1789, recognized the whole of the Boundary Line of the said Parish next to the River Thames as capable of affording the accustomed Conveniences of Public Wharfs for the Accommodation of Trade in general, and that large and extensive Granaries ana Storehouses, for the Housing of Corn and Flour, have also been set up at a considerable Expence, and form a very convenient Depdt for the constant and immediate Supply of those necessary Articles of Consumption for the Metropolis: That full Four Parts in Five of the Housekeepers of the said Parish consist of Lightermen, Warehousemen, Watermen, and Persons using the Sea, and others, engaged at such Wharfs and Warehouses, who are led to reside in the said Parish on account of the local Benefits arising to them therein from its advantageous Situation immediately at the Seat of Commerce, and who, in consequence of any Removal of the present Trade therefrom (which the said Bill tends to effect) will either be totally deprived of their Connections and Livelihood, or otherwise compelled to remove therefrom, under great uncertainty of obtaining a living elsewhere ;and that the said Parish hath been, and is, greatly burthened with Poor, and the Poor Rates, heretofore collected at Four Shillings in the Pound per Annum on the Rack Rents, were found inadequate to the Support of the Poor, in so much that the Petitioners were under the Necessity of obtaining an Act of Parliament, granting further Powers in Aid of the Poor Rate, and under the Authority of which Act they borrowed a considerable Sum of Money, by Way of Life Annuities, to pay off large Debts contracted on Account of the Poor, which Annuities are secured upon the Faith and Credit of the Poor Rates to be raised in the said Parish, and all of such Annuitants are now living; and that, in consequence of the great Improvements and extensive Wharfs made in the said Parish, and its advantageous and convenient Situation for Commerce, the Trade therein and thereto had greatly increased, and the better to accommodate the Public in carrying on the same, the Petitioners (with the neighbouring Parish of Saint Olave) about Eight Years ago, at a very considerable Expence, obtained an Act of Parliament for opening, widening, and improving, the Streets and Avenues leading to London Bridge, and thereby voluntarily imposed upon themselves and their Posterity, an additional Rate for the Public Benefit, and, under the Powers of the said last mentioned Act, many Thousand Pounds have been borrowed by Way of Life Annuities, which are also secured to the Annuitants upon the Faith and Credit of the Rates to be made by virtue of the said last mentioned Act; and that the Money, paid for the Relief of the Poor of the said Parish by the Occupiers of the said Wharfs, Warehouses, and Granaries, amounts to upwards of 900l. a Year, and is more than Two Fifths of the whole Monies collected in the said Parish for the Relief of the Poor, and the other Parochial and Parliamentary Rates bear a like Proportion; and that the said Bill, if passed into a Law, will tend to remove the greater Part of the Trade and Commerce of the Port of London to a considerable Vol. 51,

Distance from its accustomed Channel, will prejudice the Petitioners in their private Trade, reduce the Value of those Estates which are the great Resources from whence the Poor Rates and other Rates are drawn, and thereby render those Rates less productive, diminish the Securities of the above described Annuitants, who advanced their Monies in Faith of the Produce of such Rates, and otherwise greatly oppress and injure the Inhabitant Shopkeepers of the said Parish, who derive the greater Part of their Trade in consequence of the Influx of Vessels to the present Seat of Commerce: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table, until the Bill for making Wet Docks, Basons, Cuts, and other Works, for the greater Accommodation and Security of Shipping, Commerce, and Revenue, within the Port of London, and for making a Navigable Canal from Bla to the said Docks in Wapping, be read a Second Time; and the first-mentioned Petitioners are to be then heard, by their Counsel, or Agents, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

A Petition of the Planters of the West India Colonies resident in Great Britain, and of the Merchants trading to the said Colonies, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for making Wet Docks, Basons, Cuts, and other Works, for the greater Accommodation and Security of Shipping, Commerce, and Revenue, within the Port of London, and for making a Navigable Canal from to the said

Docks in Wapping: And praying, That the said Bill

may pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

The Order of the Day being read, for the Second Reading of the Bill for the Abolition of the Slave Trade, at a Time to be limited;

A Petition of the Planters of the British West India Islands, residing in Great Britain, and of the Merchants trading to the said Islands, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the said Bill; and Setting forth, That the Preamble of the said Bill states the said Trade to be contrary to the Principles of Justice and Humanity, an Assertion which the Petitioners expressly deny to be founded on any authentic Evidence, and which, on the other Hand, has been controverted, on Oath, by many respectable Witnesses, but which, if recognized by the Parliament of Great Britain, must lead to the most fatal and dangerous Consequences; and that the Maintenance and Avowal of such Doctrines, under such Authority, at the present Juncture, can have no other Effect on the Minds of uncivilized Men than to destroy all Manner of Subordination and good Government in the Colonies, and to induce the Negroes to make a general Struggle for a wild and lawless Freedom through Desolation and Bloodshed: That the Doctrines, advanced by the Advocates for abolishing the Slave Trade, are calculated not only to sustain the Rebellions and Insurrections at present actually prevailing in some of the said Colonies, but also to provoke them in the Islands where they are not yet excited, and, that the calamitous intestine War, now raging in Grenada, Saint Vincent's, and Jamaica, did not originate with the Slaves imported into those Islands from Africa, but from the Free People of Colour in one Case, and from the Free Blacks in the Two others; and representing to the House, that, on the Faith of a System, recognized and supported by Royal Charters and the Legislature of Great Britain Vot. 51.

for near Two hundred Years, many of the Planters in the British West Indies have been induced to invest immense Capitals in the Purchase and Cultivation of Lands in those Colonies, which, should the said Bill pass into a Law, will be totally lost, and that there are, at this Time, in the Whole of the said Islands, considerably more than One Million of Acres of Land, so purchased, remaining uncultivated, for which Quit Rents have been paid, and continue to be paid, to a very great Amount, and, if the Slave Trade is abolished, the Whole of such Lands must become an absolute Burthen and Incumbrance in the Hands of the present Proprietors; and that the Petitioners conceive it to be a leading Principle of the British Constitution, that no Man can be deprived of his Property by an Act of the Legislature without his own Consent, or Compensation allowed, which, from its Magnitude, and other Considerations in this Case, cannot even be thought of: That the said Colonies have been originally settled under the most sacred Compacts with the Mother Country, sanctioned by Royal Charters and Proclamations, as well as by a Succession of Acts of Parliament, authorizing and encouraging the Slave Trade, particularly by the Charters granted, in 1662 and 1674, by King Charles the Second, which established a Royal African Company (the last of which was granted in Consequence of an Address from both Houses of Parliament) and by the Acts of the 9th and 1 oth of King William the Third, a Period when the Principles of Civil Liberty were minutely investigated, well understood, and freely asserted, and, more recently, by the Act of the 23d of George the Second, which recites the Usefulness and absolute Necessity of the African Slave Trade: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law, and that the Petitioners may be heard, by themselves, or Counsel, against the same.

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table until the said Bill be read a Second Time; and that the Petitioners be then heard, by themselves, or Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit;

The latter Part of the said Motion, for hearing the Petitioners by themselves, or Counsel, against the said Bill, was, with Leave of the House, withdrawn.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second Time.

Mr. Thomas Williams reported from the Committee; to whom the Petition Of Thomas Morgan, John Morris, and Calvert Richard Jones, Esquires, on Behalf of themselves and other Trustees for repairing, enlarging, and preserving the Harbour of Swansea, in the County of Glamorgan, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them;-to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an1 Act, passed in the Thirty-first Year of His present Majesty's Reign, for repairing, enlarging, and preserving the Harbour of Swansea, was read; whereby it appeared, that the Trustees appointed by the said Act were empowered to erect a sufficient Building at or near The Mumbles, within the Port of Swansea, for keepings Coal or other Light burning for the Purposes therein mentioned: And,

Joseph Huddart, Esquire, being examined, said, That in pursuance of the said Act, such Building hath been erected, and Lights kept burning, which has afforded great Protection and Security to Vessels navigating those Parts, and particularly so in the recent tempestuous Weather: Then,

Mr. Gabriel Jeffreys, Clerk to> the said Trustees, being also examined, said, That the Provisions of the' said Act have been found inadequate for defraying the Expence of supporting the said Lighthouse, eveh id its present State: And,

Mr. Huddart', being further examined, said, That as the said Lights are' capable of Improvement, and may be rendered of general Advantage and Protection to Ships navigating the Bristol Channel, it is proposed that a; small Duty should be laid on all Vessels navigating within certain Limits of the said Channel.

Ordered'jThat Leave be given to bring in a Bill to amend and render more effectual an Act, made in the Thirty-first Year of His present Majesty, for repairing, enlarging, and preserving the Harbour of Swansea, in the' County of Glamorgan, and for making Improvements in the Lights at The Mumbles: And that Mr. Thomas Williams, Sir Wat kin Lewesj and Mr. Morgan, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A PETITION of the thereunder-signed Owners and Freighters of Ships and Vessels at Thome, in the Port of Hull, trading to the Port of London, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have hitherto traded to the Port of London with Ships and Vessels of various Sizes, and are not by Law chargeable with any Rates or Duties for navigating the same in or upon the River Thames j and that the Petitioners find a Bill is brought into the House for making Wet Docks, Basons, Cuts, and other Works, for the greater Accommodation and Security of Shipping, Commerce, and Revenue, within the Port of London, and for making a Navigable Canal from Blackmail to the said Docks in Wapping, by which Bill it is intended to impose certain Rates or Duties for every Ship or Vessel, exceeding the Burthen of 45 Tons, trading Coastwise betw een the Port of London and any Part of Great Britain, according to the Register Tonnage thereof, and also to impose further or higher Rates or Duties of Tonnage in case the same Ships or Vessels shall enter the said Docks, Cuts, or Canals, as there* in mentioned; and representing to the House, that, if the said Bill should pass into a Law, it would very materially injure the Petitioners, who will have no Occasion to make Use of the said Docks, Cuts, or Canals, and can never derive any Benefit or Advantage whatsoever from the same; that the Petitioners are perfectly satisfied with the present State and Navigation of the River Thames, and the Conveniencies established for the landing and shipping of Goods at the Port of London, and besides the Grievance of paying Rates and Duties without receiving any Consideration, the Petitioners are advised that the said Bill is, in other Respects, injurious to private Individuals, and unnecessary for the Public Accommodation: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not be suffered to pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second Time.

Wet Docks, Basons, Cuts, and other Works, for the greater Accommodation and Security of Shipping, Commerce, and Revenue, within the Port of London, and for making a Navigable Canal from Blackwall to the said Docks in Wtipping; and Setting forth, That the Petitioners are the Proprietors, Lessees, and Occupiers, of Warehouses situated in the Vicinity of certain Quays upon the Banks of the River Thames, in the Port of London, known by the Name and Appellation of " The legal Quays," and of Warehouses in various other Parts of the City of London, and the said legal Quays have been established, for a long Period of Years, by virtue of certain Royal Commissions proceeding under the Sanction, and by the Authority, of divers Acts of Parliament; and that the Warehouses of the Petitioners have been erected, at a very great Expence, in the Vicinity of the said Quays, and in various other Parts of the said City of London, convenient to the Merchants thereof, in Confidence that Parliament would at all Times protect the said Quays, which had been established under its own Sanction, and are occupied principally by Goods and Merchandize landed upon, or shipped from, the said Quays, and have been, and are, not only productive of considerable Profit to the Petitioners, but also of great Convenience and Accommodation to the said Merchants, and all Persons concerned in the Importation and Exportation of Goods at the said Quays; and that the Petitioners have been, for several Years past, continually erecting new and additional Warehouses for the Accommodation of the Merchants, in order to keep Pace with the Increase of the Commerce of the Port of London, and if the Business now transacted at the said Quays shall be removed to other Places at a Distance from the said Quays, the Warehouses of the Petitioners will cease to be wanted by Merchants and others for the Reception of their Goods, and consequently will become useless, the Money expended in the Erection of them will be wholly lost, and many of the Petitioners, who depend upon the Rents thereof, or upon the Money received for housing and keeping Goods therein, for the Support of themselves and their Pamilies, will be brought to Poverty and Ruin; and, by the said Bill, if the same shall be passed into a Law, the Business now transacted at the said Quays will be removed to other Places at a Distance from the said Quays, and all the ruinous Consequences above stated will ensue to the Petitioners; and that the Petitioners conceive, and submit to the House, that the Security and Accommodation, held forth as the Objects of the said Bill, may be better effected by other Measures, which will suggest themselves to the Wisdom of the House, than by the Schemes proposed by the said Bill, and without the Annihilation of the ancient Trade and Business of the said legal Quays, and the consequent Ruin of the Petitioners, who have relied on the Continuance of the said Trade under the Sanction and Protection of Parliament: And therefore praying, That they may be heard at the Bar of the House, by themselves, their Counsel, Agents, and Witnesses, against the said Bill, and that the said Bill may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second Time; and that the Petitioners be then heard, by themselves, their Counsel, or Agents, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

Petition from owe to themselves and to Posterity, as well as from Sl Mary's, an ardent Wish for the Prosperity of the Trade of the Rotherhithe, port Qf London, to represent to the House the alarming don Docks"* Situation in which they conceive that Trade will be &c. BilL ' placed, should such Bill pass into a Law: The Petitioners conceive that the said Bill, if passed into a Law, will, by the granting many exclusive Privileges to the Proprietors of such intended Docks, create a ..Monopoly in such Trade, and thereby restrain the Freedom of Commerce, to which the Petitioners, as well as all other His Majesty's Subjects, are justly entitled, and will also enable the Proprietors to exact an additional Charge for Tonnage on all Vessels entering into the Port of London, although they should not go into such intended Docks, by which every Article of Merchandize brought into the said Port will ultimately be raised, and the Price thereof enhanced to the Consumers; and that great Part of the said Parish forms a Line of Wharfing, on the Banks of the South Side of the River Thames, of the Length of nearly Two Miles, which, from the great Depth of Water flowing up to such Wharfing, is very convenient for Ships of considerable Tonnage to lay at and unload, and several Docks have been made adjoining thereto for building and repairing of Vessels using the said Port, mid, from the natural Advantages to Trade and Commerce arising from such Situations, the Petitioners and others have of late Years been induced to lay out and risque considerable Capitals in the building and improving many Docks, Wharfs, and Warehouses, for the immediate Accommodation and Convenience of landing, shipping, and storing, of Goods and Merchandize; and that many Granaries and Storehouses for the Reception of Corn, Flour, and other Provisions, have, within these few Years past, been erected at a considerable Expence, and are now used in the said Parish, thereby forming convenient Stores or Repositories for the Supply of those useful and necessary Articles of Life for the Supply of the Inhabitants of this great Metropolis: That a very considerable Part of the Inhabitants of the said Parish consist of Lightermen, Watermen, and Warehousemen, who reside therein on Account of the local Benefits arising to them from its advantageous Situation, and who, in consequence of a Removal of the Trade therefrom (which the Petitioners fear will be effected, should the present Bill pass into a Law) will be deprived of their Connections and Livelihood, or obliged to remove from their present Habitations, to their great Loss and Inconvenience; and, that the said Parish < is greatly burthened with Poor, many of whom are, at this Time, wholly maintained at the Expence thereof, whereby the Inhabitants are obliged to be rated 31. 6d. in the Pound on their Rack Rents towards such Payment and Support, and which Rate is at this Time inadequate thereto; and that the Trade on the Waterside of the said Parish having, from its advantageous Situation, greatly increased, an Act of Parliament was, a few Years since, obtained, at a very considerable Expence, for paving, lighting, cleansing, and improving, the several Streets adjoining thereto, and an Annual Tax of 2 s. 3 d. in the Pound imposed on the Occupiers and Inhabitants of the Wharfs, Warehouses, Buildings, and Messuagdk there, for repaying the Monies borrowed for that Purpose, and other Expences attending the same, all which Inhabitants will, should such Bill pass into a Law, be much prejudiced in their several Trades, and thereby rendered the less able to contribute their Proportions to such several Rates; and that the said Bill, if passed into a Law, will tend to remove the greatest Part of the Trade and Commerce of the Port of London to a considerable Distance from its accustomed Channel, to the great Prejudice of the Petitioners in their private Trade, and will greatly

reduce the Value of all the Estates situate near the Waterside of the said Parish, from whence great Part of the Poors Rates, and other Rates, are collected, whereby those Rates will be less productive, and the Securities of the several Annuitants, who advanced their Monies on the Credit thereof, greatly diminished; and that the several Powers and Privileges, by the said Bill requested to be granted, appear unnecessary, injurious in respect to the Public, and destructive of the Interests of Individuals, and (if permitted) will tend to destroy that Degree of Competition so essential to the Interest of the Public, and their increasing Accommodation: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law.

and that, if the said Bill should pass into a Law, the necessary Consequence will be the Removal of the Trade from the Quays of the Petitioners, and the Places where it has been heretofore carried on, under the Authority of the Commissioners of His Majesty's Customs, to other Places remote from the said Quays: That the Petitioners Ancestors and Predecessors, and they themselves, have laid out large Sums of Money upon the said Quays, in the just and reasonable Expectation that the Trade of the City of London would continue to be carried on as heretofore, and the Petitioners have at all Times used their utmost Endeavours to render the said Quays commodious to the Merchants of the City of London, and to the Persons appointed to conduct and manage the Affairs of the Revenue within the Port of London; and that the Petitioners believe, and are ready to prove to the House, that the Difficulties and Delays, complained of in the landing and carrying off the Goods when landed, and the Frauds and Impositions meant to be remedied by the said Bill, are such as either do not arise from the Causes to which they are attributed by the Petitioners for the Bill, or such that they can be removed or remedied by a System of Regulation calculated to suit the present State of the Property in the Quays and Wharfs of the City and Port of London; and that the Petitioners conceive, and are ready to prove, that a System of Regulation for the general Improvement of the Navigation and better Accommodation of the Shipping of the River Thames and Port of London, different from that proposed by the Petitioners for the Bill, and consistent with the Rights of Property (which the Petitioners are convinced the House will always hold sacred) may be carried into Execution, by which the Inconvenience of the Plan proposed by the Petitioners for the Bill will be completely avoided: And therefore praying, That

Petition from Watermen, &c. against London Docks, &c. Bill.

A Petition of the there-undersigned Watermen and Wherrymen, working upon the River Thames between Gravesend and Windsor, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for making Wet Docks, Basons, Cuts, and other Works, for the greater Accommodation and Security of Shipping, Commerce, and Revenue, within the Port of London, and for making a Navigable Canal from Blackwalt to the said Docks in Wapping; and Setting forth. That many of the Petitioners have numerous Families, and the Whole of their Subsistence is drawn from the Navigation of Boats and Vessels on the said River, and, if the said Bill should be permitted to pass into a Law, the Boats and Vessels of the Petitioners, employed upon the said River, will be rendered, in a great Measure, useless, and a great Majority of the Petitioners and their numerous Families deprived of the Means of Subsistence; and that, by an Act, passed in the First Year of the Reign of King James the First, the Company of Watermen, Wherrymen, and Lightermen, to which the Petitioners belong, are empowered to appoint a certain Number of Watermen to ply upon the said River between Vauxhall.above London Bridge, and Limehouse,

upon the Lord's Day, and the Overplus of the Earnings of such Watermen are directed by the said Act to be applied to the Use of the poor, aged, decayed, and maimed Watermen and Lightermen of the said Society and Company, and their Widows, and that, by the Overplus of the Earnings of such Watermen so plying on the Lord's Day, upwards of Five hundred aged and

necessitous Persons are now, and have been for some Time past, Annually relieved; and that the greater Part of the Earnings of such Watermen, so plying on the Lord's Day, arise from the carrying of Seamen and other Persons' on Board the Vessels lying in the said River, but, if the said Bill should pass into a Law, such Earnings will be wholly lost to the Company, and the numerous Objects of Distress which are supported by the said Charity will be thereby deprived of its Relief and Assistance: That, for several Years last past, the Number of Apprentices, bound into the Service of the Petitioners, hath been very considerable, and the Petitioners have Reason to believe that the Annual Number of such Apprentices would be considerably reduced if the said Bill should pass into a Law; and that, in the Course of the present War, near Four thousand Men have been furnished from the Body of the Petitioners, who are now serving, either as impressed Men or Volunteers, in His Majesty's Navy, and the Petitioners conceive that, if the said Bill should be passed into a Law, such Men will, on the Conclusion of the War, and on their Return Home, be deprived of their usual Means of obtaining a Subsistence, and the Petitioners also conceive that they should be deprived of their Employments, the Number of their Apprentices would be greatly reduced, and the Nation sustain an essential Injury in the Destruction of one of its best Nurseries for Seamen: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by themselves, Agents, or Counsel, against the said Bill, and that the same may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second Time, and that the Petitioners be then heard, by themselves, their Agents, or Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

A Petition of the Inhabitants of the Ward of Tower, Petition from was also presented to the House, and read; Likewise Tower Ward, taking Notice of the said Bill; and Setting forth, against D® That foe same in its Principle is founded on a System of Bl Monopoly, and in its Practice ensures the Annihilation of the Privileges, and the Destruction of the Property of the Citizens of London, and entails Ruin on innumerable Families resident therein: That the Petitioners, as being particularly interested in the Prosperity of foe Trade of the Port of London, would willingly exert themselves in the most strenuous Way to remove any Impediments, adopt any Improvements, and obtain any necessary Enlargement thereof, within foe Limits of the City, that in Effect would not produce those serious Evils the Petitioners are so justly apprehensive of, and so anxious to guard against; and, foe Petitioners beg leave to remind the House, that the Ward of Tower contributes a large Quota towards foe general Land Tax of the City of London, a very material Proportion of which is discharged by foe different Wharfs and Warehouses for Merchandize, situated within the said Ward, but which Premisses cannot sustain so heavy a Charge when they become unoccupied and useless by the Removal of the Trade of the Port to a distant Part, consequently the Deficiency so occasioned must be levied on the other Properties in foe Ward, which, by perhaps slow yet sure inevitable Progress, must sink under such a Pressure of Taxation; and that very many of that useful Body of Men, foe Lightermen of the Port of London, reside within the said Ward, who look up with Confidence to the House for the Protection of their Rights and Immunities, and for the Prevention of miserable Distress ito themselves and Families, in foe Preservation of ctbat great and essential Nursery for the Manning afthe British Navy, of which they form so considerable ai Part, which Object has ever been thought worthy 'foe'Consideration, and entitled to the Support, of a

488 8° Martii. A. 1196:

British House of Commons: That the Petitioners conceive, if all the Mischiefs in Reality and Extent, as stated by the Merchants, did exist, it would still he a momentous Question, whether the Abolition of the old Port, with all its concomitant Devastation, should take Place in favour of this new Speculative Plan, but the Petitioners humbly contend they are not compelled to reply to this supposed Proposition, inasmuch as the Corporation of London have pledged themselves to afford every Accommodation, large and extensive as may be required, and silence every reasonable Complaint, loudly and seriously as they may be now urged by the Merchants, without injuring the chartered Rights, or hazarding the long-established Welfare and Dignity of this Metropolis, and without indulging in a Wish to profit by any such Plans when completely carried into Effect; and the Petitioners beg Leave to add, that they cannot learn that it is the Intention of the Merchants to afford the promised Indemnification so justly to be expected, and so rightfully to be demanded by various Claimants, in case this their Scheme is carried into Execution: That the Petitioners, with all due Regard and Respect, thus presume to state, without Reserve, their well-grounded Apprehensions on this Subject, and with the most perfect Reliance on the Justice, and the most confident Trust in the Wisdom, of the House, do also venture to hope that the said unnecessary injurious Bill may not pass into a Law: And therefore praying to be heard, by Counsel, against the said Bill.

lying contiguous to the River Thames, on the Upper Side, and near to London Bridge, contains a great Number of Wharfs and Warehouses for receiving, landing, and shipping, by Barges, Lighters, and other Craft, Goods and Merchandizes imported into, and for Exportation out of, the Port of; and that

many of the Petitioners have expended large Sums of Money in erecting and supporting such Wharfs and Warehouses, and in regard to the Convenience of their Situation for Trade, and the Advantages attendant thereon, many of the Petitioners pay heavy Rents, and are consequently assessed at a high Rate, and contribute largely in Taxes to the Support of Government, and others of the Petitioners are wholly dependent upon the Employment they receive in the Business of the said Wharfs and Warehouses, for the Support of themselves and Families, and almost every Description and Class

House, and read; Also taking Notice of the said Bill; Bill-and Setting forth, That large and extensive Trades and Manufactories are carried on in the said Parishes and Hamlets, and the Carriage of Goods and Merchandize to and from the same, and to and from the great and extensive Wharfs and Warehouses there, and to be shipped and landed from the Ships and Vessels in the River Thames, require commodious Roads and Passages, and the Streets, Lanes, and Passages, leading to and from the said Parishes and Hamlets, are so narrow and confined, and are frequently so much crowded with Carriages, that Stoppages and Obstructions often happen even in Ratcliff' Highway, one of the widest of the said Streets; and that, by the said Bill, the Canal therein described is to be cut not only through Ratcliff Highway, the most important Avenue to the said Parishes and Hamlets, but also across every other Road, Street, Avenue, and Passage leading to and from the said Parishes and Hamlets, and Draw Bridges and other Contrivances are intended to be erected as a Substitute for Passengers at the Places so to be cut through as aforesaid, and the Petitioners apprehend the Stoppages and Obstructions in the said Streets and Passages, already complained of, will be so much increased, not only during the Time the Draw Bridges are taken up for the Passage of Ships, but also by Reason of the Narrowness and Length of the Passage across such Draw Bridges, that the Inconvenience must become intolerable, and, in Time, occasion the Removal of several of the Trades and Manufactories, and a great Loss of Trade and Custom thereto, and to the said Wharfs and Warehouses, as well as to the Trading Inhabitants of every Description:

That, as the said Canal is to be open to all Shipping coming into the Port of London, the Trade which is now carried on by the Ship Owners with the Inhabitants on the Banks of the Thames will be diverted, by Means of the intended Canal, to the new Inhabitants who are likely to settle on the North Borders of the said Canal, which will manifestly be most convenient for Trade, and the erecting of Manufactories, Wharfs, and Warehouses, and the Lands, through which it is intended to be cut, must consequently increase in the Value nearly in Proportion as the Petitioners conceive Estates on the Borders of the Thames must consequently decrease in Value, whereby the Petitioners,

Mr. Alderman Anderson reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Cheesemongers, and Dealers in Butter, resident in and near the City of London, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Peter Wilson, being examined, said, That he has been a Cooper at York Thirty Years, and has made a great Number of Firkins for the Purpose of packing Butter. — And being asked, Whether he has had any Firkins proper for Butter returned to him by the Farmers? he said, Many Times, owing to their not being heavy enough; that he has afterwards sold them to other Farmers (after having changed the Bottoms) by making them heavier. That he generally makes the Firkins with Ash Wood, and that when soaked they weigh very heavy. Then the Bottom of a Firkin, weighing Four Pounds and an Half, being produced to Your Committee, the Witness stated, That he has frequently made the Bottoms as heavy as that. — And being asked. Whether, after the Butter has been brought from the Standard, he had ever, been concerned with the Farmer in scraping it? he said, Yes, many Times, and likewise in changing the Heads, and that it was a common Practice. — And being asked, Whether he was ever concerned in changing the Staves, after the Searcher had marked the Firkius, as to the Quality and Weight of the Butter contained? he said, His Apprentices had done it. — And being asked, Whether he ever Vol. 51.

489

recollected Factors and Farmers buying Butter to put on the Top of the Firkin to make it weigh, so as to pass the Standard? he said, Yes, and that it was very common. — And being asked, Whether, after the Butter has passed the Standard, the Factors take off the Capping, and send it to London short of Weight? he said, It is common: Then,

William Hart, being examined, said, That he is a Cooper, and has lived at York Twelve Years; that he has made many Firkins for the Farmers, and has been told, that unless he made them of Twelve Pounds they, would not have them. That a Firkin should weigh Ten Pounds, and allowing Two Pounds more for soaking. — And the Witness added, That a Firkin of Seven Pounds would contain the Quantity of Butter. And the Firkin Bottom before produced being shewri to the Witness, he said, He never made one so thick as that. Then the Witness was asked, Whether he was ever concerned with the Factors in changing the Heads? he said, Yes. And being asked, For what Object? he said, When Factors sell Butter to Cheesemongers in London, they take out the Heads of Casks which contain good Butter, and put them into Casks of an inferior Sort. — And being asked. Whether he ever recollected changing the Staves or Heads of Firkins, after their having been marked as to the Quality of the Butter? he said, Yes; that they take out the best Mark, and change it for a Second Mark in another Firkin. — And being asked, Whether they do not get the Butter researched after its having been first searched, and the Head taken off and put to another Firkin, with Butter of an inferior Quality, which had not been searched ? he said, They do; that he recollects Butter being scraped, and likewise its being added to the Firkin, in order to pass the Standard. — And being asked, What became of that Butter when taken from the Standard? he said, It is sometimes taken off by the Factors, and sometimes by the Servants: And

Mr. Matthew Goodenoagh, being examined, said. That he is a Cheesemonger in Street, and

has been in the Business Twenty-six Years, and that in the Course of his Business he has sustained great Losses in consequence of the short Weight and bad Quality of the Butter. — And being asked. How much on an Average he though the Firkin came short of Weight? he said, From Two to Four or Five Pounds, sometimes Seven, and that the Deficiency is in general made up of Wood. — And being asked, What the Weight of the Head of the Firkin should be? he said, Three Quarters, or a Pound. — And being asked, Whether he did not attribute the Losses sustained to the improper Conduct of the Factors ? he said, Not always; sometimes it may be the Factors, and sometimes the Farmers. — And being asked, W'hether he did not sometimes receive Butter of an inferior Sort, marked as a better Sort? he said. Frequently.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to prevent the committing of Frauds and Abuses in the weighing, packing, and selling of Butter: And that Mr. Alderman Anderson, the Lord Mayor of,

and Mr. Mainwaring, do prepare, and bring in, the same.
