A Petition of the Inhabitants of the Ward of Billingsgate, in the City of London, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for making Wet Docks, Basons, Cuts, and other Works, for the greater Accommodation and Security of Shipping, Commerce, and Revenue, within the Port of London, and for making a Navigable Canal from Blackwall to the said Docks in Wapping; and Setting forth, That the said Bill, if carried into a Law, will be productive of the most melancholy Consequences to numerous Families in the City of London, many of whom reside within the said Ward, and the Rights and Privileges of the Citizens of London, which they have enjoyed for Ages past, will thereby, in a great Measure, be done away; and that the Ward of Billingsgate contributes very largely to the Quota of the Land Tax of the City of London, a great Part of which is paid by the Wharfs and Warehouses within the said Ward, but which cannot be defrayed by them if the legal Quays . are established in Wapping, consequently a very heavy additional Burthen will fall on the Petitioners; and that the Petitioners, feeling a strong Interest in the Prosperity of the Trade of the Port of London, are very anxious that every Accommodation required shall be extended to its increasing Commerce, and, as the Corporation of London are bringing forward Plans to that Effect, without violating the Rights which, by divers Charters, confirmed by several Acts of Parliament, they have uninterruptedly enjoyed, and without burthening the Trade of the Port of London with a heavy and perpetual Charge for the sole Benefit of a Monopoly, they humbly solicit the House will give those Plans the Preference which have the Public Good alone for their Object, and preserve their ancient Privileges entire: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law.

A Petition of James Jones and Bullcock, Pro- Petition from prietors of the Hermitage Iron and Brass Foundery, was also presented to the House, and read; Likewise against Lon- taking Notice of the said Bill; and Setting forth, don Docks, That the Foundery belonging to the Petitioners is &c- Bill, the most extensive and most conveniently situate of any in the City of London, and, as the Petitioners believe, is capable of doing more Business than any other Foundery in or near the Metropolis, and the Petitioners conceive their said Foundery is an Object of National Importance and Concern, in as much as great Numbers of Guns, and large Quantities of Naval Stores, are furnished therefrom to Ships of War, with the utmost Ease and Dispatch, there being a Dock of considerable Dimensions, with commodious Wharfs,

Quays, and Landing Places, attached to their Foundery; and that the Petitioners have seen a Plan of the said Canal and Dqcks, whereby it appears that their Foundery and Premises belonging to them, as aforesaid, will be cut through and destroyed by the making of the said Docks, and the Approach thereto, and should such a Plan be carried into Execution, it will be productive of the entire Ruin of the Works of the Petitioners, for which Injury there cannot be an adequate Compensation made, there being no Place to be found in any Degree so commodious for the carrying on of their Business as their present Site: And therefore praying, That Provision may be made in the said Bill to prevent any Part of their said Premises being taken or used for the Purposes of the said Canal or Docks, and that they may be heard by their Counsel, and Agents, against such Part of the said Bill as may affect them, and that the same may not pass into a Law as it now stands.

Mr. Ryder reported from the Select Committee, Report front who were appointed to take into Consideration the present high Price of Corn, and to collect Evidence j£e high relative thereto, and to report the same, from Time to Price of Corn. Time, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House; respecting That the Committee had further considered the Matters M^en; to them referred, and had came to several Resolutions, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Resolutions of the Committee were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That every Miller should be obliged to keep a Pair of Scales and Weights in his Mill.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Inspectors appointed by an Act, made in the Thirty-fifth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for the more effectual Prevention " of the Use of defective Weights, and of false and " unequal Balances," should have the Power of examining Weights and Scales used by Millers, and to seize all such as shall be found defective; and that all Millers making use thereof shall be liable to the same Penalties as are inflicted by the said Act on Persons using false Weights and Scales.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That every Person who shall bring Corn to a Mill to be ground, shall be entitled to have the same weighed in his Presence, and to have the Produce thereof weighed before he takes it away.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That it is expedient that Millers should, if required, be obliged to return all the Produce of the Corn brought to be ground (with the Deduction of the Toll, in Cases where Toll is taken) so as to make up an equal Weight with the Grain brought, except such Diminution thereof as shall be occasioned by Waste in grinding.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That Millers should be obliged, in case they dress the Corn brought to them, to return in like Manner, if required, all the Produce of the Corn brought to be ground and dressed (with the Deduction of the Toll, in Cases where Toll is taken) so as to make up an equal Weight with the Grain brought, except such Diminution thereof as shall be occasioned by Waste in dressing as well as in grinding.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That it is expedient that no Miller should be allowed to demand any Toll in Kind for grinding Corn, but should be obliged to receive, in lieu thereof, a Payment in Money, except in Cases where the peculiar.

Rights of Mills have been, or may be, established by Law.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That every Miller, except as above excepted, should be obliged to set up, in a conspicuous Part of his Mill, and renew, when necessary, a distinct and legible Table of the Prices in Money , for which the several Operations of his Mill are to be performed.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That when any Person shall bring Corn to a Miller tq be ground, and shall not have Money to pay for grinding the same, such Miller may, with the Consent of the Person bringing the same, take such Quantity of the Corn so to be ground as shall be of equal Value to the Money he may demand for grinding the same.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That it is expedient to give Power to Magistrates to exercise a summary Jurisdiction for enforcing the before-mentioned Regulations.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second

An ingrossed Bill to continue several Laws relating to the giving further Encouragement to the Importation of Naval Stores from the British Colonies in America', to the Encouragement of the Silk Manufactures, and for taking off several Duties on Merchandize exported, and reducing other Duties; to the preventing the clandestine Running of Goods, and the Danger of Infection thereby; to the encouraging the Growth of Coffee in His Majesty's Plantations in America; to the free Importation of Cochineal and Indigo; to the granting a Bounty on certain Species of British and Irish Linens exported, and taking off the Duties on the Importation of foreign Raw Linen Yarns made of Flax; to the importing-Salt from Europe into the Province of Quebec in America; to the encouraging the Manufacture of Leather, by lowering the Duty payable upon the Importation of Oak Bark, when the Price of such Bark shall exceed a certain Rate; to the more effectual Encouragement of the Manufactures of Flax and Cotton in Great Britain; to the allowing the Importation of Rape Seed and other Seeds used for extracting Oil, whenever the Prices of middling British Rape Seed shall be above a certain Limit; to the allowing a Drawback of the Duties on Rum shipped as Stores to be consumed on Board Merchant Ships in their Voyages; to the clandestine Running of uncustomed Goods, and preventing Frauds relating to the Customs; to the further Punishment of Persons going armed or disguised in Defiance of the Laws of Customs or Excise*, to the free Importation of certain Raw Hides and Skins from Ireland, and the British Plantations in America; and to the Duties on Spirits made in Scotland, and imported into England, was read the Third Time.

Resolved, That the Bill do pass: And that the Title

be, An Act to continue several Laws relating to the giving further Encouragement to the Importation of Naval Stores from the British Colonies in America; to the Encouragement of the Silk Manufactures, and for taking off several Duties on Merchandize exported, and reducing other Duties; to the preventing the clandestine Running of Goods, and the Danger of Infection thereby; to the encouraging the Growth of Coffee in His Majesty's Plantations in America; to the free Importation of Cochineal and Indigo; to the granting a Bounty on certain Species of British and Irish Linens exported, and taking off the Duties on the Importation of foreign Raw Linen Yarns made of Flax; to the importing Salt from Europe into the Province of Quebec in America; to the encouraging the Manufacture of Leather, by lowering the Duty payable upon the Importation of Oak Bark, when the Price of such Bark shall exceed a certain Rate; to the more effectual Encouragement of the Manufactures of Flax and Cotton in Great Britain; to the allowing the Importation of Rape Seed and other Seeds used for extracting Oil, whenever the Prices of middling British Rape Seed shall be above a certain Limit; to the allowing a Drawback of the Duties on Rum shipped as Stores to be consumed on Board Merchant Ships in their Voyages; to the clandestine Running of uncustomed Goods, and preventing Frauds relating to the Customs; to the further Punishment of Persons going armed or disguised in Defiance of the Laws of Customs or Excise; to the free Importation of certain Raw Hides and Skins from Ireland, and the British Plantations in America; and to the Duties on Spirits made in Scotland, and imported into England.

A Petition of the Inhabitants of the Ward of Vintry, Petition from was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, VinV

That the Petitioners cannot help feeling the utmost do^Dock*"* Alarm and Apprehension when they consider the Na- Ac. Bill, ture and Tendency of the Bill now depending in the House for making Wet Docks and Navigable Cuts from Wapping to Blachvall, and erecting Warehouses in that Vicinity, a Measure, which, if adopted, will divert the Trade of the Port of London into a new and untried Channel, destroy the Hopes and fair Expectations of Men who have spent Years of Industry in establishing their respective Trades, and deprive a Number of honest laborious Citizens of their chartered and unalienable Rights: That the Project of making Wet Docks deserves the most serious Consideration in a National Point of View, as tending most essentially to supersede the Necessity of employing working Lightermen, a hardy and gallant Set of Men, who form one of our principal Nurseries for Seamen, which, in a Maritime State like ours, cannot be too much encouraged; and the Petitioners beg Leave to observe, that the said Ward, from its local Situation, having the River on one Side for its Boundary, is particularly interested in the Fate of the said Bill, being burthened with a very numerous Poor, and their Revenues, both Ward and Parochial, are derived in a great Measure from Waterside Premises, and should the Scheme of making Wet Docks take place, those Premises will of course feel a considerable Declension in Value, and be less able to afford that Revenue which an increasing Poor so loudly calls for: And therefore hoping, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for making Wet Docks, Basons, Cuts, and other Works, for the greater Accommodation and Security of Shipping, Commerce, and Revenue, within the Port of London, and for making a Navigable Canal from Blackwall to the said Docks in Wapping, be read a Second Time.

Sir John Mordaunt reported from the Committee, to whom the Bill for dividing, allotting, and inclosing, the several Commons and Waste Lands, within the Manor and Hamlet of Balsall, in the Parish of Hampton in Arden, in the County of Warwick, was committed; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, relative to > Bills of Inclosure, had been complied with; and that the Committee had examined the Allegations of the Bill, and found the same to be true; and that the Parties concerned had given their Consent to the Bill, to the Satisfaction of the Committee (except the Owners of Lands, assessed to the Land Tax at 20/. os. 8 per Annum, who refused to sign the Bill; and also, except the Owners of Lands assessed at 6/. 7#. 10 per Annum, who declared themselves neuter; and that the Whole of the Lands intended to be inclosed are assessed at the Annual Sum of 243/. 16$. 3 and that no Person appeared before the Committee to oppose the Bill); and that the Committee had gone through the Bill, and made several Amendments thereunto, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Bill, with the Amendments, in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Amendments were Once read

throughout; and then a Second Time, One by One; and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, were agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendments, be ingrossed.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Bailiffs, and Common Council of the Town of Liverpool, in Council assembled, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, as Trustees of the Corporate Fund of the ancient and loyal Town of Liverpool, have always been ready, from Motives of Duty, to give every Encouragement in their Power to the Commercial Interest of that Part of the Community under their Care, and to promote the Public Welfare: That, the Trade of Liverpool having met with the Countenance of the House in many Acts of Parliament which have passed at different Times for the constructing of convenient Docks for its Shipping, and particularly for the African Ships, which, from their Form and Construction, require to be constantly

afloat, the Petitioners have been emboldened to lay out very large Sums, and to pledge their Corporate Seal to a still greater Amount, for effecting those laudable Purposes, and from these superior Conveniences of the Docks, and other local Advantages, ‘added to the enterprizing Spirit of the People, the Trade of pool, and particularly the African Trade, which forms the most extensive Branch thereof, and, in Effect, gives Strength and Energy to the Whole, is arrived at such a Pitch of Consequence as cannot but affect and improve, and is materially, and inseparably, connected with, the Wealth and Prosperity of the Kingdom at large; and that the Petitioners observe, with real Concern, the repeated Attempts and Endeavours to effect a total, and almost immediate, Abolition of this Branch of Commerce, which has hitherto received the Protection of the Legislature, and been encouraged by continual Bounties and large Annual Grants, and they trust that the Restrictions and Regulations which have lately taken place in the said Trade, under the Directions and Authority of Parliament, have now removed the objectionable Parts of it, and leave no fair or reasonable Ground of Complaint: And therefore praying, That the Bill, now depending before the House, for the Abolition of the African Slave Trade, may not pass into a Law, which must in its Consequences so materially and essentially affect, not only the Revenues and Estates of the said Corporation, and the general Welfare and Prosperity of the Town and Port of pool, but also the Public Revenue, the Landed Interest, the Manufactures, and the Maritime Strength, of the Kingdom in general.

A Petition of the Merchants, principal Tradesmen, and other Inhabitants of the Town of , was

also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners, observing that a Bill has been brought into the House for a total Abolition of the African Slave Trade, within a very limited Period of Time, beg Leave to express, with the greatest Respect, that many of the Petitioners having, under the Protection of the Legislature, embarked a considerable Part of their Property in that Trade, will be very materially injured if the said Bill should pass into a Law; and that such Abolition, in the Petitioners Judgment, would not only be a great Detriment to the Port of Liverpool, but in its Consequences produce great Distress to the extensive Manufactories of the County of Lancaster, and to many of the other rich, opu-

lent, and industrious manufacturing Towns in the Kingdom, and would in no Degree answer the benevolent Purposes of Humanity, but only serve to remove the Benefits and Advantages of that Trade to Foreign States: And the Petitioners therefore, confiding in the Justice and Wisdom of the House, entertain great Hopes that the said Bill may not pass into a Law, but if, contrary to their Expectations, the Bill shall receive the Sanction of Parliament, the Petitioners pray, That an adequate Compensation may be made to them for the grievous Losses they will thereby sustain.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table.

At the Court at St. James's, the 1 sth of August

*795;

PRESENT,

The KING's Most Excellent Majesty in Council:

His Majesty, with the Advice of His Privy Council, hath thought fit to order, and it is hereby ordered, That no Person or Persons whosoever shall, from and after the Publication of this Order in The London Gazette, until the 25th Day of December 1795, directly or indirectly, export, transport, carry, or convey, or cause or procure to be exported, transported, carried, or conveyed, out of or from any Port or Place in Great Britain, or load or lay on Board, or cause or procure to be laden or laid on Board of any Ship, Vessel, or Boat, in order to be exported, transported, carried, or conveyed, out of any Port or Place in Great Britain, any Sort of Rock Salt whatsoever. His Majesty, nevertheless, by the Advice aforesaid, hath thought fit to order, That nothing herein contained shall prevent the same being carried Coastwise under the usual Rules, Regulations, and Restrictions, nor the Exportation of the same to Ireland, or to any other of His Majesty's Dominions, under the usual Conditions and Regulations, and upon Security being given by the Exporter and Two other Persons (of whom the Master of the Vessel shall be one) by Bond in such Penalty as shall be directed by the Commissioners of His Majesty's Customs, that the said Rock Salt shall be exported to some Port or Place in His Majesty's Dominions, and none other; and that a Certificate shall be produced within Six Months from the Date of the Bond if such Rock Salt shall be entered out for any Part of His Majesty's Dominions in Europe, ana within Twelve Months if for any Part of His Majesty's Dominions in America or the West Indies, and

within Eighteen Months if for any of the British Settlements or Factories in Asia or Africa, under the Hand of the principal Officer of the Customs at the Port or Place where such Rock Salt shall be so landed; and if there shall be no Officer of the Customs, then under the Hand of the Chief Magistrate of the Place, testifying that the said Rock Salt has been duly landed at the Port or Place for which the same was entered out; and the Right honourable the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty's Treasury, the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty, and the Lord Warden of the Cinque Ports, are to give the necessary Directions herein, as to them may respectively appertain.

(Signed) Steph. Cottrell,

At the Court at St. James's, the 30th of December 1795;

PRESENT,

The KING's Most Excellent Majesty in Council:

Whereas the Time limited by His Majesty's Order in Council of the 12th Day of August last, for prohibiting the exporting out of this Kingdom any Sort of Rock Salt whatsoever, expired upon the 25th Day of this Instant December; and whereas it is judged expedient for His Majesty's Service, that the said Prohibition should be continued for some Time longer; His Majesty, therefore, by and with the Advice of His Privy Council, hath thought fit to order, and it is hereby ordered, That no Person or Persons whatsoever do, at any Time during the Space of Eight Weeks, to commence from the said 25th Day of this Instant December, directly or indirectly, export, transport, carry, or convey, or cause or procure to be exported, transported, carried, or conveyed, out of or from any Port or Place in Great Britain, or load or lay on Board, or cause or procure to be laden or laid on Board of any Ship, Vessel, or Boat, in order to be exported, transported, carried, or conveyed, out of any Port or Place in Great Britain, any Sort of Rock Salt whatsoever, except as excepted in His Majesty's former Order in Council of the 12th of August last, and subject to the Conditions therein expressed; and the Right honourable the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty's Treasury, the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty, and the Lord Warden of the Cinque Ports are to give the necessary Directions herein, as to them may respectively appertain.

(Signed) Steph. Cottrell.

A Copy of the late Mr. Hunter's Will was produced, which, among other Things, directed as follows:

" I also give to the said Matthew Baillie and Everard Home, all my Collection of Natural History, " and the Cases and other Things belonging thereto, " or used therewith, upon Trust, that they offer the " same to Sale, in One entire Lot, to the Government " of Great Britain, at such Price that may be considered as reasonable between both Parties, and in " case of Refusal, then that it may be offered to Sale " to any Foreign Government or State, upon the like " Terms, and in Failure of such Sale, then to dispose " of the same in an entire Lot, in such Manner as they " shall think proper."

Then your Committee proceeded to examine

Dr. Matthew Baillie, Physician, and Lecturer on Anatomy.

What are the Reasons which make you offer the late Mr. Hunters Collection to Parliament ?

We are obliged to do it by a Clause in Mr. Hun-, ter's Will.

What is the Nature of the Collection ?

It consists of a great Number of Preparations of the various Parts of different Animals, intended to illustrate the various Functions of Animal Life, as subservient to a better Knowledge of Physiology, and likely to improve very much the Knowledge of Medicine and Surgery.

What is the Object of the Collection ?

To make us better acquainted with the Functions of Animal Life generally, and more particularly with those of Man, therefore to make us better able to reason accurately about the Nature of Diseases, and their Remedies.

Do the Answers to the Two last Questions apply to the Whole of this Collection ?

Every Animal whatever has Circumstances in its Structure, which, when considered, tend to illustrate the Functions of Animals generally, therefore every Part of this Collection has the same great important Object in View.

Sir George Augustus William Shuckburgh Evelyn reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of Matthew Baillie, Physician, and Everard Home, Esquire, Surgeon, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and, that the House might be the better enabled more fully to understand the Circumstances of the Case, the Committee had directed him to report specially the Minutes of the Evidence taken before them; and he read the

What Advantage can the Public derive from it?

That the different Functions of the Animal Economy will be better understood. Physicians and Surgeons better acquainted with the Nature of Diseases, and therefore more able to apply Remedies, which may-be likely to remove or relieve them.

What Length of Time can such a Collection be preserved ?

I should believe that Part of the Collection, which is preserved in Spirit, will last for Centuries, because preserved in a Fluid that has a strong antiputrescent Power; and that as long as the Fluid retains the same Property, it appears impossible that these Preparations should decay — that this Opinion, as far as we can judge by Experience, seems to be well founded — that Specimens, prepared in this Way, for a great Number of Years, seemed not to be sensibly changed — that Preparations made the Beginning of Mr. Hunter's Collection, above Forty Years ago, still remain without any sensible Change — those of Albinus are in the same State of Preservation as at first, which must be Sixty Years old at the least — with respect to the dried Preparations in Mr. Hunter's Collection, a great Proportion of them must, from their Nature, be preserved unimpaired for Centuries — that those considered as the most perishable have not as yet shewn any sensible Signs of Decay.

What

36 Geo. III.

What Annual Expence will be required to keep it in its present State of Preservation ?

Two hundred Pounds a Year >vill do it amply — in this Sum the Salary of a Person, who might take Care of the Collection, and make it useful to the Public, is included.

Does this Collection form a systematic Series, so arranged that it cannot be replaced if suffered to be dispersed ?

Yes, certainly; unless the same Labour and Sagacity were continued for a long Series of Years, and unless a Person should arise with the same Reputation in these Pursuits; which last Circumstance induced many Persons of different Countries to send Specimens of various Animals to Mr. Hunter for Examination, which would not have been sent to a Person of less Celebrity.

Withdrew.

Everard Home, Esquire, Surgeon, and Lecturer in Anatomy.

What are the Reasons which make you offer the late Mr. Hunters Collection to Parliament ?

A Clause in Mr. Hunter's Will, requiring us so to do.

What is the Nature of the Collection?

It consists of Parts of Animals so prepared as to shew their internal Structure, collected from the whole Animal Kingdom.

What is the Object of the Collection ?

To expose, at One Point of View, the Mechanism of the different. Orders of Animals, from the most simple to the most perfect; by this Means to enable us to distinguish between those Structures essential to Life, and those superadded for other Purposes; also to enable us to discover the Uses of the different Parts of the Organs of the more perfect Animals, by comparing them with the same Organs of Animals of inferior Orders, which are made up of fewer Parts, and therefore more easily understood.

Do the Answers to the Two last Questions apply to the Whole of this Collection ?

The Collection comprehends One great System, of which, every Preparation constitutes a Part, the Whole being subservient to One great View.

What Advantage can the Public derive from it ?

It tends to improve our Knowledge of the Anatomy, Physiology, and Diseases of the Human Body, which, as it is most perfect in its Construction, is too complex to admit of Investigation; and therefore, when the same Parts are found in other Animals, applied to different Purposes, it enables us to understand their Use in the Human Body; for there are many Parts of the Human Body, which, probably, could never be investigated without comparative Anatomy.

What Length of Time can such a Collection be preserved ?

There is in that Collection a Preparation preserved for Three Centuries and an Half, which had been kept in a Liquor, probably less antisceptic than that used for the other Preparations; from this Fact, and my own Knowledge of the Collection of above Twenty Years,- I should consider the greater Part of it capable of being preserved for many Centuries — the other Parts of the Collection, which are considered the most, perishable, have undergone no Change in Forty Years, and therefore they may likewise be preserved for Centuries.

What is the Value of the Collection?

It cost Mr. Hunter upwards of Thirty Years Vot. 61.

Labour; and from living in it the greater Part of Mr. Hunter's Twenty Years of that Period, I feel myself justified Collection of in the Assertion, that he laid out more than 15,000l. in bringing it to its present State, exclusive of the Presents that were made to him, which were very considerable; the Value of the Time he employed, and the System which the Whole contains, being the Produce of superior anatomical Skill and mental Ability.

What Annual Expence will be required to keep it in its present State of Preservation ?

Two hundred Pounds per Annum would appear a sufficient Sum to keep up the Collection in its present State, including a Salary of 100l. a Year to a Person employed for that Purpose.

Does this Collection form a systematic Series, so arranged that it cannot be replaced if suffered to be dispersed ?

To replace it would require the same Abilities, the same Length of Time, and the same Expence, should a Person of Mr. Hunter's anatomical Skill, and Enthusiasm for such Pursuits, ever be found to make such an Attempt; and even then many particular Preparations essential to the System could not be procured.

Withdrew.

Henry Cline, Esquire, Surgeon to St.

Hospital, and Teacher of Anatomy.

Have you seen the late Mr. Hunter's Collection ?

Frequently.

What is its present State of Preservation?

Very good.

Do you know of any Anatomical Collection, in this or any other Country, of the same Extent or Value?

I know of none which is so extensive in the Number of Anatomical Preparations to illustrate the Structure of Animals in general, and the Human Body in particular; consequently it is more valuable than any other Collection of the same Kind.

In what does this Collection differ from other Anatomical Collections?

In illustrating, from Animals generally, the Structure of the Human Body, by a comparative View of the Parts of such Animals.

Of what Importance do you consider such a Collection to the Public ?

It has a Tendency, by explaining the Economy of the Human Anatomy, to give more clear Ideas of different Diseases.

What do you consider to be the Value of such a Collection ?

It is not possible to make any exact Valuation, because, if this Collection was lost, I don't conceive it could be replaced for 20,000l., if at all.

How long can such a Collection be preserved ?

That Part of it which is preserved in Spirits does not appear subject to Decay, provided a reasonable Care is taken to keep it in Repair — with respect to the other Parts of the Collection, they probably would last for some Centuries with equal Care.

What Annual Expence will be required to keep up the Collection in its present State ?

About 200l. Annually would be sufficient to pay the Salary of a proper Person, and find Materials for the necessary Repairs.

Withdrew.

Have you seen the late Mr. Hunter's Collection?

I have known it about Twenty-five Years.

What is its present State of Preservation ?

In the greatest Perfection, and superior to any I have ever seen.

Do you know of any Anatomical Collection, in this or any other Country, of the same Extent or Value ? Certainly not.

In what does this Collection differ from other Anatomical Collections r

In being a Whole more complete.

Of what Importance do you consider such a Collection to the Public?

Anatomical Collections have given more Ardour to Young Men, and been the Means of making better Physicians and Surgeons than ever existed before.

What do you consider to be the Value of such a Collection ?

I should consider it as almost invaluable.

How long can such a Collection be preserved ?

For some Centuries I should believe — Ruych's Collection is an Hundred Years old, which was sold to Czar Peter the Great, and which I am informed is still in high Preservation.

What Annual Expence will be required to keep up the Collection in its present State ?

Two hundred Guineas at least, including the Salary of a Person to look after it.

Does this Collection form a systematic Scries, so arranged that it cannot be replaced if suffered to be dispersed ?

The finest in the World, and I don't believe it ever could be replaced.

Withdrew'.

William Blizzard, Esquire, Surgeon to the London Hospital, and Lecturer in Anatomy.

Have you seen the late Mr. Hunter's Collection ?

I have.

What is its present State of Preservation ?

The best possible.

Do you know of any Anatomical Collection, in this or any other Country, of the same Extent or Value ?

I know of no other, in this or any other Country, of equal Extent and Value.

In what does this Collection differ from other Anatomical Collections ?

It is comprehensive of Articles illustrative of the Structure and Functions of the Organs of Animals in general, of their Distinctions, Links, and Dependants, from the most simple Progress from Vegetable Existence, proceeding to the most complex and perfect, that of Man, by which Light is thrown upon the Structures and Functions of the Parts of each Particular, by which their Diseases are rendered better understood.

Of what Importance do you consider such a Collection to the Public ?

Of the greatest, while Health, and Life, and the Knowledge of Diseases, are considered of Importance} since the Collection tends to improving the Means of maintaining Health and Life, and of preventing and removing Diseases.

Does this Collection form a systematic Series, so

arranged that it cannot be replaced if suffered to be dispersed ?

I do not believe that all the known Collections would constitute a Collection, in Point of systematic Arrangement, equally valuable.

What do you consider to be the Value of such a Collection ?

I believe, in what I have been assured, that some of the Articles cost 15,000l., others were obtained without Cost; but every Article has the Stamp of the Finger directed by the Judgment of a Man superior, I believe, to any one that ever existed in Point of practical Anatomy, and every Article, I conceive, must thence acquire at least double its original Value, from the Art employed upon it — in respect of the Arrangement and the Application of the Whole, I consider the Collection as inestimable.

How long can such a Collection be preserved ?

It consists of certain Articles little liable to change from any Cause, such as Bones, Calculi, &c.; these may last for Ages with little or no Attention — of Casts in resinous Substances, Plaister of Paris, &c.; they will also last for Ages with Care and Attention — of Things preserved in Spirits, which, I conceive, may be preserved so long as the Medium is supplied — and of some Things perishable through Insects, &c. which yet may be preserved for a great Length of Time with Care and Attention.

What Annual Expence will be required to keep up the Collection in its present State ?

I believe 200l. a Year may be sufficient, including the Salary to a Curator.

Withdrew.

John Abernethie, Esquire, Surgeon, and Lecturer in Anatomy and Surgery.

Have you seen the late Mr. Hunter's Collection?

I have.

What is its present State of Preservation ?

In very perfect Preservation.

Do you know of any Anatomical Collection, in this or any other Country, of the same Extent or Value?

I do not.

In what does this Collection differ from other Anatomical Collections ?

In shewing the Structure and Uses of the Parts of the Human Body, by comparing them with similar Parts in almost every Species of Animals.

Of what Importance do you consider such a Collection to the Public ?

Of the greatest, inasmuch as it explains the Uses and natural Functions of the Parts of the Human Body, which being known, their Diseases will necessarily be understood, and the Mode of curing them pointed out.

What do you consider to be the Value of such a Collection ?

I cannot appreciate it — many Preparations, I believe, cannot be replaced, and the Remainder not without the Exertion of similar Talents and Industry.

How long can such a Collection be preserved ?

The Preparations in Spirits are never likely to suffer Change, and the perishable Part of the other Preparations is very small, when compared to the Whole.

Sir George Baker, Baronet, President of the College of Physicians.

Have you seen the late Mr. Hunter's Collection ?

Yes; within these Ten Days.

What is the present State of its Preservation ?

I did not observe that any Part had received any Injury.

Do you know of any Anatomical Collection, in this or any other Country, of the same Extent or Value?

I do not conceive that there is any Anatomical Collection in Europe equal to it either in Extent or Value.

In what way can it promote Medical Education ?

I believe that it would extremely promote Medical Education, if it were to be committed to a Society of Men conversant in Anatomical Pursuits, who might superintend the Care of it, and appoint a Person competent to the reading Lectures upon the several Parts of it, by which the Animal Economy would be greatly illustrated; and I likewise think it would tend more to Medical Improvement, if, under certain Regulations and Restrictions, it were accessible to Students; I think likewise a descriptive and explanatory Catalogue should be made of it

What should you consider the Value of such a Collection ?

This Collection must have been very expensive; and it is well known that Mr. Hunter never regarded Money when in Pursuit of his favourite Object; but the Question is not what it cost, but what it is ? — It is the Produce of great Ingenuity, unexampled Labour, and Perseverance for Forty Years, or nearly, of a Man's Life; and if it can tend to the Improvement of Medicine, by that Consideration it acquires an intrinsic Value, and gives the Family of Mr. Hunter a Claim to an adequate Compensation.

Withdrew.

Sir Charles Blagden, Knight, formerly Physician

Dr. George Fordyce, Physician to St. Thomas's Hospital, and Lecturer on the Practice of Physic.

Have you seen the late Mr. Hunters Collection ?

I have, through the whole Period of its Formation, and have likewise seen it several Times lately, and particularly about Ten Days ago, for the Purpose of giving my Opinion with regard to its Preservation.

What is the present State of its Preservation ?

In a perfect State of Preservation, as far as I was able to judge.

Do you know of any Anatomical Collection, in this or any other Country, of the same Extent or Value.

I do not.

In what Way can it promote Medical Education ?

Its Usefulness in promoting Medical Education arises from the Explanation of several of the Functions of the Human Body, which may be procured from it, and which could not be known from the Anatomy of the Human Body itself. — I conceive, undoubtedly, that its being in the Possession of the Public, and proper Persons being appointed to take Care of it, and explain the several Parts and Uses of it to Students in Medicine, would be the best Manner of rendering it useful.

What should you consider the Value of such a Collection ?

I believe that Mr. Hunter has expended what would have been a very large Fortune for his Family, as near as I can judge above 25,000l. in forming it; and that such a Collection could not have been formed by a Man of less Ingenuity, Perseverance, and Industry.

Withdrew.

Dir. David Pitcairn, Physician to Christ's Hospital.

Have you seen the late Mr. Hunter's Collection ?

Frequently; and particularly within these Ten Days.

What is the present State of its Preservation ?

It seems to me to be at present in a very good State of Preservation.

Do you know of any Anatomical Collection, in this or any other Country, of the same Extent or Value?

I know of none in this Country so extensive or valuable; and, never having been out of this Country,

I cannot speak as to those of other Countries — to the best Information I have had on the Subject, I believe there is not any.

In what Way can it promote Medical Education ?

It may be applied in various Ways — perhaps the best Mode would be that which Mr. Hunter himself proposed to apply it to, which was, by giving Lectures upon the general Physiology of Animal Nature, and illustrating those Lectures by shewing the Preparations contained in his Museum.

What should you consider the Value of such a Collection ?

I cannot answer — I know it cost Mr. Hunter above 20,000l., without considering his Labour of near Forty Years, and exclusive of ail Presents.

How long might such a Collection be preserved ?

Spirits, which constitute the largest and most important Part of the Collection, have not changed, and are in their Nature almost imperishable, and the dried Preparations have suffered very little Alteration in Twenty Years.

Is there any Collection in Great Britain by which Students could acquire the Knowledge of comparative Anatomy ?

I know of none.

Upon what Principle or System was Mr. Hunter's Collection formed ?

The Object of it was to enlarge- our Knowledge of the Human Body and its Functions; to improve therefore the Art of Preserving it in Health, and remedying its Diseases.

Does Mr. Hunters Collection of Comparative Anatomy contribute materially to this Purpose ?

It certainly does.

Are not Anatomical Preparations of Animal and Vegetable Substances essential for illustrating the Science of the Anatomy of the Human Body ?

The Human Body being the most complicated of all Animal Machines, in order to understand and explain its various Parts it becomes necessary for us to examine similar Parts in Vegetables and Animals of a more simple Form, and from such Examination we are often enabled to illustrate and explain the Functions of more complicated Parts in the Human Body.

Withdrew.

Sir Joseph Banks, Baronet, K. B. President of the Royal Society.

Have you seen the late Mr. Hunters Collection ?

I have, several Times, and have viewed it lately, in order that I might be prepared, in case I should be called upon, to give an Account of it.

What is its present State of Preservation?

It appears to me to be in a very good State of Preservation.

Do you know of any Anatomical Collection, in this or any other Country, of the same Extent or Value?

Not having been educated to Anatomy, or having any particular Knowledge in that Branch of Science, it is impossible for me to form a satisfactory Opinion on that Subject.

Of what Importance do you consider such a Collec-lection to Natural History and general Science ?

I conceive such Parts of the Collection as illustrate the comparative Structure of different Animals with those of Men, and shew the nicer Parts of the Structure of Vegetables, which cannot be observed unless they are displayed with much Skill and Accuracy, as extremely interesting and useful to the Promotion of Natural History, and of Science in general.

What is the Value of the Collection ?

Not being in the Habits of buying Matters of this Nature, I do not feel myself able to put a Value on it.

I believe they might visit it with great Advantage, inasmuch as Comparative Anatomy serves to illustrate and explain many obscure Parts of Human Anatomy.

A Petition of the Rector, Churchwardens, Overseers, Petition for and Inhabitants, of the Parish of S Martin Outwich, Leave to in the City of London, whose Names are thereunto sub- Pe*

scribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting Ie_bui)d or forth, That the Church of the said Parish, which repair the was built in the Thirteenth Century, hath, for a Series Church of of Years, occasioned to the Inhabitants of the Pa- Q^"^gbartin rish a continued Expence for Repairs, and is now become absolutely ruinous, and, from that Cause, Divine Service hath not been performed in it for upwards of Eighteen Months, and the said Church stands in a very conspicuous Situation in the City of London, being at the Corner of Bishopsgate Street and Thread-needle Street, occupying a prominent Part of those Streets, which are very public Avenues to the Centre of the Metropolis: That, the said Parish being very small, the Inhabitants found themselves unable to undertake the re-building of the said Church, as was advised to be done, a Repair being reported by Surveyors to be only temporary, though very expensive, and they therefore applied to the Patrons of the Living, the Company of Merchant Taylors of London, and to the South Sea Company, whose Flouse is situate in the said Parish, for Assistance, and that, in July 1795, the Churchwardens of the said Parish signified to the Parishioners, that the Merchant Taylors Company had agreed to contribute a Donation of 500l., and the South Sea Company a Donation of 200l., on the express Condition that the Church should be rebuilt, and set back so as to form a Curve to widen the Street in such Way as should be approved by a Surveyor to be named by them; and the Parishioners, assembled at that Vestry, appointed a Committee to consider of the best Mode of raising the Residue of the Money that would be wanted; and that, at Vestries held in September and December 1795, Plans and Estimates from different Surveyors were ordered to be procured, and, on the 13th Day of January 1796, a Surveyor's Report and Plan were laid before a Vestry, who thereupon directed that an Estimate of the Expence of the Edifice, agreeably to the Plan produced, should be made, and, on the 20th and 22d Days of January 1796, the Committee of Inhabitants, appointed to conduct the Business, met, but were unable to come to any Determination, because they were apprehensive that re-building the Church, with the consequent Expence? of an Act of Parliament, would occasion Rates too heavy for the Parish to bear, and they therefore proposed to try the Mode of doing it by a Subscription from the Parishioners of the Whole of the calculated Amount of each Person's Rates at One Payment, and, with Hopes of this Plan being adopted, they, on the 29th of January, approved the Surveyor's Plan for a new Building: That the Time between the 27th of

St. Martin's Outwich Church Petition.

36 Geo. Ill 17° Martii. 523

January and the 15th of February was employed in collecting the Opinion of the Parishioners as to the proposed Mode of a Subscription, on which Day it appeared to the Committee above-mentioned, that the Sense of the Parishioners was against that Method of raising the Money, that of course it could not be carried into Effect, and, as the only Means left, they gave Direction for an Application to Parliament, such Application to be sanctioned by a Vestry, which was called for the 19th of February, on which Day, without waiting for a regular Report, the Proceedings of the Committee were approved and confirmed, and the Petition to Parliament was immediately prepared; and that the said Committee were further induced to adopt the Plan of re-building the Church in the Manner above-mentioned, instead of repairing it, in consequence of having had Intimation that the Corporation of London would favourably receive a Petition from the Inhabitants for Assistance in rebuilding the Church in the Manner proposed, as tending to provide a great Accommodation to the Public, and a Petition was accordingly presented to the Court of Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Common Council, on the 18th of February last, and by that Court referred to the Committee of City Lands; that there are Hopes their Report will be in Favour of the Petition, but the Petitioners, not thinking prudent to defer any longer their Application to Parliament, finally determined, on the said 15 th of February, to present a Petition to the House, and gave the necessary Orders accordingly; and that, by Reason of the Time necessarily and unavoidably taken up as aforesaid, the Petitioners were prevented applying to the House before the Time limited for receiving Petitions for Private Bills was elapsed, and, that the Petitioners are now without any Place of Public Worship, and so must remain until Parliament shall interfere for their Relief: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to exhibit a Petition for a Bill to re-build, or partly to repair and partly to re-build, the said Church, in such Manner, and under such Regulations, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That, in Consideration of the particular Circumstances set forth in the said Petition, Leave be given to present a Petition, as dasired by the said Rector, Churchwardens, Overseers, and Inhabitants, of the Parish of Saint Martin Outwich.

Then a Petition of the Rector, Churchwardens, Overseers, and Inhabitants, of the Parish of Saint Martin Outwich, in the City of London, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Church of the said Parish, which was built in the Thirteenth Century, has, for a Series of Years, occasioned to the Inhabitants of the Parish a continued Expence for Repairs, and is now become absolutely ruinous, and, from that Cause, Divine Service has not been performed in it for upwards of Eighteen Months past; and that the Petitioners have caused various Surveys to be made by Builders of Eminence, who have reported the Church to be in a very dangerous State, and declared their Opinion of the Necessity of a general Repair, which would be but temporary, or, of its being partly taken dowrn and re-built: That the said Church stands in a very conspicuous Situation in the City of London, being the Corner of Bishopsgate Street and Threadncedle Street, occupying a prominent Part of those Streets, both of which are very public Avenues to the Heart of the Metropolis, and that the Petitioners are induced, by the Offer of certain Donations, to re-build, or partly repair and partly re-build, the said Church, in such Way as shall accord with the Public Convenience, but the same cannot be done without the Aid and Authority of Parliament: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to rebuild, or partly to repair and partly to re-build, the Vo L. 51.

said Church, in such Manner, and under such Regulations, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Alderman Lushington, the Lord Mayor of London, &c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker's Chamber; and have Power to send for Persons, Papers, and Records.

Report respecting the

Sale of Com by Weight.

Mr. Ryder reported from the Select Committee, who were appointed to take into Consideration the present high Price of Corn, and to collect Evidence relative thereto, and to report the same, from Time to Vo l. 51.

Time, withi thehr Opinion thereupon, to the House; That the Committee had further considered the Matters to them referred, and had come to several Resolutions, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Resolutions of the Committee were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the buying and selling of Com by Weight, or by Measure regulated by Weight, is more certain, and less liable to Deception, than by Measure alone.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, notwithstanding the Bushel, commonly called " The Winchester Bushel," is the only Measure of that Description authorized by Law, there are various customary Measures used in different Parts of this Kingdom, to the great Inconvenience of the Buyers and Sellers of Com.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Adoption of Weight, or Measure regulated by Weight, in the Sale of Corn, instead of Measure alone, will tend to remedy these Inconveniences, and to equalize all Descriptions of the Quantities of Com bought or sold in this Kingdom.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Standard of Weight ought to be the Avoirdupois Pound, One Hundred and Twelve of which Pounds shall be considered as the Hundred Weight, and Twenty Hundred Weight One Ton, standing Weight, with an even Beam or Balance.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the following Weights, Avoirdupois, of the respective Sorts of Grain, shall be deemed equal to a Standard Winchester Bushel; viz. Wheat 6o lb. — Rye 561b. — Barley 5olb. — Beer or Bigg 44lb. — Oats 40-lb. — Beans 60 lb. — Pease 6olb.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all Contracts, Bargains, Sales, and Dealings in Com, ought to be taken and adjudged to be according to the Standards aforesaid; and that no Person should recover the Price of Com sold, or the Corn itself, or any Damages on Account of any Contracts, Bargains, Sales, or Dealings, but according to the Weight of the Avoirdupois Poutid, or of Measure regulated by that Weight; and that all Contracts, Bargains, Sales, or Dealings, made otherwise, should be void.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the giving and receiving, as an Allowance or Addition to the Weight, a Quantity of Corn above what is really and bond side agreed for, by which a higher Price is paid to the Seller than the nominal Weight or Quantity is worth, tends to raise the Return of the Average Price of Com, and is thereby injurious to the Consumers of Bread.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That any Person, demanding or taking any Addition or Allowance of Com to the Pound, Hundred, or Ton, or other Weight, or to the respective Weights of the Bushel, as before-mentioned, should be made liable to a Penalty.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That, by several ancient Acts, it is directed that Market Towns should have a common Balance, and Standard Weights and Measures; and that by an Act, made in the Thirty-fifth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, the Use of defective Weights, and false and unequal Balances, has been prohibited; and the Justices are empowered to purchase Standard Weights out of the County Rates.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Chief Magistrate of every City or Market Town, or the Justices in their Sessions, should be directed and required to cause to be erected, in a convenient Place within the Corn Market of such City or Market Town, or in other Places where Corn is

sold,

528 ' 18° — 21°

sold, sufficient Beams or Balances, with proper Scales thereunto affixed, with a competent Set of Iron Weights; and that the Expence thereof shall be paid for out of the County Rate, as is directed by the Act of the Thirty-fifth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, unless the City or Town does not contribute to the Rate of the County in which it is situated.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, where Weights are provided for the above Purposes, they shall be made of Cast Iron, with the Contents thereof marked on each particular Weight; and that Four Weights of 561b. each, and One of each of the Weights of 281b. 141b. 7lb. 4lb. 2lb. and 1 lb. Avoirdupois, by compounding of which a Sack of Corn, or any smaller Quantity, can be weighed, shall be considered as competent.

Ordered, That the said Report do lie upon the Table.

Ordered, That such a Number of Copies of the said Report be printed, as shall be sufficient for the Use of the Members of the House.

A Petition of the Company of Proprietors of the Petition re-Undertaking for recovering and preserving the Navigation of the River Dee, was presented to the House, r,na| and read; Taking Notice of the Bill to explain and (between amend an Act, passed in the Thirty-third Year of the Ruabon Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for Clweter-)

" making and maintaining a Navigable Canal from " the River Severn at Shrewsbury, in the County of " Salop, to the River Mersey at or near Netherpool,

" in the County of Chester, and also for making and " maintaining certain Collateral Cuts from the said " intended Canal," and for varying and altering certain Parts of the Course of the said Canal and Collateral Cuts between Ruabon and Chester, and for extending the same, and for making and maintaining several other Branches and Collateral Cuts to communicate therewith; and Setting forth, That the Petitioners have, under the Faith of several Acts of Parliament, expended very large Sums of Money in improving the Navigation of the said River Dee, and in recovering and embanking large Tracts of Land near or adjoining thereto, and they are advised, that, unless proper Clauses are inserted in the said Bill, their Navigation may be injured, and the Tolls and Duties, payable to them in respect thereof, considerably lessened, and the Safety and Security of their Lands very much endangered: And therefore praying, That proper Clauses may be inserted in the said Bill effectually to preserve and secure the Navigation of the said River Dee, and the Petitioners Tolls and Duties payable in respect thereof, and the Lands and other Property of the Petitioners.

Ordered, That all have Voices who come to the Committee to whom the said Bill is committed.

Mr. Ryder presented to the House, by His Majesty's Command,

A Copy of His Majesty's Order in Council for continuing the Prohibition on the Exportation of Rock Salt for four Weeks, to commence from the 18th Day of this Instant March; dated 16th March 1796.

And the Title of the said Paper was read.

The said Paper is as followeth; viz.

Order in Council for continuing the Prohibition on Exportation of Rock Salt, presented.

At the Court at Saint James's, the 16th March

»796;

PRESENT,

The KING's Most Excellent Majesty in Council:

Whereas the Time limited by His Majesty s Order in Council of the Twelfth Day of February last, for prohibiting the exporting out of this Kingdom any Sort of Rock Salt whatsoever, will expire upon the 18th Day of this Instant March; and whereas it is adjudged expedient for His Majesty's Service, that the said Prohibition should be continued for some Time longer; His Majesty therefore, by and with the Advice of His Privy Council, hath thought fit to order, and it is hereby ordered, That no Person or Persons whatsoever do, at any Time during the Space of Four Weeks, to commence from the said 18th Day of this Instant March, directly or indirectly, export, transport, carry, or convey, or cause or procure to be exported, transported, carried, or conveyed, out of or from any Port or Place in Great Britain, or load or lay on Board, or cause or procure to be laden or laid on Board of any Ship, Vessel, or Boat, in order to be exported, transported, carried, or conveyed, out of any Port or Place in Great Britain, any Sort of Rock Salt whatsoever, except as excepted in His Majesty's former Order in Council of the 12th of August 1795, and > subject to the Conditions therein expressed; and the Right honourable the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty's Treasury, the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty, and the Lord Warden of the Cinque Ports, are to give the necessary Directions herein, as to them may respectively appertain.

(Signed) Sleph. Cottrell.

A Message from the Lords, by Mr. and

Mr. Smith:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to continue several Laws relating to the giving further Encouragement to the Importation of Naval Stores from the British Colonies in America', to the Encouragement of the Silk Manufactures, and for taking off several Duties on Merchandize exported, and reducing other Duties; to the preventing the clandestine Running of Goods, and the Danger of In-.section thereby; to the encouraging the Growth of Coffee in His Majesty's Plantations in America; to the free Importation of Cochineal and Indigo; to the granting a Bounty on certain Species of British and Irish Linens exported, and taking off the Duties on the Importation of Foreign Raw Linen Yarns made of Flax; to the Importing Salt from Europe into the Province of Quebec, in America; to the encouraging

the Manufacture of Leather, by lowering the Duty payable upon the Importation of Oak Bark, when the Price of such Bark shall exceed a certain Rate; to the more effectual Encouragement of the Manufactures of Flax and Cotton in Great Britain; to the allowing the Importation of Rape Seed and other Seeds used for extracting Oil, whenever the Prices of middling British Rape Seed shall be above a certain Limit; to the allowing a Drawback of the Duties on Rum shipped as Stores to be consumed on Board Merchant Ships in their Voyages; to the clandestine Running of uncustomed Goods, and preventing Frauds relating to th Customs; to the further Punishment of Persons going armed or disguised in Defiance of the Law's of Customs or Excise; to the free Importation of certain Raw Hides and Skins from Ireland, and the British Plantations in America; and to the Duties on Spirits made in Scotland, and imported into England; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for defraying the Charge of the Pay and Clothing of the Militia in that Part of Great Britain called England, for One Year, beginning the Twenty-fifth Day of March One thousand Seven hundred and Ninety-six; without any Amendment: And also,

A Motion was made, and the Question being put, That it he an Instruction to the Select Committee, to whom the Bill for facilitating the Division and Inclosure of Waste Lands and Commons, by Agreement among the Parties interested therein, or a certain Proportion thereof, and for removing certain legal Disabilities that might otherwise stand in the Way of such Agreement, is committed, that they have Power to turn the said Bill into Two Bills, if they think fit:

It passed in the Negative.

The Order of the Day being read, for the House to resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the Bill for amending, and reducing into One Act of Parliament, Two several Acts, passed in the Thirty-fourth and Thirty-fifth Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, for the better ordering the Militia of the City of London, and for the further regulating of the Trained Bands or Militia of the said City.

Resolved, That this House will, upon this Day Three Weeks, the nth Day of April next, resolve itself into the said Committee.

A Motion was made, and the Question was proposed, That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, that He will be graciously pleased to give Directions that there be laid before this House, Copies of such Intelligence as has been received by any of His Majesty's Ministers relating to the Mode of carrying on the War against the Maroons in Jamaica.

And the said Motion was, with Leave of the House, withdrawn.

The other Orders of the Day being read;

Ordered, That the Bill for regulating the Conveyance of printed Votes, Proceedings in Parliament, and printed Newspapers, by the Post, in Great Britain, be read a Second Time Tomorrow Morning.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Wednesday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Wednesday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Wednesday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the Bill for amending an Act, made in this present Session of Parliament intituled, "An Act for allowing Bounties, for a limited Time, " on the Importation into Great Britain of any Wheat, " Wheat Flour, Indian Com, Indian Meal, or Rye, " in British Ships, or other Ships, the Property of " Persons of any Kingdom or State in Amity with " His Majesty, or on the Delivery of the same out of " Warehouse for Home Consumption.

Mr. Ryder reported from the Select Committee, who Were appointed to take into Consideration the present high Price of Corn, and to collect Evidence relative thereto, and to report the same, from Time to Time, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House; That the Committee had further considered the Matters to them referred, and had come to several Resolutions, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Resolutions of the Committee were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it is expedient that Magistrates should, in Times of Scarcity and high Price of Corn, have Power to make certain Regulations relative to the Manufacture and Sale of certain Sorts of Meal and Bread, which they do not now by Law possess.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, whenever the Average Price of middling British Wheat shall be above a certain Sum, Magistrates, at their General Quarter Sessions, or at any Sessions to be specially appointed for that Purpose, shall be empowered, within their respective Jurisdictions, to prohibit, for a limited Time, the Separation at the Mill of more than Five Pounds of Bran from every Sixty Pounds of Wheat; and also, to prohibit the Sale of any Wheaten Meal from which a greater Proportion of Bran shall have been separated.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That no Miller should be prevented from making fine Flour for the Consumption of any Persons who reside within the Districts where the Use of fine Flour is not prohibited, so far as the making such Flour, for the Consumption of such Persons, hath been the usual Course of his Trade.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Magistrates be also empowered to prohibit, within their respective Jurisdictions, for a limited Time, the making for Sale any other Bread, made of Wheat Meal alone, than such as shall be made of the whole Meal, deducting only at the Rate of Five Pounds of Bran out of Sixty Pounds of Wheat.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Magistrates be empowered, within their respective Jurisdictions, to prohibit, for a limited Time, the making of any Bread for Sale, except such as shall be made of the whole Meal of Wheat, as above described, or of such Mixtures of wholesome farinaceous Food, and in such Proportions, as they shall appoint.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for the Purpose of carrying the last Resolution into Effect, Magistrates be empowered to oblige the Millers within their respective Jurisdictions, for. a limited Time, to grind and dress, if required, and, if

Vor,. 51.

consistent with the Powers and Mechanism of their Mills, such Sorts of Grain as shall be necessary for making the said approved Mixtures.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That Magistrates shall not make any of the Prohibitions before-mentioned without sufficient Public Notice.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That within the City of London, and the Liberties thereof, the Company of Bakers of the said City, and in any other County, City, Division, District, Town, or Place, any Baker or Maker of Bread for Sale,

Miller or Mealman, may, within the respective Jurisdiction to which he or they do belong, or wherein he or they do exercise their Trade, Occupation, or Mystery, nave an Opportunity of offering to such Justices as aforesaid, all such Objections as such Company of Bakers, or such Bakers or Makers of Bread for Sale, or such Millers or Mealmen, may have, and think fit to offer, against any such Prohibition or Regulation as aforesaid, at the Time when such Justices as aforesaid ' shall have under Consideration the ordering any such Prohibition or Regulation.

Ordered, That the said Report do lie upon the Table.

Ordered, That the said Report be printed.

A Petition of the cutting retail Butchers of London, Westminster, the Borough of Southwark, and the Places adjacent thereto, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That a very heavy and great Distress hath, for a long Time, and doth still continue to affect the Petitioners, and also the Public in general, especially the middling and lower Orders thereof, by the Yearly Rise of the Necessaries of Life (among which Butchers Meat is one of the most considerable) occasioned, so far as relates to that specific Article, they conceive, not only by the Practices of monopolizing Jobbers, Forestallers, Regraters, and Engrossers, but also by that Dealing which hath of late so much prevailed of Carcase-butchering within the Districts of the Trade of the Petitioners; and, as the said Description of Men suppose that the Statute, passed in the Twelfth Year of His present Majesty's Reign, for repealing the Laws against Badgers, Forestallers, §c. to extend not only to the Statutes particularly named therein, but also to the Eleventh Clause of the 31st of George the Second, Cap. 40, and to every other prohibiting Statute whatever, they deem themselves unrestrainable as to the Practices and Dealings they have uniformly exercised and persisted in since the passing the said repealing Act, in consequence of which, by the Influence they have acquired over the Salesmen, they so obstruct and prevent the Petitioners Vo uSL

from the Advantages of an open and fair Market of live Cattle, that they are compelled in too many Instances to have Recourse to the said Jobbers, Carcass Butchers, &c. for a Supply of those Goods they formerly had the Opportunity of buying alive and at the first Hand, by which several considerable Profits are unnecessarily made by those middle Men, to the certain progressive Enhancement of the Price of Meat, and to the manifest Injury of the Public, and of the Petitioners as a trading Body; and representing to the House, that the said Evil hath of late extended to so alarming and grievous a Height, that it hath raised the Price of Meat in most Cases to more than double at which it was sold in the Years 1765, 1766, 1767, and 1772; and that, during many Weeks of the last Spring, the Petitioners were under the Necessity of selling Meat to many of the lower Class of People at a less Price than it cost them, in order to allay the Discontents and Murmurs so prevalent at that Time, and, notwithstanding this was well known at that Period, they had the Mortification of experiencing that the Jobbers, Forestallers, Carcass Butchers, &c. continued in the unfeeling and sordid Practice of enriching themselves through the Medium of the Petitioners calamitous Situation; and that those Men not only engross to themselves the greatest and best Part of the live Stock brought into Smithfield Market, as before stated, but also that which is brought Weekly into the small Markets within Fifteen Miles of the Metropolis, and this System of Forestalling, &c. is another real Cause of the progressive Rise in the Price of Meat, and also tends to concentrate a great and valuable Part of the Trade into the Hands of those middle Men, to the Exclusion, as well as to the manifest Injury, of the fair Traders, who were the original Purveyors and Venders of this Article of Sustenance to the Public: The present, as well as the future evil Consequences attending this Practice, the Petitioners hope the House will protect them from; and they beg Leave, finally, to observe, that, it having been suggested the dry Summer of 1794, and the Winter which succeeded thereto, might, in a great Degree, have contributed to the excessive high Price of Meat, and that a more kind and productive Season would not only lessen, but in some Measure do away so much of the Cause as doth arise from those Sources, they entertained the fullest Expectation that the mild and genial Time which hath succeeded, and which still continues, would have effected so desirable and beneficial a Change; but, alas! this Blessing hath not altered the Face of Things, the Hand of Avarice yet grasps the obvious Good, God means to all, and thus that Hope, which supported the Expectation of the Petitioners, is rendered abortive, and no longer a Consolation to them; for although, the Markets have, for many Months past, been superabundantly supplied with Stock in the best Condition, no perceptible Alteration for the better hath been the Consequence, the Price of this Article of Sustenance is now as high as ever remembered, and the Petitioners conceive will progressively rise unless timely prevented by the House; and, from Information of undoubted Veracity, they learn that Meat hath in common been sold, and in many Places Continues so to be, at the Rate of a Halfpenny to Three Halfpence a Pound cheaper, at the small Distance of Twenty to Forty Miles only from London, than in that Metropolis, and its Environs: That the Petitioners, thus surrounded by the sordid Arts of Monopolizers, &c. on the one Hand, and of approaching Ruin (to many if not averted) on the other, of all which, as well as of every other Allegation in this Petition, they are prepared to give the most satisfactory Evidence, therefore pray, That their grievous Condition may induce the House to take the same into Consideration, and that such effectual and speedy

Petition for A Petition of the Lancaster Canal Company, was kaveto presented to the House, and read; Setting forth.

Petitioner That, by virtue of an Act, made in the Thirty-

amending the second Year of the Reign of His present Majesty,

Lancaster intituled, "An Act for making and maintaining a

Canal Act. " Navigable Canal from in the County of Westmorland, to West Houghton, in the County " Palatine of Lancaster, and also a Navigable Branch " from the said intended Canal, at or near Borwick, " to or near Warton Cragg, and also another Navigable Branch from, at, or near, Gale Moss, by Chorley, to or near Duxbury, in the said County Palatine of Lancaster," and also by virtue of another Act made in the Thirty-third Year of His present Majesty's Reign, to alter and amend the said former Act, by making a Navigable Branch from the said Canal at . or near Galgate to Glasgon Dock, in the said Vol. 5J.

County Palatine of Lancaster, the Petitioners, being certain Proprietors therein particularly named, are united into a Company for carrying on, making, completing and maintaining, the said intended Navigable Canal and Branches, and for that Purpose are thereby made one Body Politic and Corporate, by the Name of The Company oj Proprietors of the Lancaster Canal Navigation, and shall have a Common Seal, and by that Name have Power and Authority to purchase Lands to them and their Successors for the Use of the said Navigation, and are thereby authorized and empowered, from and after the 25th Day of June 1792, by themselves, their Deputies, Agents, Workmen, and Servants, to cause and complete a Canal, to be called The Lancaster Canal, to be made passable and navigable through the several Parishes and Places therein particularly mentioned; and, it is thereby enacted, that it shall and may be lawful for all Bodies Politic, Corporate, or Collegiate, Corporations aggregate or sole, who are, or shall be, seised or possessed of, or interested in, any Lands or Grounds through which the said intended Canal shall pass, to contract for, sell, and convey, unto the said Company of Pro prietors, their Successors or Assigns, or to such Person or Persons as they shall nominate and appoint, for the Use of the said Navigation, all, or any Part of, such Lands and Grounds which shall from Time to Time, be set out and ascertained for the Purposes aforesaid; and that the Petitioners have made a considerable Progress in carrying on the Works of the said intended Canal, and now find that, for the Purpose of completing the same, it will be necessary for them to make a Cut through a considerable Part of an Estate called Myerscough Park, in the County of Lancaster, Parcel of the Possessions of His Majesty, in Right of His Dutchy of Lancaster (subject to a Lease thereof granted to James Heatley, Esquire, for a Term of Years yet unexpired) which intended Cut the Petitioners are prevented from carrying into immediate Execution by His Majesty's Name being inadvertently omitted to be made Use of in the said Act, and, it is conceived, that His Majesty not being expressly empowered, under the said Act, to convey and assure any Lands to the Petitioners, it is expedient for the Purposes of carrying on the said Works, which are now entirely at a stand, and the Petitioners prevented from proceeding for the before-mentioned. Reasons, that a Bill should be brought into Parliament, this present Session, to alter and amend the said Act, by enabling the Chancellor and Council of the Dutchy of Lancaster for the Time being, to contract for, sell, and dispose of, and thereupon to grant and assure, in the Name of the King's Majesty, His Heirs and Successors, under the Seal of the said Dutchy, unto, or to the Use of, the Petitioners, their Successors, and Assigns, so much and such Quantities of Land, being Parcel of the Possessions of His said Dutchy, and within the Survey and Receipt of the same, as shall be necessary and expedient to be made Use of for the Purpose of completing the Works of the said Canal, at and for such Price or Prices as shall be agreed upon between the said Chancellor and Council of the said Dutchy and the Petitioners, to be paid into the Hands of the Receiver General of the said Dutchy, or his Deputy, for the Time being, for His Majesty's Use; and that the Petitioners were not aware of the Necessity of making this Application till after the Time limited by the House for receiving Petitions for private Bills had elapsed: And therefore praying. That they may be at liberty to present a Petition for Leave to bring in a Bill for altering and amending the said Act for the Purposes . before stated.

Ordered, That, in Consideration of the particular Leave Circumstances set forth in the said Petition, Leave be given to present a Petition,. as desired by the said Lancaster Canal Company.

Whereas we have issued our Orders to the Earl Hence, Admiral and Commander in Chief of His Majesty's Fleet, to hold a Court Martial at Portsmouth, on Monday next, the 4th Instant, or as soon after as conveniently may be, for the Trial of the Honourable William Cornwallis, Vice Admiral of the Red Squadron

of His Majesty's Fleet, upon Charges exhibited against him by us, for not proceeding to Barbadoes, pursuant to our Orders to him of the 25th of February last and 15th Ultimo: And whereas we think proper that you should, take the said Vice Admiral the Honourable William Cornwallis into your Custody; you are hereby required and directed to repair forthwith to Portsmouth, and acquaint him therewith. But as it is notour Intention that he should be put under greater Inconvenience or Confinement than is absolutely necessary, you are to take his Honour for his Appearance at the Court Martial, and attend him to and from the Court during the Continuance of his Trial, and then to dispose of him as the Court Martial shall direct; for which this shall be your Warrant. Given under our Hands and the Seal of the Office of Admiralty, the 2d April 1796.

H. Seymour.
