A Petition of the Subscribers thereto, being Mer- Petition from chants and Ship Owners in the City of Bristol, was Merchwits, presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, a^joStswan-That the Petitioners are informed that a Bill, is now Light-depending in Parliament for repairing, enlarging, and house Bill, preserving the Harbour of Swansea, and for making Improvements in the Lights at The Mumbles, by which a Tax is intended to be laid on all Ships and Vessels (a few only excepted) passing within certain Limits therein described, and which will include all Ships passing from the Westward of those Lights to Bristol, or from Bristol to the Westward thereof; and that the Petitioners are fully convinced, from the Testimony of the most experienced and judicious Navigators, that those Lights, so far from being of any Advantage to the Trade of Bristol, will be prejudicial thereto, es4 pecially to Foreigners, and Ships of any considerable Burthen, who, trusting to the discovering those Lights, may make for that Coast, where there is not sufficient Depth of Water for large Ships, and thereby run the Risque of being totally lost, whereas, if there were no such Lights, they would endeavour to keep near the English Shore, where there is no Danger from Shoals or Sand Banks: And therefore praying, That no Tax may be laid on the Trade of Bristol for the Improvement of the Harbour of Swansea, and for which the proposed Alteration in the Lights is principally intended, but that the Tax may be confined to Vessels frequenting the Harbour of Swansea, and Ports contiguous thereto, or on coasting and other Vessels not exceeding the Burthen of One hundred Tons per Register, and that all larger Ships and Vessels may be exempted therefrom.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill to amend and render more effectual an Act, made in the Thirty-first Year of His present Majesty, for repairing, enlarging, and preserving, the Harbour of Swansea, in the County of Glamorgan, and for making Improvements in the Lights at The Mumbles, be read a Second Time.

St. Martin's Mr. Alderman Lushington reported from the Com-O-ch mittee, to whom the Petition of the Rector, Church-don reported warc'cns> Overseers, and Inhabitants, of the Parish of ' Saint Martin Outwich, in the City of London, whose

Names are thereunto subscribed, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as v it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the . Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at

the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. John Scott being examined, said, That the Church of the said Parish, which was built in the Thirteenth Century, has for a Series of Years occasioned the Inhabitants of the Parish a continued Expence for Repairs, and is now become absolutely ruinous, and from that Cause Divine Service has not been performed in it for upwards of Eighteen Months past. That various Surveys have been made by Builders of Eminence, who have reported the Church to be in a dangerous State, and declared their Opinion of the Necessity of , a general Repair, or of its being partly taken down and

re-built.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for re-building the Parish Church of Martin Outwich, in 77 ircadneedle Street, within the City of London: And that Mr. Alderman Lushington and Mr. Alderman Anderson do prepare, and bring in, the same.

An Amendment was proposed to be made to the Question, by leaving out the Words " Articles of Charge exhibited against the said John Fenton " thome, Esquire, with the Opinion and Sentence of " the Court Martial thereupon," and inserting the Words "Whole of the said Proceedings" instead thereof.

And the Question being put, That the Words proposed to be left out stand Part of the Question;

It passed in the Negative.

And the Question being put, That the Words " Whole of the said Proceedings " be inserted instead thereof;

It was resolved in the Affirmative.

Then the main Question, so'amended, being put;

Ordered, That such a Number of Copies of the Whole of the said Proceedings be printed, as shall be sufficient for the Use of the Members of the House.

The said' Book is preserved amongst the Other Papers of this Session.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

James Dixon, Reeve of the said Manor, being examined, said, That the Manor of Stepney is very extensive and populous, and that such of the Streets, and other public Passages within the said Manor, as are not included under any particular Act of Parliament for paving and regulating, are not paved, or very ill paved and repaired, and are greatly obstructed, and rendered incommodious, by various Nuisances and Annoyances, and divers Offences are frequently committed therein: Then,

John Bowles, Esquire, Steward of the said Manor, being examined, said, That the above Inconveniences are, in a great Measure, owing to the Want of sufficient Powers being lodged in the Court Leet of and belonging to the said Manor, and in the Steward of the said Court, to compel proper Persons to take on them the Office of Jurymen in the Court Leet; and also to the

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That such Ships and Vessels, with their Cargoes, as have been admitted to Entry, by Orders in Council, since the Expiration of the last of the said Acts, should be considered as entitled to take the Benefit of the same, and of the Orders in Council of the 16th and 2ist Days of January 1795, and be subject to the same Duties, and entitled to the same Drawbacks, as if such Ships and Vessels, with their Cargoes, had been admitted to Entry during the Continuance of the said Act.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it may be proper to permit all Ships and Vessels described in the said Acts, and also certain other Ships and Vessels belonging to Persons in Amity with His Majesty, to come to any of the Ports of this Kingdom, in the same Manner as if they had been entitled to take the Benefit of the said Acts, and of the said Orders in Council of the 16th and 21st Days of January 1795; and that the Cargoes of such Ships and Vessels should be subject to the Duties, and entitled to the Drawbacks therein mentioned, except in Cases wherein any of the said Duties or Drawbacks have been altered by any Act, passed in the present Session of Parliament.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the Gentlemen who are appointed to prepare, and bring in, a Bill to indemnify all Persons who have acted in Consequence of Orders in Council, issued since the 2 2d Day of November 1795, for the Admission of certain Articles of Merchandize in Neutral Ships, that they do make Provision in the said Bill, pursuant to the said Resolutions.

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for indemnifying all Persons who have been concerned in advising, or carrying into Execution, an Order of His Majesty in Council, respecting the Exportation of Rock Salt, for preventing Suits in Consequence of the same, for authorizing His Majesty to prohibit the Exportation, or carrying Coastwise, of Rock Salt, and for making further Provisions relative thereto; without any Amendment: And also,

AN ingrossed Bill from the Lords, intituled, An Act for vesting certain detached Parts of the Real Estate late of Sir Edward Vaughan Mansell, Baronet, deceased, situate in the County of Carmarthen, in Trustees, in Trust, to be sold, and to apply the Money to arise from such Sale, in the Reduction of the several Mortgages, or other Incumbrances subsisting upon, or affecting, such Real Estate, and also for enabling such Trustees to demise the Mines, Veins, or Seams of Coal, lying under the Residue of such Real Estate, in such Manner, and with such Consent, as therein is mentioned, was read the First Time.

Resolved, That the Bill be read a Second Time.

An ingrossed Bill from the Lords, intituled, An Act for making a Partition and Division of divers Messuages, Lands, and Hereditaments, in the several Counties of Carmarthen and Glamorgan, devised by the Will of William Powell, Esquire, deceased, and now held in undivided Moieties, and for settling and assuring the specific and entire Messuages, Lands, and Hereditaments, which, upon such Partition, are respectively allotted to be held in Severalty, for, or in lieu of, each of the said undivided Moieties, to the several Uses, and subject to the several Charges and Incumbrances now subsisting upon, or affecting, such undivided Moieties respectively, was read the First Time.

Resolved, That the Bill be read a Second Time.

An ingrossed Bill from the Lords, intituled, An Act for vesting Part of the settled Estates of William Parker Hamond, Esquire, in the County of Middlesex, in Trustees, to be sold, for discharging Incumbrances, and for laying out the Residue of the Money arising by such Sale in the Purchase of other Lands and Hereditaments, to be settled to the same Uses, and for enabling the said Trustees, and the said William Parker Hamond, to grant Leases of Part, of the said Estates for the Purpose of Building, was read the First Time.

Resolved, That the Bill be read a Second Time.

A Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, directing that every Miller shall put up a Table of the Prices in Money, or of the Amount of Toll, for which the several Operations of his Mill are to be performed.

And the said Clause was Twice read, with Blanks.

And it being proposed to fill One of the said Blanks with a pecuniary Penalty;

Resolved, That the said Clause be committed.

Resolved, That the said Clause be committed to a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House will, immediately, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the said Clause.

The House accordingly resolved itself into the said Committee.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Mr. Hobart took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair:

Mr. Hobart reported from the Committee, That they had gone through the said Clause, and made several Amendments thereunto; which they had directed him to report, when the House will please to receive the same.

Ordered, That the Report be now received.

Mr. Hobart accordingly reported from the said Committee, the Amendments which the Committee had made to the said Clause, and which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Clause, with the Amendments, in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Amendments were Twice read; and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, were agreed to by the House; and the said Clause was added, by the House, to the Bill.

Another Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, to exempt Mills kept by private Persons from the Regulations and Provisions of this Act.

And the said Clause was Twice read; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the Bill.

Then several Amendments were made, by the House, to the Bill.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendments, be ingrossed.

Ordered, That the said Bill be read the Third Time upon Tuesday Morning next, if the said Bill shall be then ingrossed.

Re-commit- Mr. Mainwaring reported from the Committee, on Petition *° w^om the Report was re-committed, which was respecting the made from the Committee, to whom the Petition of Land Tax As- several Owners of Estates, and Inhabitants House-Vol. 61.

holders, within the Parish of Saint Martin in the Fields, segment for within the City and Liberty of , in the the Salt

County of Middlesex, on Behalf of themselves, and re' the several other Owners of Estates, and Inhabitant por Householders, within the said Parish, was referred;

That the Committee had further examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerks Table: Where the same was read; and is as followed); viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

William Hewlett, Collector of the Land Tax in the said Parish, being examined, said, That the Salt Office was from 1703 to 1789 exercised within the said Parish, and the Commissioners, Clerks, and other Officers for the Management of the Salt Duties were, during that Period, constantly assessed to the Land Tax to the said Parish; that the said Office has been removed to Somerset Place, within the Liberty of the Dutchy of Lancaster, and if the said Office should not be assessed within the said Parish a heavy Burthen will be laid on the Inhabitants: That the Commissioners of the Land Tax for the Dutchy Liberty have, since the Removal of the Office, assessed it, as also have the Commissioners for Saint Martins, but whose Assessments have been returned in super.

Matthexo Chessall, Esquire, being examined, said,

That the Commissioners of the Salt Office have, since their Removal, paid the Assessments made upon them by the Dutchy of Lancaster.

Frederick Booth, Esquire, being examined, said, That the Parish of Saint Martin in the Fields, and the Dutchy of Lancaster, have agreed that a Moiety of the Land Tax to be assessed upon the Salaries of the Commissioners, Clerks, and other Officers for the Management of the Salt Duties within the said Parish of Saint Martin, shall be paid to the Collectors of the Land Tax of the said Liberty of the Dutchy: And also the Whole of the Land Tax for all additional Commissioners,

Clerks, and other Officers of the Salt Duties which shall or may be hereafter created.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for assessing the Commissioners, Clerks, and other Officers, of the Duties on Salt, for their Salaries, and the Profits of their respective Offices, to the Land Tax, in the Parish of Saint Martin in the Fields, within the City and Liberty of Westminster, notwithstanding the said Office has been removed into Somerset Place, within the Dutchy Liberty in the Strand, in the County of Middlesex: And that Mr. Mainwaring and Mr. Hobart do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A Petition and Representation of those, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, Members of the Cornwall Agricultural Society, and other Inhabitants of the said County, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, convinced that the Prosperity of this Kingdom depends principally upon the flourishing State of its Agriculture, and understanding that the Produce of Grain, although formerly fully equal to the Consumption of the Country, has, of late Years, from a Variety of Causes, become very inadequate thereto, beg Leave to represent to the House, that the Welfare of the Country may be greatly advanced, and a Remedy applied to the Grievance of an excessive Consumption, by an Attention to the Cultivation and Improvement of the large Tracts of Waste Lands throughout this Kingdom; and the Petitioners therefore desire to express their Persuasion, that the readiest Means of obtaining that Object will be by passing a general Inclosure Bill, and they further beg Leave to observe, that the County of Cornwall is peculiarly interested, both in the general Object (an Inclosure of Waste Lands) and also in that Mode of carrying it into execution, because it has larger Tracts of Waste Lands in proportion to its Extent, capable of Improvement, than are to be found 4n most other Counties, and because Property is usually so minutely divided as to preclude any Application for private inclosure Bills, from the Expence and Trouble of procuring the m: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to adopt such speedy Measures as the Wisdom of the House may suggest, for carrying the Object of the Petitioners into Effect.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A PETITION of the thereunder-signed Manufacturers of Paper, on Behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Paper Makers in England, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That a dangerous Combination has, for some Time, existed Vol. 51.

amongst the Journeymen Paper Makers throughout Combination! this Kingdom, for enforcing a general Increase of their of Workmen Wages, preventing the Employment of North Britons, and others, who do not join in their Confederacy, and Manufactory, for other illegal Purposes; and that, from the Year 1789 to the present Period, frequent Conspiracies of this Sort have been set on Foot by the Journeymen, and the Masters have been as often obliged to submit, and so lately as the Month of April last they obtained an Advance of Wages, and they now demand a further Addition of Five Shillings per Week each Man, which (considering the Variation in the Hours of Work, as a Day and a Half's Work can be performed in Fourteen Hours) at some Mills is equal to an Advance of Seven or Eight Shillings per Week, and with which it is impossible to comply, without occasioning so considerable an Advance in the Price of Paper as would most effectually injure the Exportation of that Article to Foreign Parts, and otherwise materially affect the Manufacture; and that in Support of the said Combination (notwithstanding the y complain of the Insufficiency of their Wages) the Journeymen have established a general Fund, and raised Subscriptions, and so regular and connected is their System, that their Demands are made by all the Workmen at some one particular Mill, and, in case of Non-compliance, that Mill is wholly deserted by the Men, the other Journeymen are prohibited from applying for Work at that Mill till the Master is brought to Compliance, and the;

Men who have thus thrown themselves out of Employ receive Support from their general Fund: That the only Method of punishing such Delinquents, under the present Laws (as a Magistrate has no Power of Commitment in Cases of Conspiracy) is to prefer an Indictment at the Sessions or Assizes after the Offence, but before that Time arrives the Offenders are usually separated, and removed into different and remote Parts of the Country, so that, even if their Places of Residence should be discovered, it would be at least Nine or Twelve Months before they could be brought to Trial, and the Expence of apprehending and bringing them by Habeas to the County where the Offence was committed is so enormous to the Manufacturer, whose Business has been so stopped by the Desertion of the Men, that (aware of those Difficulties) the Journey- j

men carry on their Combinations with Boldness and Impunity; and that, in Consequence of these Proceedings, it became necessary for the Manufacturers of Paper to hold Meetings, in order to consider what Means of Redress might be attainable, and it was not till after the last Day fixed by the House for receiving Petitions for private Bills was elapsed, that the Necessity of an Application to Parliament was ascertained:

And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to exhibit a Petition for Leave to bring in a Bill for the

etc7e"ks°in Petition of the Clerks in the Offices of His Male Offices'of jesty's principal Secretaries of State, for the Home ie Secreta- and Foreign Departments, was presented to the House, es of State, and read; Setting forth, That by the Act, passed in the Ninth Year of her late Majesty Queen Anne, Chap. io, for establishing a General Post Office, the Petitioners were allowed the Privilege of sending and receiving Letters, free of Postage, to and from any Part or Parts of Great Britain or Ireland, and by the Act of the Fourth of His present Majesty, Chap. 24, the Privilege of franking Letters was taken from the Petitioners, and their Privilege was limited to the sending and receiving, free of Postage, to and from any Part or Parts of Great Britain or Ireland, printed Votes and Proceedings in Parliament, and printed Newspapers; and that by an Act, passed in the Ninth Year of His present Majesty, Chap. 35, a Compensation was granted to the Petitioners for the Advantages they enjoyed from their Privilege of franking Letters before the Commencement of the Act, passed in the Fourth Year of His present Majesty, and by the Act of the Twenty-fourth of His present Majesty, Chap. 6, the Privilege of sending and receiving printed Votes and Proceedings in Parliament, and printed Newspapers, to and from the Kingdom of Ireland, was taken from the Petitioners, but they were still permitted to send and receive them, free of Postage, to and from any Part or Parts of Great Britain; and that by the Act of the Twenty-fifth of His present Majesty, Chap. 60, an Allowance of 1,000l. per Annum, charged upon the Revenue of the Post Office, was granted to the Petitioners as a Compensation to them for the Advantages they enjoyed from their Privilege of sending and receiving printed Votes and Proceedings in Parliament, and printed Newspapers, free of Postage, to and from Ireland: That the Petitioners have learned, froth the , Votes of the House, that there is a Bill, now pending the rein, by which the Privilege of sending and receiving printed Votes and Proceedings in Parliament, and printed Newspapers, free of Postage, will, under certain Restrictions therein stated, become general, and by which the Incomes of the Petitioners will be considerably diminished, inso much as they will be no longer applied to for the Purpose of sending the said printed Votes and Proceedings in Parliament, and printed Newspapers, to different Parts of Great Britain, as they have been hitherto accustomed, and for which they have received, from the Persons to whom they were sent, a stipulated Sum: And therefore praying, That as, at the afore-mentioned preceding Periods, Compensations were made to them by Parliament for partial Losses of their aforesaid Privilege, the House

will now be pleased to grant them such a Compensation for the remaining and most advantageous Part of it as shall appear meet and proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Canning, Mr. Plumer, &c.:

And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker's Chamber.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee^ That an additional Custom Duty of Twenty Pounds be charged for every Ton of Portugal or Madeira Wine, and Wine of the Produce of Spain, or of any of the Dominions of the King of Spain, which shall be imported into Great Britain, and so in Proportion for any greater or less Quantity, and for which all the Duties payable thereon shall not be paid before the 18th Day of April 1796.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an additional Custom Duty of Thirty Pounds be charged for every Ton of all other Wine which shall be imported into Great Britain, and so in Proportion for any greater or less Quantity, and for which all the Duties payable thereon shall not be paid before the 18th Day of April 1796.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an additional Custom Duty of Twenty Pounds be charged for every Ton of Portugal or Madeira Wine, and Wine of the Produce of Spain, or of any of the Dominions of the King of Spain, and so in Proportion for any greater or less Quantity, which shall have been imported into Great Britain on or before the 18th Day of April 1796, or which, on the said 18th Day of April 1796, was in any Cellar, Vault, or Warehouse, of the United Company of Merchants of England trading to the East Indies, or in any Warehouse under the Locks of the Officers of the Customs or Excise.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an additional Custom Duty of Thirty Pounds be charged for every Ton, of all other Wine, and so in Proportion for any greater or less Quantity, which shall have been imported into Great Britain, on or before the 18th Day of April 1796, or which, on the said 18th Day of April 1796, was in any Cellar, Vault, or Warehouse, of the United Company of Merchants of England trading to the East Indies, or in any Warehouse under the Locks of the Officers of the Customs or Excise.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an additional Excise Duty of Twenty Pounds be charged for every Ton of Portugal or Madeira Wine, and Wine of the Produce of Spain, or of any of the Dominions of the King of Spain, and so in Proportion for any greater or less Quantity, which shall have been found on the first actual Survey by the proper Officer of Excise, on or after the said 18th Day of April 1796, in the Stock, Custody, or Possession of any Dealer or Dealers in, or Seller or Sellers of, Foreign Wine.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an additional Excise Duty of Thirty Pounds be charged for every Ton of all other Wine, and so in Proportion for any greater or less Quantity, which shall have been found on the first actual Survey by the proper Officer of Excise, on or after the said 18th Day of April 1796, in the Stock, Custody, or Possession, of any Dealer or Dealers in, or Seller or Sellers of, Foreign Wine.

Petition from A Petition of the Gentlemen, and other Inhabitants, ao^nsflT"1 reeic*'nS *n an<l near the Town of Nottingham, whose ton'and Rad- Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the ford Inclosure House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners Bill- observe, by the Votes, a Petition hath been presented

to the House from George de Ligne Gregory, Esquire, Lord of the Manor of Lenton and Radford, in the County of Nottingham, and other Proprietors of Estates within the Parishes of Lenton and Radford aforesaid, for the Purpose of inclosing the Forest, Commons, and Waste Lands, lying in those Parishes, and praying, that Leave might be given to bring in a Bill for those Purposes: That the Ground whereon Nottingham places are run is within, and Part of, the Ground intended to be inclosed; that, in the Year 1767, the said George de Ligne Gregory, and the other then Proprietors of Lands and Estates within the said Parishes of Lenton and Radford, obtained an Act for dividing and inclosing the Open Fields, Meadows, Common Pastures, and Commonable Lands, lying South of the Turnpike Road leading from Nottingham to Alfreton, within the Liberties and Townships of Lenton and Radford, in the county of;

that, for Time immemorial, and, in Fact, ever since the Establishment of Races, and particularly since the King's Plate hath been given as an Encouragement for the Breed of a certain Description of Horses, the Race Ground, whereon the Races of Nottingham are held, hath uninterruptedly, and without any Acknowledgment required or paid for the Privilege, been used and enjoyed for such Purpose; that there are no Commons or Waste Lands in either of the said Parishes of Lenton and Radford left uninclosed, except only the said Forest Lands, which belong to the Crown, and is Part of the ancient Forest of Sherwood, but subject to Common Right for the Deer in Thorney Wood Chase, being within such Jurisdiction, of which the Earl of Chesterfield is Hereditary Ranger, as appears more particularly by a late Examination of the Original Grant to the Ancestors of the said George de Ligne Gregory, the present Lord of the said Manor, wherein all Forests and Chases are expressly exempted and reserved out of that Grant: That, from the increased Population of the Town of Nottingham and Neighbourhood, and by many others fond of encouraging the Turf, and the particular Aptitude of the Ground for such Diversions, a very liberal Subscription was entered into in 1776 for the Purpose of erecting a handsome Stand, and for improving and embanking the Race Course, upon which, at least, 2,500l. hath been expended, and also upwards of 1,500l. for enlarging and ornamenting the Assembly Rooms for the Accommodation of the Company at the Races, it not being apprehended that any Attempt would ever be made even for abridging, much less for the inclosing and taking away, the Privilege the Public had constantly enjoyed of using the Race Ground, which has always been presumed, and is supposed, to belong to the Crown; and that, should such an Act of Parliament be obtained, the Races will be totally destroyed, the Town of Nottingham and the Public be deprived of a Diversion they have Time immemorially enjoyed, and the large Sums of Money expended upon the Stand, Race Course and Assembly Rooms, will, in a great Measure, be lost to the Subscribers, as the Property without the Races will be but of little or no Value: That, in the Year 1793, Barracks were erected near Nottingham, and contiguous to the Forest, at a very considerable Expence, for the Accommodation of His Majesty's Troops, which Forest, if inclosed, will deprive such Troops from exercising their Horses, there not being any other Ground suitable for that Purpose within Seven Miles of the Place: And therefore praying, That the BUI for such Inclosure may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for dividing and inclosing the Forest, Commons, and Waste Lands, within the Liberties or Townships of Lenton and Radford, in the County of Nottingham, be read a Second Time.

Mr. Amyatt reported from the Committee, to whom Paper Mum-the Petition of the thereunder-signed Manufacturers facturere of Paper, on Behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Paper Makers in England, was referred; That the por Committee had examined the Matter of the said

Petition,

r

36 Geo. III. 21° April595

Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared, to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. William Phipps being examined, said, That he is a Paper Maker at River, near , in Kent, and has

been in the Blue and Brown Line of that Business, for Sixteen Years and upwards. — That in the Year 1789 a dangerous Combination broke out amongst the Journeymen in the Paper-making Business, in order to obtain an Increase of their Wages, and that his Mill was attacked, in consequence of which all his Journeymen left the Mill, and that the Combination at that Time extended to an alarming Extent; that he proceeded to indict Two of the Ringleaders, but before the Grand Jury could find the Bill, they absconded, and he was not able to cause them to be apprehended.

That in 1794 and 1795 similar Combinations were entered into by the Journeymen for an Increase of their Wages, to which the Masters have been obliged to submit. — That about May 1795 his Journeymen joined in the Combination, and gave him warning to leave his Mill unless he complied with their Demands, when he was obliged to submit to an Advance of from Three to Four Shillings per Week, according to the different Departments of their Work. — And the Witness further said, That from the Year 1789 to this present Time, the Journeymen have uniformly refused to work at any Mill where Scotchmen or Irishmen were employed, and the Masters have been obliged to submit, or to stop their Mills from working.

That about Christmas last he hired a Person who had been a Foreman at Mr. Payne's Mill, at Buckland, in Kent, upon which his other Journeymen insisted that he should quit the Service, because he had not joined in the former Combinations, otherwise they threatened they would all leave his Mill, and the Man being unwilling to cause any Disturbance, wTas obliged to leave the Mill in consequence of that Combination. That the Journeymen raise Money by Subscriptions, and have a regular established Fund in Support of such Combinations. — That in the Line of Business he is in, it is customary to pay the Workmen a Day's Work for making a certain Quantity of Paper, which Work can be performed in about Eight Hours; and by working Four Hours more, the Demand now made and insisted on by the Journeymen of an Advance of Five Shillings a Week in their Wages, will, in Fact, amount to Seven Shillings and Sixpence; and that the complying with such Demand will materially affect the Price of Paper, and considerably diminish the Exportation thereof: And the Witness added. That in consequence of such Combinations, the greatest Part of the Mills in Surrey,

Bucks, Hants, Berks, and Herts, are now stopped from

working. That the Practices of the Journeymen, in Support of such Combinations, are by demanding an Advance of Wages at some one particular Mill, and in case of Non-compliance, the Journeymen desert such Mill, and prohibit their Brethren from applying for Work there until Compliance; and that the Men thus leaving their Employment, are supported from their general Fund.

Mr. John Taylor, a Paper Maker at Wrolham, in the County of Kent, being examined, said, That his Mill was stopped in 1789 in consequence of the Combinations mentioned by the preceding Witness, and he confirmed his Evidence with respect to the Journeymen refusing to work with particular Persons, to their raising Subscriptions, and making a Demand of Five Shillings a Week, and to the Injury to the Trade, if such Demand should be complied with; and also to the Stoppage of Mills in the before-mentioned Counties. Vol. 51.

That his own Mill was stopped in January last by the Men, because be would not submit to an Advance of Wages of Five Shillings per Week per Man, and that it has ever since remained unworked on that Account.

Then Mr. Finch Hollingworth being examined, said, That he is a Paper Maker at Maidstone, that he was induced to stop his Mill in consequence of the Combinations of the Journeymen at other Mills; and he added, that the Trade will be greatly prejudiced if the Combinations and Refusals to work with particular Persons are not stopped.

Then he produced to your Committee, a Letter, under the Hand of William ,who was formerly a Workman to him, and whose Hand Writing he is acquainted with, whereby it appears that the Workmen belonging to the different Combinations have paid the Sum of Three Shillings each as a Support for the Journeymen entering into such Combinations; and he confirmed the Evidence of the first Witness with respect to those Matters confirmed by the last Witness.

All the before-mentioned Witnesses concurred in saying, That it is indispensably necessary that Measures should be taken to stop such Proceedings; and for which Purpose it is expedient that a Law should be made to prevent Combinations amongst Journeymen Paper Makers, and to regulate the Amount of their Wages.

Mr. Nathaniel Davis, the Solicitor for the Paper Makers, being examined, said, That the present Laws are defective, in as much as the Persons combining, if any Proceeding against them is begun, elope to distant Parts before a Bill of Indictment can be found against them.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to prevent unlawful Combinations of Workmen employed in the Paper Manufactory, and for the better Regulation of their Wages: And that Mr. Amyatt and Sir Edward Knatchbull do prepare, and bring in, the same*

Personal Liberty of the Petitioners, are so liable to be affected and interrupted by the Prosecution of Claims upon them for Tythes, &c. more especially in either the Ecclesiastical or Exchequer Court, that they trust they shall not now be deemed importunate in referring their Case to the House, seeing so long a Time has elapsed since the Petitioners have made any Application on the Subject: That the Petitioners cannot ascribe to the Legislature a Disposition to place them and their Posterity in a State of Suffering on account of a Religious Scruple, which they can neither evade or desert, without violating their Integrity, yet such is the Effect of the Law, as is painfully manifested in sundry Instances, particularly in the deplorable Case of Seven of their Brethren now Prisoners in the Gaol at York, and without any present Prospect of Release, though convicted of no Crime, except it be a Crime scrupulously to adhere to what they conceive to be the plain Precepts of Christ respecting the Ministry of the Gospel: And therefore earnestly requesting, That the House will bestow a serious Consideration on their Case, and grant such Relief as may appear proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Mr. Canning reported from the Committee, to whom Petition from the Petition of the Clerks in the Offices of His Ma- the Clerks in jesty's principal Secretaries of State, for the Home and of

Foreign Departments, was referred; That the Com- taries of State, mittee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, reported, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, passed in the Ninth Year of her late Majesty Queen Anne, for establishing a General Post Office, was read, whereby it appeared, that the Petitioners were allowed the Privilege of sending and receiving Letters free of Postage to and from Great Britain and Ireland.

And it appeared, by an Act of the Fourth of His present Majesty, that the above Privilege was taken away, and limited to the sending and receiving free of Postage, printed Votes and Proceedings in Parliament, and printed Newspapers: Then,

Another Act, passed in the Ninth of His present Majesty, was also read, whereby it appeared, that a Compensation was granted to the Petitioners, for the Advantages they enjoyed from their Privilege of franking Letters previous to the Commencement of the said Act of the Fourth of His present Majesty.

It further appeared, by another Act passed in the Twenty-fourth of His present Majesty, that the Privilege of sending and receiving printed Votes and Proceedings in Parliament, and printed Newspapers, to and from the Kingdom of Ireland, was taken away, but the Petitioners were still permitted to send and receive them free of Postage to and from any Part of Great Britain.

And it appeared, by an Act of the Twenty-fifth of His said Majesty, that an Allowance of i,oooo/. a Year charged upon the Revenue of the Post Office, was granted to the Petitioners as a Compensation to them for the Advantages they enjoyed from their Privilege of franking to and from Ireland: Then,

George Randall, Esquire, One of the Clerks in the Secretary of States Office for the Home Department, being examined, informed your Committee, That by a Bill now depending in the House, the Income of the Clerks in the said Office will be considerably diminished, as they will no longer be applied to for the Purpose of franking Newspapers. — That his Loss, being one of the Ten Clerks that have that Privilege,

he

36 Geo. III.

£1° Aprilis.

597

he estimates at Fifty Pounds a Year; some will be more, and others less, but he thinks his Loss will be about the Average of that of all the Clerks; this Privilege is of a fluctuating Nature, and he does not think it by any Means at its Height. — That he considers it a more valuable Privilege than that of flanking to Ireland was, which was abolished by the Act of the Twenty-fourth of His present Majesty, and for which a Compensation of 1,0001, per Annum was granted: Then,

Charles Robert Broughton, Esquire, a Clerk in the Office for the Foreign Department, being examined, said, That he is One of the Eleven Clerks in that Office who have the Privilege of franking Newspapers, that he estimates his Loss at 133/. 10$. being the Amount of his Receipt last Year, and which has been regularly increasing, and he thinks will be more. — He conceives the Privilege more valuable than that of franking to Ireland was, and for the Loss of which a Compensation has been given.

Stephen Rolleston, Esquire, being also examined, informed your Committee, That this Privilege is of a fluctuating Nature, and is by no Means at its Height — and that his Profits have been gradually increasing within the last Ten Years.

Mr. Alderman Lushington reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons, of the City of London, in Common Council assembled, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, An Act, passed in the Second Year of His present Majesty's Reign, intituled, "An Act for the better supplying the Cities of London and Westminster with " Fish; and to reduce the present exorbitant Price " thereof, and to protect and encourage Fishermen," was read; whereby it appeared that Persons are restrained from selling or exposing to sale in Billingsgate Market, or within the Space of One hundred and Fifty Yards from Billingsgate Dock, or in any other Market in the City of London, or within the Weekly Bills of Mortality, any Fish which, in the same Day, shall have been before sold in the same Market: Then,

Mr.. Thomas Peete, Supervisor of Billingsgate Dock and Market, being examined, said. That the retailing of Fish at the said Market, is of great Public Utility and Convenience, and tends materially to reduce the i exorbitant Price of Fish, but cannot be continued to be

practised, whilst the Restrictions contained in the said Act remain in Force,

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to authorize the Sale of Fish at Billingsgate, by Retail: And that Mr. Alderman Lushington and Mr. Alderman Anderson, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Mr. Alderman Anderson reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Coalheavers working on the River Thames, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, made in the Tenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act to repeal an Act, " passed in the Thirty-first Year of the Reign of his " late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, "An Act for the Relief of Coalheavers working upon " the River Thames, and for enabling them to make " Provision for such of themselves as shall be sick, " lame, or past their Labour, and for their Widows " and Orphans," and to regulate the Price of their " Labour, to prevent Frauds and Impositions on such " Labourers, and for their further Relief," was read, by which it appeared, that the said Act was to continue in Force for the Term of Three Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament only: And,

Mr. Peter Potter being examined, said, That the said Act has long since expired, and the Petitioners have been thereby deprived of the Benefit arising from the Provisions thereof. That they have for several Years past laboured under the greatest Hardships

3

through the Impositions of some of the Coal Under-takers, who oblige the Petitioners to give them Part of what they earn, in order to obtain Employment for them, by which Means the Petitioners and their Families are reduced to great Distress, and Disturbances and Inconveniences are occasioned. That the Coal Trade would be much better carried on if the Coal Undertakers were under proper Controul, and the Wages of the Coalheavers secured to them by Authority of Parliament.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the Relief of Coalheavers working upon the River Thames, between London Bridge and Greenwich, and to regulate the Price of their Labour, and to prevent Frauds and Impositions on such Labourers: And that Mr. Alderman Anderson, the Lord Mayor of London, Mr. Alderman Lushington, and Sir Watkin Lewes, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Mr. Mainwaring reported from the Committee, to whom the Bill to regulate the buying and selling of Hay and Straw, and for repealing so much of Two Acts, made in the Second Year of the Reign of King William and Queen Mary, and in the Thirty-first Year of the Reign of King George the Second, as relate to the buying and selling of Hay and Straw within the Limits therein mentioned, was committed; and to whom the Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Farmers and Growers of Hay, in Behalf of themselves, and the several other Persons supplying the Hay Markets of London and Westminster', and also, the Petition of the several Persons whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Salesmen of Hay and Straw in Smithfield Market, in the City of London, on Behalf of themselves and others, exercising that Business in the said Market, were severally referred; That the Committee bad considered the said Petitions, and had heard Counsel in Support of the said Bill; and that the Committee had gone through the Bill, and made several Amendments thereunto, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Bill, with the Amendments, in at the Clerk's Table: Where the

Report was read.

Ordered, That the said Report be taken into further Consideration upon Thursday Morning next.

Ordered, That such a N umber of Copies of the said Bill, as amended by the Committee, be printed, as shall be sufficient for the Use of the Members of the House.

A Petition of the Owners and Occupiers of Lands and Tenements in the Township of with Harrogate, and the adjoining Townships, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill to continue and enlarge the Term and Powers of an Act, made in the Seventeenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for repairing and widening the Road from the Town of Skipton to the Turnpike Road leading from Leeds to Ripon, near Olcbeck, in the Township of Bilton with Harrogate, and from thence to communicate with the Road leading from Knaresborough to Wetherby, in the West Riding of the County of York; and Setting forth, That, under the Management of the present Trust, the Public have not received the Benefit intended, and the Petitioners and others have been greatly aggrieved, the Money raised and collected having been chiefly expended in making and repairing that Part of the Road which adjoins to Skipton, and, at the same Time the nearest Toll Bar is placed at a Distance of Six Miles from Skipton, by which all the Persons within that Distance, and whose Resort is to Skipton, contribute nothing; that another Bar has been placed in Harrogate, where, by reason of the Resort of Company to that Place, a great Part of the Money received upon the said Road hath been collected, but the Township of Bilton with Harrogate, through which the said Road passes for about Three Miles and an Half, hath only been allowed at the Rate of Four Pounds per Annum, so that the Burthen of making and repairing about One Seventh Part of the Length of the whole Road hath been borne by the Occupiers of Lands in Bilton with Harrogate, and the Petitioners have Reason to believe that, if the Accounts of the Trustees were inspected, it would appear that, by extravagant Salaries, and other unnecessary Expences, the Sums applicable to the Purpose of the Act have been greatly diminished; and that the Petitioners apprehend, that the Abuses of the past Management are intended to be continued and increased by the Bill proposed, which contains a Clause, that no Toll Bar shall be erected at any other Place than where the present Toll Bars stand, unless it shall be found expedient to erect a Bar at some Place between the Turnpike Road from the South West Corner of the Inclosures of Harrogate to Knaresborough and Plompton Corner, and by the said Provision the Inhabitants of Harrogate may be subject to pay at Two Bars within a Distance of less than Three Miles, and all the adjoining Townships Southward and Westward of Harrogate, which use Knaresborough Market, may be subject to pay Toll for little more than crossing the Road, from which the Inhabitants of Skipton and that Neighbourhood enjoy, in Effect, an Exemption by the placing of the Bar which is provided to be fixed in its present Position; and that the Petitioners, on the Expiration of the present Act, are desirous of making and maintaining (as they have hitherto done) the Road which leads through Harrogate, at their own Charge, and to be free from the Burthen of a Toll of which they receive so little Benefit: That the Petitioners also observe, that a Clause is inserted in the intended Act to repeal so much of the former Act as exempts Carriages, Horses, Mares, Mules, Asses, or other Cattle, going for, or returning with, any Lime, Dung, Mould, Manure, or Compost, of any Nature or Kind soever, to be employed in Husbandry, or for manuring or improving of Land, or carrying any Hay, Straw, or Corn in the Straw, from the Payment of Toll, and the Petitioners are satisfied, if the above-mentioned Repeal takes place, that it will be a great Check to Agriculture, as

Mr. Hobart, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Eight hundred and Eighty-five thousand Six hundred and Seventy-three Pounds Nineteen Shillings and Ten Pence, be granted to His Majesty, for defraying the Extraordinary Expences of the Army, incurred and paid by the Right honourable the Paymaster General of His Majesty's Forces, from the 15 th of November to the 24th of December 1795, both inclusive, and not provided for by Parliament.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Two hundred and Ten thousand One hundred and Ninety-four Pounds Fifteen Shillings and Eleven Pence, be granted to His Majesty, for defraying the Expence of Services performed by the Office of Ordnance, previous to the 31st Day of December 1795, and not provided for by Parliament.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Provision be made for making Allowances, in certain Cases, to Subaltern Officers of the Militia, in Time of Peace.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Mr. Hobart, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to w'hom the Bill for continuing and making perpetual an Act, made in the Thirty-second Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for the more effectual " Administration of the Office of a Justice of the Peace " in such Parts of the Counties of Middlesex and Surrey " as lie in and near the Metropolis; and for the more <£ effectual Prevention of Felonies," was committed, the Amendments which the Committee had made to the Bill, and which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Bill, with the Amendments, in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Amendments were Once read throughout; and then a Second Time, One by One; and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, were agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendments, be ingrossed.

Ordered, That the said Bill be read the Third Time upon Monday Morning next, if the said Bill shall be then ingrossed.

Mr. Hobart, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of so much of an Act, made in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act for " granting certain Duties of Customs on the Importation of Fruit, Sallad Oil, Waste Silk, and Timber, " and on the Exportation Of British Rock Salt, and " Coal," as imposes a Duty on Mahogany imported into this Kingdom, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Duty granted on the Importation, and the Drawback allowed on the Exportation of Mahogany, by an Act made tin the last Session of Parliament, do cease and determine.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of One Pound Ten Shillings be charged upon every Ton, containing Twenty Hundred Weight, of Mahogany of the Growth of any of the Bahama Islands, or of the British Limits within the Province of Yucatan, in the Bay of Honduras, and imported directly from thence into this Kingdom.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of Three Pounds be charged upon every Ton, containing Twenty Hundred Weight, of Mahogany not imported directly from any of the Bahama Islands, or the British Limits in the Bay of Honduras, or being the Growth of any other Country or Place, imported into this Kingdom.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Drawback of the said Duties be allowed upon the Exportation of any such Mahogany imported into Great Britain, and exported to any Place beyond the Seas as Merchandize.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That a Bill be brought in upon the said Resolutions: And that Mr. Hobart, Mr. Rose, and Mr. Charles Long, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Sir Watkin Lewes reported from the Committee, to Petition to whom the Petition of David Steel, of Great James Tte Street, Bedford Row, Esquire, was referred; That the ThLtre re-Committee had examined the Matter of the said Peti- ported. ' tion, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

Thomas Winde being examined, said, That The Royalty Theatre, in Well Street, in the Liberty of the Tower of London, was built in the Years 1785 and 1786, by Mr.

John Palmer, Comedian, at the Expence of 18,000l.; and that the same was licensed by His Majesty's Justices of the Peace for public Music, Dancing, and other Entertainments of the like Kind: Then,

Mr. George Holmes being examined, said, That the said Theatre became the Property of the Petitioner in the Year 1789, and that he has since expended several Sums of Money in improving the same, which, together with the Purchase Money, have amounted to the Sum of 10,000 /.: And,

Mr. Winde being again examined, said, That the Petitioner opened the said Theatre for public Entertainment with such Amusements as were authorized by the said Licenses, but finding he thereby incurred considerable Losses, the Petitioner caused the same to be closed. — And being further examined, he said,

That the said John Palmer raised the Sum of 7,0001. or thereabouts by the Sale of Renters Shares, each Holder of which is entitled to free Admission to all Performances at the said Theatre, and also to a certain Annuity therefrom, for Twenty-one Years, from the Year 1787, who, by closing of the said Theatre, have become considerable Sufferers. — And the Witness added, That if the Petitioner was enabled to open the said Theatre for the Purposes of the Drama during the Summer Season, his own Losses, and those of the Renters, would be in a great Degree compensated; and that he (the Witness) apprehends the Public will receive a Benefit by such rational Amusements. Mr. Alderman Lushington reported from the Committee, who were appointed to take into Consideration an Act, made in the Thirteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act to explain and amend, and reduce into One Act of Parliament, " the general Laws now in being lor regulating of " Turnpike Roads in that Part of Great Britain called " England, and for other Purposes and also, an Act, made in the Fourteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for explaining and " altering an Act, made in the Thirteenth Year of His present Majesty's Reign, intituled, "An Act to " explain and amend, and reduce into One Act of Parliament, the general Laws now in being for regulating of Turnpike Roads in that Part of Great Britain called England, and for other Purposes," so far as the same relates to the Payment of additional Tolls at Weighing Engines, and the Number of Horses to be used in Carriages drawn on Turnpike Roads; and for allowing certain Exemptions with respect to Weight and Payment of Toll in particular Cases," and to report the same, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House; That the Committee had considered the said Acts, and had come to several Resolutions, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Resolutions of the Committee were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Traffic upon the Roads in the Neighbourhood of London is exposed to considerable Inconveniencies by the present Limitation of Weights.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Horses used in the Neighbourhood of the Metropolis are capable of drawing greater Weights than are allowed by Law.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Carts, having the Fellies of the Wheels Six Inches in Breadth, and the Tire perfectly flat and cylindrical, should be allowed an additional Weight of Ten Hundred to the respective Weights now allowed in Summer and Winter, on paying an Addition of 50/. per Cent. upon the Tolls now paid at the respective Turnpike Gates.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Waggons, having the Fellies of the Wheels Six Inches in Breadth, and the Tire perfectly flat and cylindrical, should be allowed an additional Weight of Thirteen Hundred to the respective Weights now allowed in Summer and Winter, on paying an Addition of 50/. per Cent, upon the Tolls now paid at the respective Turnpike Gates.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, as Weighing Engines are intended to prevent excessive Weights, and not to increase the Revenues of the Turnpikes, the Trustees of Roads should be restrained from leasing or otherwise letting the same.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Weighing Engine should be inspected by and under the Regulation of The Inspectors of Weights and

Balances, or of such Persons as the Magistrates of the County shall appoint.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the Roads suffer materially from the conical Shape of the Sixteen Inch Wheels, and from the projecting Tire, and the improper Form of Nine Inch Wheels now iu Use.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Wheels of all Waggons and Carts, of the Breadth of Six or Nine Inches, should be perfectly flat and cylindrical.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Weights, now allowed to Waggons with Sixteen Inch Wheels, are injurious to the Roads.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Regulations proposed, with respect to the Weights to be carried in Carts and Waggons, should be limited to a Distance within Twenty-five Miles of the Metropolis, and to continue for a limited Time.

Ordered, That the said Report do lie upon the Table.

Mr. Hotting- A Petition of Finch Hollingworth, of , in

vaith's Peti- the County of Kent, on Behalf of himself and others, Pa" a*Manu- ^whers of Paper Mills and Works, in the County of fkturers Bill. Kent, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That it has been usual with the Petitioner, and other Owners of Paper Mills and Works as aforesaid, to give extraordinary Reward and Encouragement to such of their Workmen as are most skilful, sober, and industrious, from which Practice the Petitioner and others have reaped great Advantages, and the Articles manufactured by them have been made of a superior Quality; and that there is a Bill now depending in the House to prevent unlawful Combinations of Workmen employed in the Paper Manufactory, and for the better Regulation of their Wages, which, by limiting the precise Quantum of Wages to be given, directly or indirectly, to each Individual Workman, will make it, as the Petitioner is advised, unsafe to give any Distinction or Reward as an Encouragement to superior Skill or Merit, and, by destroying all Emulation amongst the Workmen, would, if suffered to pass into a Law, be productive, as the Petitioner apprehends, of the most serious Inconvenience; and that the said Bill also contains several other Provisions and Regulations, which, the Petitioner apprehends, will be very injurious to the Trade, and disadvantageous to the Public: And therefore praying, That he may be heard, by himself, or Counsel, against the said Parts of the said Bill, and that the same may not pass into a Law as it now stands.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second Time.

Mr. Mainwaring reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Cutting Retail Butchers of London, Westminster, the Borough of Southwark, and the Places adjacent thereto, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report tlje same, together with their Opinion thereupon, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Thomas Willed,a Cutting Butcher, being called in,

was asked, What was meant by a Jobber of Cattle? he said. They buy Cattle of the Graziers and Farmers, which would come from them to Market were they not prevented by these People, which is the Means of considerably enhancing the Price — That there is not a Doubt but that more than Half the Cattle, both Beasts and Sheep. (but more particularly the Beasts) are jobbed that come into Smithji — That in the Month of June last he was cheapening some Cattle of a Mr. Pooiey, a Salesman in Smithfie who asked a great Price for them, that he (the Witness) asked what could be the Cause of it, and he (the Salesman) told him he believed it was in consequence of jobbing; and that a Mr. Ltncdon and Co. of had,

during the Spring of 1795, jobbed upwards of a thousand Beasts, by which they must have cleared at least 2,000l.: And the Witness further said, that Air. J. Earle, a Salesman in said to him,

he wished jobbing to be done away within Thirty Miles of London, for that it was arrived to a very alarming Heighth, and that by Means of the Jobbers he could give no Satisfaction to his Employers the Graziers, who did not deal with Jobbers; that the Practice of jobbing has existed for a considerable Time, but never to that Excess which it has done for the last Two Years. — And being asked, Whether there would be any Difficulty in the Farmers and Graziers getting their Stock to London were there no such Men as Jobbers? he said, None at all, for there are Drovers for that Purpose, as regularly calling for the Stock as the Butchers send their Journeymen round with Meat to their Customers. — And being asked, 'Whether he

conceived the Practice of jobbing enhanced the Price of Cattle in the London Market? he said, Very consi- derably. — Then,

Mr. John Hawkes, a Cutting Butcher, being called in, was asked. What Information he could give respecting the jobbing of Cattle ? he said. He has seen reat Quantities brought to Market by Men who were nown to be Jobbers, and never fed Cattle — That several of the Salesmen complain very much, and think they are a very great Evil, and the Cause of enhancing the Price of Meat very much; and that he (the Witness) is of the same Opinion — That no longer ago than Friday he saw' a Jobber in Smithfield, who had got some very fine Scotch Beasts, and asked at the Rate of 7 id.per lb. — that Mr. Self, a Salesman, came

up, and said, he hoped the Jobbers would be deceived, and not get the Price they had given for their Cattle, and that he wished to see all Jobbers suppressed, for they caused so much Confusion among the Graziers in the Country, that it was impossible for the Salesmen to give Satisfaction to the Graziers who employed them — that the Jobbers rode about the Country, and if they found a Grazier who was not inclined to sell them his Cattle, but determined to send them to the London Market, they very often tempted them with Prices more than they were really worth, to induce the Graziers to let them have them, and so get the Stock into their own Hands — That when the Graziers have sent their Cattle to Market after the Jobbers have been with them, it was impossible for the Salesmen to give Satisfaction, because the Jobbers had bid more for their Cattle than they knew they were worth — That he (the Salesman) had many Times been bid a very good Price for Cattle by Butchers, and frequently more than they could make of them, which he has been obliged to refuse, as he knew the Jobbers had been with the Graziers, and offered more — That he (the Salesman) wras very certain, while Jobbers were allow'ed, Meat w:puld never be cheap in this Metropolis — That the Markets all along the Road up to London were so infested with Jobbers, that the Graziers could not get their Cattle up to London, although they had sent them out with Drovers, with Orders for them to be drove to the London Market. — That a Butcher at Stevenage told him (the Witness) that the Cattle were so entirely in the Hands of Jobbers, that he was often obliged to come to Smithfield to buy Cattle of them, though many went through the Place from wffience he came. — That the Witness has a Brother in Worcestershire (a Butcher), who lately wrote to him to know the Price of Meat in the London Market, for that the Jobbers so infested the Fairs, and monopolized the Cattle, that they are obliged to give any Price they demand — That he (the Witness) has seen the same Thing in Smithfield Market an hundred Times — That his Brother likewise informed him by his Letter, that there is a Jobber in store Sheep comes to their Market every Week, and very seldom buys so few as an Hundred, and that those Sheep are brought there by Jobbers, so that none of the Farmers or Graziers in the Neighbourhood can have any until such Time as the above Person has had the Refusal of them, and taken as many as he thinks fit — That he (the Witness's Brother) could have pointed out Twenty of these Sort of Jobbers within this Twelvemonth — -that they have the Market entirely in their own Hands, and that he never saw a greater Plenty of fat Cattle at this Time of the Year than there is at present. — And being asked. Whether there would be any Difficulty in the Farmer or Grazier conveying his Stock to London, if there were no such Persons as Jobbers? he said, Not the least, as the Graziers know as well how to have their Cattle conducted to Smithfield Market, as if they were within Two Miles of it — That it is the Custom of the Salesmen, where they are not interrupted by the Jobbers, to send thek Drovers round to the different Farmers

and Graziers for their Cattle, and write to them, when they find the Market is likely to want a Supply. — And being asked, Whether the Farmers and Graziers would not get rather more than less for their Cattle, while the Consumer got his Meat cheaper, if there were no Jobbers? he said, He believed they would, though there might sometimes be an Exception — That it is the general Opinion of those who frequent field Market, that Three Fourths of the Cattle are jobbed before they get there; and that he has been frequently informed by Salesmen, that Cattle are jobbed Four or Five different Times before they reach Smithfield Market. — And being asked, Whether he knew a Mr. E. Cramp ? he said, Yes, and that he attends different Markets — That Mr. Turpin, a Salesman and Butcher at St. Ives, informed a Mr. Smith and him, that Cramp generally attended St. Ives and Stevenage Markets, and had bought Eighty-one Head of fat Cattle that were on the Road coming to Smithfield and that he was going again to Stevenage for the same Purpose. — Then,

Mr. Thomas Smith, a Cutting Butcher, being called in, was asked, What Information he could ive respecting the bringing of Cattle to Market ? — e confirmed the Evidence given by the last Witness, as to the jobbing of Mr. Cramp, and said, That that Practice must necessarily increase the Price of Meat to the Consumer — That Tunbridge, Sevenoaks, and Maidstone, have been the Seat of jobbing for some Time, and that jobbing is now become almost general throughout the Kingdom, by which is obtained a Command over the Graziers, and enhance the Price in the London Market — That he knows a Person at Stowe on the IVolds, a very considerable Dealer in that Way, and that the Butchers about can buy nothing for him. — Then,

Mr. John Bate, a Cutting Butcher, being called in, was asked, When Beef first made any considerable Advance? he said. About Seven Years ago — That about that Time one Godson, a Carcase Butcher, informed him, that he had some Cattle in Smithfield which netted to him from 3/. to 5/. per Head by jobbing. — And being asked, What he conceived to be a fair Profit on his Meat? he said, 3 d.per Stone of 8lbs. — And being asked, Whether he knew what a Carcase Butcher's Profit is? he said, Nearly equal to the Cutting Butcher's — That if the Cutting Butchers were to kill their own Meat, they would gain after the Rate of 6 d. per Stone; but, owing to the Jobbers, they are unable to purchase live Meat. — Then,

Mr. John Pope, a Cutting Butcher, being called in, was asked, What he knew respecting jobbing? he said, That he has heard from Salesmen, with whom he has dealt, that the Beasts he had been about to purchase were jobbed; and that they wished jobbing was totally abolished, as it bred such Confusion in the Country; and that if they could have the Cattle immediately from the Graziers to the Market, they could sell them at a Price to satisfy the Butcher. — And being asked, What further Information he could give respecting the Practice of jobbing? he said, From the Salesmen he has heard that the Cattle sent to Smithfield, particularly on a Friday, are Three Parts jobbed Beasts, and that it was impossible to sell those Beasts that were Graziers Beasts to the Satisfaction of their Employers, as the Jobbers had been many of them endeavouring to buy those Beasts, and finding the Graziers not inclined to sell, they have used this Argument, that the Beasts would fetch more then than if kept Five or Six Weeks longer, by which Means they have drawn off the Beasts before they have been ready to come, so that there must be lost, out of every Score of Beasts that come, at least One Fourth in Quantity, by Means of being drawn away by Jobbers — That when the Jobbers go to the Graziers, and they are not inclined to sell them, they endeavour to tempt them Vot. 51.

by a Price far more than they even intend to give; so when those Beasts are sent to Smithfield, the Salesmen are not able to make the Money for them as bid by the Jobber, and the next Quantity of Beasts the Grazier has to dispose of, he is inclined to sell to the Jobber, fearing the y may not fetch in the Market so much as before — That he (the Witness) thinks that it is impossible for the Public to have meat at any fair Price whilst this Practice is continued, nor the Cutting Butcher be enabled to get a Living. — And being asked, Whether he ever enquired the Price of Sheep in Smithfield Market, and found they were not to be sold till a Jobber had the Refusal, and which Jobber afterwards sold them to him ? he said, Yes; and that they were sold to him by the same Salesman on the Jobber's Account. — That a Grazier in Bedfordshire informed him (the Witness) that he could not get a Lot of store Sheep into his Hands that had not been jobbed before, and that he wished it was abolished, as it was an Injury to the Public. — And being asked, If Jobbers were entirely abolished, would it put the Grazier under any Difficulty in sending his Stock to the London Market ? he said, There are Drovers belonging to all Parts of the Kingdom, w ho collect Cattle from the Graziers. — Then,

Mr. Edward Adams, late a Salesman in Smithfield, being examined, said, He had been Salesman near Fifty Years. — And being asked, What has been the Practice of jobbing ? he said, That Beasts have been jobbed ever since he could remember, and that he has sold many such Cattle — that the Jobbers buy their Oxen of the Graziers in the Country — that he has sold for Graziers as well as Jobbers; and that the Cattle take all the same Chance in the Market. — And being asked, Whether the Farmers and Graziers would be under any Difficulty in sending their Cattle to Smithfield, ,w'ere there no such People as Jobbers? he said, They would not. — And being asked, Whether he knew of any Instances of Jobbers meeting the Droves? he said, That Butchers sometimes met them at Hounslow, and bought them for their own Use. — And being asked, If he knew of any Practice of forestalling in the London Market ? he said, That such Things are done, but that he never sold Beasts in the Market twice over — That the Graziers and Farmers consign their Cattle to the Salesman in London, and send a Letter, informing him, that on such a Day they intend sending so many. — And being asked, Whether those Cattle always arrive? he said, Sometimes an Accident happened on the Road — That he never knew any Cattle jobbed on the Road. — And being asked, How the Jobbers deal? he said, They sometimes bought Beasts at Smithfield, and other Markets in the Country — That he would never have any Thing to do with Jobbers, because he did not like them, as they bought Cattle to sell again in the same Market. — And being asked, How often he has known the same Beast sold in the same Market? he said, He could not tell how often, but that there has been a good deal of that Practice, and by People who make it their Business to job Cattle. — And being asked, If those People were not suffered, would the Market be as well supplied? he said, Yes; for the Cattle must come. — And being asked, Whether he has not heard One and all declare that the enormous Price given for lean Stock was entirely owing to the Practice of jobbing? he said, Yes, most certainly; and that he fully concurred in that Opinion. — And being asked, Whether he did not attribute the enormous Addition in the Price of Oxen at the Country Fairs to the Practice of jobbing ? he said, He did. — And being asked, If there was an End put to the Practice of jobbing, whether the Butcher would not be enabled to sell his Meat cheaper than at present ? he said, It might certainly make a Difference. — Then,
